### On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

Since it is necessary that causes precede the things they create, and that simple things precede those composed from them, we must begin our methodical division with the most simple or primary meteorological member: **Wind**. Its beginning or root is so ancient that we find in Holy Scripture that it took its origin from the mouth and nostrils of the Almighty Jehovah. Therefore, in this chapter, we shall speak somewhat more abundantly concerning wind in general, for it is a creature of a divine condition and a truly marvelous nature.

The Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy, known for walking while they taught</term> assert that wind is a hot and dry exhalation, difficult to ignite, springing from the earth and raised up to the middle region of the air. They say that, being repulsed by the cold of that region and resisting upward movement—partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other exhalations rising from below—it is observed to move laterally across the earth in the lowest region of the air. It stirs and fans this air so that it does not rot from a lack of motion or through a kind of sluggishness. We will first insist upon this definition of Aristotle's here, because certain spurious Christian Philosophers have not hesitated to defend and support his opinion with all their might—as if it were published to the world by divine decree or issued from a holy oracle—driven by a kind of unbridled madness in both public schools and their private studies. From Aristotle's aforementioned definition, they attempt to teach: first, that the matter or substance of wind is a hot and dry exhalation. Second, that the place in which it is generated and from which it is derived is the earth, while they say the place to which it tends is the middle region of the air, which it cannot penetrate; the medium in which it moves upward, downward, and laterally is the lowest region of the air. Third, they seem to establish a double mover of this exhalation: namely, the cold of the middle region of the air, which presses that barely imaginable exhalation down toward the earth, and subsequently other exhalations rising successively from the earth; these, by their upward motion, encounter the exhalation depressed by the cold and are accustomed to struggle with it, consequently creating a noise in the air. Finally, this definition seems to succinctly outline the end or purpose of this motion ordained by nature: namely, that the air might be refreshed, preserved from all rot, and purified by this kind of ventilation.

<margin>Exodus 15:8</margin>
<margin>Job 37:9 and 28:25</margin>
But whoever wishes to give any credit to this Pagan definition—especially if he is a lover of true wisdom—we believe he will do something worthwhile if he first examines every small part of that definition. After careful inquiry, he should see whether it agrees with the laws of divine wisdom or not; that is, whether this opinion of Pagan Philosophers ought to be approved by us Christians by the right of stronger reason, or rather rejected. In the first place, let us ask whether there is any probability of truth in the first part of his definition: namely, is the matter of wind a hot and dry exhalation springing from the earth? We are taught by the Holy Scriptures (to which we Christians must give faith above all things) that wind has its origin from the spirit of Jehovah. *At the blast of your nostrils,* it says, *the waters were piled up;* and it continues (ibid. 10), *You blew with your wind, and the sea covered them.* Elsewhere, *God brings forth ice by His breath, and the frost is frozen by the breath of God.* And elsewhere, the royal Psalmist says that the very angels of God are winds when he says (Psalm 104:4), *He makes His angels winds, and His ministers a flaming fire.* And hence it is that Doctors more profound in the mysteries of nature have said that the manifest or external part of the angels was the air or worldly spirit, but they made their hidden part a divine fire; for which reason they are called by Dionysius <note>original: "Dionysio"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose works on the celestial hierarchy were highly influential.</note> *Agalmata*—that is, the clearest mirrors receiving the light of God and representing His image. By the royal prophet in the place cited above, both the hidden wind and that which is manifest, flashing, or fiery, is described as an angelic spirit animated by divine fire. For this reason, the commentator on that passage speaks thus: *For* (says he) *God uses the winds and fire as ministers of His will and judgments, so that they also have the name of angels, where by flaming fire, lightnings and thunderbolts are understood. Thus he says.* But concerning the explanation of this matter, we shall deal more fully in the following sections, where the supernatural efficient cause is to be discussed. It must be confessed, therefore, that either the breath of the nostrils or the treasure-house of God is an exhalation subject to preternatural passions coming out of the earth (which is certainly profane to say), or that this part of the Peripatetic definition is entirely false. But from the examination of what follows, this will be more clearly depicted and debated; we shall therefore hasten to the inquiry of the second part.

The second part is that the place in which it is generated and from which that exhalation (the material cause of wind) is derived is the earth; the place to which it tends is the middle region of the air; and the medium in which it moves upward, downward, and laterally is the lowest space of the air. How many gross errors and absurdities are found in this assertion of the Pagan will be clear from the following. Therefore, for a better examination, we divide this clause of his definition into three: in the first portion, we must explore by diligent inquiry whether the matter of the winds is extracted from the terrestrial body or not; in the second, whether that substance makes its way upward seeking only the convex surface of the middle region of the air; in the third, whether the place in which the wind moves is only in the lowest region of the air. To the first, we say that either the Holy Page (which is the source of all truth) is not true, or this portion of the second part of his definition is most false—

Aristotle himself affirms that the wind moves from the earth and ascends to the middle region of the air, and is driven back down from there. But Saint John says that it moves not by force or accidental impulse, but voluntarily according to its pleasure; and that although its voice or sound is familiar to the ears, it is not known where it comes from or where it goes. For it is the heaven, or the air, which is the treasury-chest of GOD, and not the earth; from the heavens (I say) proceed the meteors, which are finally rained down upon the earth for its blessing or its curse. Hence David says: **He opened the doors of heaven and rained down Manna upon them to eat, and gave them the corn of heaven, etc.** and elsewhere, **GOD covers the heaven with thick clouds, who prepares rain for the earth.** But also to this doubt—namely, whether the origin and passage of the winds is from the earth into the heaven—a man far more learned and wise in natural matters than Aristotle directly responds in these words: **Man knows not the way of the wind** <note>original: *Venti viam ignorat homo*</note>, **nor does man know the work of GOD himself, by what way He does all these things.** But Aristotle was a man—indeed, a Pagan—to whom it was consequently granted much less to judge rightly of such abstruse matters. Hence, Jehovah, as if mocking the audacity of such a man and rebuking him, speaks thus: **Do you know where the way is in which the exhalation is divided, which scatters the wind over the earth?** arguing from every side the impossibility of this thing to a man to whom divine wisdom (which alone teaches all these things) has not been granted by the Creator. And yet Aristotle seems to answer Him impudently: "I know it; for the way of such an exhalation is from the earth upwards, where, partly through <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being concentrated by surrounding cold</term> from the cold driving it downwards, and gradually by other exhalations striving upwards, it is dispersed and driven laterally over the earth." But the impossibility of this reasoning of his we shall show immediately in what follows.

<margin>2 Samuel 22:8 <note>In the Vulgate, 2 Samuel is often listed as 2 Kings (2 Regum).</note></margin>
<margin>Job 37</margin>
Regarding the second and third parts of this clause, we say that the medium through which the winds move is far more vast than what Aristotle busies himself with ascribing to them. For the wind does not blow only in the lowest region of the air, but also in the middle, and likewise in the highest—indeed, even in the Empyrean and Ethereal world. But the actions of the wind in any of these regions of the world vary according to the different action of resistance—that is, the thinness or thickness of the moved air—as will be seen more clearly in the following chapter. If, therefore, the wind blows in the middle region of the air, the vigor of that Aristotelian definition will be utterly destroyed; for its efficacy consists chiefly in this: namely, that exhalation is not permitted to penetrate through the diaphragm of the middle region of the air, but is reverberated downward by the force of the cold resisting the heat of the exhalation. For the cause of the wind—if there be any in the middle region of the air—is totally taken away from the fact that it is not driven downward by the cold, but is observed to blow in the very midst of it. But truly it is manifest that the clouds—both the upper ones, which are lighter, more lucid, and colored, as well as the lower ones, which are observed to be darker and heavier—are driven by winds from any quarter of the world to its opposite and fly as if on their wings; which certainly cannot happen without the presence of the winds in that middle region. Do we not also see with open eyes the South wind sometimes blowing strongly in one horizon, while at the same time the North wind holds dominion in the horizon next to it? From which it happens that we see a huge mass of clouds accumulated at the edge of both horizons, and cloud moving against cloud, bringing with them horrendous thunders and stupendous lightnings, eliciting fire like sparks from flint; which certainly cannot happen unless the winds moving them in opposite ways are also impetuous and violent in the middle region of the air. This, Holy Scripture also seems to confirm in many places, for in one place it is said: **Smoke went up from the nostrils of Jehovah, coals were kindled by him, and he bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet, and he ascended upon the Cherubim and flew, and glided upon the wings of the wind; he placed darkness in his circuit as a hiding place, sifting the waters from the clouds of heaven; at the brightness of his presence the clouds were kindled, the Lord thundered from heaven.** From which we gather that not only are clouds, thunder, and lightning moved by the winds, but even GOD himself, surrounded by dark clouds in the middle region of the air, is carried upon their wings. And elsewhere, it is said: **that the mighty GOD by his breath produces ice, and for irrigation he tires out the thick cloud.** From which it follows that it is necessary for the wind and its effects to be stronger in the middle region of the air than in the lowest. Does not Aristotle also speak against himself by confessing that the stormy wind called <term>Ecnephian: a Greek term for a sudden, violent wind that breaks out from a cloud</term>, as well as the whirlwind, are sudden winds driven downward from a cloud—and yet he seems to deny any passage of a windy exhalation in the middle region of the air? But let us immerse ourselves a little deeper into this absurdity of his. He himself confesses that the causes of ignited meteors are hot, dry, inflammable, and oily exhalations, and yet he denies them a way or passage through the middle region of the air, though permitted by the nature of the place...

<meta>This page continues the author’s systematic refutation of Aristotle’s definition of wind. Having previously argued against the material cause (that wind is a dry exhalation from the earth), the author now addresses the "formal cause" (the nature and movement of wind) and the "final cause" (its purpose), contrasting the Greek "Pagan" view with Christian Scripture and medical authorities like Galen.</meta>

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.
<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>

...is admitted. But who can be so ignorant in Philosophy as not to know that cold resists an actually fiery and inflammable thing more than one which is neither actually inflammable nor fiery by its own nature? Furthermore, the material cause of ignited meteors <note>Such as lightning or fireballs.</note> is heavier than that of the wind, seeing as it is more compact and oily, and consequently not as fit for ascending or tending upward as the material of the winds, which is exceedingly light and rare. Therefore, it would be even more impossible for the matter of ignited meteors to ascend into the middle region of the air, and through the middle into the highest, both because of the vigorous resistance of the cold in that place and because of the heavier and more compact composition of its substance (whose inclination is to tend downward), than for the path of the winds into the middle of the air to be denied by the cold. For cold stands in the way of an actually fiery and inflammable thing more than one that is only potentially so, and that which is light by its nature ascends more quickly than that which is compact and more ponderous.

But we shall now hasten to the examination of the third part of his definition, where he describes a double action of the winds, which he makes out to be "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a non-essential quality that happens to a thing, rather than being part of its internal nature.</note>—as if one were to say that the wind is not at all moved or excited by an internal principle, but rather by external accidents. Specifically, he claims it is driven downward by the cold of the middle region of the air through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>The supposed intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being squeezed and intensified by surrounding cold.</note>, and that it meets other ascending exhalations, and by such an encounter its direct motion is hindered. From this, he seems to assert that the wind is compelled by force and contingency to move to the side, and by such lateral motion it agitates the air or the medium in which it moves, which causes a din and sound to be emitted. How beautiful a lie this is, and how very similar to the fictions of the poets! As if the wind were nothing other than something accidental! 

But the Holy Bible stoutly defends the idea that the wind proceeds primordially from the divine breath <note>original: "flatu diuino"</note>; indeed, it even calls the wind an "angel," which it acknowledges to be spread everywhere by the divine spirit. <margin>Exodus 15:8</margin> Hence Moses says in the passage cited before, *By the blast of your nostrils the waters were gathered together*, <margin>Psalm 103</margin> and elsewhere, *You blew with your wind, and the sea covered them*, and elsewhere, *By the breath of God frost is given*. Does not King David also say, <margin>20</margin> *Bless Jehovah, you his angels, who are mighty in strength and perform his word*, of whom he says elsewhere, <margin>Psalm 104:4</margin> *Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire*? And in the prophet Baruch, chapter 5, verse 60: *The wind performs the command of God*. And elsewhere: *O you winds, bless the Lord, and exalt him above all forever*, in the Song of Ananias. 

And yet, nonetheless, this Pagan of ours <note>Aristotle</note> wishes the wind to be something merely accidental, and is not ashamed to assert that its very motion comes from external principles and not from an internal one, which is the "first act" of all things. He makes the motion of the wind involuntary (I say) and arising from contraries in nature, rather than voluntary; and yet we are taught by Saint John *that the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the author plays on the dual meaning of 'spirit' and 'wind'.</note> blows where it wills*, that is, by its own voluntary motion, which is prompted and always ready to serve any command of its Creator by its indwelling nature. Aristotle extracts this dead fiction of his from the earth according to his own fantasy, whereas God, on the contrary, produces this living creature of His from His treasuries by means of His breath in truth, as the Royal Prophet <note>David</note> and Jeremiah testify. 

But in this part of his definition, he seems to conclude that the lateral motion of the wind is due to the resistance and hindrance of ascending exhalations. O, what a most wretched argument! As if anyone could prudently say that a motion so constant as that from the North to the South, etc., proceeds from a cause so uncertain and varied. I say that the North, South, East, and West winds have their lateral motions from an accidental struggle so frivolous and uncertain! What, I pray you, my Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note>, was that reason for the struggling of exhalations, and what was the order of their gushing from the earth, when the Prophet, by divine admonition, said to the spirit: <margin>Ezekiel 37:9</margin> *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live*? It seems to me that they themselves, and indeed the Christians inspired by them, are plainly mute and destitute of tongues with which to respond. The wise man says: *Awake, O North wind, and come, O South wind, and blow upon my garden*. How deaf would that invocation of the wise man be if the matter and life of the winds were such as Aristotle ascribes to them? And finally, why is there such a great variety in the condition or quality of the winds—so that one is hot and moist, another cold and dry, a third hot and dry, and the last cold and moist—if the Aristotelian opinion were to remain in its vigor, namely, that all winds are created in a single way and moved laterally by the same accidents?

Finally, regarding the last clause of his definition, in which he placed the "end" <note>The purpose or final cause.</note> of the winds or ventilations—namely, for the sake of purifying the air and preserving it from putrefaction—we say, taught by experience, that this is most false. For we observe with Galen and Hippocrates <note>Famous ancient Greek physicians.</note> that the Southern winds are very contagious and pestilential, inasmuch as they thicken the air and render it putrid with their malevolent heat and moisture; a fact which we have confirmed by the Holy Scriptures, which support us in this matter. <margin>Psalm 91:5</margin> *Do not fear* (says the Psalmist) *the plague or the demon that wastes at noonday*. <note>original: "lue seu dæmonio vastante in meridie"; referring to the 'Noonday Demon' often associated with the hot South wind.</note> And Habakkuk says in his prayer: *When God came from the south, his glory covered the heavens and the earth was full of his praise; the pestilence went before him and burning coals went forth at his feet*. Indeed, the holy page teaches us that the winds in general, as well as the other meteors of heaven, were ordained by the Creator as much for a scourge as for doing kindness. <margin>Job 37:14</margin> Therefore, Aristotle and his disciples have erred no more in the final cause of the winds than they have in everything else under heaven. We conclude, therefore, that the definition of that Pagan Philosopher, which Christians worship and follow with such devotion, is in every way false.

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

...and spurious, since winds are creatures by nature far more excellent and divine than Aristotle or any of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who generally focused on physical rather than spiritual causes.</note> ever understood, seeing as they are not inanimate things endowed only with accidental motion—that is, exhalations springing by chance from the earth and disturbed and driven by the cold of the ascending upper exhalations. Rather, as the Angel taught Zechariah, *Chapter 6*: The winds, animated by an angelic spirit, go forth and stand before the ruler of all the earth; they are hidden in the power or the treasury-chest of their Lord, who brings them forth quickly to fulfill His will, just as we are taught by the royal Psalmist in the place cited above.

But I know well there will be some Christian followers of Aristotle who, in the common manner, will want to reply that in a dispute there should be no progression from one art to another <note>A logical rule in Scholasticism (the "metabasis" rule) stating one shouldn't mix disciplines like physics and theology.</note>, and that it is therefore irregular to make a progression from Philosophy to Theology, or to reject the authority of one through the authority of the other. To these we easily respond that **Theosophy** <term>Theosophy: Literally "divine wisdom," referring here to a philosophy derived from sacred scripture rather than pagan reasoning.</term> and sacred Philosophy differ very little from one another. Furthermore, if the laws of Philosophy disagree with those of Theosophy, that Philosophy must be regarded as false and spurious by concession, and consequently rejected entirely and relegated to the eternal oblivion of Christian men. For the Holy Bible, which is the true source and origin of Theosophy or Theology, is the only truth, and whatever is dissonant with it is false and Diabolical. Of such a kind are those deformed inventions of the Pagans, which shall vanish like shadows; whereas, on the contrary, the characters of the divine word—carved in eternal monuments of memory and inscribed as if by the finger of GOD—shall remain until the very end. For in this word the spirit of all truth is to be found, which, as the holy scripture testifies, will teach all things, and without which nothing can truly be learned or acquired.

Very well: let it be (someone might say) as you say, but I would like to know, what then is wind? How is it to be defined or described by the consensus of the sacred letters? To which we say this can be provided in many ways under a single essence. We think it may be described quite relevantly in these ways:

->**Wind is an airy spirit, of moderate consistency, inspired or animated by the breath of Jehovah, which He brings forth from His treasuries at His will, whether to execute a scourge or a blessing.**<-

Every part of this definition is proven from many places in the sacred letters. For that its internal substance is air, in its moderate consistency, is clear from the fact that air, spirit, and wind are called by the same Hebrew word **Ruach** <note>original: "Ruach"</note> in many places of the sacred scriptures. Furthermore, that its internal or moving soul is the divine breath is argued by those places of sacred scripture cited before, <margin>Exodus 15:8</margin> namely: *by the blast of your nostrils the waters were gathered together*, Exodus 15:8. And again, *You blew with your wind and the sea covered them*. And elsewhere, *The mighty GOD produces ice by his breath*. It is as if he were saying: GOD inspired the air with His mighty spirit, so that there is no difference between an angel and the air inspired by GOD. For air is the external or manifest aspect of an angel (whether malignant or good), animated by the divine spirit for either benevolence or malediction; just as the immediate breath of GOD is its hidden aspect. Hence they are also called **Agalmata** <gloss>Divine mirrors</gloss>, that is, the clearest mirrors receiving the light of GOD, as was narrated. And from this it is said that the name of GOD was in the Angel who preceded the Israelites, who also moved in the pillar of cloud and fire—which was composed partly of dense, moist air (as if from a thinner air) and partly from a thin fiery substance. And this angel, as we read elsewhere, was called **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia"</note>; for we read in Ecclesiasticus: *I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne is in a pillar of cloud, I alone encompassed the circuit of heaven, and I walked in the depths of the abyss, in the waves of the sea, in all the earth, and in every people and nation I have rested.* (Ecclesiasticus 24). For this reason, the Cabalists and the more skilled of the Hebrew Doctors called this angel **Metattron** <note>Metatron: A supreme celestial being in Jewish mysticism, often associated with the voice of God or the mediator of the physical world.</note>, whom the Platonists also made the universal soul of the world. Thus the universal spirit or air of the world, animated by the divine emanation called Wisdom, is that angel or spirit and great wind whose heart or source is in the Celestial sun; whence the royal Psalmist says, *He has set his tabernacle in the sun*. And this is the reason why the angel preceding the Israelites, who also moved in the pillar of cloud, is called a "creature" in respect to the external spirit or air which was created, and is sometimes called **Jehovah** in respect to the name of GOD, or the divine and uncreated light that animated him. From this it is clear that GOD is the center of every spirit, and air is its vehicle; which, being so inspired, is the soul of the cloud and of every other meteor—nay, indeed, even of a perfectly mixed body, as the internal soul moving within. And this seems to be the same as what the deeper students of the **Cabala** <note>A school of Jewish mysticism; the author is likely referencing Christian Cabala which sought to find Christian truths in Hebrew texts.</note> hold (Reuchlin, *On the Cabala*), asserting that an Angel is a middle power between GOD and nature, by which operations are done in things which their own nature either would not do, or would do differently—things which others say come from an "occult property" and others because "it is so." This great angel, called Wisdom, therefore seems to be the one who appeared to John in the Apocalypse, who was said *to be like the son of man in the midst of 7 golden candlesticks, whose eyes were as a flame of fire, in his right hand he held 7 stars, and his voice was as the murmur of many waters or winds: under whose command the other angels were seen to be subject, as it was given to him to command 4 angels who had power over the winds, ordering them not to harm the earth and the water etc. Apocalypse 1 & 3.* <margin>Apocalypse 1 & 3</margin> We conclude, therefore, that just as GOD is **Identity** <note>Refers to the Monad or absolute unity.</note>, namely pure uncreated form, so also the angel is **Alterity** <note>Refers to the first departure from unity into "otherness" or the created realm.</note>.

...namely, from His uniform breath, and compacted from the mundane air; that is, from the uncreated spirit or breath, and the created air or wind. In our aforementioned definition, therefore, we have expressed first what the **material cause** <term>Material cause: The physical "stuff" something is made of—in this case, air.</term> is; we have said, namely, that it is air of a moderate existence. **Wind is an invisible spirit or air, animated and quickened by the divine light from the face or sight of Jehovah, issuing forth like breath from his nostrils, to execute his pleasure as much in the heavens as on the earth.**

**Wind is a certain angelic spirit, or subtle air, inspired and animated by the fiery spirit of Jehovah—sometimes visible and manifest, as in lightning and flashes, sometimes invisible and hidden, like that which is heard but not seen—sent forth from some quarter of the world in a divine and secret manner to execute the divine will, whether for salvation and benevolence, or for punishment and cursing upon the earth.**

**Wind is an invisible and hidden spirit, endowed with a fiery soul, and inspired by GOD in the manner of an angel; which, flying hither and thither at the pleasure of the one who inspires it, as if on invisible wings, sometimes even delights to carry the Inspirer upon its pinions. Or thus:

**Wind is an angelic spirit, breathing hither and thither, secretly and invisibly, according to the abstruse good-pleasure of the creator; though its noise may be heard, the limit of where it comes from or where it goes is unknown to mortals. *John 3:8: The Spirit breathes where it wills, and a man hears its voice, but knows not whence it comes or whither it goes.*** Furthermore, the sacred writings testify that the way and place of GOD is unknown to men.

Or thus, then, from the mouth of the Savior:

**Wind is a spirit that breathes where it wills; although its voice is heard, yet the goal is unknown, and the place from which it comes or where it goes is uncertain.**

Or thus, as we perceive or gather from the places alleged above:

**Winds are the angels of GOD, most mighty in strength, fulfilling his word, hearkening to the voice of his command, his flaming ministers, doing his pleasure. *Psalms 103 and 104.***

This, therefore, is the reason why the men of this age, though capable of the divine mind, have forgotten their illustrious origin and nobility—inasmuch as they are led by prestiges and the "lights" of darkness—and are so rude and unskilled in both true **Theosophy** <term>Theosophy: Divine wisdom or a philosophy built upon the study of God's nature through scripture and creation.</term> and in the sincere arts, that they know neither GOD as He truly is, nor His creatures...

Elsewhere, they also call this חכמה <note>original Hebrew: "Hochma"</note> or Wisdom, which they describe as a holy spirit of intelligence, and a certain flow or emanation of brightness—that is, the spirit or luminous breath of the eternal light, and a spotless mirror of the majesty of GOD. The Cabalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), whose ideas were often integrated into Christian Hermetic philosophy.</note> have, not without reason, frequently called this spirit *Ruach* the "Soul of the World," which they understood through the great angel Metattron <note>Metatron, a high-ranking angel in mystical traditions often associated with the presence of God.</note>. From this, they argue that the entire created spirit of the world, which we call the general air, is animated by the divine and uncreated spirit, or breath, or emanation. They even believed this angel was the one who went before the Israelites in the desert, of whom God spoke: *Behold, I send my angel before you... pay attention to him... for my name is in him. Exodus 23:20.* The Poets also called this spirit the "Bread of God," <note>Likely referring to the "Pan" of Greek myth, interpreted as "Universal Nature" (Pan = All).</note> by which they understood the universal spirit or nature of the world. This is that spirit or breath and divine wind, the *Ruach Elohim* proceeding from the mouth of the Most High (according to the passage in Ecclesiasticus, *I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High*), with which God inspired the potential spirit of the world with the actual spirit of life. From this, the Empyrean spirit or wind <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most refined part of heaven, associated with fire and light.</note>—the thinnest of all creatures—was formed and animated, and was moved by the divine will in the manner of gently stirred air. Therefore, the air or created spirit in this heaven, when gently moved, is a creature, but the soul moving it is *Elohim*; hence, this Angelic composition is called *Elohim Ruach*: because it is that immediate form through which the winds are inspired and animated, according to what was previously cited from David. Furthermore, this angelic composition is, as it were, the "form" that gives shape to the ethereal spirit produced on the second day of creation. In the center of this spirit, God placed His tabernacle in the sun; thus, the entire cavity of the heavens is filled with true or "animated" air. Indeed, even the stars themselves are animated by angelic winds and are driven by them in their many different motions. But because the uncreated wind or spirit of the highest degree established its tabernacle primarily in the sun, all the winds or spirits of the stars look toward its central treasury and show it reverence, no differently than subjects to their king and emperor. This, then, is the reason why the Platonists believed the seat of the World Soul was in the sun. Finally, the celestial wind along with its super-celestial soul (which, joined together, are called "Ether"—that is, fiery air, or air and fire joined) is the formal soul or wind, moving from within and centrally stirring the sublunary air from the inside, and...

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

In this way, the wind—or the air of the world's lowest region—is animated by an inspiration that is as much super-celestial as it is celestial, just as we see a body moved by a soul. Furthermore, the wind thus animated serves as the soul of all "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>. From these winds, or portions of air inspired by angelic powers, all the world’s meteors—both visible and invisible—are procreated. For example, we see that clouds and other meteors, whether bright or dark, are not only moved centrally by the winds but are also materially "blown together" or forged from the air itself.

From this, we see that the divine breath <note>original: "spiraculum"</note> is the central and internal principle of every worldly thing, the simplest and primary agent of all, according to the words of the wise man: *The incorruptible Spirit of GOD is in every thing.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 12:1; original Latin: "Spiritus DEI incorruptibilis est in omni re"</note> By its blowing, the angelic spirit or wind is moved and animated; in turn, the aerial spirit is moved by the angelic wind; the elemental or ethereal spirit by the ethereal wind; and the meteors (or "imperfect mixtures") by the aerial wind. This aerial wind, along with its own souls—namely the empyrean and ethereal—drives and moves all composite things. These composites are nothing other than "spermatic meteors" <note>The author views all physical matter as a kind of "seed" or "sperm" that is still developing.</note> brought to the perfection of maturity. It is their nature either to retreat back into the air from which they came (moving from an imperfect mixture back to simplicity) or to proceed toward the completion of a perfect composition. These movements are always mediated by internal agents which, according to their nature governed by the divine will, work either toward generation by maturing or toward destruction by rotting and corrupting. We observe, however, that the uncreated spirit <note>The Holy Spirit or the direct breath of God.</note> blows in different ways, even though it is one and the same spirit. We see this in fire, which can act benignly and naturally by providing warmth, or malignantly, either by drying and heating unnaturally or by totally consuming and burning a subject "contrary to nature." These various effects exist not because of the agent (God/Fire) but because of the resistance or poor reception of the thing being acted upon. Hence, just as GOD is the first and principal act in every creature—whether His intent is inclined toward destruction, affliction, and the infliction of suffering, or toward generation and benevolence—He is attributed various names in Holy Scripture according to these properties. Thus, following the various arrangements of the ten Cabalistic Sephirot <note>The ten attributes or emanations of God in Jewish mysticism.</note>, ten names are ascribed to GOD. Nevertheless, all these seem to tend toward two ends: either toward severity, by which He punishes sinners and corrupts the elements for the sins of men; or toward kindness, as will be discussed more extensively in our discourse on the efficient causes of meteors.

This was the reason why the Greek sages called Him "Dionysus" during the night, at which time He is said to tear apart the seven composite parts; but during the day, they called Him "Apollo," as He is thought to reconstruct those seven parts and rebuild them through generation—the same parts He caused to fail through putrefaction under the name of Dionysus during the night. But since GOD is understood to act through "ordination" and the angels (as His ministers) through "execution," those versed in the deeper mysteries of Theosophy <note>Divine wisdom or mystical philosophy.</note> attribute the execution of His severity to the angels: Gabriel, who presides over the Northern Winds, and Samuel or Uriel, who governs the Southern ones. Consequently, it is through the spirits of these angels that effects "beyond nature" are often produced in the world, as you will find explained abundantly in our treatise *On Mystical Anatomy* <note>original: "de Anatomia mystica"</note> and more copiously in the section on the efficient cause of meteors. Conversely, the angels who provide evidence of divine clemency and mercy are Michael, who holds dominion in the East and blows benevolent breaths of life and generation from that quarter, and Raphael, to whom the guardianship of the Western quarter is attributed, as he has dominion over the winds of that region—for the name Raphael signifies "the medicine of GOD." From these winds, under the dominion of the Archangels, all meteors in the sublunary world are procreated, whether they reach the goal of generating a composite thing or return to the simple end of corruption. For at the center of any "seed" <note>original: "spermatis"</note>, a certain wind is seen to animate the mass, inflating it and making it swell. Experience is our teacher here: a seed is nothing other than a cloud or thickened air, which is centrally inspired and animated by the spirit of life. It moves toward the point of perfection just as we see air reduced by an angelic wind or spirit into vapor, from vapor into mist, and from mist gradually into a dense cloud. The flashing soul of such a cloud sometimes appears to our eyes and sometimes remains hidden, until finally the substance of the cloud is observed to change into hard stone through the operation of that formal, lightning-like wind. In the same manner, for the generation of a human being, the "will of the father"—which is also a wind—stirs the paternal soul. Then the animal, vital, and natural winds are enclosed in the seed; within a few days of being poured into the womb, they raise up three "vessels" <note>original: "ampullas," referring to the primary embryological structures.</note> from which the heart, brain, and liver are formed by their breathings. Then, like an inflated bladder, they are observed to gradually forge the shape of a fetus and finally the human form. Indeed, the entire life of a human is spirit and wind, whose duty is to inspire and expire at every moment. Does not the Holy Page call it the "breath of life"? Furthermore, every passion of the soul—whether violent and unnatural or according to the laws of nature—is stirred up by winds. Thus anger, madness, fury, fear, and other such things are the effects of microcosmic <note>The "microcosm" is the human being, viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> stormy and tempestuous winds, similar to Typhoons, Whirlwinds, and Fire-storms <note>original: "Typhonis, Ecnephiæ & Presteris"</note>, and even the effects of thunder and earthquakes. Among diseases, epilepsy, vertigo, and "suffocation of the womb" <note>Hysteria.</note> are of this same kind. This is also confirmed by the testimony of the wise...

### CHAPTER VI.

->On the types of Macrocosmic winds, and first on the Cardinal winds.<-

<image-desc>A classification diagram for winds using curly braces to show hierarchy. On the left, a central bracket groups two main types: "Cardinales" and "Collaterales". There are two types of Macrocosmic <note>term: Macrocosmic — relating to the "Great World" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the Microcosm (the human being).</note> winds. Some are:
*   **Cardinal**, which are four in number, namely:
    *   **Boreas** (the North wind), blowing from the Northern pole of both heaven and earth.
    *   **Auster** (the South wind), breathing from the Southern pole of both heaven and earth.
    *   **Subsolanus** (the East wind), leaping forth from the eastern equinox of heaven and earth.
    *   **Favonius** (the West wind), blowing from the western equinox of both heaven and earth.
*   **Collateral.** See G.

The ancients knew, or rather focused upon, only these Cardinal types among the winds, because they used to stand at each distinct region or "quarter" of the world; all those called "collateral" winds were contained within the power and naming of these four. These were called **Cardinal**, **principal**, and **primary**, partly because their duties vary from one another—since each is observed to breathe a blast different in position and condition—and partly because of their site and position, as we shall show below in the proper place. The cardinal number is four, according to the four quarters of the world from which they are observed to emit their blasts. For **Boreas** has its place and dominion from the arctic pole, namely from the seven northern stars <note>The "seven stars" refers to the Big Dipper or Ursa Major, used to locate the North Star.</note>; thus it is entirely contrary to **Auster** (or Notus) in both location and nature. Conversely, **Auster** is said to breathe from the Southern pole, and is likewise opposed to the nature, condition, and position of Boreas. **Subsolanus** usually expires its breath from the eastern point of the equinoctial line, just as **Favonius** does directly from the western point opposite to it.

We have this confirmed by the Bible of all truth. For in the prophet Jeremiah we find these words: *I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds.* <note>Jeremiah 49:36</note> And from the Apocalypse: *I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that the wind should not blow on the earth.* <note>Revelation 7:1</note> And in the prophet Ezekiel: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain.* <note>Ezekiel 37:9</note> And in the prophet Daniel: *Behold, the four winds of the heaven strove upon the great sea.* <note>Daniel 7:2</note> This is also found in many other places. 

In the specific naming of these winds, the Holy Scriptures seem to differ slightly from modern writers. For what the moderns call **Boreas**, the Scriptures call **Aquilo**; likewise, the **Subsolanus** of the moderns is the **Eurus** of the Scriptures, which is generally accepted for every wind blowing from the East. If it inclines more toward the South, it expresses a stormy and furious force, as the Psalmist testifies: *The storms of the sea are stirred up by Eurus; by Eurus you break the ships of the Ocean.* <note>Psalm 48:7 (referenced as 48:8 in the Latin text).</note> And Job: *With Eurus a whirlwind brought the sea in a storm; with Eurus he brought the Red Sea back to dryness.* <note>Job 27:21 and Exodus 14:21.</note> If it inclines more toward the summer solstice, they assign to it greater powers of heat and dryness; thus in Genesis we find fruits scorched by Eurus <note>Genesis 41:6</note>, and also plants dried up, as is held in the prophet Jonah. In its middle disposition: *By Eurus light is scattered upon the earth, and by Eurus Jehovah brought the locusts.* <note>Job 38:24 and Exodus 10:13.</note> So too they accept **Aquilo** for every Northern wind, where it is said by the wise man: *Aquilo produces rain* and *Aquilo brings forth cold.* <note>Proverbs 25:23 and Job 37:9.</note> And: *Arise, O Aquilo... come, O Auster, blow through my garden.* <note>Song of Solomon 4:16.</note> Finally, **Favonius**, and all other winds of that quarter of the world under the common...

### On the Formal Cause of Meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, lightning, and even magnetic effects.</note>

...they seem to be comprehended by this common word: *By a wind from the West (says Moses) in its strength* <note>original: "Vento ab Occidente... in suo robore"</note>

Indeed, it is not without cause that in our division of the Cardinal winds, we mentioned the poles and the equinoctial circle, and consequently the winds blowing from them both on earth and in the heavens. We are taught by the experiment of the magnetic stone (which is also called a **terella** <term>terella — literally "little earth"; a small, spherical magnet used by early scientists to model the Earth’s magnetic field</term>) that the earth itself possesses an excellent proportion to the heavens and its circles. By an almost airy spirit, the earth lives and breathes in imitation of its celestial parents, mediated by that "spirit of the world" <note>original: "spiritu illo mundano"</note> from its four quarters, just as the heavens do. The human body is seen to emulate this in every respect, for as a "son of the world," it possesses its own poles, circles, and winds proper to each of its quarters, as was explained in our *Mystical Anatomy*.

The experiment concerning the magnetic terella, by whose arrangement we are accustomed to judge the nature of the Macrocosmic Earth <note>The Earth as a whole</note> and even the Microcosmic Earth <note>The human body</note>, is of this kind:

First, it is certain and proven by experience that the magnetic terella emits its forces from the center into a sphere. This same phenomenon is undoubtedly observed in the earth, of which the magnet is a minute offspring; it possesses the disposition of the whole within itself, no differently than a single drop of water possesses the nature of the great sea. For in the center of the earth is a **Central Sun**, possessing within itself an exactly magnetic power by which it draws its like to itself. Indeed, just as we observe two poles in the mathematical heavens that rotate the machine of the world, so too do we find natural poles, endowed with Macrocosmic virtue, in the terrestrial globe: one tending toward the arctic pole, and the other reclining toward the opposite part of the world. This can be most easily demonstrated by the nature of a round magnet (which is no more a small portion of the earth than a drop of water is of the element of water). When this stone is fashioned into a spherical shape like the earth, it indicates through its effects not only the poles, but also the **equinoctial** <note>The equator</note> and other circular lines distant from one another in latitude. For the closer the parts of the magnetic sphere are to its equator, the more obliquely they will move; but the parts of the spherical body are observed to draw iron or a needle to themselves more directly the closer they are to the pole. We have expressed the figure of the spherical stone with its various formulas of attraction here:

A similar magnetic force is also present in the human body, which is also a "terella." Its magnetic spirit is observed to be so strong that the wise were well aware that it could allure not only elemental but also celestial virtues in an admirable way, joining earthly things with heavenly things through this magnetic faculty of spirits. Indeed, just as a pure and clean spirit is able to draw clean things to itself from the heavens and elements, so too an evil and impure spirit, by the opposite reasoning, attracts spirits like itself—the good attracting divine inspirations, the evil attracting diabolical ones. And within this magnetic virtue of spirits, those most well-versed in **natural magic** <note>The study of the hidden powers of nature, distinct from "black magic"</note>, and even **sorceresses** <note>original: "veneficae" — those who use potions or charms for harm</note> themselves, are accustomed to produce astonishing and scarcely imaginable things, using this occult mastery to malignly infect the spirits of men from a distance.

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. III. Membr. I.

### The Relational Application of the Aforementioned Macrocosmic Distinction to the Human Microcosm.

The same must also be said concerning the cardinal winds of the body, or the "human earth," as was said regarding those of the Macrocosm. Therefore, we divide the Microcosmic winds in this manner:

**Winds in the Microcosm**, both cardinal and principal, which blow in imitation of the cardinal winds found in both the heavens and the earth of the Macrocosm, are either:

*   **Cardinal**, which are understood as a group of four:
    *   **Boreas** <note>The North Wind</note>, blowing from the region of the spleen, or the microcosmic north.
    *   **Auster** <note>The South Wind</note>, breathing from the region of the liver, or the microcosmic south.
    *   **Subsolanus** <note>The East Wind</note>, sending forth its life-breaths from the station of the heart and the spiritual organs.
    *   **Favonius** <note>The West Wind</note>, breathing from the spermatic vessels, the entrails, and the stomach, as if from the west.
*   **Collateral Winds. I.**

Just as we see that the earth—following the example of the magnetic **terella** <term>terella — a "little earth"; a spherical magnet used to demonstrate the Earth's magnetic properties</term>—contains its own quarters of the world, namely the Poles, the Equator, and the Tropics, so too the "little earth" of the human body undoubtedly possesses within itself its own quarters and principal regions. The various spirits of these regions attract the "spirit of the world" <note>original: "spiritum mundanum"</note> to themselves in different ways through a magnetic virtue. 

From this, it follows that just as different parts are found in iron which, by the property of their essence and a certain natural inclination, seek out one part of the magnet or another (as is clearly shown in the aforementioned experiment), so too in the "spirit of the world" drawn into the human body through breathing, one may find various conditions and natures that naturally adhere more to this or that portion of the body's spirit. 

For example, that portion of the world-spirit introduced into the human body through inhalation has some northern parts, some southern, others eastern, and finally some western. But in its general inclination, it participates more in that wind whose dominion was strongest at the time it was inhaled. This is why a certain spirit or wind makes the spirits of men more fluid and prone to catarrhs <note>A buildup of mucus; a "cold"</note>—namely, the Southern wind. The same applies to the others: even the spirit attracted at the very first birth, or rather at the hour of the fetus's life, causes it to have a phlegmatic, melancholic, sanguine, or choleric complexion <note>The four "humors" or temperaments of medieval medicine</note>, according to the nature of the wind first inhaled at that time. 

Similarly, the spirit of natural life is derived from all the winds (as Ezekiel seems to assert when he prophesied to the bones, saying, *Come, O spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live* <note>Ezekiel 37:9</note>). From the inhaled Macrocosmic spirit, it divides those parts proper to each wind of the Macrocosm and distributes them by magnetic virtue into their own quarters within the human "little earth." That is, the Northern part of the Microcosmic spirit is attracted by the Northern part of the Macrocosmic spirit, both for its own sustenance and to perform those duties in the human body which must be provided by the styptic <term>styptic — contracting or astringent; a quality associated with cold and dryness</term> and cold temperament of that part—namely, to restore the Melancholic humor, which is the food of the Spleen. 

In the same way, its southern portion performs this same task in the service of the blood for the sustenance of the liver and the procreation of blood; just as the portion destined for life performs this same task in the heart and arteries. For like always delights in like, and by a certain magnetic attraction, they embrace each other closely in the bonds of love, since nature rejoices and exults in nature. 

Have we not experienced and proven this very thing most exactly in our "anatomy" of wheat and bread? In that study, we divided the matter into its distinct elements, which we found to be nothing other than wind and air when examined by the test of fire, inasmuch as they were dissolved by the application of a very gentle heat into a smoke very similar to atoms. From these things, we can argue—and clearly so—that a composite body stands in relation to its internal animating spirit as a cloud stands to the wind. For just as a cloud was formerly air, which is condensed into mist and cloud by the breathing of winds blowing from opposite directions, so indeed an opaque composite body was nothing but a cloud reduced into a perfect mixture by the benevolent breath of the winds. 

This is proven in this way: namely, because every thing is resolved back into that from which it was originally created. Thus wood, wheat, and the animal body are reduced by the violence of fire into smoke or a thick vapor and something like a cloud, which also gradually dissipates into invisible air, from which air all things are seen to depart. Thus is verified that axiom of Plato: *Upon that which the beginning of any thing depends, in the same shall be its increase.* Since no creature can either grow or live if deprived of air, we say therefore that the whole composite body is nothing other than air of various conditions, fashioned into that which it is.

...fused; I mean air of varying condition, insofar as it includes the **seeds** <note>original: "spermata," referring to the formative principles or germs of things</note> of different winds: namely, **choleric** <note>Yellow bile, associated with fire and heat</note> seeds from the Eastern winds; **phlegmatic** and watery seeds from the Western; **melancholic** and earthy from the Northern; and **sanguine** <note>Blood, associated with air and moisture</note> seeds, along with putrefaction, from the Southern. And hence it is that the fiery oiliness of wheat becomes air through the seed of the wind Eurus <note>The South-East wind</note>; its ethereal quality [becomes air] through the Subsolanus <note>The East wind</note>, as it is the central salt; its aerial medium, the instrument of vegetation, becomes air through the seed of the southern winds. Its earth, which binds all things together, partakes of the northern winds, just as its phlegm or watery substance is nourished by the western winds. 

And hence it is that from the same subject, the oil or choleric humor is separated by the **natural chemistry of man** <note>original: "chymia hominis naturali"</note> and stored in the gallbladder; the aerial part is refined in the liver and changed into blood; and the earthy part or "glue" is transported to the Spleen, as if to its own natural place. Sweet phlegm is carried to the stomach and the hidden passages of the viscera, while the false serosity <note>Thin, watery fluid</note> is sent to the kidneys and bladder. And yet all these parts of bread or wheat are nothing other than air, infected by the different natures of the winds blowing from the four quarters of the world—which is indeed evident from the fact that, by a light fire (as has been said), they are gradually converted back into air or wind.

By these things, therefore, it is clearly explained that in the **Spleen** there is a magnetic power to attract to itself those things of a northern nature, both from nourishment and from the air drawn in through breathing; in the **liver**, those which participate in the southern winds; in the **heart**, those which, by the natural power of life, are descending from the ether; in the **gallbladder**, those from the bilious winds (such as Eurus and Caecius); and finally, in the **stomach** and **viscera**, those which receive their life from the western winds. From these effects upon the parts of man, we can deduce the points of the poles and the equinoctials (both eastern and western), in the same way that we deduce the equator, poles, and vertical axis of a magnet through the experiment of applying iron to its parts, as previously described. Is it not also established by similar reasoning that air is converted into a cloud by the application of various winds, containing within itself bodies of diverse nature—namely stones, flames, waters, and so on?

### The relationship or application of the aforementioned Macrocosmic distinction to the human microcosm.

The same thing that was said regarding the cardinal winds of the Macrocosm must also be said regarding the cardinal winds of the body, or the human earth. Therefore, we divide the Microcosmic winds in this manner:

*   **The cardinal or principal winds in the Microcosm**, which blow in imitation of the cardinal winds in both the heavens and the earth of the Macrocosm, are either:
    *   **Cardinal winds**, which are comprised in a grouping of four:
        *   **Boreas** <note>The North Wind</note>, blowing from the region of the **spleen** <note>associated with the "Microcosmic North"</note>.
        *   **Auster** <note>The South Wind</note>, breathing from the region of the **liver** <note>associated with the "Microcosmic South"</note>.
        *   **Subsolanus** <note>The East Wind</note>, emitting its life-breaths from the station of the **heart** and the spiritual organs.
        *   **Favonius** <note>The West Wind</note>, breathing from the spermatic vessels, the viscera, and the stomach, as if from the West.
    *   **Collateral winds**.

Just as we see the earth (following the example of a **magnetic terella** <note>original: "terellæ magnetis"; a small, spherical magnet used by early scientists like William Gilbert to model the Earth’s magnetic field</note>) contains its own world-quarters—namely the Poles, the Equator, and the Tropics—so too the "little earth" of the human body undoubtedly possesses its own quarters and principal regions. The various spirits of these regions attract the mundane spirit to themselves in different ways through a **magnetic virtue** <note>An invisible, attractive force thought to operate similarly to a magnet</note>. 

From this, it follows that just as certain parts are found in iron that seek out one part of a magnet or another due to their essential properties and a certain natural inclination (as is clearly shown in the experiment mentioned above), so too in the mundane spirit drawn into the human body through inhalation. One can find various parts that, by their condition and nature, are naturally more inclined to adhere to this or 그 portion of the human body’s spirit. 

For example, that portion of the mundane spirit introduced into the human body through breathing has some northern parts, some southern, others eastern, and finally some western. But in its general inclination, it participates more in whichever wind held the strongest dominion at the time it was inhaled. This is why a certain spirit or wind might make a person's spirits more fluid and prone to **catarrhs** <note>Excessive buildup of mucus or inflammation</note>—namely, the Southern wind—and so on with the others. Even the spirit attracted at the first moment of birth (or rather, the hour of the fetus's life) causes the person to have a **phlegmatic, melancholic, sanguine, or choleric complexion** <note>The four temperaments or "humors" believed to determine a person's physical and psychological makeup</note>, according to the nature of the wind first inhaled at that time.

Similarly, the spirit of natural life is derived from all the winds (as **Ezekiel** <note>A reference to Ezekiel 37:9</note> seems to have affirmed when he prophesied to the bones, saying: *“Come, O spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live”*). From the inhaled Macrocosmic spirit, it divides those parts proper to each wind of the Great World and distributes them by magnetic virtue into their own quarters within the "human little earth." That is, the northern part of the Microcosmic spirit is attracted by the northern part of the Macrocosmic spirit, both for its own sustenance and to perform those duties in the human body which must be provided by the astringent and cold temperament of that part—namely, to restore the **Melancholic humor**, which is the food of the **Spleen**. 

In the same way, the southern portion performs this same task in the **sanguine** <note>Blood-related</note> office for the sustenance of the liver and the procreation of blood; just as the portion destined for life performs the same in the heart and arteries. For "like always rejoices in like," and they embrace each other closely in the bonds of love through a certain magnetic attraction, because nature delights and exults in nature. 

Do we not have this very thing most exactly tested and proven by us in the **anatomy of Wheat and Bread**? In that study, we divided the subject into its distinct elements, and we found these elements to be nothing other than wind and air when examined by the "trial of fire." This is because, with the application of a very gentle heat, they were dissolved into a smoke very much like atoms. From this, we can argue—and clearly so—that a composite body relates to its internal animating spirit as a cloud relates to the wind. For just as a cloud was formerly air, which is condensed into mist and cloud by the blowing of opposing winds, so too an opaque composite body was nothing but a cloud reduced into a perfect mixture by the benevolent breath of the winds. 

This is proven in this way: namely, because every thing is resolved back into that from which it was originally created. Yet wood, wheat, and the animal body are reduced by the violence of fire into smoke or a thick vapor, much like a cloud, which also gradually dissipates into invisible air—the very air from which all things are seen to depart. Thus is verified that axiom of **Plato**: *“Upon whatever the principle of any thing depends, in that same thing shall be its increase.”* Since no creature deprived of air can either grow or live, we therefore say that the entire composite body is nothing other than air of varying condition, fashioned into that which it is.

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

...blown together; an air, I say, of varying condition, insofar as it includes the seeds <note>original: "spermata"</note> of different winds. These include the **choleric** <note>associated with yellow bile, heat, and dryness</note> from the Eastern winds, the **phlegmatic and watery** from the Western winds, the **melancholic and earthly** from the Northern winds, and the **sanguine** <note>associated with blood</note> with putrefaction from the Southern winds. 

From this, it follows that the fiery oiliness of wheat is "air" containing the seed of the South-East wind <note>original: "Euri"</note>. Its celestial or "ethereal" part comes from the East wind <note>original: "subsolani"</note>, which serves as the central salt of life and its airy medium of growth. The "air" containing the seed of the southern winds is the instrument of its vegetation. Its "earth," which binds all parts together, partakes of the northern winds, while its "phlegm" or watery substance is nourished by the western winds. 

And so it is that from the same substance (such as bread), the "oil" or choleric humor is separated by the natural chemistry <note>original: "chymia"</note> of man and stored in the gallbladder. The airy part is processed in the liver and changed into blood. The terrestrial part, or "gluten," is transported to the **Spleen**, as if to its own natural place. Sweet phlegm is carried to the stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"</note> and the hidden passages of the organs, while the "false" salty fluids <note>serosity</note> are sent to the kidneys and bladder. Yet all these parts of bread or wheat are nothing other than "air" infected by the different natures of the winds blowing from the four quarters of the world. This is clearly proven because, as has been said, when a light fire is applied, they are gradually converted back into air or wind.

By these things it is clearly explained that a **magnetic force** <note>original: "vis magnetica"</note> exists in the **Spleen** which attracts to itself those things of a northern nature, both from nourishment and from the air drawn in through breathing. In the **Liver**, it attracts those things participating in the southern winds; in the **Heart**, those things which, by the natural power of life, descend from the ether; in the **Gallbladder**, those things from the bilious winds (such as the East and North-East winds); and finally, in the **Stomach** and viscera, those things which receive their life from the western winds. 

From these effects upon the parts of man, we can determine the points of the poles and the equinoctials (both East and West), just as we determine the equator, the poles, and the vertical axis of a magnet through the experiment previously described involving the application of iron. Is it not also established by a similar logic that, through the application of various winds, the air is converted into a cloud containing bodies of different natures—namely stones, flames, waters, and so on?

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

For example, the North-East wind <note>original: "Aquilo"</note> carries the cold and dry nature of the North wind <note>original: "Boreae," the direct polar wind</note> in every respect, except that its coldness is mitigated by a single degree because of its proximity to the place of the rising sun, which is intensely hot. For this reason, it is observed to differ from the nature of the North wind in certain ways; for while the North wind's role is to drive away dense clouds, the North-East wind does not dispel or scatter them, but rather binds and constricts them. This can be gathered from the etymology of its name. For as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar</note>, Constantius, and others maintain, *Aquilo* is so named because it is like "binding the waters and clouds" <note>original: "aquas & nubes ligans"</note>. In Holy Scripture, this wind seems to be used generally for every wind blowing from the northern quarter. Another wind collateral to the North, situated opposite the arctic circle, is called the North-North-West <note>original: "circius"</note>; it leans slightly away from the dryness of the North toward the moisture of the West wind <note>original: "Favonii"</note>, and thus is observed to differ slightly in its condition from its principal, the North wind. So too, the South wind <note>original: "Auster"</note> has the South-East wind <note>original: "Euro-Austrum"</note> on its right side, whose moisture is somewhat mitigated by eastern dryness; just as on the left side of that Cardinal wind, the heat of the South-West wind <note>original: "Austro-africi"</note> is somewhat—though imperceptibly—blunted by western cold. Thus, its effects are somewhat different from those of its Cardinal wind.

In a clearly similar way, the collateral winds of both the East <note>original: "subsolani"</note> and the West <note>original: "Favonii"</note> differ. For that wind which is North-of-East, called *Caecias* <note>the North-East wind</note> from its "wickedness" and *Hellesponticus* from the region of the earth where it blows, increases its dryness because of its proximity to the Northern region. In this respect, it sometimes puts on a "cold garment," for it is very inconstant and changeable in its nature; it does not drive away clouds like the North wind, but rather attracts them because of its dryness. From this comes the proverb concerning a miser: **"He draws coins to himself, as the North-East wind <note>original: 'caecius'</note> draws clouds."** In the southern part of the East wind, there is the South-East wind <note>original: "Eurum"</note>, which, insofar as it faces the South, participates slightly in its moisture.

This wind, named *Eurus*, is used in Holy Scripture generally for every wind blowing from the eastern quarter.

Of the collateral winds of the West, the moisture of the one to the North, called *Coridicti* <note>the North-West wind</note>, is slightly altered by Northern dryness; thus its condition varies in some respects from its principal. So also the South-West winds <note>original: "Africi"</note>, named after the region from which they blow, are seen to vary from the West wind's disposition in several ways because their cold is affected by Southern heat. But we shall discuss the various qualities and natures of these winds, both Cardinal and collateral, more copiously below in the treatise on the final causes of meteors.

> * **The Western** is the descendant of the North-North-West <note>original: "Circii"</note>, which is observed to blow from the lowest region of the spleen, and as if from the left kidney and the region adjacent to it, partly into the organs and stomach, but especially into the right **hypochondrium** <note>the upper abdomen under the ribs</note>, that is, into the cavity where the **liver** <note>original: "hepar"</note> is located.

> **The Southern or Liver Region**
> * **The Eastern** is the offspring of the South-East <note>original: "Euro-austri"</note>, which blows from the right kidney and the region situated around it toward that part of the hollow of the liver where the small veins lead bile from the liver to the gallbladder; from there it is accustomed to blow into the stomach, the intestines, and through the entire hypochondrium by means of the mesenteric veins <note>original: "venis meseraicis"</note> and other passages, both hidden and those noted by common observation.
> * **The Western** is of the lineage of the South-West <note>original: "Austro Africi"</note>, which is observed to blow from the right-side organs located immediately below the liver to the left hypochondrium (in whose cavity the **Spleen** is located).

That a portion of every wind, whether cardinal or collateral, exists both in the wind (or air) breathed into a man and in the juice of his nourishment (which also comes from the winds), has been quite fully declared before. It is also observed by a sound mind that there is a certain **magnetic force** <note>original: "vis quædam magnetica"</note> in the human spirit, implanted in it from the first breath of the fetus, which by a certain natural instinct attracts its like from the air of the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or universe, which the human "Microcosm" reflects</term>, whether it be from the simple air or from its waves in complex nourishment; it extracts these and unites them with its own substance. 

Thus, the internal force of the **Spleen** is to attract and preserve styptic and acid humors, as well as the muddy and earthy substance of the blood (or prepared chylous juice), by a natural appetite. Likewise, the nature of the **Liver** is to gather chylous clouds and convert that chylous juice into the nature of warm and moist blood, and sometimes to produce catarrhal rains, in the manner of the **South wind** <note>original: "Auster"</note>. There is also a point of magnetic attraction in the intermediate places, whose role is to draw to itself the intermediate parts of the air infected by the lateral winds. In this way, the entire portion of the human spirit, fabricated from infinite particles, is bathed in the dominion of all the winds blowing in the Macrocosm, which proceed from the seeds <note>original: "seminariis"</note> of all the winds of the world’s spirit, though in unequal proportions. 

This, therefore, is the reason why the bodies of men—and their airy spirits—are necessarily altered by the surrounding air (according to the rules of Galen and Hippocrates <note>Ancient Greek authorities on medicine who emphasized the influence of environment/air on health</note>). Thus, the most skillful physicians have not hesitated to forecast the types of future diseases according to the dominion of malignant winds. 

We say, therefore, that the offspring of the collateral winds of the world exercise their powers and blasts within the human air no differently than their parents do in the Greater World. For this reason, we call them the "offspring," "sons," and "descendants" of the collateral winds of the world, since they are procreated and exercise their powers in the human body from those seeds scattered and sown everywhere in the open air, which is drawn in through the lungs and pores. 

But as we see in childbirth, not all wombs <note>original: "matrices"</note> are suited for propagation—some are too cold, causing the seeds to be deadened and fail to move toward the desired goal of a fetus; others are too hot, and either scorch the seeds or absorb their radical moisture; others are almost suffocated by a mass of superfluous humors, and are hindered in their movement of generation by infinite other obstacles. In the same way, the **seeds of the winds** <note>original: "seminaria ventorum"</note>, whether malignant or benevolent, are dispersed everywhere in the air. When they are drawn into the human body (as if into a womb), whether by breathing or by the nourishment of animal or vegetable, they are not perceived to act either malignantly or benignly if they encounter a material contrary to the nature of that wind. This is because the growth of such seeds is hindered and, as it were, extinguished by the quality of the contrary wind predominating in that same body. 

For example, we see that not everyone is infected during a time of **plague** <note>original: "tempore pestifero"</note>, and yet we perceive that everyone breathes that same contagious air. This is because we see the natures of some men are not at all suited to nourish such seeds received into their bodies, because they abound in a disposition of a contrary wind. For instance, if the constitution of the spirit at the first breath of human life is **Northern** <note>original: "septentrionalis"</note>, and it persists strongly in that condition, the contagious blasts of the Southern winds cannot harm it much. But if such spirits are weakened by the inspired air and the gathered nourishment from opposite winds blowing for a long time, then they are infected, either lightly or heavily, in proportion to the weakness of the Northern spirit.
