### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

...contagious, it very easily absorbs and nourishes the seeds of the "meteors" <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric or bodily phenomenon, such as vapors, winds, or sudden illnesses.</note> belonging to that same wind; for this reason, such people are infected more quickly and more fatally by this kind of plague or epidemic disease than others. And this doctrine of ours seems not to differ or dissent much from that of **Galen** and **Hippocrates**, who both arrived at this opinion: namely, that those of a **bilious** <term>bilious: a temperament associated with yellow bile, characterized as being hot and dry</term> temperament endure the hot temperature of summer with greater difficulty and fare better in the winter and northern cold; conversely, those of a **phlegmatic** <term>phlegmatic: a temperament associated with phlegm, characterized as being cold and moist</term> temperament tolerate the Southern, rainy, and wintry disposition with greater difficulty, while the heat of summer is more pleasing to them. Their words are these: *In summer (says Hippocrates, Aphorisms book 3, 18), the elderly are healthier, as they are naturally cold.* And Galen, commenting on that passage: *In the elderly, because of the coldness of their temperature, summer is most beneficial.* And elsewhere: *Phlegmatic types live best in summer, and bilious types in winter.*

Do we not also have this confirmed in the blowing of the worldly winds, in which those from the North <note>original: "Boreales"</note> seem to cure and uproot the effects of the Southern ones? For just as the condition of the **South Wind** <note>original: "Australis venti"</note> is to generate clouds, dissolve frozen things, thicken the air, produce rain, and even generate contagious diseases; so indeed the spirit of the **North Wind** <note>original: "Boreæ"</note> scatters clouds, or freezes those that have dissolved, thins the air, drives away rain, and opposes the growth of the plague. Similarly, when the dry winds of the **Spleen** <note>original: "Lienis"</note> predominate, thin vapors and flowing rheums <note>excessive watery discharge or fluids</note> are thickened, frozen, and halted. Likewise, the vapor emitted by the **Liver** <note>original: "Hepate"</note> dissolves those things frozen and condensed by the winds of the Spleen, and opens the pores that were constricted and locked by them; and so it is with the others. But although we write these things taught by their effects and common experience—as if by a "demonstration from the effect"—nevertheless, the reason for this matter is deeply hidden and mystical, and can only be indicated by a "demonstration from the cause." For there are healthy winds of mercy, and there are unhealthy winds of severity; there are also great angels or **Archangels** who have been ordained by God to preside over these winds, and who send out their legions either for vengeance and punishment, or for beneficence, according to the good pleasure of their Creator (before whom they stand). There is also a certain universal angel, the first emanation from the brightness of the Almighty, called **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia"</note> by the author of Ecclesiasticus, **Metatron** <note>original: "Metattron"</note> by the Kabbalists, and **Messiah** and **Soter** or **Savior** by the mystics, in whose power it is to preserve men from the violence of the "Windy Demons" <note>original: "Cacodaemonum Ventosorum"</note>. He, I say, is the solar soul itself, the presiding officer of life and health, acting kindly to protect health in no other way than the office of **Raphael** is ordained to drive away diseases (as is clear from the etymology of his name <note>The Hebrew name Raphael means "God heals."</note>). He is the one who "ascends from the rising of the Sun, having the seal of the living GOD, and crying with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to hurt the earth and the sea, saying: Hurt not the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads" (Revelation 7). But concerning this mystical method of being affected by disease or of preserving health, we shall discuss more at length, God willing, in our treatise on the *Metaphysics of Meteors*, regarding both healthy and unhealthy causes. However, you will find the history of the **Microcosmic winds** described and treated more fully and extensively in our treatise on *Mystical Anatomy*, an ocular demonstration of which you have depicted here.

### Chapter I. Of Member II.

->Where meteorological bodies produced from the winds are treated in general.<-

The condition of meteorological bodies, both in substance and form, is the same as that of perfectly mixed bodies. These were previously "imperfectly mixed" bodies arising from aerial simplicity through motion, and in that state, they took on the form of meteorological bodies. This occurs, namely, between the "limit from which" <note>original: "terminum à quo"</note>—which is the simply aerial state—and the "limit toward which" <note>original: "illum ad quem"</note>—namely, perfect composition. This has been sufficiently demonstrated to you in the preceding sections. 

From these points, it seems clear enough that everything which exists, as far as its consistency is concerned, is originally nothing but one and the same thing: namely, air. There is no composite thing in the world that is not either a meteor or made from a meteor. It is a "meteor" (I say) if it is an imperfect body; it is "from a meteor" because, by the very nature of things, a transition must occur from a simple nature to one that is perfectly composite. 

For it is impossible for a progression from a starting point to a finishing point to happen without an intermediate middle. In the number two <note>The Pythagorean "Dyad."</note>, no perfection is found, since only two limits are present; for this reason, the Pythagoreans called it a confused and imperfect number. They most rightly attributed the dignity of perfection to the number three <note>The "Ternary."</note>, because in it three limits are found: the beginning, the middle, and the end. These limits in composition are like an "imperfectly mixed" or meteorological body. 

We see this, for instance, when a paste or dough is formed from impalpable flour as if from air; the dough acts as the middle limit or the "composition in middle motion" between the bread and the flour. Then, by the reduction of moisture and by baking, that imperfect composite is confirmed and reduced into the perfect form of bread. Does this not also appear in the examination of wood, or of an animal body, or even of a metal—such as lead, iron, or copper—within a cupel? <term>cupel: a small, porous bowl used in assaying or refining precious metals to separate them from lead and other impurities.</term> Under the violence of fire, those bodies first turn into a dense smoke or cloud—

We find that the **Form** is a single, simple thing, the primary act, central, acting, the offspring of primary light, forming and effecting all things, supernatural and uncreated in origin, but clothed in natural effect and spirit, natural and created. Whence it is said, *heaven and earth shall pass away, but the word of GOD shall remain forever; for the spirit of GOD is incorruptible, and consequently is subject to no corruption, wherefore it exists into eternity.*

## CHAPTER III.

### On Universal Water and its species, and that it is the passive matter of any mixture, whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed.

Just as the internal form of all things, whether mixed or simple, is a certain uncreated light or an incorruptible spirit instilled in them by the divine since creation—without whose presence they could not live, or indeed exist at all—so also that spirit is the garment or the closest vehicle of this light. By this light, the invisible air (namely, the wind) is moved at the command of this God-like spirit dwelling in the center. Its remote covering, and the one closest to the air carrying it, is the **invisible water**, both thick and thin, from which the bodies of creatures are fashioned. 

From this it follows that all things in the world were created primarily from water and through water, by the operation of that central spirit; but secondarily from heaven (as the internal and spiritual part) and earth (as the external and physical part), since these two are what fill and complete the vast cavity of the world. And this is confirmed by Saint Peter, in the passage cited many times by us previously, who says: *That the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of GOD.* From this it follows that those things which are immediately fashioned from heaven and earth mixed together are originally made from water and through water—yet not from water alone, which is the passive part in the composition, but by the mediation of the acting divine Word, without which (according to John) *nothing was made, as it is that in which the life of the creature resides.* Or, as was said before, by the mediation of Wisdom, *which was the brightness of the eternal light emanating from the mouth of the Most High before any creature was made,* and which (by the testimony of the wise man) *was standing by her father in his works.* Or, as the leader Moses would have it, *by the mediation of the spirit of the Lord, which moved over the waters,* providing them with fiery vigor or life.

We see, therefore, that the waters created primarily from worldly creatures are the whole of that which is called heaven and earth; and consequently, it is certain that they fill the vast concavity of the world. Whence also, just as the heavens or the air are spread everywhere in their spiritual nature and are of an invisible consistency, the "earth" is actually thin water that has become visible, while the thick dregs or "dead head" <note>term: caput mortuum; an alchemical term for the useless residue left after distillation or chemical reaction, representing the most solid, inert matter.</note> of the whole is the opaque earth itself, whether of a wetter substance like mud and mire, or a drier and harder one. So also we think it would not be absurd to distinguish between visible and invisible waters, namely into the celestial and the terrestrial. But indeed, it is certain that the invisible waters preceded the visible ones in creation, both in time and in order, for it was in them that the heaven was established before any land or sea appeared.

# CHAP. II.
## On the general distinction of dark Meteors.

| Dark meteors in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world" or the universe at large.</note> collected and animated by the winds are twofold, namely: | **Watery** : See M. |
| :--- | :--- |
| | **Earthy** : See N. |

**S**ince all things in the world proceed from the marrow and fountain of dark Chaos as if from a material source, and from the bright emanation of the Creator as if from a formal origin—the light informing the general matter—we do not think it absurd that we have made a vast distinction in this meteorological discourse between dark meteors and bright ones. Yet, by "dark meteors" we do not imagine such chimeras in which no portions of primary light exist; for without the participation of formal light, meteors would be nothing and entirely potential. Rather, we call them "dark" because the formal light is hidden within them, and the entire mixture appears opaque and not at all translucent to our eyes. Thus it is also said by the testimony of the Holy Bible, *Darkness was upon the face of the abyss* <note>original: "Tenebras fuiſse ſuper faciem abyſsi"</note>, *Genesis 1.* And yet Wisdom walked in the depths of the abyss, as we have in Ecclesiasticus: *Ecclus. 24.* For darkness, according to the royal Psalmist, is not darkness to God, *Psalm 139.* And as elsewhere: *Thick clouds are a hiding place for GOD, who walks upon the circuit of the heavens, Job 22:18.* And elsewhere: *Thick clouds are the vehicle or chariot of GOD, who goes upon the wings of the wind, Psalm 104.* Indeed, GOD himself said that he dwells in darkness or under a thick cloud, *2 Chronicles 6:1.* And elsewhere: *He made darkness his secret place, and with very black waters and thick clouds he surrounded his tabernacle, so that they might serve him in place of a veil, Psalm 18:11.* Is it not also said that the darkness in Egypt proceeding from divine power was so great that one person could not see another? And yet, like a dark mist, they were palpable [able to be felt], *Exodus 10.* And these are the darknesses that are watery or moist in condition.

Furthermore, the earth itself is taken for darkness, and is called dark, as can be seen in many places of Holy Scripture; and consequently, we have not ineptly or rashly called all compact and opaque meteors of an earthy consistency "dark." Such things include the <term>Ceraunian stone</term> <note>original: "lapis Ceraunius"; also known as a "thunderstone," these were prehistoric stone tools that early modern scholars believed fell from the sky during thunderstorms.</note> or lightning stone, manna, metallic bodies, and other things of this sort.

### CHAP. III.

#### First Part: On the dark, watery meteors in the Macrocosm.

Dark **Meteors** of a watery consistency are either thinner or thicker in their substance. We call those "thinner" meteors which are more spread out, softer, and less compact in their parts—the kind which are, as it were, at a midpoint in their journey from simple, invisible air toward what we commonly call water. We call those "thick" which are either liquid water or frozen, or those compacted with earth, which we will discuss below. Watery meteors of a thinner consistency are various grades of vapors or fumes, where one is denser or heavier than another, or closer to the state of water toward which they tend. These include the Halo, Mist, and Cloud, which we shall discuss here in more detail—first explaining Aristotle’s opinion on the origin or generation of such meteors, and then how that opinion either agrees or disagrees with the testimony of Holy Scripture. Aristotle, along with the rest of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note>, defines a **Halo** as a whitening circle surrounded by blackness at its edges, appearing around the Sun, Moon, or a luminous star. It is formed from moist vapor rising from the earth and waters, condensed into a thin cloud or "cloudlet," which creates a circular shape in the eyes of the beholders because of the light. This is usually a sign of rain if it gradually turns black and becomes thicker overall; but if it breaks with a great gap on one side, it portends winds from the direction where it first opens and bursts. These are their views. <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author of a massive encyclopedia of natural history</note> also acknowledges that the Halo circle is sometimes the color of blood, due to the density of the cloud surrounding the sun (Pliny, Book 2, Chapter 30).

**Mist** (or fog), according to the opinion of the Peripatetics, is a kind of "sterile" cloud—that is, one without rain—which remains from the residue of vapor gushing from the earth and waters that could not be raised high enough or condensed into a cloud. Or it can be defined thus: Mist is vapor drawn upward from the waters and earth by the heat of the sun, but because the solar heat is not strong enough to lift that vapor into the middle region of the air (where it would be contracted into a cloud by the cold of that place), the heat fails and allows the vapor to gradually descend back to the earth after only a slight condensation.

A **Cloud** (which is the most general category for all the others mentioned) is vapor elevated from the lands and waters into the middle region of the air by the force of solar heat. There, it is contracted and, as it were, frozen into the consistency of a cloud by the power of extreme cold. Afterward, it is driven here and there through the middle region of the air, partly by the sun's heat and partly by the force of the winds.

Finally, they define a **Small Cloud** (or cloudlet) as a tiny cloud that grows to a massive size through the union or addition of vapors successively flying upward; hence the common proverb: "from a small cloud a great storm can often arise."

In conclusion, then, all these meteors seem to differ not only in their material cause but also in their external form, insofar as some are more or less compact than others, and some are smaller or thinner in quantity. Therefore, once the matter and form of one type are sought out with diligent focus, the others will also reveal themselves more clearly by that light, since they are all of the same nature and condition.

In defining the condition of any such meteor, three things are worthy of observation: namely, the matter, the location, and the efficient cause.

Aristotle makes the matter of the halo, the mist, and the cloud the same: namely, moist vapor gushing from the earth and water as the places appropriate for its generation. But let us hear what the <term>Sacred Page</term> <note>A traditional way of referring to the Bible</note> relates concerning the origin of such small clouds and clouds, so that we may see by the testimony of the whole truth...

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

<gloss>On the Formal Cause of Meteors.</gloss>

...let us see whether that pagan Aristotle is a liar or a truth-teller; in those [Scriptures] we find it written: *That God fits the weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure, he makes a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders. Job 28:25.* <note>The author uses this verse to argue that air has a physical weight and role in creating rain, contrary to some ancient views.</note> From these words, the order or stages in the procreation of watery meteors is gathered, and consequently their original material can be sought out: the order is of this kind. Specifically, from air to mists, small clouds, and larger clouds; and from clouds to rain; and finally to lightning. Therefore, in a description of this kind, the primary **material cause** is declared to be air, which is gradually thickened into a vaporous small cloud, and from there into a firm cloud. Through the penetration of this cloud, its fiery soul sometimes reveals itself, and by the heat of that same soul, that material is condensed and reduced into rain. And this is the progression in nature from the "point of departure"—namely from air or invisible water—to the "point of arrival"—namely into visible water—with smoke, mist, or clouds acting as intermediate compositions or "imperfect mixtures" that necessarily occur during the transition of one element into another. Likewise, in the regression of the watery element back into air, it is necessary that these same intermediates or imperfect mixtures intervene: just as in the conversion of water into air by fiery power, a thick vapor is first placed between the watery consistency and the airy one, which is gradually thinned into an airy condition. 

We conclude, therefore, that the general matter of all species of clouds is **air**, expanded everywhere throughout the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The region below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change and the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, and not vapor raised from the earth and terrestrial waters by the heat of the sun. This can also be more easily gathered from the story of Noah’s flood, in which the water overflowing the land far surpassed the earth itself in quantity and dimension. Furthermore, Aristotle seems to be ignorant of what those "windows of heaven" were which were opened to bring about that flood, and even today the Christians of this age doubt this question and cannot answer such a doubt. 

But truly, if they inspect the holy writings with an attentive mind, they will perceive that waters hide everywhere in the air potentially and in a hidden manner, which are revealed according to the Divine will. In this way, the air or the "heaven" of God’s treasury is opened, and the windows of heaven are said to be unlocked. And this is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Bible: *The Lord will open to you his best treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to your land in its season. Deut. 28:12.* Where by "heavens" he understands the **air**: because clouds are procreated in the air, and similarly air is called "heaven" in many places of holy scripture. Hence it is said, *The birds of the heaven, etc. Gen 1.* Similarly, we read elsewhere: *Therefore the treasures were opened and the clouds and mists flew out like birds. In his greatness he placed the clouds etc. Ecclesiasticus 43:17.* But Job also seems to confirm this in the clearest words, saying, *Chap. 37:21. And now men see not the light; suddenly the air is gathered into clouds and the passing wind will drive them away.* In this discourse he seems to declare clearly not only that clouds are procreated from the air, but also that the agent in this kind of creation—the soul moving them—is the **wind**: which will be discussed more widely below. 

From these things it is manifest that Aristotle himself was deceived regarding the material origin of the <term>Halo</term>, mist, and cloud, and is inconsistent in that assertion of his, since he deduced the material cause of clouds *a posteriori*—that is, from the earth and dense water. It is as if someone were to say that creation received its existence from a composite and visible thing by moving backward, rather than from a simple and invisible thing by moving forward. We are taught that this is most false by the testimony of the Apostle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul in Hebrews 11:3: "so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."</note> often cited before: who indicates to us that visible things were originally first made from invisible things, and not the opposite. 

For if the material cause of clouds (as declared in Book 7 of our *History of the Macrocosm*, chapter 4) were vapor from the earth and terrestrial waters raised toward the middle region of the air by the heat of the sun, it would follow that clouds would be more frequent in the summer than in the winter. This is because in summer the sun is observed to sublimate vapors from the waters and earths into the heights more easily with its more direct rays; and also because in the warmer time, the terrestrial pores vomiting such vapors allow the smoke to exit without any hindrance of cold blocking the way through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>A scientific theory of the time suggesting that a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as internal heat increasing when the outside air turns cold.</note>. 

For we see that according to the doctrine of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because he famously walked while teaching.</note>, the air in summer is most thick because of the constant vapors rising from the earth and water; indeed, they say that ponds, springs, and rivers are converted—either entirely or in great part—into the substance of air by thinning. Just as, conversely, in winter, when the thicker part of the air is condensed by the power of cold, the air is observed to be changed first into a misty substance, then into a cloud, and finally into rain or water. Hence springs, ponds, and rivers are filled in the winter time by the change of air into water, and torrents arise; and hence the entire surface of the earth, dried out in summer, is rendered moist and slippery in winter. This is their doctrine, although we, taught by experience, are compelled to dissent from this opinion of theirs, as we shall say more widely below where the generation of springs is discussed. 

From this it is evident, even according to their own doctrine, that it is not vapor elevated into the middle region of the air immediately, but the **condensed air itself** that is the cause and material origin of the substance of a cloud. It is also evident that clouds are produced more in winter than in summer, both because of the contrary blast of opposing winds, and because the blasts of the Northern winds are more frequent, whose nature it is to congeal, as will be explained more fully below. Therefore it follows that this portion of the Aristotelian definition is false and lying, both in respect to the material cause of the cloud and because he is deceived regarding the place where that material originates. Furthermore, it is most certain (contrary to that assertion of the Peripatetics) that clouds are procreated even in the lower region of the air, especially in winter time, as they are observed to move below the peaks of mountains and not far from the earth; indeed...

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

...and sometimes, when thunders occur in summer, clouds are observed almost touching the tops of tall trees; from which it is clear that clouds do not consist of vapor sublimated from earth and water, elevated into the **middle region of the air** <term>The middle region of the air was believed by early scientists to be a place of intense cold where vapors condensed into clouds and snow.</term>, and there condensed and frozen by the power of that place’s intense cold, as those Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici," referring to Aristotle and his followers</note> would have it.

Then, he [Aristotle] proceeds to the efficient and procreating cause of the cloud, which he says is solar heat; by its power, such vapor is not only sublimated from the earth and water, but is also moved here and there—partly by that heat and partly by the winds. He makes the cold of the middle region of the air the "constricting cause" of the vapor. Thus, two agents, contrary in nature and condition, seem to concur to complete the cloud: namely, solar heat and the cold of the middle region. However, he provides no *internal* moving cause for the cloud, as if it were by its nature shapeless and inanimate.

In this specific part of the definition, many doubts occur to the subtle observer that must be resolved. First: Is the heat of the sun the cause that elevates the matter of the cloud into the middle region of the air from the lower parts for the completion of the cloud? Second: Is the cold of the middle region of the air the cause of the thickening or condensation of vapors into the compact substance of a cloud? Third: Is the cloud moved only by the winds and the heat of the sun—destitute of any internal principle—or is it rather animated by an internal spirit and moved centrally or naturally? I shall attempt to respond to these in order, in this manner.

To the first point, therefore, we say: Solar heat does not contribute much to the production of clouds (in the Aristotelian sense), nor to the elevation of their matter, nor to its sublimation from earth and water. This you have already had sufficiently declared from what was said before; for there is a certain divine, incorruptible, and God-like spirit expanded everywhere through the air, which we previously called **Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientiam"</note>. This divine spirit, universally diffused, performs all things in the heavens and on the earth; it is this which disposes all things, and is accustomed to perform so many secrets and miracles daily in the moist nature of the world. Regarding this, Jehovah speaks, mocking the bold philosophers of the world and their fictions:

> *Who has counted the clouds in his wisdom? And who can tilt the water-skins of heaven?* <note>original: "Quis sapientias nubes effecit sapientia? & vtres cæli quis prosternat" — Job 38:37</note>

To which Aristotle seems to respond (impudently attributing the power and efficacy of the Creator to created things): "The heat of the sun along with the cold of the middle region of the air." But let us look for a moment at whether this was uttered well by him, or rather erroneously. By the testimony of the very fountain of truth, we have:

> *That God weighs the waters by measure, and sets a law for the rains, and a path for the sounding storms.* <note>original: "quod DEVS aquas appendat in mensura, & ponat pluuiis legem, & viam procellis sonantibus" — Job 28:25</note>

He does not say that the heat of the sun supplies the material for the clouds or moves them, nor does He mention condensation by cold. Rather, He says that God Himself weighs the clouds in the air, makes a way for them, and moves them here and there according to His pleasure by His Word or Wisdom. The Wise Man [Solomon] also confirms this in these words:

> *When Jehovah established the clouds above, when he strengthened the fountains of the deep, when he imposed his decree upon the sea... I, Wisdom, was with him as a foster-child.* <note>original: "Cum fortificaret Iehoua superiores nubes... ego sapientia sui apud ipsum velut alumnus" — Proverbs 8:27-30 (cited in text as Prov. 4.27)</note>

By this speech we are taught that Jehovah is the author of the clouds and their sustainer, through the mediation and assistance of Wisdom, or 그 divine emanation, which is the brightness of the indivisible Divinity. Thus also David acknowledges in express words:

> *That Jehovah himself has covered the heavens with clouds, which appear to the earth, and makes rain so that they bring forth grass; and that when He sends His speech to the earth, His word runs most swiftly—He who gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes.* <note>original: "Ipsum Iehouam nubibus obtexisse cælos... qui edit niuem sicut lanam" — Psalm 147</note>

But truly, in all these places, no mention is made of the sun's heat or the condition of cold, since these are merely instrumental causes and not efficient ones. Instead, he places the first and principal agent who immediately works these wonders: namely, **GOD**, through His Word or the Holy Spirit of discipline, present everywhere, acting both secretly and manifestedly to fulfill the will of the Father.

Therefore, Aristotle spoke in a pagan manner, and his aforementioned Christian followers speak with pagan hearts when they refuse to—or rather, do not know how to—ascribe all these things immediately to the Creator rather than to created nature. For since all things are ordered by God; by that Great Angel <note>referring to a high celestial mediator or the Logos</note> as the most powerful minister of God (proceeding first from His mouth before all things); by this immense **World Soul** <term>Anima Mundi: a vital force that early modern thinkers believed permeated and animated the entire physical universe</term>; by this flow of eternal clarity filling all things with its lucid goodness; and by this Divine Word and first-born Wisdom of God, through which all things were made and without which nothing exists; it follows that it is no small error—and one to be severely corrected by the lash of ignorance—to attribute to creatures those things which are to be attributed to the immediate act of the Creator. Indeed, if it is not a portion of blasphemy, it is certainly a manifest and apparent form of Idolatry to prefer the effects of the Sun, Moon, stars, and elements over those things which truly and immediately proceed from God. For what else did they do, who offered their sacrifices to the Sun, Moon, stars, and the host of heaven, while the due worship of Jehovah, the God of Gods, was forgotten?

As for the resolution of the second doubt: We say that the reason for the vaporous cloud being constricted and composed is something other than that brought forward by Aristotle (namely, that it occurs because of the cold of the middle region of the air). Truly, in the aforementioned fourth chapter of the seventh book of our *Natural History* <note>original: "Physicæ nostræ historiæ"</note>, I have expressed the manner and stages of cloud procreation, having been instructed by ocular experience.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of cloud formation. On the previous page, he challenged the Aristotelian view that solar heat and the cold of the "middle region" are the sole causes of clouds. Here, he provides personal observations from his travels in the Alps and at sea to argue that clouds are actually formed by the physical compression of air, either against mountains or by opposing winds.</meta>

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.
<term>Meteors: In the early modern period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including clouds, rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</term>

This was the nature of my experience. While I was traveling from Venice toward Augsburg in Germany among the Alpine mountains and crags, on the summit of a certain cliff of immense height which the solar rays were striking vigorously, I perceived a very thin mist appearing at first—hardly visible, like a vapor—from the front part of the cliff. By thickening more and more, it was gradually reduced from a barely visible vapor to the consistency of a mist and finally into a cloud, clinging to the front face or peak of the mountain. Meanwhile, I observed that the other parts of the cliff, and even the surrounding air, were free of clouds and clothed, as it were, in the garments of a most serene season; that is, they were shining everywhere with solar rays.

Therefore, being somewhat curious to investigate the cause of such a sudden appearance of a meteor, I descended from my horse. Having plucked some blades of grass and scattered them into the air, I noticed that a wind blowing quite vigorously against that side of the mountain peak was the cause of this arriving meteor. For the wind, driving the thinner air before it with its blast, compressed it against the resisting substance of the cliff or mountain, which rose up perpendicularly. Because of the hard resistance of the rock, the air was unable to flee further and was thus successively retained, united, and gathered together. That is, the parts of the air following behind were pushed by the force of the wind and added to those preceding them. In this way, by such compression, they gradually and little by little escaped into and were transformed into the consistency of a dense cloud. Finally, the solar rays striking the peak of the cliff dissolved this cloud into drops, bringing on rain.

From these things we can gather that the substance of a cloud is nothing other than air, transformed from its moderate and invisible substance into an increasingly visible meteor by means of addition and compression. But perhaps someone will object that clouds appear where mountains and crags are not found at all. To this it must be answered that the condensation of air is produced by similar compression, albeit by different efficient causes. For two opposing winds blowing—even if one is stronger than the other due to its predominance in the air—are very often accustomed to compress and condense the thinner air into the appearance of a cloud of any consistency. These winds, if they act and react strongly against one another, produce a sound in the air similar to that which two rivers make when falling with contrary motion into the same bay or abyss.

But some will undoubtedly reply that two winds cannot blow at the same time, futilely turning over that old axiom of the inconsistent philosophers: *That the greater always contains the lesser within itself, and the greater force repels and overcomes the lesser.* Nevertheless, we see, taught by experience, that a small force resists a stronger force in proportion to its mass. For a candle is not deprived of its power simply because it is inferior to the light and brightness of the sun and is reduced to nothing in the human eye.

For I remember being on a ship plowing the sea with sails spread, with a stronger wind blowing as we made our way toward England, and also toward Marseille and Italy. Although a predominant wind was serving our journey, I observed a somewhat weaker opposing wind blowing against our path and pushing the sails backward, until that wind favorable to our navigation overcame the one adverse to us and finally carried us happily to our desired goal. During that time, I perceived various clouds gathered in the air, sometimes sweating out rain. Is it not also apparent to the common eye that a cloud armed with lightning, appearing at the furthest edge of the horizon, moves against the motion of the wind on that horizon? From this it happens that thunder and tempest are procreated from the clash of two clouds moving oppositely in such a way, as is shown more clearly in the said chapter.

But lest anyone believe these things are reported by us pointlessly or falsely, we shall proceed to establish our assertion with the testimony of the sacred truth itself. Did not Ezekiel, by divine command, call upon the spirit to come at the same time from the four winds of heaven and breathe upon the slain so that they might live again? <note>Ezekiel 37</note> And the Prophet Daniel said: *Behold, the four winds of heaven fought upon the great sea.* <note>Daniel 7</note> And in Zechariah we have: *These four horses are the four winds of heaven, which go forth and stand before the ruler of all flesh.* <note>Zechariah 6:1</note> Furthermore, we have in Jeremiah: *And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and I will scatter them into all those winds.* <note>Jeremiah 49:36</note> From these things it is clear enough that not only one wind or another, but indeed all four have been given at times to blow at the same time, by which clouds and tempests, whirlwinds and thunders, and things of this sort are stirred up for the destruction of the impious. That divine poet Homer also seems to argue this same thing in these verses, where he understands by the "gods" spirits struggling in the air (as Daniel said) and fighting among themselves in the aerial sea, singing thus in interpretation:

> *So great a clamor spread through the heavenly hall*
> *When the cruel gods rushed into alternating battles;*
> *Phoebus Apollo fought against Neptune,*
> *And Pallas Athena contended against Mars, etc.*
<note>original: "Tantus cælesti rumor percrebuit aula / Cum sæva alterni ruerent in prælia diui / Neptunum contrabellabat Phæbus Apollo, / Aduersus Martem certabat Pallas Athene, &c."</note>

Where by Neptune he seems to indicate the west wind, which is cold and humid, and by Phoebus the east wind or the spirit presiding over it. Similarly, Ovid is eager to reveal the contest between Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> and the other winds with words of this sort, speaking in the person of the Northern Wind:

> *I myself, when I have found my brothers in the open sky*
> *(For that is my field of battle), struggle with such great effort*
> *That the middle air resounds with our shocks,*
> *And fires, forced out, leap from the hollow clouds.*
<note>original: "Idem ego quum fratres cælo sum nactus aperto / (Nam mihi campus is est) tanto molimine luctor, / Vt medius nostris concussibus insonet æther, / Exiliantq; cauis elisi nubibus ignes." From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note>

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

Where by "brothers" he understands the South wind <note>original: "Austrum"</note> and the other cardinal winds, which the North wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note>, encountering them in the air, is accustomed to agitate into storms, such as thunder, whirlwinds, and other such tempestuous things. Therefore, there is no doubt that two or more winds in the same storm, either opposing or crossing each other, emit their blasts in the open air. By the compression of these winds, clouds are generated from the air within the air, and are driven hither and thither by the winds, as was previously declared according to that passage in *Job 37:21*: "Suddenly the air is forced into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away." <note>This is a paraphrase of the Vulgate Job 37:21, which discusses the cleaning of the air by wind.</note> Therefore, it follows that the assertion of Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) argued in his *Meteorology* that clouds formed primarily due to the cooling of vapors in the "middle region" of the air.</note> is most false—namely, that the vaporous substance of a cloud is formed into a cloud by the constriction of the cold in the middle region of the air. This can also be made clear from the fact that the southern winds (which are the primary parents of clouds and rain) are quite warm; consequently, the vapors emitted from that quarter ought rather to dull the power of the cold in that middle region and, as a result, produce either no clouds or at least thinner ones than the other winds. Furthermore, the blasts of the East wind <note>original: "Euri"</note> are very hot, yet experience teaches us it is far otherwise, for those winds are noted for thickening the air and producing clouds far denser and more moist than the others. Indeed, these winds thicken the middle air so much that they usually make objects appear larger to the eyes than other winds do, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 CE), a scholar whose "Etymologies" was a standard reference for medieval and early modern science.</note> testifies.

To arrive now at the resolution of the final doubt—namely: Are clouds moved hither and thither primarily by external motion (that is, by the winds and the sun and only on the surface) and not by some internal principle from the center? To this doubt, we respond that the Halo, the mist <note>original: "nebulam"</note>, the small cloud <note>original: "nubeculam"</note>, and the cloud (all of which <term>meteors</term> differ neither in matter nor in internal form, but only in shape) enjoy their own internal principles of motion from their center. By means of these, according to the will of the Creator, they move hither and thither. For since that divine spirit (which they call Wisdom) is present in the worldly spirit, by means of which the world is animated, it is necessary that this luminous soul be dispersed everywhere through the air, just as we observe the soul to be expanded throughout the human spirit and body in the smallest parts—namely, in the whole and in every part, as the Philosophers teach. Hence, it is because the condition of this luminous soul is to be situated around the center of any composite thing and not in the circumference (although it also emits its rays from the center to the circumference, which is why it is said to be in the whole and in every part). That entire portion of the World Soul (if it is permitted to think of it as divisible) which, before the air's contraction, moved in the air for the sake of informing it, now reflects and contracts itself into the center or midpoint of the air converted into a cloud. There it breathes through the mediation of its angels or spirits, sent from the quarters of the winds to execute the will of that incorruptible spirit wherever it wishes, moving hither and thither according to the will of the King sitting upon his central throne, either for the blessing or the cursing of the earth and its inhabitants. Therefore, this eternal spirit, thus enclosed by its own will in its black hut <note>A poetic reference to the dark interior of a storm cloud.</note>, partly by magnetic power attracts the air from the center to its circumference, and partly the angels, who are his windy ministers, apply air from all sides with their breathing-holes, so that suddenly and as if in a moment they may build a hut for their Creator, which they do not cease to carry hither and thither at the Emperor's pleasure. Do we not also have this very thing clearly depicted by the Holy Page in these express words: *He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet, and he ascended upon a cherub, and flew, and glided upon the wings of the wind. He placed darkness round about him as a tabernacle, sifting the waters from the clouds of the heavens; at the brightness in his presence, the clouds were kindled, etc. 2 Samuel 22:8-12.* <note>The Latin cites "2 Reg. 22", which in the Vulgate corresponds to 2 Samuel in modern English Bibles.</note> And we have it written by the Psalmist: *The thick cloud is the vehicle or chariot of God, who walks upon the wings of the wind, Psalm 104.* And elsewhere it says: *Jehovah spread a cloud for a covering, Psalm 105:39.* And in Job we find: *Thick clouds are the hiding place of God, who walks about the circuit of the heavens.* Indeed, even Jehovah himself affirmed that he dwells under a dark mist. Did not this spirit of Wisdom also say: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne is in a pillar of cloud, I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and I have walked in the depth of the abyss, etc. Ecclesiasticus 24.* <note>Ecclesiasticus, also known as Sirach, is a book of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon.</note> Therefore, it is this incorruptible spirit sitting in the midpoint of the cloud who gives rain to the earth when he wills, and again restrains it according to his pleasure, according to that: *He restrains the waters so that they dry up, and he sends them out so that they overturn the earth, Job 12:15.* Or that: *I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon the earth, Isaiah 5.* And elsewhere: *The heavens over your head shall be brass, Deuteronomy 28.* And elsewhere: *Jehovah is so kindled with anger against you, that he closes the heavens so that there is no rain, and the earth does not yield its fruit, Deuteronomy 11:17.* And elsewhere: *God covers the heavens with thick clouds, that they may provide rain for the earth, that the mountains may bring forth grass, Psalm 147:8.* This, I say, is that spirit of divinity which is centrally within the clouds, but not inclusively (as he who is present everywhere breathes where he wills), whose glory sometimes reveals itself in a flash from the struck cloud, and sometimes leads the cloud in its invisible essence hither and thither. His windy ministers follow his will or desire, for they go forth and stand before the Ruler of the whole earth, as the prophet testifies, *Zechariah 6.* Hence it is said: Wisdom was a covering for them by day, that is, a cloud or mist by day and the light of the stars by night; for as Wisdom is accepted in its angelic nature, insofar as it is "otherness" (that is, clothed in a created spirit), so it is called a "creature" by Ecclesiasticus, and the Angel Metatron <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition (Kabbalah), often described as the celestial scribe or the "Lesser Yahweh."</note> by the Cabalists, etc. etc. And that great angel having the appearance of the sun, and holding seven stars in his hand, and speaking with a voice like the murmur of waters or winds, whom the four angels presiding over the winds obeyed, as is found in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>; and that angel who went before the Israelites, in whom was the name of God. # On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

eternal, and God Himself; therefore Wisdom, in respect to its angelic garment or contracted air, can be called a mist, a pillar of cloud, and likewise a fiery spirit, or light leaping forth from a cloud or the covering of Jehovah. It is also called "smoke" from the nostrils and mouth of Jehovah—that is, from the cloud with which He is clothed, just as the soul is clothed by the body.
> Sacred scripture says: "Smoke went up from his nostrils, and fire from his mouth devoured; coals were kindled by it; the Lord thundered from heaven," etc. *2 Samuel 22:9–14.* <note>The author cites this as 2 Kings 22, following a traditional numbering where 1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings were grouped as 1–4 Kings.</note>

This spirit is that first emanation from the Father (*Wisdom 10:17*), present everywhere, which is the "Spirit of spirits," insofar as all spirits of any kind, whether angelic or otherwise, are formed by its presence; and consequently, all worldly spirits offer it obedience. It is the "Wind of winds," for it blows where it wills, and all winds—inspired by its breath—strive to carry out its commands as if it were their primary commander. No one of sound mind can deny that this Spirit is the prince of winds, since it appeared to the Apostles in its windy nature; by its presence or most powerful breath, it was given to them not only to command the winds, but also to calm stormy seas, extinguish the rage of poison, drive away diseases by a single touch or word, and bring many other astounding miracles to completion. The history expands itself with these words:
> "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting," etc. *Acts 2:2.* "By the blast of your nostrils," says Moses, "the waters were gathered together," *Exodus 15:8.* And elsewhere: "By the breath of God frost is produced, and snow is given like wool," <note>original: "sicut lana"</note> *Job 37:10.*

This was that spirit by whose power Elijah produced a tiny cloud, like the palm of a hand, rising from the sea. From this, it happened immediately that the heavens were darkened by clouds and wind through the power of that spirit of immense strength dwelling in the center of the little cloud and drawing the air toward itself from every side, *1 Kings 18:44.* Solomon also speaks of this spirit thus:
> "By his wisdom the depths were broken open, and the skies drop down the dew." *Proverbs 3:20.*

We conclude, therefore, against the doctrine of Aristotle and the other Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; refers to non-Christian philosophers whose natural theories the author is refuting.</note>, that neither earth nor water are the sources of water-based meteors <note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, rain, snow, and wind.</note>, but rather the air or heaven itself, which is God’s treasury. Nor is the cold of the middle region of the air <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology* proposed that clouds formed when vapor hit a cold "middle region" of the atmosphere and condensed.</note> the cause of the compression of vaporous substance into the substance of a cloud. Instead, it is the central spirit swimming in the cloud which, according to its pleasure and through its windy ministers, expands the cloud as a garment. Under this darkness the Spirit dwells—not by heat or solar action, but by the divine light centrally implanted within them. This light sits upon the Cherubim like a commander—Cherubim being the aerial and windy angels—and it flies upon the wings of the winds, which that Spirit inspires with its primary breath. By means of this breath, they move and blow wherever it wills. It is, I say, the Spirit of Wisdom, which is far more noble than the sun (being the "soul of the sun") and more excellent than light. It is the chief actor in this kind of business, not the sun or any other part of the "host of heaven." It is, I say, a creating spirit, not a created one, which is the "first act" in the movement of meteors, assisted by its angelic ministers breathing in the world to execute its pleasure. It is, I say, the wind blowing from the center of the cloud—the wind that blows originally—and not the created winds, which are moved by the motion of the primary breath, the prince of spirits. Hence this Spirit said in the place previously cited:
> "I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High... and as a mist I covered the earth. My throne is in a pillar of cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep," etc. <note>This quote is from the deuterocanonical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:3–5, though often attributed to "Wisdom" personified.</note>

It did not say: "I encompassed the circuit of heaven driven by the violence of the winds," but it performed this voluntarily and by its own will, for at its nod the winds are always ready. For by the divine presence alone, as an internal agent, the clouds and the earth itself are moved. David also seems to confirm this in these words:
> "The waters saw you, O God, they were afraid; the depths also were troubled. The clouds poured out water, and the upper clouds gave forth a sound," *Psalm 77:16–17.*

And elsewhere it is said:
> "Jehovah sends forth his commandment upon earth: his word runs very swiftly. He gives snow like wool," *Psalm 147:15–16.*

From this it is clear that the principle of cloud motion is in the "middle-heart" of the cloud, in which this Spirit has its throne—that is, from an internal "prince-wind" and not from an external agent. This remains true even though external winds are also always ready to move and blow according to the disposition of the universal spirit. But so that every Christian may set aside all doubt in such a controversy, let him first consider the words of Saint John: namely, that *all things were made or created by the Word, and without Him was nothing made.* Since the question now concerns the daily creation of clouds, I would like you to tell us seriously: is the creation of such a meteor from the uncreated Word, as holy scripture teaches us, or from created things—namely, the Sun and the cold of the middle region of the air compressing and forming it? How can you thoughtlessly refer the reason for the cloud’s formation to an external accident and not to an internal and central principle? If we agree with the Pagan, then the doctrine of the sacred page must be rejected, and thus falsehood embraced instead of truth.

Here, therefore, one may see with open eyes how inconsistent that doctrine of the Pagans regarding clouds is, and how fragile and filthy are the foundations of those who, neglecting the Holy Spirit moving centrally everywhere, ascribe the motions of meteors to external acts and not to internal principles. By doing so, they make these things seem to arise purely by chance and not at all naturally—or rather, not supernaturally and divinely. Indeed, they falsely attribute to creatures those things which sacred scripture teaches us are derived most closely and immediately from the Creator. Nevertheless, their Christian disciples are so stuck and entangled in the "birdlime" of that erroneous doctrine that they do not hesitate to hold the things brought forth by them as if they were oracles sent down from heaven. Thus it happens that, intoxicated by such deceptive Pagan fictions, they cannot rightly engage in any science—nay, not even in sacred theology—nor can they recognize God in his creatures...

...they are able to comprehend within their own boundaries; indeed, they confidently believe and do not blush to boldly pronounce: that God is only in the heavens—that is, in the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, fiery part of heaven in medieval and Renaissance cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>, which is above the starry sphere according to His essence—but in all other places, they claim He exists only "virtually" (through His power). As if the divine power could be more divided or separated from the divine essence or spirit than a ray of sun could be from the sun itself! 

But if they were willing to consider the matter a little more correctly and accurately, they would perceive that God, according to His essence—that is, by His actual presence—is everywhere: namely on the earth, in the sea, in the air, in the heaven, and in every single creature, as is read more widely and clearly in the Sacred Pages. For God is in the "heaven of heavens," that is, in the third and innermost heaven, or in the third and most worthy region of the Tabernacle, specifically in the **Holy of Holies**. Yet God is also present everywhere: in the heaven as commonly understood, in hell, in the farthest reaches of the sea, in the night, and in the darkness, according to that saying of the Psalmist (*Psalm 139:7*); or as Moses testifies, "in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (*Deuteronomy 4:39*). 

Wherefore it follows that even the "heaven of heavens," which is the mystical heaven, is everywhere, as it is the seat of the divinity. Nor should it be believed that Paul was caught up into the Empyrean heaven of the physical world—that is, above all the orders of the stars—but rather that, while remaining on earth, he was caught up and sublimated in his spirit into the "third heaven," which is not at all distant from the earth, wherein he asserted that he saw wonders that the tongue is not permitted to utter. Does not the wise man confess that "the incorruptible spirit of God is in all things"? (*Wisdom 12:1*). Does he not also recount elsewhere that the "holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world"? 

And yet these **pigs**—distinguished only by the name of Christians but not by their virtue—fattened on ethnic (pagan) wisdom, which is worldly and vain philosophy, do not hesitate to strip away the "life" (which is in the Word, as John testifies) from the clouds and other meteorological bodies. O vanity of vanities, how great is this vanity!

But if they should finally say: "If this definition of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who generally sought physical rather than mystical explanations for nature.</note> is false and erroneous, show us a definition of the **Halo**, the mist, and the cloud that is more fitting and consistent with the truth."

I respond, therefore, that according to the smallness of my own understanding, and indeed not without the approval of the sacred writers, I am prepared to accomplish the task they seek. Thus, I shall begin courteously.

### CHAPTER IV.

->In which the Halo and clouds are described according to the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures.<-

A **Halo** is invisible air, condensed into the consistency of a thinner and transparent cloud by the "magnetic" attraction of divine Wisdom (which presides centrally within it) and by the compression of its windy ministers. Through this, the rays of the Moon, Sun, Jupiter, or Venus—prepared and adapted for this kind of reception—penetrate in a circular fashion, typically prefiguring a "crown" or a circle of various colors within it. 

Or defined thus: 

A **Halo** is the direct and voluntary application of the incorruptible spirit of Wisdom—which has its throne in the middle of a mist, as if in its vaporous covering or garment—to the orbicularly diffused rays of this or that stellar creature; or, it is a peripheral reception.

In these definitions of the Halo, and also of its other species, we primarily understand what their "primary matter" is: namely, **invisible air**. Hence it was said (as you have recorded in the preceding sections): "Jehovah will open to you his best treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to your land" (*Deuteronomy 28:12*). This means that from the air—which is the "heaven" or "expanse"—clouds of every consistency are procreated, and from these, through resolution, rains are produced. 

This was also why Elijah heard the "sound of an abundance of rain" before any cloud appeared (*1 Kings 18:41*): that is, he heard the motion of the invisible spirits in the air, the windy ministers of Wisdom. By their agitation, the air was first compressed into a small cloud the size of a man’s hand, and then immediately afterward, the heavens were shaken by winds and darkened by clouds. Thus, it was necessary for the winds to precede the appearance of the clouds, as the clouds had to be gathered by the blowing of the winds. For the wind, or the motion of the spirits in the air, began first as a sound; by its agitation, the little cloud was procreated, and then the winds grew, and that little cloud was increased to an immense size. 

All these things, however, are done by **Wisdom**, which hides centrally and primarily in the middle of the air (which was first invisible and then contracted into clouds) as if upon its throne, performing all things according to its pleasure. The Psalmist also seems to confess this generally when speaking thus: "Your works are wonderful and vast, which you have made in wisdom" (*Psalm 104:24*). And Job says: "God by his wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs out the waters by measure; he makes a decree for the rain and a path for the lightning of the thunder" (*Job 28:25*). 

This means that divine Wisdom sometimes converts the air into the consistency of either a Halo, or a mist, or a cloud, or some other **meteor** <note>The term "meteor" here refers to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, snow, or halos, not just shooting stars.</note>. For this Spirit is everywhere dispersed in the air, though invisibly, serving it in the place of its primary form. For just as the moist nature of the world (which we call the universal air) is the universal passive prim... <note>original: "primi-"</note>

...created spirit, so the eternal light emanating from God, and proceeding as if from His mouth, is an uncreated act, informing that created or passive spirit. This is also confirmed by Holy Scripture: *By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens (that is, the entirety of the air), Job 26:13.* <note>The author uses "garnished" or "adorned" to describe how God's breath gives structure and beauty to the atmosphere.</note> This spirit, moreover, is the central light, dwelling in inaccessible light, whence it is written, *GOD is clothed with light as with a garment.* This light, appearing at times with its "garment," is seen in lightning and the sun; for this reason, it is sometimes called a consuming fire, the fire of GOD, and so on. This, therefore, is that hidden spirit which does all things in the heavens and on the earth, in whose power it is (as stated before) to open the heavens, His greatest treasury, at His pleasure—that is, to bring forth from His storehouse the mists, clouds, and all other atmospheric phenomena <term>meteors: In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</term>. Whence it is said elsewhere, *He opened the doors of heaven and rained down manna, Psalm 78:25.* We conclude, therefore, that air is the primary material of the Halo as well as other atmospheric phenomena, which will be discussed more broadly in the description of the mist and the cloud: but Wisdom is the primary efficient cause, and her ministers are the secondary, or rather instrumental causes, as will be detailed below.

As for the consistency of the Halo, it is in the form of a transparent mist—that is, a vaporous substance through which stellar rays can most easily penetrate. This consistency is applied to it in a denser or thinner measure according to the will of divine Wisdom, in whose power it is *to make the weight for the winds; and he weigheth the waters (or vapors) by measure. Job 28:25.* Thus it happens that, according to the variety of quantity in density and thinness, it usually produces various effects according to the creator's will, as will be more clearly explained in our treatise on the final cause. It is necessary, therefore, that the consistency of this kind of atmospheric phenomenon is not plainly of the natural constitution of air—which is invisible and consequently cannot visibly receive such impressions—nor of that dense mist or cloud, since a stellar body <note>meaning a star or planet</note> could scarcely be seen through such bodies, and consequently could not print its coronal image <note>the circular "crown" of the halo</note> upon it. Rather, it is a medium between corporeal darkness and that incorporeal state in which air is rendered invisible; here, the light is not so obscured by darkness that it is not transparent, yet surely this transparency must not be without some obscurity. For otherwise, the reflection of the image cannot occur, and consequently, there will be no visible impression of the rays or the received image, just as can be clearly seen in glass and in the air itself. Hence **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian philosopher whose works on optics and light were influential in Europe.</note> rightly says in *On the Nature of the Mirror*: *That no part of the sphere of the stars appears to the sight because, he says, that sphere is more rarefied in other parts toward the light itself, and is not bright because it is not subject to color, for it is not visible.* **Haten** <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), known in the West as Alhazen, the "father of modern optics."</note> also seems to confirm this in Book 1 of *On Optics*, saying *that which has no color is not visible, since (says he) a thing is not visible except according to the light in the seen thing; for visible light occupies only that which is colored.* From this, it is clear that the substance of the Halo must be misty, and of a consistency halfway between invisible spirit and an entirely opaque body, so that it may better receive the forms of the stars within itself. Whence **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on nature and science.</note> says that the images of bodies can be most easily expressed in moist air, no differently than in a mirror or its reflections. From this, it is also told that it happened to a certain person, on account of the weakness of his sight, that the nearby air in a time of moisture served him in place of a mirror, because the rays could not perfectly penetrate through it but were partly reflected. The same thing also tends to happen to those afflicted with most ruinous and dangerous illnesses and pestilential fevers; seeing their own faces in the air due to the weakness and lack of visual faculty, they think, struck with terror, that they are seeing demons and foul forms. But I shall proceed to the description of the Mist.

# Chapter V.
## On the description of the Mist.

**M**ist <note>Latin: *Nebula*</note> is a transmutation of air from its natural and invisible consistency into a visible and thick vaporous substance, performed by the light of wisdom centrally—that is, by contracting the air toward itself from within—and by its windy ministers from without, lightly compressing it with contrary blasts.
->Or thus:<-
Mist is the primary species of dark visible atmospheric phenomena, constituted and procreated from the first degree of air contracted into vapor, by the divine will operating centrally and circumferentially.
->Or thus:<-
Mist is the vaporous dwelling-place of God-like Wisdom, fashioned and contracted from the air by the magnetic attraction of the Lord dwelling centrally within it, and by the external compression of His winds.

Mist is therefore of the same matter as its body, and of the same form as that of the Halo; the only difference is in thinness and density—that is, in the formula of its composition.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 65 regarding the causes of atmospheric phenomena. Having established Divine Wisdom as the "formal cause" (the guiding intelligence), the author now examines the "material cause"—the actual substance of the air—and how it transitions from an invisible, spiritual state into visible forms like clouds, rain, and snow through the power of God’s Word.</meta>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member II.

Regarding the matter of this subject, although we have spoken quite abundantly in the preceding sections, something still remains to be explained in this place that was not fully demonstrated before. We have said, therefore, that air is the immediate origin of the first level of "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and clouds, not just falling stars.</note>, namely vapor, which, by thickening more and more, is reduced into the consistency of a cloud. This invisible spirit is that from which all visible things were made, according to that passage so often cited before: *through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear; Hebrews 11:3.* It is as if he were saying that from "nothing"—that is, from an imperceptible spirit—something, or a thing subject to the senses, was created. Thus the world was created from nothing, and its creatures were produced from an equal "nothing" (at least according to our meager capacity for understanding), to be remembered by faith alone. This thing, which exists in potential, is brought into "act" <note>A philosophical distinction: "potential" is the possibility of being, while "act" is the reality of being.</note> in relation to us by the mediating Word or the Spirit of Wisdom, which first shone forth before all things.

Does not St. Paul also seem to acknowledge this same thing in these words? *God chose the lowly things of this world, and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: that no flesh should glory in his presence. 1 Corinthians 1:28-29.* By these words, he seems to argue that things of no apparent value or existence are, through the mediation of Wisdom, the cause both of the existence and the abolition of those things that do exist. For all generation and regeneration, all corruption, and the resurrection from corruption, stem from that invisible source through the mediation of that Christ, who is called by the Apostle the <term>Power of GOD and the Wisdom of GOD;</term> whence it follows in the next verse, *Christ Jesus is made unto us wisdom from GOD, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, 1 Corinthians 1:30.* Therefore the Apostle also says elsewhere, *For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory and honor, Romans 11:36.*

But this same concept is best expressed by the mystical Doctors and the Kabbalists. For Rabbi Bahir says that there is no principle except Wisdom; which, contracted in darkness or invisibly within the invisible spirit (according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus, "The Monad generates a Monad and reflected its heat into itself"—that is, it shone back upon itself), remained as if in an idle state, destitute of action. That is to say, it had regard for "nothing," and in such a state it is called by the Hebrews **אין** <note>original: "Ein" (Ayin)</note>, which means "Nothing," or "Non-being," and "the Limitless." Our perception is so barren, and our capacity for contemplating divine objects so meager and powerless, that we judge those things which do not appear as if they did not exist at all.

But truly, when it appears in reality in some form or substance, then the Kabbalists say that the "dark Aleph" is converted into the "lucid Aleph." And just as *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing unity.</note> is held by them to be the hieroglyphic of God because of its unity and simplicity, so also by that "dark Aleph" they understand the "Hidden God," and by the "lucid Aleph" they understand the "Manifest God." Whence they also call the lucid Aleph *Beth* (which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabetical order, just as Aleph is the first); therefore if *Beth* is added to the letter *Aleph*, it is read as **אב** <note>original: "AB"</note>, which is interpreted as "Father." The Father always has a relation to a Son; thus "AB" denotes the Father of all generation, where Aleph is the sign of the Father, and Beth of the Son, proceeding from the Father by divine emanation.

And this order is estimated by the Kabbalists as the first deduction in divinity, and the primordial beginning of all change, which Moses called <term>Berefchit</term> <note>Bereshit: The first word of Genesis, "In the beginning."</note>, that is, the "Principle," or the immediate emanation of light from infinity. This is the second Kabbalistic numbering called <term>Hochma</term> <note>Chokmah: Wisdom.</note> or Wisdom, over which the benevolent name of GOD, "JAH," presides. Through the mediation of this property of GOD, all things were made from nothing—that is, from unknown, or invisible, or formless matter—according to that passage in the Book of Wisdom: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of formless matter,* according to Pagninus’s interpretation; or, as Tremellius has it, *created the world from formless matter*; or as Jerome translates it, *created the orb of the earth from invisible matter, Wisdom 11:18.*

This passage agrees with that of the Apostle cited from Hebrews 11, where we find that visible things, such as all bodies are, come from the invisible (or unseen, or formless, or unknown)—namely, from the mundane spirit, which is called "the heavens and the air," distinguishing it from visible corporeal things of earthly composition. Hence it is said, *Jehovah shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heavens, to give the rain unto thy land; Deuteronomy 28:12.* He does not say "He will open his treasure, the lands and the waters," as Aristotle would have it, but "the heavens"—and this through the mediation of His wisdom.

Does not Moses also make a difference between the "vapor of the earth" and the "cloud of the heaven," where he says: *For Jehovah had not caused it to rain upon the earth, nor had any vapor gone up from the earth to water the surface of the ground, Genesis 2:5-6.* Furthermore, it is said: *Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail? Job 38:22.* And elsewhere, *He bringeth the wind out of his treasuries, Psalm 135:7.* And elsewhere, *He opened the doors of heaven (as if of the air), raining down manna, etc.* From these passages, the nature of the "place" is generally gathered from the words of Holy Scripture.

But truly, what that thing is which is shut up and hidden within those secret places of the invisible treasury of GOD is beyond the grasp of the common man to understand—except that it is in the power of Divine Wisdom to detect and reveal, at her good pleasure, the things reserved and hidden in that secret way: I mean the "seeds" hidden in the air, which exist only in "potential" to us, and to produce them into a visible "act." For through the mediation of the Word, all things were wonderfully created as if from nothing, according to that saying of King David: *O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all, Psalm 104:24.* And elsewhere: *Remember (he says) his marvelous works that he hath done; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth, Psalm 105:5.*

Hence it is said, *Hearken unto this, O Job: stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God. Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine? Dost thou know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him which is perfect in knowledge? Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong as a molten looking glass? By what way is the light parted? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? Where is the way where light dwelleth? and as for darkness, where is the place thereof? Job 37 and 38.*

But indeed, the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle; the author is criticizing them for claiming to understand nature through logic while ignoring the divine mystery.</note> in their vain manner boast that they know all these things; and yet, nonetheless, the wisest of all men spoke thus—
