# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

<note>The "Formal Cause" refers to the blueprint or shaping principle of a thing; "Meteors" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, wind, or clouds.</note>

...speaks. I perceived that man cannot attain the whole work of God, that work which is done under the sun; however much a man labors to seek it out, he shall not find it; even if a wise man thinks he knows it, he shall not be able to attain it. *Ecclesiastes 8:17 <note>The text says Ecclef. 9.2, but the quote corresponds to 8:17.</note>* By this, Solomon understands the effort of man on his own, without the attainment of divine wisdom, which elsewhere he seems to verify thus: *For what man can know the counsel of God? Or who can think what the will of the Lord is? For the deliberations of mortals are timid, and our plans are uncertain. Wisdom 9:13-14.* For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that muses upon many things. And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth, but the things that are in the heavens, who has searched out? And who has known your counsel, unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit from the highest places? For so the ways of those who live on earth were corrected, and thus through wisdom were they saved. *Wisdom 9:15-19.* From these words it is evident that human or worldly wisdom is vain; therefore, the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> teaches us to beware the vain philosophy of the Heathens and to diligently look upon the fountain of all truth. And we are taught by the prophet Baruch that the fountain of all wisdom must by no means be abandoned, so that we do not seek art, science, and understanding in foreign regions—that is, from the Heathens—as did the Hagarenes and those who were in Teman, *Baruch 3*; for they never acknowledged the way of true wisdom. Therefore, wisdom must be acquired first, and then through it we shall understand all things. *Seek first (says Christ) the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you.* Hence Solomon confesses that by the enjoyment of wisdom he arrived at a certain knowledge of the constitution of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle of times, the changes of the solstices, the varieties of seasons and weather, the circuits of the year, the positions of the stars, the natures of living creatures, the furies of wild beasts, the violence of winds, the thoughts of men, the differences of plants, the virtues of roots, and the understanding of all things, both hidden and manifest. *Wisdom 7:17-21.* From this we may see that although the human spirit by itself cannot draw out the mysteries of meteors, and knows not how to search through divine mysteries, yet a man can accomplish all this in the light of wisdom. But let us return to the proposition.

That the matter of a **mist** <note>original: *nebula*</note> is air, condensed into a thick vapor, is clear from what has preceded. And although someone might object that vapor leaping up from the surface of the earth is the cause of the mist, yet we have declared in the earlier sections that the earth itself is necessarily filled with air, no differently than a human being or any other body—whether animal, mineral, or vegetable—which it continually breathes in through its pores for its own sustenance, after the manner of an animal or plant. For there is in the air a hidden food and spiritual nourishment for every creature. Here also, when Wisdom works with her ministers in the earth—*(for the spirit of discipline fills the world, and the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing, Wisdom 1:7 and 12:1)*—she is seen to procreate within the earth, through various degrees of condensation, smokes, vapors, clouds, and waters. For Wisdom "weights the air according to her pleasure and appends the waters in measure," both in the earth and in the heaven, *Job 28:25.* Whence the earth enjoys all its meteors, and even the human body does as well, no differently than the Macrocosmic heaven, seeing as air is present in them which is of the same kind as the worldly air, as we have disputed more fully in the preceding pages. From this, therefore, we discern that there is another species of mist besides that which rises from lakes, rivers, and valleys—namely, that which is suddenly formed from the universal coagulation of the air in a miraculous and hidden way through the operation of Wisdom, which fills the entire lower region of the air. Hence it is written in the sacred fountain: *I came out of the mouth of the most High, and covered the earth as a mist. I dwelt in high places, and my throne was in a pillar of a cloud. I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep; in the waves of the sea, and in all the earth, and in every people and nation I rested. Ecclesiasticus 24:3-6.* Furthermore, Wisdom, who made the cloud her tabernacle (no differently than the body is held to be the tabernacle for the soul, whence "man" is taken to mean both soul and body, and in Holy Scripture "living soul" is sometimes used for the whole composite being), is sometimes herself called a cloud. Whence it is said: *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites (that is, a pillar of cloud) and a light in the starry night, Wisdom 10:17.* But in the Psalms it is said: *That God led the Israelites with a cloud by day, and all the night with a light of fire, Psalm 78:14 <note>Text cites Ps. 73.15</note>.* And in Exodus: *God went before the Israelites in a pillar of a cloud by day, Exodus 13:21.* And yet God said: *Behold, I send my Angel before you: beware of him, and obey his voice, for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him, Exodus 23:20-21.* That is, "my essential power." Those who are versed in angelic mysteries say, therefore, that an angel is forged from air and fiery light; whence he is called a "duality," seeing as there concur in his composition a created spirit (which is his external part serving in the place of a body) and uncreated light (which is his internal part and holds the place of a mind). Thus, with respect to his external part, he is called in that same chapter an "angel" or "creature," but by reason of his internal center, he is called there "Jehovah." This angel was called **Metatron** by the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> and the **World Soul** <note>original: *Anima mundi*</note> by the Platonists; it was that Wisdom proceeding from the mouth of the Father. Indeed, this uncreated emanation, insofar as it was mixed with the worldly spirit, is called a "creature." The words are as follows: *The Creator created Wisdom before the world in the beginning, and she shall not fail in the world to come; in the holy tabernacle she ministered before him. Ecclesiasticus 24:9-10.* But truly, this emanation in its simplicity is called the Creator and the Word; whence St. John said: *All words <note>original: *verba*</note> were made [through him], and without him was nothing made; for in him is life.* And this is the reason that the divine Plato not unwisely called it the soul or life of the world, and the royal Psalmist in Psalm 33: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and all the power of them by the spirit of his mouth.* From him, in him, and through him are all things.

To Him be praise and honor, as St. Paul testifies. This spirit (I say), with the angels as administrators, draws out from its excellent treasury—the heavens, or the treasury-chest of the air—the matter of mist, whether thick or thin, according to its own good pleasure. It spreads this out as a covering, according to the words of the Royal Psalmist: *God spread out a cloud for a covering* (*Psalm 105:39*). And *like a mist, it covers the earth* (*Ecclesiasticus 24:10*). And elsewhere: *He holds the surface of his throne under the clouds; he spreads his cloud over it* (*Job 26:9*). And elsewhere: *I, Wisdom, have my tent in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud* (*Ecclesiasticus 24:3*). We conclude, therefore, that just as the uncreated light in an angel—which was the essential <term>Name of Jehovah<note>In the Western esoteric tradition, the "Name of God" was often viewed as a literal, potent force or light residing within celestial beings to give them power and form.</note></term> within the angel—was the central point in the angelic composition and its primary mover (whence Wisdom is said to do all things according to the Father's good pleasure), and just as it is the soul or mind to the angel's external form; so indeed this good and incorruptible spirit of God is the internal motor and actor of the cloud and of every <term>meteor<note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or rainbows.</note></term>, directing it wherever it wishes. Whence Job says: *The clouds scatter their light, which wanders over all things in a circuit, wherever the will of the governor leads them, to do everything he commands them upon the face of the world* (*Job 37:12*), whether for a scourge <note>meaning as a punishment or plague</note> or for performing acts of kindness and mercy. Finally, a mist is nothing other than a cloud of medium consistency, between the vaporous substance of a <term>Halo<note>Original: "Halonis." A reference to the thin vapor that creates rings around the sun or moon.</note></term> and that of a dense cloud. We have now arrived at the description of the dense cloud itself.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the Christian description of the cloud.

**A** cloud is air that has been compressed and condensed, first into the degree of a dense or misty vapor, and from that gradually into a thicker and darker consistency. This happens through the blowing of two winds—either opposing or transverse—by the will of God, who operates centrally to fulfill His purpose. Or thus:

->The cloud is the revelation of the world-spirit <note>original: "spiritus mundani"</note> in the treasury-chest of God—that is, in his heavens—hidden by divine wisdom operating from the center, and by his windy ministers compressing it from the outside at God's nod. That is to say: it is a gathering into a misty heap by the divine breath, which Jehovah spreads out as his covering, and which he holds as a booth or a vehicle to fulfill his will both in the heavens and on the earth.<-

->Or thus:<-

->A cloud is a vaporous and dense mass of air, which Divine Wisdom, expanded everywhere through the spirit of the world, has made as if out of nothing—that is, out of the invisible and unknown sanctuary or treasury-chest of the air. It has brought this forth into the common light and revealed it publicly to the world to execute its will, both in the heavens and on the earth.<-

In such definitions, or rather descriptions, we have the <term>material cause<note>The substance from which something is made.</note></term>: namely, the dense and vaporous mass of air, or misty heap, in which the <term>formal cause<note>The design or shaping principle that makes a thing what it is.</term></note> is also depicted. We also have its <term>efficient cause<note>The force or agent that brings the thing into being.</note></term>, both the central one, acting first by its will—namely, Divine Wisdom—and the external and superficial one: namely, the ministers of wisdom, who compress and move it. We have also the "mine," or treasury-chest, from which the matter of the composition is drawn: namely, the heavens, which are the treasure of God. Finally, the <term>final cause<note>The ultimate purpose or goal of the thing.</note></term> is expressed in the last place: namely, the effects of the Creator's will, whether they are healthful and leaning toward mercy, or unhealthful, destructive, and tending toward the property of divine severity.

To defend the first part of our definition, we have several testimonies from the Holy Page. For instance, we find that *God by his wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs out the waters by measure; he makes decrees for the rain and a path for the lightning of the thunders* (*Job 28:25*). That is to say, according to the will and ordination of the divine spirit, the air is changed from a lighter state or weight into a denser or heavier one. The degrees of this change are explained in the following sections: namely, toward clouds (which he calls "waters"), and from clouds to rain (or common water). Furthermore, he makes the internal, formal light of the cloud the lightning, which is not revealed except by the dissolution of the compound—that is, by the removal of darkness—which is achieved through the blowing of the winds. Whence it is said: *As soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow* (*Psalm 147:18*). That is, it rains, or the snows, clouds, and ice are dissolved. And elsewhere: *Men do not now look at the light when it is bright in the upper clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed*—that is, separated from the waters or the dense clouds (*Job 37:21*).

The efficient cause of the cloud in the definition is also confirmed by the authority of the fountain of all truth, in which it is written: *God weighs the waters* (that is, the clouds) *by measure* (*Job 28*). And elsewhere in the same place: *Who has made the sapphire clouds by wisdom?* And elsewhere: *God covers the heavens with dense clouds* (*Psalm 147:8*). And elsewhere: *God spread out a cloud for a covering* (*Psalm 105:39*).

The "mine" or treasury-chest, from which the matter of the cloud is drawn, is expressed in this passage of the Holy Bible: *Jehovah shall open his best treasure, the heavens* (or the air), *giving rain to your land in its time*, etc. (*Deuteronomy 28*). Just as it is said of the "mine" of the winds: *He brings the wind out of his treasures* (*Psalm 135:6*). And of the treasures of snow and hail it is said: *Have you entered into the treasure of the snow? Or have you seen the treasure of the hail?* The storehouse or "perfume-closet" <note>original: "myrothecium"</note> and sanctuary for all these things is a single one, in which the general matter of the world was originally extracted: namely, the spirit or universal <term>Mercury of the World<note>original: "Mercurius mundi." In alchemy and natural philosophy, this refers to the underlying, fluid substance of all matter that can be transformed into different shapes.</note></term>, which, at God's command and with His wisdom assisting, is transmutable into any form like <term>Proteus<note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note></term>. ->### On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 69<-

By the truly Christian philosopher, this spirit—taken generally and endowed with the power of Wisdom—is defined as an infinite nature, procreating like from like, generating and increasing all things, and containing within itself the names of all things. Inasmuch as it is an animal by nature, it is also stone, wood, a tree; and all bodies that are seen—whether they are imperfectly or perfectly mixed—are animated by this kind of spirit through divine Wisdom and stabilized by its bond. It is the ligament of the elements and the power of mixing which, by means of its central soul in any thing of this world, effects the mixtures of the elements and impresses the form appropriate to its species, through which that thing is distinguished and separated from every other thing. Yet, this "occult nature" is of no specific color, though it participates in and produces all colors; it is of no weight or quality, yet it is the fruitful mother of all weights, qualities, and things. 

Hence, it was because of this that Anaximenes <note>Anaximenes of Miletus (c. 585 – c. 528 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "Air" was the primary substance of the universe.</note> boldly asserted that air was the cause of all things, and Anaximander <note>Anaximander (c. 610 – c. 546 BC) preceded Anaximenes; while he proposed the "Apeiron" (the Infinite) as the beginning, the author here groups them as focusing on the material "receptacle" rather than the divine source.</note> wished it to be held as God, as the first author of all things. But that good man did not at all notice that this universal spirit is the vehicle and receptacle of the divine and god-like emanation, at whose command this spirit is accustomed to be transformed into this or that species. Therefore, in the manner of the Heathens and Idolaters, by looking at the circumference and being ignorant of the center, he foolishly held the creature in place of the creator, and erroneously offered divine worship to the external body instead of the internal soul. Finally, the "final cause" proposed in our definitions is also supported by the authority of Holy Scripture. For in those writings we read:

> For irrigation, he tires the thick cloud, and scatters the light of his cloud; whatever he commands them to do on the earth, whether for a scourge or for doing kindness, he brings it to pass. <note>original: "pro irrigatione fatigat densam nubem, & dispergit lucem nubis suæ, quodcunque præcipit illis faciendum in terra sive ad flagellum sive ad faciendam beneficentiam efficit, vt præsto sit." A variation of Job 37:11-13.</note> Job 37.

And in the Prophet Baruch we read:

> When the clouds are commanded by God to go over the whole inhabited world, they accomplish what has been commanded. <note>original: "Cum nubibus mandatum est a Deo vt obeant totum orbem habitabilem, perficiunt quod imperatum est." Baruch 6:60 (often found in the Letter of Jeremiah).</note> Baruch 6:60.

But someone will no doubt object—indeed, very many will—that God and his Wisdom have not always been in the clouds, mists, and other <term>meteors<note>In early modern science, a "meteor" was any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note></term>, but only sometimes and in a prodigious or miraculous manner. They might argue that in this current time (all miracles having ceased), or even in those times from the origin of the world to the birth of the Savior of the world, God or divinity was not in the clouds except in an extraordinary way; and that at other times, clouds are procreated by the order and disposition of nature, and have produced their fruitful effects by a natural progression.

To these people we certainly respond in the first place: that miracles (however much some may blather with open mouths and claim with a profane spirit that they have ceased) will remain in their efficacy for as long as God, the author of miracles, has the power of acting in this world. For the Word of God (by means of which all miracles are performed) shall remain forever and ever. But let those infidels, who have dared to put an end to miracles, read the prophets—among them Joel especially—and let them read the Apocalypse; then let us see with what forehead or what audacity they dare to defend an error of such great weight. 

But let us now make a more particular inquiry into Holy Scripture, so that it may appear more clearly whether God acts immediately through his Wisdom in the production of clouds and other meteors or not. We find, therefore, in the place cited before:

> That God opens his best treasury, the heavens, to give rain to the land in its time, and by blessing every work of the hand of the just. <note>original: "Quod Deus aperit thesaurum suum optimum cœlos, ad dandam pluuiam terræ suo tempore, & benedicendo cuique operi manus justi." Deuteronomy 28:12.</note> Deuteronomy 28:12.

And elsewhere it is said:

> that with thick clouds, God covers the heavens, which prepare rain for the earth, which makes the mountains bring forth grass, and gives food to the cattle. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 147:8.</note>

And elsewhere:

> by his wisdom the depths broke themselves open, and the heavens drop down dew. <note>original: "sapientia eius abyssi ruperunt sese, & cœli stillant rorem." Proverbs 3:20.</note> Proverbs 3:20.

And elsewhere:

> God restrains the waters so that they dry up, and he sends them out so that they overturn the earth. <note>Job 12:15.</note> Job 12:15.

And elsewhere:

> He who gives snow like wool, and scatters the mist like ashes; who can stand before the face of his cold? <note>Psalm 147:16-17.</note> Psalm 147:5.

And elsewhere:

> He binds the waters in his thick clouds, so that the cloud is not rent under them; he holds back the face of his throne, and spreads his cloud upon it. <note>Job 26:8-9.</note> Job 26:9.

These passages are not to be understood as referring to miraculous things, but to the extent that God acts commonly through his Wisdom in the production of clouds in this world. Whence elsewhere:

> Who made the sapphire clouds by wisdom? and who can tilt the bottles of heaven? <note>original: "Quis sapphiricas nubes effecit sapientia? & vtres cœli quis prosternit?" Job 38:37.</note> Job 38:37.

To which question it is answered elsewhere:

> God by his wisdom adjusts the weight for the air, and weighs the waters by measure, he makes statutes for the rain, etc. <note>A paraphrase of Job 28:25-26.</note>

And elsewhere it asks about this:

> Do you know about the balancing of the thick cloud, the wonders of him who is perfect in knowledge? <note>Job 37:16.</note> Job 37.

From these places it is explained clearly enough that all these wonders do not arise centrally from any *created* nature, but have been from the beginning from the Wisdom of the great Creator, and are daily in the present time, and will be made and procreated in the future until the final "Let it perish" <note>Referring to the end of the world.</note>; according to that word of the Royal Psalmist:

> Your works are wonderful and ample, which you have made in wisdom. <note>Psalm 104:24 (Vulgate 103:24).</note> Psalm 103:24.

And elsewhere:

> Not one iota of the word of God shall fall to the ground.

Indeed, it is no wonder that these and all other things are effected in this divine Wisdom, seeing that by its spirit—more effective than any other thing—that mundane spirit is animated and quickened, without whose presence it would vanish into nothingness, in which state it was before the creation of the world. But truly here the presence of the word of the Lord will remain forever. Hence it is said:

> by his spirit he garnished—that is, he formed with beauty—the heavens, etc. <note>original: "spiritu suo ornauit, hoc est, decore formauit cœlos." Job 26:13.</note> Job 26:13.

We conclude, therefore, that it is impossible that any meteor, whether it be visible or invisible, could be procreated without the presence and assistance of the Creator, who acts principally and primarily from the center in this world; for the incorruptible spirit of God (as the Wise Man testifies) is in every thing (*Wisdom 12:1*) and consequently in meteors, which are the seeds of things. This spirit is defined by him elsewhere to be a spirit that has all power in itself, containing all intelligible spirits (*Wisdom 7*), as being more mobile than all movable things, and reaching everywhere because of its purity, insofar as it is a vapor of the power of GOD, or a pure emanation of the glory of the almighty GOD, and the brightness of eternal light, and a mirror without spot.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*On the diversity of clouds, according to the testimony of Philosophers, Pagans, and the followers of Christ, as well as the Holy Scriptures.*<-

Those who were well-versed in Aristotelian philosophy proposed many differences among clouds. Most notably, they distinguished one from another by a general difference in substance and quantity. Then, they divided each of these members into their own species. They categorized their substance into "dense" and "rare," insofar as thick, heavy clouds or thin, subtle clouds are procreated in and from the spiritual medium of the lower world. They claim that the former are composed and fashioned from many thick terrestrial fumes, while the latter come from a more subtle and less dense vapor. In this opinion—concerning the difference in density and thinness—they have hardly erred, as they were acquainted with the various consistencies of clouds through common experience.

However, regarding the idea that the material cause of a cloud's density is a thick and terrestrial "fume," they are entirely deceived. This is because the cloud's consistency, in both thinness and density, is actually homogeneous air <note>original: "aer homogeneus"</note>, accumulated in either a larger or smaller mass and constricted in a more compact order. For do we not see that the rainwater from a very black and dense cloud is of the same homogeneity and clarity as that from a thinner, whiter cloud? Therefore, the arrangement of terrestrial fumes is not the cause of the density or darkness of a cloud, but rather the density of the air itself, or rather the gathering of its vaporous consistency into a deep mass. In a mist, we see that the matter of the mist is the same—namely, condensed air—but its diversity lies in the depth of its composition and its compact union.

But let us proceed. They were also accustomed to distinguish clouds according to their colored quality. From this, they said that black clouds arose from terrestrial smoke, or from something reinforced and compact. We, however, confess that they arise from air that is strongly and deeply thickened. Those reddish or yellowish clouds with blackness, they said, arose partly from stellar light or fiery exhalation, and partly from thick terrestrial smoke. We, on the other hand, affirm that they are made by the various spirits of the winds compressing the luminous or fiery lights expanded everywhere through the air, without any exhalation from the earth. Furthermore, they say that those red clouds with greenish-black tints are procreated from exhalations with thick and copious vapor, along with a great quantity of water and moisture. We assert that those are born from various vapors or air gathered into one mass according to the various winds blowing from different quarters of the world during their procreation. Thus we see that opposing winds usually produce clouds and lightnings of various colors. Finally, they say that white clouds are made from a scarcity of vapor, whereby it happens that, due to the thinness of the subject, stellar light very easily penetrates the mass and makes it bright.

They also have another distinction for clouds, making some of them "empty" and as if hollow—specifically those that are dispersed through the sky like flakes of wool. The Aristotelians claim these are fashioned more from hot and dry exhalations than from moist vapors or those drenched in wetness. But we, following the Holy Scriptures, say that these "luminous clouds" are purged of their liquid substance by a passing wind. For the Holy Page speaks of them thus: *“And now men see not the light when it is bright in the clouds: but the wind passeth, and cleanseth them.”* <note>Job 37:21; the author cites Job 37:18 in the text, but the quote corresponds to verse 21 in standard numbering.</note> From this passage, that opinion of Aristotle regarding the winds (mentioned above) is also refuted—namely, his idea that the matter of winds, which he calls "exhalation," does not penetrate the middle region of the air. Yet, by this testimony, the wind seems to blow in the highest part of the middle air, specifically where the "upper clouds" have their positions. Others, however, are overflowing with water—those which dissolve into rainy matter. 

But we, following in the footsteps of the Holy Bible, divide clouds first by their different positions into "upper" and "lower." Whence it is said: *“Men do not look at the light when it is bright in the upper clouds.”* <note>Job 37:21</note> And elsewhere: *“The upper clouds gave a sound.”* <note>Psalm 77:17</note> And elsewhere: *“He commanded the upper clouds of heaven, and opened the doors of heaven.”* <note>Psalm 78:23</note> And elsewhere: *“The upper clouds were strengthened above.”* <note>Proverbs 8:28</note> This is found in many other places, thereby signifying that there are also lower clouds which are grosser and denser in their substance.

Furthermore, clouds are seen to be distinguished from one another by sacred authority with respect to their substance—namely, into dense and thin. Into "dense," I say, because we find it written in that place: *“God covers the heavens with dense clouds, that he may provide rain for the earth,”* etc. <note>Psalm 147:8</note> And elsewhere: *“Dense clouds are his pavilion.”* <note>Job 22:14; the author cites 22:15</note> And elsewhere: *“Clouds are the vehicle of God.”* <note>Psalm 104:3</note> And elsewhere: *“Jehovah binds up the waters in the dense clouds, so that the cloud is not rent under them.”* <note>Job 26:8</note> Furthermore, this passage argues for the thinness of a cloud: *“Behold, the Lord ascends up-“* <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "per" indicates the next page begins with "per-", likely completing the word "persuper," referencing Isaiah 19:1: "The Lord rideth upon a light cloud."</note>

In the preceding sections, it has been demonstrated how necessary the relationship is between the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World," or the universe at large.</note> and the human <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," or the individual human being, viewed as a reflection of the universe.</note>; because this one is surely shaped according to the pattern of that one, just as that one is formed in the image of the Creator. Whence it is written: "In man is a spirit, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding," Job 32:8. By these things we see that the divine spirit is the central actor in both the mundane and human spirits, which breathes and incites the created spirits of both wherever He wills, and makes them perpetually ready and prompt to carry out His wishes; and it is not the heat or cold of the creatures, which are only effects of the divine action or breathing, as will be explained elsewhere.

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

### Cap. VIII.

### *On the Halo, the Mist, and the Cloud.*

Since air is the medium in which aqueous <term>meteors</term> <note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and clouds, not just falling stars.</note> are produced—both in the macrocosmic sky and everywhere within its earth—it is necessary that such meteors are also produced in every part of the human air, whether solid or fluid; that is to say, every degree of cloud. Indeed, because the eyes in the highest heaven (or the head of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," meaning the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>) are strictly related to the two luminaries of the greater world <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>—inasmuch as the rays of the human spirit emit their sight through them—any species of cloud, such as the **Halo**, the mist, the little cloud, etc., can be very easily distinguished by their effects. For just as in the greater world we sometimes see a **Halo** or a very thin mist interposed between our eye and the sun or moon—sometimes denser, and sometimes very thick—and a cloud that can hardly be penetrated by solar rays, so too in the ocular medium (namely, in the humors as well as in or between the membranes of the eye) we sometimes see these kinds of meteors mixed between the visual rays and the objects seen. These are mists, <term>white spots</term> <note>original: "albugines," referring to opacities of the cornea.</note>, and <term>suffusions</term> <note>original: "suffusiones," an early term for cataracts.</note> or cataracts. 

For mist in the eye is said to be a thin and superficial whiteness or darkness of the membranes of both eyes; this kind of disease is called a **little cloud**, because a certain thin humor exists, in the manner of a thin and small cloud impressed in the air, clinging to the corneal membrane. Because of this, the sufferer thinks they see all things through a mist, vapor, or smoke. However, if this humor or vapor thickens even more, it coalesces into the second degree of cloud and is then called <term>Albugo</term> <note>A dense white opacity of the cornea.</note>, in which all clear sharpness of sight is dulled, and things are seen as if in a dark shadow—just as in the densest mist of the greater world, we see the image of an object once visible completely taken away from our sight. Furthermore, sometimes due to the excessive density of the corneal membrane, vision is rendered dark, which is why this occurrence is called "darkness." There is also another species of cloud produced in a deeper place, namely in the <term>crystalline</term> <note>The lens of the eye.</note> or vitreous humor, by reason of which that humor is changed into a bluish-gray or dark color; hence people affected in this way think they see through smoke or mist, and such an alteration of vision is called **Glaucoma**. 

Finally, we have another species of these meteors through which that effect in the eye is produced which they call a **suffusion** or **cataract**. This is produced from the thickening of misty air, occurring either in the seat of the pupil, or between the <term>uvea</term> <note>original: "Rhagoidem tunicam," the grape-like middle layer of the eye.</note> and the crystalline humor. This happens gradually and little by little, so that it can scarcely be discerned at the beginning. Thus, even in the production of a celestial cloud, we observe various stages: namely, a progress from air into a scarcely perceptible vapor, and from that into a very thin mist, and from that into a denser one, which finally thickens into a dense cloud. Furthermore, when the air is condensed into the first degree, and remains around the circumference of the pupil while the center is untouched (or obscured only by the thinnest smoke), it is observed to take on the appearance of a **Halo**. 

However the matter stands, we see here that the reasoning for turning air into thin or dense mist, and to the consistency of a cloud, is the same as we have in the worldly air. Indeed, we have even observed that the aqueous humor of the eye, when decreasing, is nourished and preserved in its full state by such air compressed into dense vapor and thickening into dew. That this substance was previously air is shown to us in two respects: first, because it proceeds step by step from invisibility to the visibility of the onlooker, and second, because it could not have penetrated through the spongy and porous substance of the optic nerve except in an aerial and spiritual condition. The reason why this kind of aerial substance sometimes thickens in the aforementioned places is due to the various conditions of the air penetrating that seat—specifically, because of its central force, convertible into various dispositions, which it received from some constricting wind. By this means, it gradually contracts itself into a mass; whereas air from a wind of the opposite nature remains dissolved in its own nature, the better to perform the roles and duties of the aqueous humor according to the laws of Nature.

In the ventricles of the brain, aerial whirlwinds, vapors, mists, and clouds are also generated, either by the natural path or according to laws beyond nature. For just as in the cells of the brain, vapors of air drawn through the nostrils are condensed into a sweet and natural mist by the stirring of the good and healthy spirit of nature, and by circulating they are lightly condensed—partly into the dewy moisture of the anterior ventricles, and partly dispersed through the passages of the <term>choroid plexus</term> <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain ventricles that produces cerebrospinal fluid.</note> into the invisible spirit called "animal spirits"—the superfluous part of them is contracted into the disposition of dense water. This is excreted through the <term>infundibulum</term> <note>The funnel-like stalk of the pituitary gland.</note> and the pituitary gland, and finally through the openings of the <term>sphenoid bone</term> <note>original: "cunei foramina."</note>, distilling into the palate. 

In this way, air filled with the seeds of preternatural meteors, drawn in and out through the <term>olfactory bulbs</term> <note>original: "processus mammillares."</note>, is sometimes observed to be reduced into a misty or cloudy substance by preternatural means. From this, **Catarrh**, **Scotomia**, **Vertigo**, and other such effects of meteors are accustomed to be produced in the ventricles of the brain. These occur with their own afflictions according to the aerial substance and the qualities of the winds predominating in it, as well as according to the site and place in which they are formed.

*   **Entire body**, as seen in the vapors expelled <term>diaphoretically</term> <note>Through sweating or perspiration.</note> to the surface of the body through the pores.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### On the Halo, Mist, and Cloud.

Since air is the medium in which watery <term>meteors</term> <note>In Renaissance science, a "meteor" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, clouds, and wind, rather than space rocks.</note> are produced—both in the <term>macrocosmic</term> <note>The "greater world" or the universe at large.</note> heaven and everywhere in its earth—it is necessary that meteors of this kind also be produced in every part of the "human air," whether solid or fluid, namely every stage of a cloud. In truth, because the eyes in the highest heaven (or head) of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "lesser world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> hold a strict relationship to the two great lights of the world <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, as it is through them that the rays of the human spirit emit their sight, every species of cloud—such as the **Halo**, the **mist**, the **little cloud**, and so on—can be very easily distinguished by their effects in the eyes. 

Just as in the greater world we see sometimes a **Halo** or a very thin mist interposed between our eye and the sun or moon, and sometimes a thicker one, and occasionally a very dense and heavy cloud that solar rays can barely penetrate, so too in the ocular medium—namely in the humors as well as in the membranes or between the membranes of the eye—we sometimes see these types of meteors mixed between the visual rays and the objects seen. Specifically, we see **mists** <note>original: "nebulas"</note>, **white spots** <note>original: "albugines"</note>, and **suffusions** or **cataracts**. 

Mists in the eye are said to be thin and superficial whitenesses or darkenings of the membranes of either eye; this disease is called a **little cloud** <note>original: "nubecula"</note>, because a certain thin humor exists like a thin and tiny cloud impressed in the air, clinging to the corneal membrane. Because of this, the sufferer thinks they see all things through a mist, vapor, or smoke. However, if this humor or vapor thickens even further, it congeals into the second stage of a cloud and is then called **Albugo** <note>A white opacity of the cornea.</note>, in which all clear sharpness of vision is dimmed, and things appear as if in a dark shadow—just as in a very thick mist of the greater world, we see the image of an object once visible completely taken away from our sight. Furthermore, sometimes due to the excessive density of the corneal membrane, it becomes faulty and dark, which is why such a darkening is called an "accidental dimness." 

There is also another species of cloud produced in a deeper place, namely in the **crystalline** <note>The lens of the eye.</note> or **vitreous humor**, by which that humor is changed into a gray or brownish color; hence people affected this way think they see through smoke or mist, and such an alteration of vision is called **Glaucoma**. Finally, we have another species of these meteors by which that effect in the eye is produced which they call a **suffusion** or **cataract**. This is produced by the concretion of "nebulous air" formed either in the seat of the pupil, or between the **Rhagoides** membrane <note>The uvea or iris, named for its resemblance to a grape skin.</note> and the crystalline humor. This happens gradually and little by little, so that at the beginning it can scarcely be discerned at all. 

Thus, we also observe various stages in the production of a heavenly cloud: a progression from air into a barely perceptible vapor, and from that into a very thin mist, and from that into a thicker one, which finally congeals into a dense cloud. Furthermore, when the air is condensed into the first degree around the circumference of the pupil while the center remains untouched (or only clouded by the thinnest smoke), it is observed to take on the appearance of a **Halo**. 

However the matter stands, we see here that the process of converting air into a thin or dense mist, or even to the consistency of a cloud, is the same as that which we have in the mundane air. Indeed, we have even observed that the watery humor of the eye is nourished and preserved in its full state by such air, compacted into a dense vapor and congealing into dew. That this vaporous substance was originally air is shown in two ways: first, because it proceeds gradually from invisibility to the visibility of the onlooker; and second, because it could not penetrate the spongy and porous substance of the optic nerve except in an aerial and spiritual condition. The reason why this aerial substance sometimes congeals in these places is due to the varying nature of the air penetrating that seat—namely, because of its "central force," which can be converted into various dispositions received from some "constrictive wind." By this means, it gradually contracts itself into a mass. Conversely, air from a wind of the opposite nature remains dissolved in its own nature, the better to perform the roles and duties of the watery humor according to the laws of Nature.

In the ventricles of the brain, aerial whirlwinds, vapors, mists, and clouds are also generated, either by a natural path or contrary to the laws of nature. Just as the vapors of the air drawn through the nostrils into the cells of the brain are—by the stimulation of the good and healthful spirit of nature—congealed into a sweet and natural mist through circulation, and by light condensation are dispersed partly into the dewy moisture of the anterior ventricles and partly into the invisible spirit through the passages of the **choroid plexus** <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain ventricles that produces cerebrospinal fluid.</note> (which are called **animal spirits** <note>The refined "breath" or energy that Renaissance science believed traveled through the nerves to cause movement and thought.</note>), their superfluous part is contracted into the disposition of dense water. This is excreted through the **basin** or **funnel** <note>The infundibulum and pituitary gland.</note> and the pituitary gland, and finally through the openings of the wedge-bone <note>The sphenoid bone.</note>, dripping into the palate. 

In this same way, air filled with the "seeds" of preternatural meteors is observed to be reduced into a misty or cloudy substance through inspiration and expiration made through the **mammillary processes** <note>The olfactory bulbs, once thought to be processes that drew air/mucus from the brain.</note>, sometimes by a preternatural cause. From this, **Catarrh**, **Scotomia** <note>Dizziness with darkened vision.</note>, **Vertigo**, and other such effects of meteors are usually produced in the ventricles of the brain. These occur with their various symptoms according to the nature of the aerial substance and the qualities of the winds predominating in it, as well as according to the site and place in which they are formed...

...these kinds of <term>meteors</term> <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric-like phenomenon occurring inside the body, such as vapors or mists.</note> are observed to vary. This is why the air, filled with the "seeds" <note>original: *seminariis*; a reference to the "seminal principles" or microscopic origins of physical phenomena, a common concept in Renaissance science.</note> of a turbulent wind, once drawn in, is so disposed that its central mover, incited by natural heat, rotates it in a circle—much like a whirlwind or the effect of clouds clashing with other clouds, or a river meeting a strong opposing current. This occurs in the anterior ventricles of the brain, whereby everything appears to the imaginative faculty as if rotating in a circle like a wheel; for this reason, this condition is called **vertigo** <note>original: *vertigo*, derived from the Latin *vertere*, "to turn."</note>. 

But if the inhaled air, due to a different arrangement of these "seeds," is reduced into a misty matter that is even darker and thicker, and it remains more stable in the front part of the brain than the air which causes vertigo, then dark objects appear to the person, like flies or gnats. This is because of the loose and disjointed constitution of the "cloud" appearing to the imaginative sense. Indeed, all physicians acknowledge and frankly confess that this type of affection or effect is generated by dark vapors existing in the brain, yet nearly all of them are plainly ignorant of where they originate, and some perceive it only vaguely. But we shall discuss the efficient cause of this type of preternatural meteor more extensively elsewhere. 

Such is also the origin of **catarrh** or **rheum** <note>original: *catarrhi seu Rheumatis*; refers to the discharge of mucus.</note> in most cases. This can be very easily discerned from the fact that we perceive thick air through the "tears of marble" <note>A poetic reference to condensation on cold stone surfaces, compared here to bodily secretions.</note> and a heaviness of the head arising from the blasts of cloudy winds. From this it follows that unless a person's nature is strong, they are easily overwhelmed by such impressions when the air is altered into a moist disposition, for the body's nature is conquered by the air's nature. 

On this point, **Hippocrates** (*Aphorisms* 5.3) and **Galen** agree: namely, that when the **Southern wind** <note>original: *flatu Australi*; the South wind was traditionally associated with heat, moisture, and pestilence.</note> dominates for a long duration, hearing is dulled, vision becomes clouded, the head grows heavy, dizziness occurs in the eyes and brain, the intellect feels sluggish, and the **falling sickness** <note>original: *morbus caducus*; a historical term for epilepsy.</note> and similar conditions are produced in men. This is because the moist spirit of that wind brings in thick and dark clouds; its function is to make the air gross and thick, and to produce corruption and decay because of the foulness of the "seeds" it releases into the universal air. However, because this wind produces warm moisture, it is suited to produce all meteors of that same moist condition, tending either toward destruction or toward benevolence according to the arrangement of the order.

Furthermore, such meteorological impressions—both natural and preternatural—are generated in the **stomach** <note>original: *ventriculo*; here referring to the stomach as the "middle region" of the body's internal atmosphere.</note>, which primarily performs the role of the "middle region of the air" within the human body. The seeds of these kinds of meteors are derived both from terrestrial winds and from those of the elementary heaven in this manner: For just as we see that the "seeds" of the world's meteors are drawn by breathing to the left chamber of the heart, and from there scattered through the arterial vessels into the members of the entire body—and even dispensed everywhere through the vessels of the brain by means of the <term>mammillary processes</term> <note>The olfactory bulbs, thought to be channels for vapors.</note>—so too vapors, mists, and clouds are generated in the stomach. Whether they are healthy or unhealthy, and in whatever size they are produced, they arise from the varied nature of fruits, foods, or nourishment (both liquid and solid), according to the various disposition of the winds that predominate in the air during the time of growth, increase, or nutrition of animals and even vegetables.

Thus it happens that when the **Southern winds** preside over the air during the time of growth or vegetation of plants—namely grain, herbs, fruits, and roots—they order the temperament of the air according to their own disposition. They make the plants prone to their own nature and fill them with putrid seeds, since vegetables receive the "hidden food of their life" from the air at every moment. For in the air, both celestial and terrestrial, there is a hidden food for the life of every thing. 

Plants have a **magnetic virtue** implanted centrally within them, by means of which they constantly attract an "aerial life" similar to themselves. As explained in our *Anatomy of Bread and Wheat* <note>original: *Anatomia Panis & Tritici*; a reference to another work by the author, likely Robert Fludd.</note>, by this faculty and succession they daily acquire more and more growth and increase, both in their spirit and their bulk. Similarly, such vegetables—grasses, fruits, grains, etc.—make the animals that eat them (whether terrestrial or winged) into the same condition as the plants themselves, since the temperament of the nourished follows the temperament of the nourishment; for that which creates a certain quality is itself even more possessed of that quality. 

Therefore, the air which contributes to their nourishment and growth, and is condensed into their substance, always retains the seeds of the wind that predominated during their growth. When that air is restored to its original freedom through dissolution and refinement (digestion), the vaporous air extracted from the food by the circulation of the "first concoction" <note>The first stage of digestion in the stomach.</note> in the stomach—and then reduced again into chyle and later into blood by compression—always holds the spirit of the presiding wind as its internal character. Consequently, it gradually brings the entire body it nourishes into its own condition, according to its preceding constitution. 

For this reason, **Epidemic diseases** <note>original: *morbi Epidemici*</note> that spread among the people are so varied and diverse in succeeding years, following the different disposition of the winds blowing in them. Thus, if the winds from those quarters of the world are more frequently healthful and suited to the life of animals—such as the **Northern and Eastern winds**—they herald a healthy year. This is because vegetables are nourished by such air and such "seeds" of the winds, and through the vegetables, animals are nourished; furthermore, the brains and hearts of the animals themselves are purified through breathing. But conversely, the Southern winds, because of their corrupt disposition and bad habit, [taint] fruits and grasses with their long-lasting breaths...

But we shall discourse more fully, by God’s favor, on the mysteries of winds and also of spirits in food, and on their roles in the efficient and final causes of meteors.

By a similar logic, meteors of this kind are produced in both ends or chambers of the heart, though in different respects and through different works of alteration. In the left chamber <note>original: *thalamo*; literally "bedroom" or "inner room."</note> of the heart, vapors, mists, and in a certain way, clouds are generated immediately from the condensation and contraction of the air inhaled through the lungs. In this kind of operation, the final consistency of the "cloud" and the effect of the whole action of nature is **arterial blood**, which is animated by the life-giving seeds of the air. These seeds of the **vital spirit** swim in the vehicle of the arterial blood like a soul in a body. Thus, this operation (the reduction of air into a misty substance for the sake of life) is a path *from the cause* <note>original: *a priori*</note>. 

However, to produce a cloudy or misty substance in the right chamber of the heart, the operation is the opposite, proceeding *from the effect* <note>original: *a posteriori*</note>. Specifically, it proceeds from the reduction and resolution of the thick blood—which was perfected in the "workshop of the liver"—into a vaporous substance (by means of preparation and circulation). This is then condensed into a liquid or blood much more subtle than it was before (so that it might be better adapted for the nutrition of the light and delicate substance of the lungs). From this, it is clear that the first circulation (or rotation of the elements) completed in the left ventricle was a progression starting from the condensation of simple celestial air; the second was an alteration by the <term>chemistry of nature</term> <note>original: *chimia naturae*</note> of terrestrial air (or the "earthy" element) into thick blood first, and afterwards into a more subtle blood. This blood is then reduced by a further degree of **Alchemy** into an invisible spirit, together with the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance.</note> of the air drawn in through the nostrils, from which the **animal spirits** are afterwards formed, serving as the most fit ministers of the intellect and reason, or the human mind. Concerning this kind of progress of human nature, we have spoken more copiously in our *Treatise on Mystic Anatomy*, regarding the mysteries of the blood, in the chapter where we discuss the Alchemy of Nature in the human body.

For the most subtle substance of the **chyle** <note>The milky fluid produced during digestion.</note> is drawn from the intestines through the mesenteric veins; in the workshop or laboratory of the liver, it is transmuted from its white or "tin-like" substance into a golden and reddish color by circulation, and is refined into a vaporous mist. For in every work of Nature, this must be considered above all: that in her paths toward perfection, she always proceeds by purifying; she purifies by thinning; she thins by dissolving; she dissolves by cooking <note>original: *concoquendo*; the physiological process of "digestion" or "maturation."</note>; she cooks by a light and natural circulation; and finally, she returns the circulated and cooked substance—by means of placement, union, and assimilation—to the perfection or preservation of those parts for which nature intended them. 

For example, the bloody nature is perfected in the **Liver**, in which completion the misty substance of the refined matter is coagulated into fibrous blood, and that, in a further progress of nature, is transmuted into flesh and solid parts by condensation. Here, therefore, we must consider that air which is primarily coagulated into a terrestrial mass is, through dissolution, made more suitable and fit for the rectification and nutrition of solid bodies (namely, the air found in nutrients). Conversely, that celestial air, free from all composition, contributes primarily to the rectification and refreshment of the animal and vital spirits. From this, it is very easy to recognize what kind of air is prone to infecting the human spirit with diseases, and what kind, in turn, tends to corrupt only the solid parts while the spiritual parts remain well.

Finally, all types of cloudy meteors concur in the completion of the **semen** contained in the seminal vessels. On the side of the arterial vessels—in which the internal seed or "sperm" (which is the quintessence of arterial blood, containing within itself, though invisibly, the hidden image of the entire species) lies hidden like a soul in a body—the quintessence of coagulated air is contracted into an invisible smoke immersed in the arterial blood. This is in the form of an invisible wind, which breathes into and animates that thick, elementary smoke into the visible consistency of sperm, in the same way that the spirits of the world's winds act as the souls within the clouds. ...is moved toward the completion of the fetus, until the species to which the seed belongs is depicted anew in its own sperm, and the sperm is converted into a rational animal. This happens by a kind of attraction from every limb; this air—suddenly and in a moment, by the inclination of nature or rather by the voluntary action of Divine Wisdom acting as the central mover—is drawn into the seminal vessels which were previously empty. There, it is first converted into vapor (in which form it is strained and separated from the blood, as if through a sieve, by the wonderful <term>anastomosis</term> <note>The connection or opening between two vessels, such as blood vessels</note> of the networks of the seminal vessels). Then, indeed, it coalesces into a cloudy and mucilaginous substance, where afterward, through the mediation of the concocting vessels, it is reduced by coagulation into the consistency of a thick cloud. Then this meteorological body—or "imperfectly mixed" substance—proceeds toward the completion of a "perfectly mixed" body (inasmuch as it is the <term>meteor</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "meteors" included all atmospheric phenomena like clouds, rain, or wind; here, the author describes the stages of fetal development as internal versions of these weather patterns</note> of generation); that is to say, it becomes a fleshy mass, part of which we later see migrate and convert into bones, cartilages, tendons, and membranes, and into the complete fabric of the external man.

And indeed, all of this is done by Divine Wisdom acting from the center to execute its will, which we also have confirmed from various passages of the Holy Scriptures. *Have you not* (says Job, addressing Jehovah) *poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese? You have granted me life and favor, and your visitation has preserved my spirit: Job 10.* By these words it seems to be exactly declared that the "visitation" and real presence of the Divine Spirit is found in the reduction of the body’s consistency—that is, the human "earth"—from the invisible elemental air through the stages and degrees of condensation. This means passing through a thin vapor into a white, cloudy substance, and from that into a spermatic cloud, and from this coagulation (in the manner of milk into cheese) into flesh and bones. Indeed, the Spirit is always present, visiting every creature, albeit invisibly, for without its presence nothing can be preserved. Hence it is also said that when God sends forth his spirit, creatures are recreated; *when he hides his face, they are troubled; when he takes away their breath, they expire: Psalm 104:29.*

Furthermore, our preceding assertion is established elsewhere by the words of the Royal Psalmist: *You are He who took me out of the womb, making me hope at my mother’s breasts; I was cast upon You from the womb; from my mother’s belly, You have been my strong God: Psalm 22:10.* And elsewhere: *You possessed my kidneys from the time You covered me in my mother’s womb. My frame was not hidden from You, when I was made in secret, as if in the lowest parts of the earth; Your eyes saw my unformed mass, and in Your book all these things were written, from the days they were being fashioned, when as yet there were none of them: Psalm 139:13.* By these words, he seems primarily to argue that the central act of man, from the point of his generation until his completion, must be referred to God and His Holy Spirit acting within. Secondly, he argues that the movement in human generation is, as it were, "out of nothing"—that is, from a thing that is least apparent, namely, the nature of air. Finally, Job says: *The Spirit of the strong God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life: Job 33:4.* And elsewhere: *The hands of God have fashioned man: Psalm 119:73.*

From these things, therefore, we can conclude that just as air is the principle from which generation occurs, so a "misty meteor" is the middle point in its motion. From the manifest part of this meteor, with the addition of its like, the external part or "Body" of the offspring is made; but from the internal spirit or "wind" of the spermatic cloud, the internal part or "Soul" of the offspring is made. This middle state, by progressing toward the goal of a "perfect mixture," creates a creature similar to the paternal species through a various rotation of the elements: namely, of air into a vaporous mist, of mist into a compact cloud, and of this into dense water, which again—like milk—is curdled into flesh and bone in the manner of cheese.

The motion will be the same when proceeding backward from a "perfect mixture" to a "misty meteor," and from that into air, which is the final goal in dissolution. For whatever was the principle in generation, such will be the end of the same in corruption. Hence the King said, not without consideration: *Man is flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return; Remembering (he says) that they were but flesh, a wind that passes away and does not come again: Psalm 78:39.* And elsewhere: *Man born of woman flees like a shadow and does not continue.* But this is also taught by common experience; for all flesh and bones are resolved by the violence of fire into smoke, and from that into "nothing," as it were, or invisible air. By this it is possible to see that "meteors" <note>intermediate vapors</note> are the middle states, as much for dissolution as for generation, and for disease as much as for health. Above all these things, we can consider that the "seeds" of sickly meteors—whether through the air into the body by means of breathing, or by the attraction of food in which they lie hidden—very easily convert the spirit or the body (already prone to corruption) into their own sickly nature by a certain hidden malice. Like a poison, they infect the entire human composition or a part of it; that is, they either disturb it with diseases or attempt to drag the vital spirits from a state of health into the borders of infirmity, and finally to the ultimate goal of corruption.

## CHAPTER X.

### *Concerning aqueous meteors descending from heaven. And first, concerning those of a more liquid consistency.*

->P.<-
->Aqueous meteors descending from heaven are either:<-
->Liquid, such as:<-
->Dew<-
->Rain<-
->Frozen: See S.<-

Those aqueous meteors which are of a thick and more compact consistency than those that are either cloudy or misty, are different from one another with respect to the place or seat from which they arise. Indeed, some of these descend from heaven, some rise up from the bosom of the earth, and others draw their origin and growth from the sanctuary of both—namely, from both heaven and earth.

Furthermore, those that descend from heaven are observed to differ evidently in their consistency; for some take on a liquid and flowing form, while others are frozen by the Northern cold and are made, as it were, fixed and not at all fluid. Those which fall from heaven in a fluid and liquid form are Dew <note>original: *Ros*</note> and Rain <note>original: *Pluvia*</note>, which are the primary subjects we intend to treat in this section. In the first place, therefore, we shall express the arrangement of these two meteors according to Aristotle and the Peripatetic sect <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note>; and then afterward, we shall declare in a few words what the opinion of the Holy Scriptures <note>original: *paginae sanctae*</note> is concerning them.

According to the opinion of the Peripatetics, therefore, **Dew** is defined as a vapor, mixed with a small amount of earthy matter, condensed in the lowest region of the air; they assertively say that as soon as it settles, it dissolves into water. Or they define it thus:

> **Dew** is a vapor which, in the spring and autumn seasons, by the power of the sun during the daytime, is attracted on high; but because it does not reach the middle region of the air, it is frozen by the night cold in the lowest region of the air, and is forced to descend in the form of drops of water. Or thus: That which is generated from a weakly warm, thick, and moist vapor, not raised very far from the earth in the lowest part of the air, condensed by the night cold and resolved into water. **Rain**, however, they define as a liquefied cloud, resolved into water, dripping drop by drop. Or otherwise thus: **Rain** (they say) is a warm, smoky, and thick vapor, raised from moist bodies by the heat of the sun and other stars, up to the middle region of the air; it is condensed there by the cold of that region and converted into a cloud, which cloud is again liquefied and resolved into water falling to the earth, for the health of living and growing things.

Rain falling more copiously with force they call a **Shower** <note>original: *Imber*</note>.

From these definitions of Dew, the Aristotelians seem to place no difference between the matter of a cloud and that of dew: for they assign to the composition of both a warm, moist, and sufficiently compact vapor, rising from the earth and water, and attracted upward by the force of solar heat; hence they have not hesitated to attribute the same agent to both. Therefore, the entire difference they make between the constitution of each is placed in the diversity of their locations—namely, in the varying disposition of the cold found in them. For if that vapor had been raised into the middle region of the air, it would follow from their doctrine that, by the intense cold of the place, it would turn into the consistency of a cloud.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of dew, shifting from the traditional Aristotelian (Peripatetic) view to a more mystical and scriptural interpretation. It challenges the idea that dew is merely terrestrial vapor, arguing instead that it is a product of the "universal sea of air" and Divine Wisdom.</meta>

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. III. Membr. II.

...might be condensed by the cold; but indeed, since it has not been raised beyond the summit of the middle region of the air <note>Early meteorology divided the atmosphere into three regions; the "middle region" was thought to be where clouds and cold resided.</note>, it is therefore raised only by the light cold of that place and of the nighttime through a gentle constriction, and falling down little by little by its own weight, it is transformed into drops clinging to the herbs. Hence, they have defined dew as nothing other than a small rain, but without clouds.

Certainly, these thinkers assign a very beautiful and, at first glance, a quite probable description of the meteor of dew. But indeed, if we look into the matter a little more deeply, we shall perceive it to be otherwise, and that as far removed as possible from what they imagined. For first, we consider those things which were said concerning the origin of clouds, and we shall discern that the whole matter brought forward by the Philosophers <note>Referring here to the followers of Aristotle, known as the "Peripatetics."</note> from the beginning is closer to external probability than to central truth. Furthermore, we add in this place that the cause of dew is not originally from the earth, but from heaven—or rather the lowest part of the air. If any air or vapor is exhaled from the earth, it is solely by way of expiration after the inspiration of the common air. It does not follow, however, that the air breathed out by a living creature must be condensed into a dewy substance by the night cold, even if this sometimes happens through a freezing or northerly blast. By the same reasoning, we affirm that although vapor exhaling from the bowels of the earth is sometimes congealed into dewy drops, it does not follow from this that all dew is produced from vapors rising out of the earth. 

For just as air is accustomed to penetrate everywhere, even to the center of the earth—since it provides life and spirit—so it is necessary that, being homogeneous with the air of the universal world, it has the capacity to be both condensed and refined by that sea of air. Indeed, let us boldly affirm that the treasury-chest of the dewy substance is the universal sea of air, whence there is no necessity for it to be breathed out from the cavities of the earth, since the greater contains the lesser within itself, as you will have confirmed below by the testimony of the sacred fountain. The reason for its condensation is the will of Wisdom, moving and contracting from the center, at whose command the winds—namely the North and the South, the latter blowing more strongly and the former more weakly—very easily condense the nighttime air by a light compression. This condensed air, drawn in by the pores of the earth through inspiration, clings to the herbs and grasses and appears in the form of little drops. 

Does it not seem that Aristotle, contrary to the description of his own dewy limit, recognizes a great thing—albeit secretly—existing in the blast of the South winds that concurs in the constitution of dew? For there he says, taught by experience, that there is no dew unless the South wind is blowing. Upon these words of the Philosopher, Bartholomew <note>Bartholomaeus Anglicus, a 13th-century Franciscan author of a famous encyclopedia on the properties of things.</note> concludes thus: *Because (he says) dew is a tiny rain, and rain is a great dew;* and in this respect, he concludes that the southern wind generates dew because of its humidity, just as, conversely, the northern wind licks up and consumes dews with its dryness, or condenses and freezes their substance by means of its cold. Furthermore, in this doubtful resolution regarding what the origin of dew might be, many have written many things, often contrary in their reasoning. For Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> attributes the generation of dew upon the moist earth to the constitution of the moon, *because (he says) the Moon is the mother of dew.* In these matters, one may see that the Philosophers are by no means consistent with themselves regarding the procreation of dew, inasmuch as various men have spoken of it in various ways.

What the Holy Scriptures feel regarding dew and its origin, we shall now show in a few words. We find the Holy Scriptures speaking of dew in general in the person of GOD to man:

> Gird up now your loins like a man <note>original: *Accinge nunc ut vir lumbos tuos*</note> (says Jehovah, speaking to Job in the whirlwind) and make known to me what I shall ask of you, etc. Is there a father for the rain? Or who has begotten the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth? Or who has begotten the frost of heaven?

From this, it is argued that it is beyond human grasp to explain such mysteries without the revelation of the divine spirit; and yet the Peripatetics nevertheless seem to answer Jehovah's objection boldly, asserting that the womb or matrix of the dew is the earth with its water, and its father is the solar rays, mediated by nighttime cold and humidity. But let us proceed to a more particular explanation of this matter.

<margin>Gen. 2.</margin> From a twofold consideration of the holy letters, we have observed that there is a twofold difference of dew in the world. Namely, we gather that one kind springs from the earth, whence it is said: *No vapor had ascended from the earth to water the whole surface of the earth;* but Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has it: *A fountain ascended from the earth which watered the whole surface of the earth.* But let the exposition of the text be made in the following manner: we say (as in the preceding pages) that meteors are generated in the spirit or air enclosed in the earth no differently than in the open air. We have also said that Wisdom is everywhere—in heaven, in earth, in the depths of the sea, etc. And we say that the earth, at the command of that terrestrial Wisdom (which is a single and simple spirit, existing everywhere through the world, enclosed nowhere), has its expirations and inspirations, which we call vapors. 

Yet, that vapors of this kind are condensed into dews is a mystic and secret work of divine wisdom, not something that requires material from the earth; for in His hands are the spirit of the universal world and all bodies which are animated by it, whence it is said: *GOD of the soul and the body, the strong GOD of spirits, the GOD of all flesh.* <margin>Num. 16. 22.</margin> But since at His command and breath the air, both celestial and terrestrial, is changed into this or that disposition: we say, indeed, that heaven is the father of the earth, as it was procreated from it from the beginning, whence it is said: *GOD created the heaven and the earth,* and not the earth and the heaven, arguing from this that the earth was created after the perfection of the Heavens. But just as GOD is said to be in heaven, so we recognize Him to be in the earth, and consequently, it is certain that heaven is found obscurely in the earth, which is also God's tabernacle. We conclude, therefore, that the matter of dew is principally from the celestial spirit, although that spirit is also inspired and expired by the earth for its vivification. Air is therefore the treasury-chest of God...
