...things were created: both as formal causes, namely the created light. Indeed, by "darkness" and "the deadly shadowy shadow," he intends the dark abyss, over the face of which there was darkness, and from which they remained without a soul. *Job 12:22.*

From these things, therefore, it is right to gather—so far as it is possible for the human mind to grasp—what the nature of this divine spirit is, generally speaking, and from where its emanation flows, and what its particular property or office was in the creation of the world. Now, in the following sections, we shall speak more particularly of its essence, power, and office in the creation of the world and its creatures from nothing, or from formless or invisible matter. These will be more extensive words, supported by the authority of Holy Scripture, God willing.

# CHAPTER IV.

## What this divine spirit is that creates all things, and how it is sometimes called the Word, and occasionally Wisdom.

In the preceding sections, we have demonstrated through the opinions of both sacred letters and philosophers that this spirit of immense power is God Himself, as it is no more to be divided from the divine essence or the fountain of light than the rays of the sun are from the solar body. In what follows, we shall explain how, by its emanation from the darkness, the darkness or the abyss was overwhelmed and illuminated, and how waters, both thin and thick, were given life and brought from a state of "nothing" into action and being. Indeed, we have already stated this quite clearly: for it is written, *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters* <note>Genesis 1:2</note>, imparting vigor to them. These waters, before this liquid spirit went out from the fountain of light or the bosom of the Father, were called the "abyss," over the face of which there was darkness, as it is held in the sacred text. Finally, we are taught by many passages of the sacred context that this spirit is the *Alpha and Omega*, the beginning and the end of all things, as it is the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. *I am the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord, Revelation 1.* And elsewhere: *I am the first, I am the last, my hand founded the earth, my right hand measured the heavens; I will call them and they shall stand together, Isaiah 48.* And it is established that *in God himself we live, move, and have our being, Acts 17.* This is also to be understood regarding every created thing, since the incorruptible spirit of God is said to be in every thing, *Wisdom 12:1.* For this cause and reason, it was said of this spirit by the Apostle, *that God works all in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* From this, the said Apostle concludes elsewhere that God is the father of all, *whom he says is over all, and through all, and in us all, Ephesians 4:6.* Elsewhere he says, *That God gives life to all things, 1 Timothy 6.* This also seems to be verified by the Evangelist, affirming that all things were made by the Word <note>original: "verbo"</note> and without it nothing was made that was made, and *that in it was life. John 1.* Elsewhere we are taught by the Apostle *that from Christ and through Christ are all things, Romans 11.* And in another place he says: *Christ fills all things, Ephesians 4:8.* And elsewhere: *from him, in him, and through him are all things, to whom be praise and honor.* In the same epistle, he acknowledges *that God created all things through Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:9.*

And this name "Jesus" is said by the Kabbalists <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism, whose ideas were often adapted by Christian scholars during the Renaissance.</note> to encompass all the names of God in its power; indeed, even that most essential name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah.</note> or Jehovah. This is because at that name—namely, Jesus—every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, *Philippians 2.* Hence it happens that everything ascribed in the Old Testament to the ineffable name "Jehovah" is transferred in the New Testament to "Jesus." Thus says Job (speaking of this creating spirit and its efficacy): *Jehovah stretches out the North over the empty space, hangs the earth upon nothing, binds up the waters in his thick clouds so that the clouds are not torn under them: he encloses the face of the pole, and spreads his cloud over it. By a decree he circled the face of the waters, until the completion of light with darkness: by his power he breaks the sea, and by his understanding he divides the deep; by his spirit he adorned the heavens, etc. Job 26:7.* From this it is clear that the work in creation which is ascribed to GOD is also assigned to Jehovah in the Old Testament and to Jesus Christ in the New.

That this name, however, is the Word of God, and that this Word is God Himself, is declared by the speech brought forth by the Evangelist: *In the beginning,* he says, *was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it, etc. He was the true light, he was in the world, and the world was made through him, etc. John 1.* By these words, he argues: first, the most exalted lineage of this divine spirit, namely that it is of Divine and God-like origin; second, that the place from which it emerged is darkness, which nevertheless did not comprehend it. Hence it is said: *Not even the darkness can be so darkened that you cannot see, but the night shines for you as the day, and darkness to GOD is as light itself, Psalm 139:11.* Furthermore, its essence and pure formality are indicated by the fact *that it is the light of the world and the light shining in the darkness*; indeed, it is the light not only of the world but of man himself. Finally, its office is explained in that all things were made by it; and the reason is that in it is the life of every single thing. Hence it is written elsewhere, *In GOD himself we live and move and are, Acts 17.* And elsewhere, *God gives life to all things, 1 Timothy 6.* And elsewhere, *I am God your redeemer, making all things, stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth and none with me, Isaiah 44:24.* Hence also the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were formed, and by the spirit from his mouth all their power.* Finally, all that has been said by us is most clearly confirmed by St. Peter: *The heavens were before, and the earth consisting of water and in water, by the word of God, 2 Peter 3:5.* By which words...

...by these words he clearly indicates to us the primary matter of the world, which he tells us is the waters; he then depicts the form as the act—namely, the uncreated divine word—creating them and preserving them so far that they persist in the same state even to this day.

But indeed, this *Jesus Christ*, this *Jehovah God*, this divine word, appears from other passages of the sacred scriptures to be the holy spirit of discipline, that is, the very spirit of divine wisdom. For to this spirit was given the same property or office in the creation of the world, both in the quickening <note>Original: "vivificatione," the act of giving life or animation to matter.</note> of creatures and in the execution of the Father's will, both in the heavens and on earth. Regarding its divine lineage and eternity, it is said in the Holy Bible: *I, wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before every creature. Ecclesiasticus 24.* <note>The author cites "Eccles.", referring to the Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, a book of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon highly valued by Renaissance philosophers.</note> And elsewhere: *From the beginning and before the ages I was created, and unto the future age I shall not cease, and in the holy dwelling place I have ministered before him.* And elsewhere: *Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting. Ecclesiasticus 24.* And elsewhere: *The word of God on high is the fountain of wisdom, and her ways are everlasting commandments. Ecclesiasticus 1.* Similarly, we learn from Solomon that the Lord possessed wisdom in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything; from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity, and from ancient times before the earth was made. *Proverbs 8.* Finally, it is said that wisdom is from the Lord and has been with him always, that is, before time; *Ecclesiasticus 1.* In its simple essence or nature, it appears to be the supreme light; and hence it is called a breath of the power of God, a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty, the brightness of eternal light, the unspotted mirror of the divine majesty, and the image of his goodness. *Wisdom 7.* Indeed, that divine light is so excellent and incomparable that it is said to be more beautiful than the sun, and being compared with the light of all the stars, it is found to be prior to them, as the wise man testifies in the same chapter. Furthermore, we find properties unique to it alone, as it is the fountain and origin of those things in the world: namely, that it is a holy spirit of understanding, manifold, unique, subtle, eloquent, mobile—indeed, more mobile than all mobile things—undefiled, certain, sweet, loving that which is good, sharp, which nothing hinders from doing good, humane, benign, stable, sure, secure, having all power, overseeing all things, and reaching everywhere because of its purity. Though it is one, it can do all things, and remaining in itself, it makes all things new, etc. *Wisdom 7.* Armed therefore with these virtues, this spirit was prepared for the office assigned to it by the Father: to create the world and all things in the world, and to bring those formless darknesses into actual being. Hence it is said: *By wisdom God prepared the earth in eternal time, and filled it with two-footed and four-footed creatures, etc. Baruch 3.* And elsewhere: *By wisdom God founded the earth, by prudence he established the heavens; by his knowledge the depths were broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew. Proverbs 3:19-20.* And elsewhere: *I, wisdom, was present when he prepared the heavens, when with a certain law and circle he enclosed the depths, when he established the upper ether. Proverbs 8.* And in another place: *Wisdom made an unfailing light to rise in the heavens, and like a mist she covered all the earth; she alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and penetrated the bottom of the deep; she walked in the waves of the sea, and stood in all the earth. Ecclesiasticus 24.* And elsewhere: *By his wisdom God made the clouds, and stayed the bottles of heaven. Job 38:37.* And elsewhere: *By his wisdom God makes the weight for the winds, and he weighs the waters by measure. Job 28:25.* He makes a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders. *Job 28:26.* He who by his wisdom or power stilled the sea, and by his understanding struck down its pride; who by his wisdom made a covering for Israel by day and the light of the stars by night. *Wisdom 10:17.* Finally, God made all his wonders in his wisdom, and in it he confirmed and adorned the heavens. *Psalm 104:24.* Indeed, whatever is done, whatever is created, and whatever is altered—whether by quickening, multiplication, or corruption—in this world, it possesses the force of its mutation from this created, central, and internally acting principle. For as the Wise Man testifies: *The incorruptible Spirit of God is in all things. Wisdom 12:1.* And in another place it is said that God pours out wisdom upon all his works, and upon all flesh according to his gift, and he has given her to them that love him. *Ecclesiasticus 1.* By these things it is primarily indicated that this divine spirit is present in every work of God, according to the aforementioned assertion of the wise man; and then afterwards, this holy spirit of discipline can be revealed to those who love and fear the Lord, and be brought forth out of the darkness of the creature into the light for the benefit and happiness of those he loves, according to that saying of the Prophet: *Let the earth open and bring forth a Savior.*

## CHAPTER V.
### How this wisdom or emanation of divine brightness is a creature, and is sometimes called by the name of an angel.

**I**f wisdom be the word, and the word be GOD, and GOD be not a creature but the eternal creator, it will seem a thing of wonder to us that in many places of the scriptures wisdom is found to be "created first of all." *Ecclesiasticus 1.* And again it is said that *wisdom was created from the beginning before the ages, and unto the future age I shall not cease, and in the holy dwelling place I have ministered before him.* But if we consider the matter a little more accurately, we shall perceive that this is not to be understood of that pure wisdom which emanated from the fountain of light (being immune to all material constitution)—for that is Wisdom, the Word, and indeed Jehovah God himself creating all things—but rather of the moist worldly spirit, inspired, animated, and reduced into act from potentiality <note>A reference to the Aristotelian transition from "potentiality" to "actuality."</note> by the presence of that bright emanation or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).</note>. For before this emanation, it is written that darkness was upon the face of the deep, but when the spirit was moved upon the waters,

...then the waters appeared entirely in their actual state, which before were empty in shapeless darkness and existed only in potential; from which (says Augustine) that spirit was divine love, imparting a fiery vigor to the waters. From these waters, thus revealed and created by that luminous spirit, the heaven and the earth were afterward created, as St. Peter testifies in 2 Peter 3, by the operation of the same Word. And to this matter, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure viewed by Renaissance thinkers as a contemporary of Moses and a fountainhead of ancient wisdom.</note> seems to agree in the most expressive words: *Thus having spoken, Pimander <note>Original: "Pimander," the "Divine Pymander" or "Shepherd of Men," the title of the first book of the Corpus Hermeticum.</note> changed his form, and instantly I conceived all things in a moment of time; then I saw an indefinite spectacle, for all things became a sweet and cheerful light, which I loved as I waited. And a little after: A shadow or darkness was carried downward in an oblique revolution, so that I imagined I saw the darkness changed into a certain moist nature, agitated beyond what can be said, and as if vomiting smoke from fire and emitting a certain unspeakable sound. Following these things, an inarticulate voice was emitted from it, such that I suspected it to be the voice of light; from the light, the holy word stood by the moist nature and cherished it.* These are his words; with which vivid colors he seems to depict the manner of the primordial light emanating from the dark abyss, and the light sent forth by God, like a forming and creating "form" mixing with matter—which he says the holy word cherishes and stands by. Then, in that passage, he narrates the order of creation and the arrangement of the elements: *Pure fire, he says, leaped out from the moist nature into the heights above, for it was light and sharp, as well as effective; but the agile air followed the spirit while it ascended toward the fire from the earth and water, so that it was believed to hang from it; the earth and water indeed remained mixed in themselves.* These things, however, were moved by the spiritual word which was carried over them, etc. We see, therefore, that this high priest <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus as a "priest" of ancient wisdom.</note> does not disagree with the aforementioned opinion of St. Peter. From this it is clear that this emanation from the mouth of the Most High—or the lucid **Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the primary point of creation or the "First Principle."</note> of the Cabalists proceeding from the dark and hidden **Aleph**—animates and informs the universal spirit of the world, or the moist nature (which is called water), as a universal soul. It exists in the manner of a soul in a body, within the whole mundane spirit and in every part of it; hence it was written by the Poet <note>Referring to Virgil in the Aeneid.</note> that *mind moves the mass.* And elsewhere, *The spirit nourishes within,* and of this spirit it is written that it fills all things and is present everywhere and in every place. And the prophet says that God is everywhere, namely in heaven, in hell, in the heights, in the furthest reaches of the sea, in the night and in the darkness (Psalm 139:7). And hence it is also said that God does whatever He wills in the heavens and on earth, through the seas and all the abysses (Psalm 135:7). *I alone (says Wisdom) have compassed the circuit of the heavens, and walked in the bottom of the deep.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:5). From which we conclude that this divine emanation (which is no more to be divided from the divine essence than solar rays from the Sun, as Hermes Trismegistus says) is the life of the spirit of the world, and that this spirit of the world is brought into action by that emanation.

Hence it is that this emanation in itself—though uncreated with respect to the spirit in which it dwells as if in a vehicle (which in itself is nothing, except regarding the presence of such uncreated light)—is sometimes called "created" and a "creature." But in respect to itself, having no relation to any created matter, it can be called *Jehovah*, the incorruptible spirit, the spirit of wisdom, and the power of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>. But we will demonstrate this more clearly from the sacred letters. First, it is said that Light was created on the first day: and yet it is certain that this light is not understood as the simple divine emanation, nor indeed as some high, absent part of said divine emanation—without which no creation can occur. Therefore, it is certain that by this light is meant the spirit of the world, created by the presence of divine light, or a ray of the spirit, which was carried over the waters, animated, and adorned with beautiful splendor. Thus, the spirit so illuminated is called a creature, or created light—that is, the external name for the whole. Yet, if we look at its internal nature, it is indeed the creator, the informer, the first act, and the first mover in the world: God, the Word, Jehovah, Jesus, the Messiah, who is the power of the Tetragrammaton.

Here, however, we think it will not be useless to explain in passing the foolish and vain opinions of Aristotle and Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an influential early Christian monk and theologian.</note>, who wish for light to be an **accident** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change or be absent without the thing ceasing to be what it is (like the color of a shirt). The author argues light is a "substance" or essential force instead.</note> and not something substantial. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> of this age adhere vehemently to these opinions. But if they wish to be consistent with themselves, it is certain beyond all doubt—and according to their own doctrine—that the nature of an "accident" is to "inhere" in something. Therefore, if light created on the first day were an accident, it would be necessary that some body or substantial subject preceded or pre-existed it, which is certainly against the sense of the sacred letters, which make light the work of the first day. But back to the point.

For it is from this that this uncreated spirit, mixed with the spirit of the world in the manner of a soul with a body, is called by the Platonists the "Soul of the World" (Anima Mundi). Hence even the world itself is called a creature, although its internal agent is the uncreated spirit itself, from which the whole world is sometimes named: whence the poet says:

->*Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever moves.*<-

Which speech indeed seems to agree with the holy letters: *Christ God fills all things,* says the Apostle in Ephesians 4:8. But He is hidden from our eyes by a lethal shadow, so that we discern Him only from afar and from behind <note>Original: "a posteriori," meaning reasoning from effects back to causes.</note> in his creatures; but once those Cimmerian clouds <note>A classical reference to a mythical people living in perpetual darkness; here used to mean spiritual or intellectual ignorance.</note> are removed, all things will be God. For those things which are not of God are in truth nothing, and will vanish into smoke, whence elsewhere the Apostle says: *Christ will be all in all, when he shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father* (1 Corinthians 15).

We say therefore, that in respect to the exterior or the creature in which wisdom dwells, she is said to be as if created and a "creature," that is, insofar as she inhabits a created thing. Thus Christ as man is called a creature—a man, certainly, although...

...in respect to the eternal spirit that inhabited him, he might be called GOD, the Word, and Wisdom. Similarly, in the composition of an Angel, we observe two things: namely, the external, which is a most subtle ethereal substance, and the form or uncreated light, which is Jehovah himself or Wisdom. For this reason, Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on the "Celestial Hierarchy" were central to medieval and Renaissance angelology.</note> calls angels *agalmata* <note>original: "agalmata"; a Greek term meaning divine images or statues, used here to imply they are clear vessels reflecting God.</note>, that is, the clearest mirrors, receiving the light of GOD and reflecting his image. These are creatures of an airy consistency, in which the divine light exists as a form or central agent; we can designate this light by the ineffable name of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah.</note>, or the Word, or eternal Wisdom. Hence, we read this written concerning that great angel who preceded the Israelites on their path through the desert: *Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on this way, and to lead you into that place which I have prepared; take heed of him and listen to his voice, do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him*, Exodus 23:20. From these words, it is right to conclude that the Word, or the uncreated light of GOD, or Jehovah himself, was within the airy constitution of that Angel, like a soul animating his airy body and directing it according to his will. From this, it is clear that in respect to his internal part, that angel was not called an angel, but sometimes Jehovah; that is, with respect to his internal light or the light of GOD, which cannot be separated from the Divinity. At other times, he is called an angel with respect to his external part, namely, to the creature. Hence it is written in the same chapter: *The Angel who preceded the camp of the Israelites in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night.* And then afterward: *Jehovah went before the Israelites by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud;* from which it is evident that this spiritual leader of the Israelites is sometimes called an Angel and sometimes Jehovah. But when he is marked by the name of Jehovah, the fiery nature of the pillar is noted, just as in the naming of the angel, the watery and vaporous nature is noted, such as the thin consistency of the angelic body.

Furthermore, it is also said elsewhere that the angel of Jehovah appeared to Moses in a flame of fire in the midst of a certain bush. Yet in the same chapter, it is said that Jehovah spoke to Moses from the midst of the fire of the bush, saying, *I am the GOD of Abraham* etc. By these things, the Prelate seems to hint that where the angel of Jehovah was, there also was Jehovah, or the divine light, or the emanation from the father, or Wisdom. Indeed, it appears evidently from the consensus of Holy Scripture that the angel who preceded the Israelites on their journey through the desert was Wisdom, considering its internal agent; for it was *Wisdom that was a covering for them by day, and a starlight by night: she brought them across the Red Sea and through many waters*, Wisdom 10:17. Finally, if anyone reads that entire chapter, they will perceive that this angel was the Wisdom created first before all things, and sometimes takes its name from its eternal nature—insofar as it is purely and simply formal light—and sometimes from the whole angelic composition: namely, for the created spirit by which that light is covered, the animating light itself, and the light together, as if one were to say the angelic soul and body together. And certainly, the nature of this Deiform angel is so immense that it fills all things in the world, and yet extends itself beyond all things. *I came out of the mouth of the most high (she said), and like a mist I covered the earth; I had a tent in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud; I alone circled the circuit of heaven, and I walked in the depth of the abyss; I rested in the waves of the sea and among every people and nation.* Ecclesiasticus 24:3 <note>Sirach 24 in many Bibles; a poetic passage where Wisdom personified speaks of her role in creation.</note>. And it is said elsewhere, Wisdom is higher than the highest heaven, indeed deeper than the abyss. We say, therefore, that the garment of this angel of immense strength, who can hardly be comprehended, is the universal <term>world-spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus mundanus"; the vital, mediating spirit that Neoplatonists believed linked the soul to the body and God to the physical world.</note>, which is the vehicle of this kind of emanation, most excellent in light and brightness. Thus, everything that the Platonists accepted as the "World Soul" is nothing other than this Wisdom, which is clothed in light as if with a garment (as David says). That is, by adorning the world-spirit and especially the heavens with its shining presence, it placed its tabernacle therein, and by the greater aspect of its beauty, it copiously enriched the Sun, adorned with its own flashing riches.

How this Wisdom—the highest minister in executing the will of its father, to whose command all other angels and demons are subjected—is called the angel **Metattron** <note>Metatron; in Jewish mystical tradition (Kabbalah), a high-ranking angel often identified as the celestial scribe or the "Lesser YHWH."</note> by the Cabalists, we shall declare more extensively in the second member of this book. Here, however, we have set forth a certain visual demonstration by which the matter may be more clearly explained to the understanding of the readers.

In the preceding demonstration, we have outlined the flow of the divine emanation from the Father—who once dwelt in darkness—which emanation or Holy Spirit of intelligence we have depicted in the form of a dove, because we read that this Spirit descended upon Christ in such a form. Furthermore, that this luminous spirit, or emanation, or the brightness and splendor of eternal light, moved peripherally <note>That is, in a circular or boundary-defining motion.</note>, is declared in that the Spirit of the Lord is said to be "carried over the waters," and that Wisdom herself has confessed *that she alone encompassed the circle of the heavens. And elsewhere, GOD who makes the earth by his power, prepares the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretches out the heavens, Jeremiah 10:12. He turns the heaven in a circle to its place in one day: 3 Esdras 4:34 <note>A book of the Apocrypha, also known as 1 Esdras in modern editions.</note>.* All of this <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works (the Hermetica) were attributed; he was highly regarded by Renaissance scholars as a contemporary of Moses.</note> seems to hint at in the *Pymander*, book 1, by saying: *That when GOD had revealed himself, all things were turned into light, pleasant to the sight: and a little after, a dreadful shadow glided down with an oblique revolution into the moist nature, etc.*

Fire created by GOD (since we distinguish it from that uncreated fire which is sometimes called a "consuming fire") [proceeds] from the act of wisdom into the <term>spirit of the world</term> <note>The "spiritus mundi" was thought to be a subtle substance connecting the soul and body of the universe.</note>, which undergoes change in various ways according to the diversity of its consistency and resisten- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "resistance" on the next page.</note>

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...against resistance, fire is produced through reflection. This fire takes various forms according to the diversity of the resistance it encounters; for the resistance that typically occurs in the thicker spirit of the world produces a grosser fire that acts more sensibly upon the senses. For example, the fire of the highest heaven is rendered more gentle, kind, and intellectual due to the cleanliness and purity of the spirit in that place. For this reason, that region is assigned to the most spiritual creatures and is called the **Empyrean** <note>From the Greek *empyros*, meaning "in or on fire." In medieval cosmology, this was the highest, most refined heaven.</note> or **Fiery Heaven**. Next, the fire in the middle region of the world, brought forth on the second day and dispersed everywhere, is created because of the twofold nature of the resisting spirit. Its nature is somewhat more violent due to greater resistance than that first degree. This fire, before the third day, was expanded everywhere into the ether through the spirit of that place, which for this reason is called **ether**, as if to say *aetha aer* <note>original: "ætha aer," a pseudo-etymological play on the Greek *aitho* (to burn) and *aer* (air), meaning "fiery air."</note>, that is, fiery air. Finally, this fire of the lowest region is more sensible and more "rebellious" than those two higher degrees; hence it consumes, as is demonstrated in lightning and terrestrial fire. Yet, the internal act of any of these fires is the very light of the world, the uncreated and incorruptible spirit, which converts fire—its own creature—into whatever act is necessary to fulfill the will of the Father. Thus it is said of the fire of the higher order: *Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire. Psalm 104.* And yet (as was said previously) the internal act of the angels is Wisdom itself. So also elsewhere: *With a light of fire he led the Israelites all the night. Psalm 78:14.* And yet Wisdom says: *My throne is in a pillar of cloud and fire. Ecclesiasticus 24.* And elsewhere: *Wisdom was a covering for them by day, and a light of stars by night. Wisdom 10:17.* Is it not also said of the celestial fire that he placed his tabernacle in the sun? But the admirable dominion of the divine spirit within created fire is proved by these words: *God sent fire in such a way that it would not burn. Wisdom 16:18.* <note>The author is likely paraphrasing Wisdom of Solomon 16:18-19, which describes how fire lost its power to burn during the plagues of Egypt to spare the righteous.</note> Indeed, God makes fire burn even amidst water; for (says the wise man) the creature serving You, who made all things, exerts its strength against the unjust for punishment, and slackens its force for the benefit of those who trust in You. From this it is clear that this Divine and uncreated spirit (which is the center and the circumference) is accustomed to move and act from the center of any creature, either by emitting its powers or by contracting them centrally to fulfill its commands. For the incorruptible spirit is in every thing, and its habitation is in the heaven of heavens, as much in the spirit of any particular creature as in the spirit of the entire world—that is, in the Holy of Holies—from which, as from an innermost center, it emits its gazes or reflects them back into itself according to its pleasure. Hence it is that Augustine and others hold that the more light something has within itself, the more of GOD it seems to claim for itself; for God (who is the fountain of light and the light of the world) is said to have *his dwelling in inaccessible fire. Leviticus 10:2.* <note>The text cites Leviticus 10:2, which describes fire coming from the Lord, though the phrase "inaccessible light" or fire is more commonly associated with 1 Timothy 6:16.</note> That is, in the center of the fire; and for this reason, mention is made in the Holy Scriptures of the "devouring fire of GOD." And elsewhere GOD is said to be a "consuming fire," by which is understood the fire from the center of which Jehovah, with an angry gaze, looked upon the impious. Thus in the same place it is said *that that fire was a burning which Jehovah kindled. verse 6.* So also elsewhere, *a fire going out from Jehovah consumed those two hundred and fifty men who offered incense. Numbers 16.* And elsewhere, *that greatest fire of Jehovah will consume us.* Finally, for this reason it is said: *God is clothed in light as with a garment. Deuteronomy 5.* <note>The text cites Deuteronomy 5, though the famous image of God clothed in light is from Psalm 104:2.</note> We conclude, therefore, that in the first creation of the world, the central form of created light was the Word or Wisdom, from which the heavens and all the heights of the world were procreated. This is the immediate act in the world, in which Wisdom or the created spirit puts on the spirit immediately created by itself as a garment; and thus light is said to be created, and that heaven to be adorned, which for this reason is called **Empyrean**. So, in this simple act, the uncreated spirit is the Mind of the world and, as it were, the center of life, and the light of every thing, whose circumference is infinite. Its created spirit or vehicle is "moist nature" <note>A term from the Hermetic tradition referring to the watery chaos or primeval matter.</note>. Then, afterward, this composition penetrating further downward is the created Soul of the World; nevertheless, its innermost actor is the Uncreated. And finally, the soul of heaven with its denser vehicle is the soul of every element and every thing composed of elements, according to that saying of the Poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 724-727.</note>:

->In the beginning, the sky and the lands and the liquid plains,<-
->The shining globe of the Moon, and the Titan stars,<-
->An internal spirit sustains; and Mind, infused through the limbs,<-
->Agitates the whole mass...<-

And this spirit, according to that saying of Saint John, is that light of the world in which is the life of every thing. We say, therefore, that the rays of the spirit of Wisdom, penetrating downward into the dark abyss, beget fire by the reflection of its rays, which leap back from the resisting gross and dark matter. For this reason, fire ascends with a contrary motion from below toward the top, according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus** in the *Pimander*, Book 1: *The holy Word stood over the moist nature*, and pure fire leapt out from the moist nature upward into the sublime, for it was light and sharp, and at the same time agile and effective.

The reason for this kind of primary reflection made in the highest heaven I have depicted in this place to the best of my ability, where the rays of Wisdom descending directly and penetrating into the chaos are explained, together with their vibrating ascent as they reflect back upward due to the repercussion. Those which tend toward the sublime are the "created fire of the first degree," consisting of the created spirit, animated by the uncreated spirit, and converted into a nature of fire or light.

## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the First Mover, the First Mobile, and the Divine Will.

We have said that the first mover of all things is Wisdom herself, inasmuch as she was created before all things, and—by her own property (as the wise man testifies in *Wisdom 7*)—is more mobile than all mobile things, reaching everywhere because of her purity. For the emanation from GOD is the most vital of all acts, and the origin and source of all acts. This Wisdom, having driven back the darkness to the region of the earth, immediately exercised her primary moving power first in that heaven which is called the **Primum Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: Literally the "first moved" sphere; in traditional cosmology, this is the outermost sphere of the universe which provides the daily rotation to all inner spheres.</term>. It is called the First Mobile because all the other spheres of the world receive their motions from East to West according to its movement. Hence we find it written, *that the most powerful GOD, who is truth, turns the heaven in a circle to its own place in one day, 3 Esdras 4.* And Wisdom herself said *that she alone encompassed the circuit of the heavens* <note>original: "se circumiuisse cœlos solam"</note>, at the movement of which—as if by the divine will—the spirit created on the first day is accustomed to move constantly, just as a body moves to the motion of its soul.

From this it is clear that divine Wisdom is, as it were, the will of GOD, emanating immediately from the Word, being continuous with it and not at all divided from it, *Ecclesiasticus 1.* Wherefore the wise man speaks in these words: *The source of wisdom is the Word of GOD on high, and her entrance is the eternal mandates.* Indeed, the Evangelist seems to suggest that the will of GOD is itself the very effect of the Word, through these words of our Savior: *I came down from heaven to do the will of the Father who sent me, John 6.* 

Therefore, as the Word is, such is the will of GOD, and such is Wisdom. The Prophet says, *The Word of our GOD remains forever, Isaiah 40.* And the wise man says, *The will of the Lord will remain forever, Proverbs 19.* The will of GOD is the word **FIAT** <note>original: "FIAT," the Latin command "Let it be done" from the creation account in Genesis.</note>. ## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the Prime Mover, the First Mobile, and the Divine Will.

We have said that the Prime Mover of all things is Wisdom itself, inasmuch as it was created before all things. According to its own nature—as the wise man testifies in <note>original: "Sap. 7," referring to the Wisdom of Solomon 7:24</note> *Wisdom 7*—it is more mobile than all mobile things, reaching everywhere because of its purity. For the emanation from God is the most living act of all, and the origin and source of all actions. This Wisdom, having indeed pushed back the darkness to the region of the earth, immediately exercised its primary moving force upon that first heaven, which is called the **First Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: In the geocentric model of the universe, this is the outermost sphere that moves all the inner celestial spheres</term>. It is called the "First Mobile" because it is the source of motion from which the other spheres of the world derive their own movements from east to west.

Hence we find it written that the most strong God, who is Truth, "turns the heaven in a circle to its place in one day," <note>original: "3. Esdr. 4," referring to the apocryphal 1 Esdras 4:34 (Vulgate 3 Esdras)</note> *3 Esdras 4*. ### CHAPTER VIII.

->*In which ways the Divine Will and the human will agree, and in what they differ*<-
->*from one another, and how the latter essentially depends upon the former.*<-

Just as two principal and primary parts of man are enumerated by Philosophers—namely, the intellect (or reason) and the will itself—so indeed we find through experience that the will is sometimes governed so much against the laws and direction of reason that it is plainly called an irrational, sensitive, and sensual appetite by the **Theologasters** <term>Theologasters: A derogatory term for petty or superficial theologians who lack true depth or spiritual insight</term>. Through this state of the will, man usually differs very little from a brute beast, and in this condition, the human will is seen to differ to the highest degree from the divine will...

...it seems, since it is always just and inclined toward the good unless it is provoked to punish the wicked; it is eternal in its being and intellectual in the highest degree. From this it follows that the true will of man (inasmuch as it derives its origin from that divine will) is of such a condition and nature that it naturally seeks things that are good and rejects those that are evil.

Just as the divine will can be defined—and quite aptly so—as the motivating power of the divine essence, by means of which God does whatever He wills both in the heavens and on earth (all of which He afterwards saw, by its effect, to be good); so also we say that the true and non-spurious will of man is the motivating power of the rational soul. By this power, a human being either desires things clearly produced by reason as good, or rejects them as wicked. From this it is evident that the human will or appetite ought to obey its own reason, and do, will, or perform nothing unless, being led by reason, it can provide a probable cause for its motion. Hence it is clear that the reason or intellect must provide the rule or the goal for the voluntary act. And although a good intention of the will sometimes produces a bad effect—which indeed happens occasionally because it occurs that the intellect, due to the uncertainty of the senses and the deception of the imagination, is sometimes deceived and goes astray—in this defect it seems to differ immensely from the divine will. 

This, however, is the true will of man: namely, the power of the intellectual soul, which holds the position of a prince over that which physicists call the "natural will." Through this natural will, we either desire things naturally and necessarily desirable to man—for example, to live, to know, to eat, to drink, etc.—or, on the contrary, we hold them in a kind of hatred, abhorrence, and aversion—namely, to die, to starve, to be afflicted by poverty, etc. The **Rational Will** <term>Rational Will: The higher faculty of choice guided by logic and morality, distinguished from basic biological urges.</term>, therefore, like a prince, is free in its movement, and in this it is made like the divine will. The natural will, however, is not free, but is swept along by the desiring corporeal nature toward its own perfection. From this it is excluded from the rational, but let us return to the matter at hand.

Just as we stated in the preceding chapter, the act of the divine will exercised its primary force in the creation of the world upon the "first mobile" of the heavens, and that this act is the motivating divine will, emanating immediately from the first and highest intelligence of all as a general source of acts, which exercises its primary force upon the most subtle **spirit of the world** <term>Spiritus Mundi: A "world soul" or subtle ether believed by alchemists and Neoplatonists to connect the physical and spiritual realms.</term>, which is more obedient to its act. In the very same way, the matter stands in man, or the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: The "little world"; the human being seen as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</term>. In man, the will, proceeding from the intellectual spirit and governed by the service of reason, first rotates the **animal spirit** <term>Animal Spirit: From the Latin 'anima' (soul); the refined essence in the body that enables movement and sensation.</term>, as if it were the substance of the Empyrean and intellectual heaven, or the "first mobile" in man. From this it is manifest that the will in man is the queen of all other faculties because, for its own pleasure and in imitation of the divine, it directs the arrows of its appetite toward the good as a desirable goal. 

For just as we see in the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: The "great world"; the universe or cosmos as a whole.</term> that the heaven of the stars is most slow in its motion—inasmuch as it moves through only one degree every hundred years (according to the teaching of Ptolemy)—and that the number one hundred is the square of the number ten, which is composed of the parts of the **quaternary elementary number** <note>This refers to the Pythagorean "Tetractys" where 1+2+3+4 = 10. The number 10 was considered the perfect number of the universe.</note>, namely 1, 2, 3, and 4, which added together constitute ten; from this it is clear that this heaven represents the elementary body. It is filled by a fourfold division of signs according to the nature of the four elements, namely: three fiery, just as many watery, and again three airy, with just as many earthy signs. This partition of signs is called a **triplicity** <term>Triplicity: In astrology, a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</term> by astrologers. For this reason, it is not inaptly called the body of the great worldly animal, whose interior organs are the seven planets. Hence also the **Zodiac** <note>original: "Zodiacus à Zoon (animal)"</note> is frequently called its "girdle," from the word *Zoon* (meaning "animal"). In the same way that this cosmic body is moved immediately by the spirit of the first mobile, as if by a soul agitated by the divine mind, so indeed the will in the Microcosm represents the image of the mind of the Macrocosmic first mobile, sweeping the entire spirit of the same along in a circuit (by whose motion the other internal or interior spheres are led). By means of this will, the whole mass of the human body is moved and swept along, just like the eighth or "starred" sphere of the macrocosm, and all its internal faculties and organs are agitated like the planetary spheres and elementary regions.

This is also what **Aristotle** himself means: namely, that the will in man is an image of the spirit of the first mundane sphere, animated by divine light, inasmuch as it passes through and turns all members and faculties no differently than the first mobile turns the other circles. And the **Platonists** hold that just as the first mobile is the leader of the heavens, moving all lower things by its vigor and virtue—yet is not led by any lower circle, but only by the holy intelligence operating within it—so indeed the human will governs and sweeps along all lower organs and faculties in the human body. It is ruled or moved by nothing, but has its primary act from that spark of divinity that moves all things, whose nature is to perpetually incline toward the good, even though reason is sometimes deceived by the delusions of the senses and the imagination. For the senses are very often deceived regarding their own objects. From this it happens that things which seem good to the senses and the flesh are sought by the will, although they are judged by their effect to be evil; and this occurs because of the phantoms of darkness and the blindness of igno- <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "rantia" suggests the next page begins with the completion of the word "ignorantia" (ignorance).</note>

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. IV. Membr. I.

...of ignorance, or the perverse madness of diabolical error, which clouds the rays of truth and overshadows the sight of truth.

We consider the divine will, therefore, to be the moving act of the divine Word or Wisdom—emanating from the essence of God—which is never to be separated from its ray. This will is eternal, just as the Word and the emanation themselves are, and is no more divisible from them than heat is from fire or light from the sun. We identify this same lineage as the God-like parent of the **divine ray** in man, which is the "first act" within the human will. For when God said, *let us make man in our image,* the word <term>Fiat</term> <note>original Latin: "Fiat," meaning "Let it be" or "Let it be made."</note>—or the moving power of the Word—was the will of God, the living signature of His will. From this root, the human will was born; for immediately following that Word, there followed an act not only of life, but of the will alongside that life.

What then follows? Shall we conclude that the will of man is the will of God? By no means. Just as we say that the life and the sublime mind of man are not separated from the essence of God—since they are the **divine breath** <note>original: "spiracula," literally vents or breathing holes through which God infuses life.</note> from God and consequently cannot be divided from His emanation, for the divine essence is indivisible—so we say that the human will proceeds from the divine. Yet, that will of God was intended to shape the human species, and to continue, govern, and direct it in this life toward good things and away from foul things that are abominable to God and human nature. This is according to the words of the wise man: *God sends wisdom to man from the holy heavens, so that she may be present and labor with him, and that he may know what is pleasing to Him (Wisdom 9).* And elsewhere: *That she may direct man in his way.* But this spark of divinity, because of the perverse error and sin of Adam, has been so obscured and clouded in darkness for those of us who followed him, that although this spark always tends toward the good in its own movement, its impressions are nonetheless poorly received due to the dark disposition of the body. The wise man seems to acknowledge this in these words:

> Who among men can know the counsel of God? Or who can know what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid and our foresight is uncertain; for the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things. We can hardly guess at the things that are upon earth, but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from the highest? Thus were the paths of those on earth corrected, and men learned the things that please you. *(Wisdom 9)*

By this polished thread of words, he seems to argue that the heaviness and obscurity of the corruptible body is the cause of the uncertainty of the human path. Furthermore, we gather that God immediately infused the ray of life and intelligence into man from these passages: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding (Job 32).* And elsewhere: *The spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.* From these, it is clear that the origin of both human reason and life is the divine spirit or breath. Similarly, we understand from the speech of the wise man that this primary ray of life and intelligence is the very spirit of wisdom: *By His wisdom, God made man to have dominion over the creatures He created (Wisdom 9:2).* And from this it is said: *God made man in His own image (Genesis 1:27).* Whence it is certain that Wisdom herself (whose act is the effect of the divine will) is the source and origin of the human will no less than the divine.

However, the darkness and corruption of the human body—brought upon it by the cunning and malice of the Devil through Adam’s sin—are the occasion for error in life and the cause of the wicked effects of the divine will within man. For in his first creation, God gave man the Holy Spirit to rule him, lead him in His paths, and defend him from corruption; hence Man was called the **temple of the Holy Spirit**. We confirm this from these sayings of the wise man:

> God created man to be immortal, and made him to be an image of His own likeness; but through the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world. *(Wisdom 2:23)*

And elsewhere:

> Seek not death in the error of your life, nor pull down destruction upon yourselves with the works of your hands; for God made not death, neither has He pleasure in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might have their being, and He made the nations of the world healthy. *(Wisdom 1:13-14)*

By these words, he indicates that the gift given by God was an act of health, prudence, and happiness, but that it is overshadowed by the vice of man, fathered by the malice of the Devil. Thus, man wanders in his life unless those shadows are illuminated by the influx of divine wisdom sent from the highest heavens—that is, unless ray is added to ray, all corporeal and diabolical darkness is removed, and so "nature shall rejoice in nature." For this reason, there is a difference between the human will and the divine will; not because they differ in essence, but because the divine never concerns itself with vain effects, while the human will—though always good in itself and possessing the most certain knowledge—is sometimes turned by the **vile and decaying flesh** from good operations into evil and vicious effects. This is just as the pleasant rays of the sun are converted into a violent, burning heat by the reflection of a **burning mirror** <note>A "speculum ustorium" or burning mirror is a curved lens or mirror used to concentrate sunlight to start a fire—a metaphor for how the body distorts divine light.</note>. It is not that the mirror or the flesh received evil impressions from that divine act, but that by receiving His good acts poorly, the flesh tends to sin, turning the direct motion of the rays into an oblique path away from truth itself through rebellious reflection. Thus, this perverse and oblique will makes man wander due to the reception of his perverse flesh.

# Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

Hence it is said that even the most just of men errs seven times a day—not, I say, because the good spirit is the cause of evil, but because the "evil object," by perversely receiving the good acts of his rays, very often produces perverse effects. This is much like a man wandering in a dark place who intends to walk the path of his own freedom and toward the vision of light, but being led astray by the darkness, unexpectedly falls into a pit. For the rays of divinity (by means of which all things subsist, and through the abundance of which man is said to rule over all other creatures) do not in themselves suffer the insults of darkness; hence it is said: *darkness is not darkness to you, but the night is as clear to you as the day.* <note>original: "tenebre non sunt tenebre tibi, sed tam clara tibi est nox, quam est dies" — a reference to Psalm 139:12.</note> Rather, the darkness deludes the animal creature, who is overwhelmed by the false vision of the senses, and seizes them toward evil in place of good. At such times, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure often cited in alchemical and philosophical texts as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> says that the divine mind in man is at rest; it does not govern him by way of the intellect, but instead provides him only with the basic functions of life. Thus it is said that *your heavenly Father makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, Matthew 5.* From this, he argues that the Father of all has granted the force and virtue of life to both the good and the bad, but intellect and prudence are granted only to those who are pure in spirit and strangers to dark actions.

Therefore, to bring the power of such a divine spark back into its intellectual action within the human body, it is required that the ray of wisdom sent from God be illuminated. By this, it may have dominion over the diabolical darkness of the body, so that in this way the sensual and brutal will of man may be brought back into such a disposition—truly intellectual (of which that central spark is the essence)—*that he may walk in the right path and observe the statutes of GOD, discerning what is just in his eyes. Wisdom 9.* <note>original: "Sap. 9" refers to the Book of Wisdom, or the Wisdom of Solomon.</note> Hence Job says: *Your visitation has preserved my spirit, Job 10:12.* And elsewhere: *Lift up the light of your face upon us,* and *it shall make us see good, Psalm 4:7.* <note>The text cites Psalm 7:4, but the quote corresponds to Psalm 4 in standard numbering.</note> And also in another place, the royal prophet <note>King David.</note> seems to confirm this same thing, saying: *If you illuminate my lamp, Jehovah my God, you will make my darkness shine.* And elsewhere: *In your light we shall see light, Psalm 36:10.* And elsewhere: *By the light of Jehovah's face we shall be saved: Psalm 80:4.* By these, he seems clearly to argue that the internal light of man—or the spark of truth granted by God for man’s existence but now obscured by his sins—is illuminated by the application of the universal ray of uncreated wisdom. It is exalted by its own likeness above the power of darkness, so that even the body, once dark and covered on all sides by gloom, now shines so brightly that it is sometimes illustrated by a stellar flash, as is read concerning Socrates—namely, that he was so transfigured that he:

->Would have surpassed the light-bringing sun with its sharp brightness.<-

It is also handed down that Zoroaster <note>The ancient Iranian prophet, often viewed by Renaissance philosophers as a great magus.</note> himself was so transfigured that he was lifted upward in his body. But if you give little credit to these accounts, we read in the Holy Bible that the face of Moses shone so brightly (once illuminated by the speech of Jehovah) that the children of Israel could not look upon him; so also Elijah ascended to the heavens in a certain fiery chariot; and we read that Paul was caught up into the third heaven, etc. Speaking of this kind of illumination, Zoroaster utters these words: *You must ascend to the light itself and to the rays of the father, from whence your soul was sent to you, clothed in much mind.* And Hermes Trismegistus says: *It will behoove you to ascend above the heavens, and to be far away from the choirs of demons.* And Pythagoras says: *if you, having left the body, pass into the free ether, you will be an immortal God,* thereby declaring that if, by means of that spark of divinity which is in us, we rightly seek the way to the place of the father, we shall be partakers of his rays. By these rays, we shall be partakers of the divine power <note>original: "numinis diuini"</note>, and we will be transfigured from this dark form into a divine appearance. This also the sacred letters seem to confirm in this manner: *He who adheres to GOD shall become one spirit with him:* And elsewhere it is said: *At last we shall be transformed into the same image:* And indeed, all those sparks in the world shall be joined into one essence of divinity and truth, leaving behind the filth of Diabolical vanity and falsehood, when Christ comes to judgment. *GOD* (says the Apostle) *will be all in all, when Christ shall have delivered the kingdom to the father. 1 Cor. 15.*

And although in truth the divine spark in man is no more divided and separated from its lucid source than the rays of the sun are from its essence, as Hermes Trismegistus testifies (for the divine essence is indivisible); nevertheless, insofar as it is within the creature he created and preserves through generations, it seems to be distinguished from the divine light, insofar as it is the "royal part" of the creature. Just as the name of God was said to have been in the Angel, and yet the whole composition of the angel was a creature, so also man's motive power—by which he is said to desire good and refuse evil—is said to be varied and different from that of divine wisdom. For in the Divine will, there is perfection in execution; for we read *that no circumspection of men can resist the divine will, Gen. 27.* And elsewhere: *Can we resist the will of God? Gen. 50.* Hence we are taught by Christ: *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven:* That this will is eternal is indicated elsewhere by the wise man: *The will of the Lord (he says) shall remain forever.* Finally, that it is produced into action by the Word both in the macrocosm <note>The great world or universe.</note> and the microcosm <note>The "little world," i.e., man.</note>, it is said in one place: *Whatever he wills, he does in the heavens and on the earth,* and the Word clothed in flesh said: *I descended from heaven to do his will who sent me, not to do my own will, John 6.* In this speech, he distinguishes the human will from the divine one, and consequently acknowledges that both the will of God and that of man are within him. Furthermore, that the will of man is varied, and divided from that of God unless it be united with God's, is declared in this: that it is inconstant, uncertain in its effects, inclining toward evil because of a bad conception, since the senses are mostly deceived regarding their own objects, and the flesh—prone to pleasures through dark and deceptive appearances—distracts it. Whence it is written: *We have done our will in the desires*

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

of our flesh. *Ephesians 2.* And Christ himself, having overcome the distress of his own flesh by first praying that God would take away that cup, said, *Nevertheless, let not my will but yours be done, Luke 22.* This is in accordance with that passage in *John 5: I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me.* But if the human will is united with that divine one, then it is accustomed to perfect that same will, and of this kind of union John speaks: *He who does the will of God remains forever, 1 John 2.* This means he has become one with God. Indeed, so that this might happen in the Royal Prophet <note>A common title for King David, author of the Psalms.</note>, he himself speaks by praying to God: *Teach me to do your will, for you are my God, Psalm 143:10.* It is as if he had said: *let your face shine upon your servant, and in your light I shall see light,* or as he has it elsewhere, *You are the Sun giving life and glory, and you illuminate my lamp; you will make my darkness shine, so that I may enter upon the right path to carry out your will, Psalm 18:29 and 84:12.*

From these things, therefore, one may see that the lamp of man <note>Referring to the human soul or intellect.</note> does not differ in essence from the spiritual sun—which gives grace, glory, and salvation—except in this: that the former resides in a created body as a particular ray of that sun, providing it with being and existence, and holds the place of a creature. This spiritual sun, however, exists in and through itself, attributing life and being to the worldly spirit, and existing so far outside all things that it is said *to fill all things, the Father of all, who is over all and through all, God giving life to all, the worker of all in all, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6.* He is the center of every thing whose circumference is nowhere <note>original: "centrum cuiusque rei cuius circumferentia est nullibi" — a famous Hermetic definition of God.</note>, the unity of unities, the father of fathers, the principle of principles, the fountain of fountains, the root of roots, the star of stars <note>original: "syderum sydus"</note> as Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century Neo-Platonic philosopher and bishop.</note> says in his Hymns. He is the good of goods, the idea of ideas, immense beauty, the hidden seed of things, the father of ages, the father of the intelligible worlds. He is the spirit instilled by Ambrose <note>Likely referring to St. Ambrose’s views on the Holy Spirit animating the world.</note>, floating upon the mass of the body, who now awakens the world; he is Jupiter or Jehovah, from whom all lower gods depend, as Orpheus and the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for their mystical view of numbers and the cosmos.</note> maintain. In short, he is everything that truly *is*; in which statement we exclude from him all things empty, deceptive, and phantasmic, like the sons of darkness, which seem to be and yet are not—as will appear in the final examination when all things are to be reduced to One.

We conclude, therefore, that God acts voluntarily and not moved by necessity (as the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whom the author is criticizing for suggesting God acts by a logical necessity rather than free choice.</note> would have it), and that nothing has been made either in the heavens or on the earth which has not received the motion of its origin from the divine will. But if the spark in a creature does not produce the desired effects—those which smile upon both God and a good man—this does not happen because of the incorruptible spirit acting from the center, but because of the deceptive mass of darkness subject to all alteration. This darkness receives the acts of the divine mind poorly, and thus obscures the rays of such great light; and the darkness in the creature does not comprehend that light dwelling in the darkness, according to that saying of Saint John: *in the Word was life, and that was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.*

We can most aptly compare this light, or spirit of wisdom, to the nature of the Sun. In itself, it is simple and always uniform in its act, and yet it is manifold in respect to the variety of operations which its rays are accustomed to produce in the world. This does not happen because of any varied action of the sun, but because its impressions are received differently according to the variety of bodies—differing according to their existence, or by the greater or lesser resistance of those receiving the solar acts. For, according to the Wise Man <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight."</note>, God, composing all things by number, weight, and measure, made one thing different from another in proportion, so that by his single and simple act he might produce various creatures, both corporeal and spiritual, in this world.

Thus we see that various effects are produced in the world by those solar rays, according to the character of the recipients. For the sun in one place causes grass and herbs to sprout and bloom, while at another time it burns and dries them up; sometimes it cherishes and refreshes animals with its beneficial heat, and sometimes it makes the weak and sick languid by its presence. Indeed, it forces healthy men to hasten to shaded places to escape the persecution of its scorching rays. Again, the rays contracted into the center of a burning-mirror set fire to and consume cities and royal palaces, reducing them to nothing; yet in water, it is observed not to act in the same way. It inflames rocks and cliffs with heat, and at other times warms them only slightly. Sometimes, therefore, the effects of generation prosper, and sometimes they tend toward corruption—and yet the sun itself, together with its rays, is the same: permanent and simple in its act. The entire difference lies in the diversity of the object, which receives the solar acts either well or poorly. The matter is no different regarding the rays of the invisible and intellectual Sun, which gives life and being to this worldly sun. And so you have my conceptions concerning the divine will with its branches, according to which all things are done in this world, in which it produces various effects according to the variety of those receiving the divine rays—varying by number, weight, and measure in this world. As for the act of the human will, both obscured and illuminated, we have depicted it in this place to the best of my ability for the better understanding of the readers.

We call that "necessary" <term>necessarium: in formal logic, something that cannot be otherwise</term> which indeed cannot be otherwise; but that which we call "contingent"—whether voluntary or accidental—is that which can be otherwise. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding the "Efficient Cause" of the world. It completes the word "sufficient" (sufficiens) from the previous page and moves into a point-by-point refutation of the idea that God acts out of natural necessity rather than free will.</meta>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...ficient. But indeed, the primary arguments of the aforementioned philosophers were these two: First, because God acts through His own essence, and not through an acquired power. Second, because the effects in the world appear to be necessary, from which they conclude that they cannot proceed from a contingent cause—that is, either by chance or by will. 

To the first of these we respond that they seem to argue against themselves; for insofar as He acts in His own substance, it is clear that He is moved to act by His own free nature, and not compelled by any necessity, whether external or internal. Furthermore, in unity there is no involuntary compulsion or incitement, because the One does not "suffer" <note>original: "patitur." In classical philosophy, to "suffer" means to be the passive recipient of an action or to be changed by an external force.</note>. Moreover, it is impossible that He be compelled or urged to such a work by any foreign cause, since He—remaining primarily and immovably in Himself and from Himself—acts as the primary source. 

To the second argument, we say that necessary effects do not imply necessity in the First Cause as the ruler, because secondary causes (which Plato and other wise men call handmaids and, as it were, servants) act either by His command and mandate, or by a necessary order, so that the necessity depends on His mandate and the order which He executes according to His pleasure. Hence, we read in the Book of Wisdom <note>Wisdom of Solomon 16:17-19</note> that God sent fire so that it would not burn; at one moment He makes fire burn amidst water—indeed, even in snow and ice without them melting—yet that same fire, on the contrary, forgot its own natural power so that the righteous might be nourished. 

From this it follows that the fire did not consume the servants of God in the burning furnace of the Chaldeans, and that the Sun in the time of Joshua stopped its course for the space of one day and rested in a firm position; and that the same Sun also moved backward ten degrees or lines on the sundial in the time of Hezekiah. Furthermore, without any evident reason in nature—the moon certainly not being at the "head or tail of the dragon" <term>head or tail of the dragon: astronomical terms for the lunar nodes, the points where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic, where eclipses naturally occur</term>—an eclipse nonetheless occurred (indeed, one that happened beyond the common laws of nature) during the full moon, while the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ was taking place. All of these things could by no means have happened if God acted in the world out of necessity; for from these examples it is clearer than light that He operates in created things according to His own good pleasure and free will, not according to the laws of nature—things which He created, made, and continually preserves voluntarily and in His pure mercy.

But come now, I pray you, O Philosophers, who wish to bind God, the ordainer and actor of all things, by the laws of necessity: what honor or glory, I ask, do we attribute to God for His command, wisdom, justice, and mercy, if He were forced by necessity not only to create all things, but also to cherish and sustain them? What thanks, what service and adoration do we owe Him if these things are so? Why, O Aristotle, according to your assertion, is it granted to the roots of nature to offer sacrifices? Or what benefit will prayers and orations bring to us humans? Even Plato, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus <note>These were famous Neoplatonist philosophers who, despite being Pagans, argued for the power and necessity of prayer.</note> teach us that these are most necessary—but why, if God were not moved to favor by prayers? Or why were Pythagoras and Socrates (who, by the testimony of the oracle, were the wisest of all at that time) accustomed to pour out their prayers, if God were compelled to perform the works He does? Why does the Prophet say:

> *Let God alone be called upon and prayed to. Psalm 30:8.*

If there were some necessity in God for the doing and preserving of things? Indeed, it has been clearly demonstrated from these points that God is accustomed to be inclined toward mercy through those means, and that in His good pleasure He acts either severely or mercifully with the world and its creatures, and especially with men; and consequently, that He is not urged by necessity in His actions.

But there are certain other philosophers who behave more modestly in the resolution of this doubt. For Avicenna <note>An influential Persian philosopher (Ibn Sina) who sought to reconcile Aristotelian logic with monotheism.</note> maintains that such actions are neither necessary nor violent, but in a middle ground between the two, which he places in the will of the agent. In this resolution, he does not seem to differ much from the Sacred Fountain, in which we read:

> *God has punished us for our iniquities, and He will save us for His mercy. Tobit 13.*

Where that chosen man intimates that will is present in God, either for doing good or for doing ill. But this is indicated elsewhere even more clearly and in more expressive words:

> *God (says the Prophet) acts according to His will both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and there is no one who can resist His hand or say, "Why have you done this?" Daniel 4.*

And God Himself says:

> *My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done, calling a bird from the east, and from a far country the man of my will.*

From which it is sufficiently clear that every operation in the world is by divine will and for His good pleasure, and not by necessity as the Pagan philosophers wished, thereby diminishing the divine prerogative and binding Him to necessity. But necessity is undoubtedly in the causes and effects, or in their operations; for example, we have it in the Prophet Baruch that the Sun, Moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds, and fire obey God in all things. That is, they are compelled to carry out the will of the commander or creator; they are, I say, compelled by necessity. But it does not follow from this that the Commander is urged by necessity to command, but rather that He does so by a voluntary motion. Hence it is said:

> *Who shall resist the will of God? Romans 9.*

We conclude, therefore, that it is not only absurd but even impious to trumpet loudly <note>original: "ebuccinare" — literally "to blast on a trumpet."</note> alongside those Pagans that He, who was all things, and in all things, and finally everything that is, cannot act voluntarily and freely when, how, or where it pleases Him—especially when we see this same privilege granted to the human soul (which is a flow proceeding from that same divinity), as is most clearly shown in the choice of good or evil, both by ourselves and by our forefather Adam.
