->CHAPTER X.<-

### *On the property of Divine numbers and names among the Cabalists, and how the various effects of the divine will follow their natures, tending toward both benevolence and malediction.*

In our "Mirror of Causes," attached to the end of this section, you have seen it demonstrated how a different name of GOD presides over each Cabalistic <note>original: "Cabalisticæ." Cabalists were practitioners of a mystical tradition (Kabbalah) that sought to understand the universe through divine emanations and the Hebrew alphabet.</note> numbering. This is not because there is any diversity in the essence of GOD itself, but because His properties in the world are varied according to His good pleasure and will, wherever it seems good to Him. Some of these properties tend toward mercy and benevolence, while others tend toward severity and harmfulness. For a fuller understanding of this matter, it should be known that although many names are attributed to God (according to the opinion of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), a famous Jewish philosopher and physician.</note>), all of them—except for one alone, namely the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, which is called the "separated name"—are assigned to Him in relation to created things. 

The Tetragrammaton is uniquely His because it signifies the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, without any shared participation with creatures. The other names assigned to Him denote Him through participation—that is, with respect to created things—and are consequently derived from His works. It was for this reason that His essential name was never spoken, except in the sanctuary by the holy priests of the Lord, specifically during the priestly blessing by the High Priest on the day of the fast <note>The Day of Atonement, or Yom Kippur.</note>. The rank of this name (says Rabbi Moses) is supreme, and it was not to be uttered rashly by the mouth, since it signified the substance of the Creator. Through this, God is noted to be "above all being," and to have existed before any thing was. But the other names denote God as He is "in all being."

For example, when Moses asked, GOD answered him: *I.H.V.H.* <note>original: "I.H.V.H." representing the Tetragrammaton.</note>—this is my name forever. Therefore, this name alone belongs to eternity, representing the Divine essence in its purity. No such name can be composed by a human voice that can equal the nature of divinity, for although various titles for GOD come from His works, this is the only name appropriated to Him before any created thing existed. Yet, insofar as the divine essence exists within created things as much as it exists outside of everything, the Tetragrammaton is also common and general, acting in every branch of the Sephirotic tree <note>The "Tree of Life," a diagram of ten spheres (Sephiroth) representing the steps of divine emanation.</note>, so that the various other titles of GOD are merely properties, or offices, or different acts of power from that one and indivisible essence.

Thus, among the various titles of God inscribed on the Sephirotic tree, *Ehieh* <note>Hebrew for "I Am."</note> signifies the source of all creatures, the primary fountain of all clemency and all graces, sparing all, the father of mercies, and the God of all consolation. Christ teaches us to pray to Him thus: *Our Father who art in heaven, etc.* And it is said of Him that the Father judges no one; furthermore, He is assigned as the Father because He is always merciful and benevolent toward His children, as *Psalm 103* teaches how God has mercy on His children. This name, therefore, is assigned as the ruler of the Sephirah <note>A specific emanation or "sphere" on the Cabalistic tree.</note>, or numbering, or "bright gate," or the first branch of the Cabalistic tree, which is called *Cheter* <note>Kether</note> or the *Crown*. For just as the *Crown* is like the root of the tree, so *Ehieh* is the father of all creation. From this, it is clear that the reason for this title of God is taken from His property in clemency and mercy, which is occupied with creatures—namely, in giving and granting life, and giving the gift of being or existence to the world and the creatures contained within it.

The second title of GOD in the Sephirotic order is *Iah*: which also tends toward the benign property of GOD—specifically, the shaping of the world and the extraction of waters from the womb of Chaos. The numbering over which it presides is *Hochma* <note>Chokhmah</note>, that is, *Wisdom*; hence it is written of her: *He who made a weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when He set a law for the rains, and a path for the sounding storms, then He saw wisdom, etc.* (*Job 28*). And elsewhere: *When He formed the heavens above, when He strengthened the fountains of the deep, when He set a decree for the sea, when He established the foundations of the earth, I, Wisdom, was with him like a foster child, arranging all things* (*Proverbs 8*). Because of its benign disposition, it is said to be mild, kind, and loving of good; and elsewhere, it is said to be given to men by God so that He might show them what His will is. Nevertheless, as it is certain that *Wisdom* stands in the middle between *Kether* and *Binah*—of which the latter denotes severity and the former clemency—the title of God *Iah*, or Wisdom, sometimes punishes, though very rarely. Hence Jehovah said when speaking of the Angel or Wisdom: *do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him* (*Exodus 23*).

The third Sephirah or Cabalistic numbering is *Binah*, that is *Prudence* <note>Often translated as "Understanding."</note>, and the title of the Tetragrammaton attributed to this is *Elohim*, which is *terror and dread*. It is through this name that severe punishments and slaughters come, for in this property GOD exercises His power by punishing the wicked. In this type of office, He employs those angels who, for this reason, are called *Bene Elohim* <note>Sons of Elohim/Sons of God.</note>, that is, the sons of Elohim. The Doctors of the Cabala maintain that the region of the world from which such demons <note>In this context, "demons" refers to spirits or agents of divine action, often those delivering judgment or natural disasters.</note> are sent...

<meta>This page continues the technical exploration of the Sephirot—the ten attributes or "emanations" in Kabbalistic thought—detailing how specific Names of God act as channels for divine power, influencing everything from the weather and minerals to human morality.</meta>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...is the North <note>original: "Aquilo." In many mystical traditions, the North was associated with darkness and the source of judgment or "evil" in the sense of physical punishment.</note>, for from it comes all evil or punishment resulting from sin. However, its property during creation is to illuminate and give form to matter; in this action, it is necessary for a "privation" <note>A philosophical term for the absence of a quality or form that ought to be present.</note> to intervene, should any preceding form have existed.

You see that the effects of these three divine titles, drawn from their properties toward created things, are varied. Specifically, the first tends toward clemency and mercy, the last toward an entire inclination for severity, while the middle title partakes of both natures yet is mostly inclined toward clemency. To this middle state is assigned the essential name *Jehovah* <note>original: "Iehoua." The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note>, because it is exercised in this world both in punishment and in beneficence, yet it is much more prone to mercy than to punishment. Thus it is written: *The LORD God is long-suffering, abounding in kindness, forgiving iniquity and transgression, who does not leave the source entirely unpunished, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, etc. Numbers 14.*

But let us proceed to the fourth numbering, which is *Chesed* <note>term: "Chesed" (Hebrew: חסד), meaning Loving-kindness or Mercy.</note> or clemency, to which grace, goodness, and mercy are attributed. Its presiding title of God is *El*, whose role is to cherish all things and succor everyone with the highest piety and clemency. Under this property, it is said that bodies received their shapes. From this numbering, grace and mercy rain down into the lower worlds through its "channel" or "bright gate."

However, we think it necessary to address an objection raised by some: of what use is this Kabbalistic <note>original: "Cabalistica."</note> science to us, or how can it be proven that this or that name of the Tetragrammaton possesses this or that property, or an inclination toward clemency or severity? To this we respond that it is proven by the effects recorded in the Hebrew text. Hence, the property of the name *El* is openly explained by Moses in the passage where it is recorded that he implored God for the gift of health for his sister Miriam, who was suffering from leprosy, in this manner: *El na rapha na la*. That is: *GOD of grace, heal [rapha], now [na], her [la], I pray.*

The fifth numbering (which is *Geburah* <note>term: "Geburah" (Hebrew: גבורה), meaning Strength, Might, or Severity.</note>) is presided over by the divine title *Elohim Gibbor* <note>original: "Elohim Gibbor," meaning "God the Mighty."</note>. Under this property, God is said to have drawn the elements out of the turbulent Chaos; it denotes power, violence, severity, judgment, and the punishment of sins. This property of God flows into the lower regions—namely, into the world—bringing the effects of plague, famine, war, plunder, and desolation. From this it is clear that just as the nature of the name *El* promised every good thing to the creatures of the world, so *Elohim Gibbor* seems to announce every evil and turbulent outcome, such as occurred during the extraction of the elements from chaos.

The sixth numbering is *Tiphereth* <note>term: "Tiphereth" (Hebrew: תפארת), meaning Beauty or Ornament.</note>, which denotes grace, ornament, beauty, and delights. The name of GOD assisting this is *Eloah*. It follows that all those influences poured out from this Channel, or this path, or divine property, give form to the sun, returning to it clarity, life, and light, and they adorn the heavens according to that passage in Job: *By His spirit He adorned the heavens, Job 26:13.* And also: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of His mouth, Psalm 33.* From these influences afterwards proceed minerals (of which the chief is gold), vegetables (among which Bread and Wine are the chiefs), and animals (whose head in dignity is man), following the positioning of the sun in the sky.

The seventh Sephirah <note>original: "Sephirota." One of the ten emanations of God.</note> is called *Nezeth* <note>Likely a variation of "Netzach" (Hebrew: נצח), meaning Victory or Endurance.</note>, namely Triumph or Victory. Furthermore, it indicates charity and the love of justice. From here also follow the influences of multiplication and generation. The name presiding over this is *Jehovah Sabaoth*, the *Lord of Hosts*.

The eighth is called *Hod* <note>term: "Hod" (Hebrew: הוד), meaning Splendor, Glory, or Praise.</note>, namely praise, honor, and beauty. The name associated with this property is *Elohim Sabaoth*, that is, *GOD of hosts*—not, however, for rigor and war, but for piety, justice, and concord.

The ninth numbering is presided over by the name of GOD *Elchai*, that is, the *living GOD*, or *Shaddai* <note>original: "Sadai."</note>, *GOD Almighty*, or He who is sufficient unto Himself. This numbering is called *Yesod* <note>term: "Iesod" (Hebrew: יסוד), meaning Foundation.</note>, that is, Basis, foundation, redemption, and rest.

The tenth and final Sephirah is called *Malkuth* <note>term: "Malchut" (Hebrew: מלכות), meaning Kingdom.</note>; that is the kingdom, the church, the empire, and the temple of GOD. Hence the Psalmist says: *for the kingdom is the Lord’s, Psalm 22.* The name of GOD presiding over this is *Adonai*, the Lord. This numbering brings severity and servitude to those upon whom it flows.

From these descriptions, it can be seen that in all the properties or operations of the divine essence in the world—whether for punishment and the lash, or for beneficence—GOD is more prone to clemency and mercy than to severity. For in the property of His first title, He extends His charity out of the darkness into the world, just as a father does for a son; hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of mystical and alchemical writings (the Hermetica).</note> calls the world the "son of GOD."

In the property of the second title, God is more inclined toward the creation of things through His wisdom than toward striking the human race with a plague for their sins, as is explained by the words of GOD to the Israelites: *Behold, I send my angel before you to keep you in the place I have prepared; take heed of his face, etc. Exodus 23.* Elsewhere, I have shown that this angel was Wisdom, which was sent to the Israelites for their preservation, yet with the precaution that they should not commit evil, for He says: *he will not bear your transgression.* Thus it is evident that God is more inclined toward benefaction than toward the lash in this property. In the property of the third title, severity and punishment are included, for the title *Elohim* is terrible in its nature. Consequently, while the title of the first Sephirah, namely *Ehyeh* <note>original: "Ehieh" (Hebrew: אהיה), meaning "I Am."</note>, is referred to the Father and attributed to the Empyrean heaven (the place of the blessed and of rest), the title of the second—namely *Yah* <note>original: "Iah."</note> or *Jehovah*...

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.
<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, thunder, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>

...is ascribed to the Son in the ethereal or starry heaven, from which Fate claims its origin, raining down both good and evil upon the lower worlds. In the same way, the name *Elohim* <note>original: "Elohim Sephirotæ"</note> presides over the third numbering <note>The third Sephira, Binah or "Understanding."</note> and is related to the Holy Spirit. This name looks toward the lowest or elementary heaven, in which all change, birth, and decay occur among earthly things—including the violence of winds, thunder, and other atmospheric phenomena in the midst of the air. This is clearly demonstrated by those who compare the most holy persons of the Godhead as creators with the properties of created things. They compare the Father to the solar body, as if to essence and "whatness"; the Son, or the Word, to the rays emitted from that essence; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, to the heat or the effect. Thus, the life or fountain of the ethereal heaven (in the center of which He placed His tabernacle) was the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven of pure light and fire.</note>, like the Son receiving His being from the Father. Again, the soul and life of the Elementary heaven is the power of the ethereal heaven. Thus, you may see more clearly than light itself that the Elementary heaven received its life and being mediately from the Empyrean heaven—as if from the first Father among created things, for the first creature was light—and immediately from the starry heaven as if from the Son, just as we see in the ideal and Archetypal world that the Holy Spirit, in personal numbering, had His progression from the Father and the Son.

From this it is certain that the effects of these most holy persons in the symbolic world are such as we have reported. Consequently, it is proven through their effects that, first, the intellectual, angelic, and Empyrean heaven is a sweet, mild, and benevolent dwelling assigned to the blessed; according to the property of the Father, it is a sacred Monastery or "Holy of Holies," appropriated for the Angels of God and holy souls, in which they live in this world under the shadow of Jehovah’s wings, secure from every severe property of God. But *Keter* <note>original: "Cheter." Usually translated as "Crown," the first Sephira.</note>, the second property <note>The author uses a specific numbering system here that differs from some traditional Kabbalistic layouts.</note>, acting as the effect of the second numbering, imposes Fate upon the world, bringing both good and evil to sublunary creatures. This denotes here and there that the nature of the divine essence is inclined toward both punishment and clemency. Just as in the Sephirot, *Chokmah* <note>term: "Hokma" (Hebrew: חכמה), meaning Wisdom.</note> is placed between *Keter* and *Binah* (or *Ehieh* and *Elohim*), so its effects are seen between the Empyrean heaven—the place of rest, grace, and happiness—and that of the lower abyss, namely the elementary heaven. In the latter, there is almost no rest and much distress, both in the heavens (that is, the air) and on the earth, for in it reigns that rebellious spirit who is called in the Holy Scriptures the "prince of this world," to whom the empire of the air is assigned. From this it is clear that although it is said that all the power of the world and the heavens is created by the breath from the mouth of Jehovah, we must nevertheless understand that through this, both good and evil are breathed upon the creature by that same Spirit according to their merits. "The Lord has power over life and death," says the wise man, "who leads down to the gates of death and brings back again" (*Wisdom 16:13*). And elsewhere: "Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God" (*Ecclesiasticus 11*). And elsewhere: "Consider the works of God, that no one can correct whom He has despised; in the good day enjoy good things, and beware the evil day; for God made this one as well as that, so that man may not find just complaints against Him" (*Ecclesiasticus 7:14*). By these words, he seems to hint that the actions of God in this world are various, indeed even opposite in nature. The Father *Ehieh* <note>term: "Ehieh" (Hebrew: אהיה), meaning "I Am," the name associated with Keter.</note> is the author of goodness, which the Son *Jah* <note>term: "Iah" (Hebrew: יה), a shortened form of the Tetragrammaton, associated with Chokmah.</note> executes in wisdom, raining it down from His luminous gate of *Chokmah*. The Spirit *Elohim*, proceeding from both, is terrible to the ungodly, yet is also assisted in His office by *Jah* as a participant in both extremes. And hence He is called the Spirit claiming the power of God and pursuing the unjust with justice (*Wisdom 11:12*).

But let us proceed. *El* is the title of the bright gate or numbering of *Chesed* <note>term: "Cheſed" (Hebrew: חסד), meaning Mercy or Loving-kindness.</note>, pouring clemency and mercy into the lower regions. But *Elohim Gibbor* <note>term: "Elohim Gibbor" (Hebrew: אלהים גבור), meaning "God the Mighty" or "God of Strength."</note> in the gate of *Geburah* denotes severity and punishment. In the sixth order, *Eloah* or *Jehovah* rains down beauty and grace through the gate of *Tiphereth* <note>term: "Tiphereth" (Hebrew: תפארת), meaning Beauty.</note>. Yet, because it is in the middle between *Ehieh* and *Adonai*, it is said to participate in both extremes, as this property sometimes punishes. So also *Jehovah Sabaoth* <note>term: "Iehouah Sabaoth" (Hebrew: יהוה צבאות), "The Lord of Hosts."</note>, presiding over the gate of *Netzach* <note>original: "Netzeth." Hebrew: נצח, meaning Victory or Eternity.</note>, signifies victory and triumph—not in severity, but in its excellence and in the love of justice—and yet it is opposed to the unjust. *Hod* <note>term: "Hod" (Hebrew: הוד), meaning Splendor or Praise.</note> also gives beauty and praise, over which *Elohim Sabaoth* predominates. Furthermore, *Shaddai* <note>original: "Sadai." Hebrew: שדי, meaning "Almighty."</note> pours out redemption and rest through *Yesod* <note>original: "Ieſed." Hebrew: יסוד, meaning Foundation.</note>, from which its influences are good and beneficial. Finally, just as *Ehieh* sends out fatherly grace and clemency through His royal gate *Keter* (the Crown) at the root of the Sephirotic tree, so *Adonai* <note>term: "Adonai" (Hebrew: אדני), meaning "My Lord."</note> from the summit of the same tree sends out servitude, miseries, and punishment into the lower worlds through His gate *Malkuth* <note>original: "Malchut." Hebrew: מלכות, meaning Kingdom.</note>.

From this it is evident that in these branches of the Sephirotic numbering, we have four testimonies of divine compassion and clemency: namely the properties of *Ehieh* (the 1st), *El* (the 4th), *Jehovah Sabaoth* (the 7th), and *Shaddai* (the 9th). We have, however, only three of extreme severity: namely *Elohim* (the 3rd), *Elohim Gibbor* (the 5th), and *Adonai* (the last). Finally, we have three that participate in both extremes: namely *Jah* (the 2nd), which nevertheless tends toward clemency; *Eloah* (the 6th); and *Elohim Sabaoth* (the 8th). For the planet to which *Elohim Sabaoth* pours its qualities is Mercury, which experience has noted to be good with the good and evil with the evil. Thus with *Elohim*—that is, with fear, dread, and finally disturbance—*Sabaoth* (or rest) is joined. But it is certain that these properties participating in both extremes are more inclined toward clemency and mercy. Hence the Prophet says: "God is gracious and merciful, patient, and of much compassion, and forgiving of wickedness" (*Jonah 4*). And again: "You, Lord, are a stabilizer and merciful, patient and of much mercy and truth" (*Psalm 86:15*). And elsewhere: "God is pious and...

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

He is merciful, and remits sins in the day of tribulation, *Ecclesiasticus 2*. Furthermore, the Apostle speaks thus: *Let the kindness, patience, and long-suffering lead you to repentance, Romans 12* <note>While the text cites Romans 12, this verse is actually found in Romans 2:4.</note>. Finally, the wise man most clearly expresses this disposition of God—which is by no means inclined toward vengeance for its own sake—in this golden discourse: *Indeed, they could have fallen with a single breath, pursued by justice and scattered by the spirit of your power; but you have ordered all things in number, measure, and weight. For great power is always present with you; you have mercy on all because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men so that they may repent. For you love all things that exist, and you hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have fashioned anything if you had hated it. How could anything have remained unless you willed it, or been preserved if you had not called it forth? But you spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of souls. Wisdom 11.* By these words, the wise man seems to imply that God is in Himself long-suffering and merciful, and slow to vengeance, even though both good and evil, life and death, etc., are in His hand, as was declared previously.

Concerning the various orders of angels who receive these types of influences <term>influxus; the flow of divine energy from the higher spiritual realms to the physical world</term> immediately, and concerning the great angels to whom these influences are committed and through whom they are poured into the planetary sphere subject to each one’s dominion; as well as concerning that influence descending from the said Planets to the lower elements of the world and the things composed of them <term>elementata; physical beings or substances formed from the four elements</term>, we will discuss more extensively in the second and third members below.

## CHAPTER XI.

->*How the Wisdom of the Spirit, spread everywhere throughout the world, and informing and nourishing its moist nature, also forms, creates, and preserves all creatures composed of the elements until their final end.*<-

The Spirit of divine wisdom, animating, forming, and creating the world, binds and arranges all discordant elements into a harmonious peace by its breath. By its harmonic spirit, it strengthens and sustains heaven and earth by its will alone, according to that saying of the Prophet: *He who made the earth by his power, prepares the world in his wisdom, and by his prudence stretches out the heavens, Jeremiah 10.* <note>original: "Qui facit terram in fortitudine sua, præparat orbem in sapientia, prudentia sua extendit cælos."</note> This Spirit (I say), having completed universal things, looked toward the particular: namely, the stars, animals, plants, and even minerals. The Prophet indicated this succinctly to us in these words: *The LORD creating the heavens, stretching them out, establishing the earth and those things which sprout from it, giving breath to the people, and spirit to those walking upon it, Isaiah 42:5.* But this is explained even more clearly and specifically in the first chapter of Genesis: namely, that by the word "LET IT BE" <note>original: "FIAT"</note> the general things were created first, and then the particular. Hence the Evangelist says: *All things were made by the word, and without it nothing was made that has been made; in it was life, and that life was the light of men, John 1.* From these words, it is evident that in every creature there is a trace of the Word; indeed, a portion of that actual divine light is situated in every creature. By means of this light, and not without it, a thing exists as it is. And this is what the wise man seems to imply with these express words: *the incorruptible spirit (he says) is in every thing, Wisdom 12.* And the Apostle has it: *from him, in him, and through him are all things, to whom be praise and honor.* And elsewhere: *God created all things through Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:9.* And elsewhere: *God the father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all, Ephesians 4:6.* And elsewhere: *God gives life to all things, 1 Timothy 6.* And elsewhere: *God works all things in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* And elsewhere: *IN GOD himself we live and move and have our being, Acts 17:28* <note>The text cites Acts 17:9, but the quote is from 17:28.</note>, as one of the poets said. From these things, therefore, it is very clear that a ray of divinity is in every thing, as it is impossible to exist without it, or to be brought from potentiality into act. In truth, a thing is nothing, but only appears to be what it is not, without that divine virtue which is the only truth inhabiting the center of every thing. That which commonly appears in the external habit is not the true reality, but is present to creatures in the place of a false image <note>original: "simulachri falsi"</note>; and in the absence of truth, it will vanish into smoke and be absorbed by darkness—that deceptive parent—and turned into nothing, which is to say, deformity. This, then, is the difference between the acts of GOD and the Devil: the latter's act is illusory <note>original: "præstigiosus"; in this context meaning deceptive or like a stage-trick, rather than modern "prestigious."</note>; it is seen but is not, the work indeed of the prince of darkness. The former’s act is true, infallible, and is rarely seen except by the elect, yet it truly exists: truly the work of the Prince and the luminous fountain.

It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that without the presence of truth (which is God alone) there is no creation, but all is void and empty. However, His infinite rays, like angels, have procreated infinite things varying in species and nature according to the will of the one ordering and emitting them. Specifically, these are the stars, differing among themselves in appearance and beauty as much as in quality and property in the starry sky or ether; and the animals, vegetables, and minerals among earthly things; and the meteors <term>meteora; in the 17th century, this referred to all atmospheric phenomena including rain, wind, and lightning</term> differing among themselves, both in the kingdom of light and that of darkness. Finally, as we have said with the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who believed in a "World Soul" (Anima Mundi) that gives life to the physical universe.</note> that the universal wisdom or emanation of divine clarity is the form and, as it were, the soul of the universal world-spirit in general, so indeed every ray or breath of it is the life-giving form of any particular thing in its species. And although this resplendent wisdom in general, and every ray of it in particular, is invisible in its nature and hidden, nevertheless we gather this uncreated nature through its effects: for (as Holy Scripture testifies) we contemplate GOD in His works. Hence Plato calls her the invisible but uncreated daughter of GOD, but calls the sun visible and created. Hence the Psalmist says: *Jehovah GOD is a Sun, giving life and glory, Psalm 84:11* <note>The text cites 84:12.</note>. And elsewhere: *If you light my lamp, Jehovah my GOD, you will make my darkness shining, Psalm 18:28* <note>The text cites 18:29.</note>; that is, if you inspire my soul with your luminous spirit, etc. Concerning this invisibility of the spirit, the wise man speaks thus: *Wisdom is drawn from hidden places, it is hidden from the eyes of all living things, and it escapes even the birds of the heaven, Job 28.*

From this it is clear that it is hidden in this world with respect to its essence, but it is manifested to us through its effects.

To these testimonies of the sacred text, several Philosophers (very deep observers of the mysteries of nature) seem to agree. For Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet often associated in this period with natural magic and deep philosophy.</note> and Heraclitus of Ephesus <note>A Greek philosopher famous for the idea that "all things flow" and that fire is the fundamental element.</note> held that nature was fire...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Divine Spirit as the animating force of the world. It bridges the gap between ancient philosophy (Pythagoras, Democritus) and mystical theology (Kabbalah), arguing that the "sparks" of divinity found in all things are rays of the one true God.</meta>

<header>Section I. Portal IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.</header>

...a certain invisible fire, from which he recognizes all things were born. It is as if they had understood that Spirit of the Lord (which is fiery love) when it was carried over the waters, imparting a certain fiery vigor and, as it were, "Being" to them. Hence, by some, the world was called a living creature <note>original: "animal"</note>, the heart of which they made the sun; likewise, they also called the stars living creatures, and understanding the souls of all particular things in the world, they thought them to be participants in the divine mind. They proclaimed, not unwisely, that these souls were rays or sparks emanating from that entire luminous nature. For this reason, they recognized that a soul presides over every single thing, and consequently Democritus and Orpheus, along with many of the Pythagoreans, were of the opinion that "all things are full of Gods." To these they assigned divine honors, dedicated sacrifices and prayers, and venerated them with various forms of worship.

Furthermore, they reduced all such souls to a single **soul of the world** <note>original: "animam mundi"</note>, and consequently referred all the Gods to a single Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. From this, therefore, proceeded all the errors of the gentiles in adoration; from here, I do not doubt, emanated the fictions of the Poets, diabolical sacrifices, and sacrilegious immolations. Whence the land of Egypt worshiped and adored certain animals and other monsters and portents. But concerning these various types of Idolatry, where namely the creatures are adored instead of the creator, the scriptures speak everywhere—specifically regarding the profane worship of stars, devils, men, and others of that kind.

In this, therefore, those Philosophers were deceived: that they did not at all distinguish the simple uncreated light—that is, the creating nature—from the moist created nature. Instead, they considered the created light—that is, the whole illuminated moist nature, namely the angel or "alterity" (as the Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalistæ"</note> have it) and not that unity which preceded it. Hence some of them said fire was God, others air; some made the earth divinity, others water, etc.

But truly, in that they said all things are full of Gods—or rather, animated and filled with sparks of divinity, all of which they referred to a single Jove—or that all things are endowed with luminous souls, which they taught have a relation to the single soul of the world: in this indeed they seem to differ neither from the sense of the Hebrew Doctors, nor even from that of Holy Scripture. For **Rabbi Breseth** <note>Likely referring to the Midrash *Bereshit Rabbah*, a commentary on the beginning of Genesis.</note> says that the creator daily creates a host of angels, whom others call "forms," inasmuch as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be born or perish is filled beyond number. Concerning these Angelic forms, the **Gate of Light** <note>original: "Porta lucis," referring to Joseph Gikatilla's *Sha'are Orah*, a famous 13th-century Kabbalistic text.</note> speaks thus: *From the earth all the way to the firmament there is no empty place, but everything is full of forms; some of them are pure, some are capable of grace and mercy, and there are below many foul, harmful, and tempting shapes, etc.* From which he seems to suggest that all forms, both good and evil, are as if they were angels—but of these, more elsewhere.

However we look at it, we see that although all these forms in the world are like sparks of divinity and rays of a single spirit (assigned with various properties and shapes either for the preservation of life or for its destruction, as is sufficiently explained in the divine properties inscribed upon the **Sephirotic tree** <note>The *Tree of Life* in Kabbalah, a diagram of ten spheres (Sephirot) representing the emanations of God.</note>), nevertheless, all these pure forms or rays of divinity are no less to be divided from their fullness of essence than solar rays are from the Sun. And although by the divine will they are enclosed in various dark tabernacles, both foul and pure, to execute His various commands, they themselves—as sparks of truth—will in the end return to the fountain of unity from which they went forth. Concerning this matter, the Apostle speaks thus: ***God will be all in all***, when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father (1 Corinthians 15). Nor do the holy scriptures seem far removed from the aforementioned opinion, in which we find that ***Christ fills all things***. And elsewhere: ***God, not needing anything, gives to all life and breath and all things*** (Acts 17). And elsewhere: ***In God himself we live and move and have our being*** (Acts 17:28). And the wise man gives the reason for this thing, for, he says, ***the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing*** (Wisdom 12:1), which in another place he calls a sincere emanation or flow of the clarity of almighty God, and the brightness of eternal light, which gives life to all things (Wisdom 7).

We conclude, therefore, that it is certain that the life and being of every thing is from God, and is like a fiery impression from the divine word's character or seal (which the Kabbalists call ***Emeth*** <note>Hebrew for "Truth."</note>), or a ray from the shining Word, which is more abundant and flowing in one creature than in another—for example, in the sun of heaven and in the Man of the earth. Whence the Evangelist says, ***in the word is life, and this life is the light of men***. And of the other it is said: ***by his spirit he adorned the heavens***. And for this reason also it is said ***that God saw all things created by him were good*** (Genesis 1): that is, insofar as they participated in the divine essence, which is alone goodness and truth, as the holy scriptures testify.

## CHAPTER XII.

### On the Void and the Full.

At this point, we believe it to be of no small value to explain to you what that "void" is, which is so avoided by nature, and what the "full" is <note>original: "vacuum... plenum"</note>. The solution to this uncertainty seems to belong primarily to our purpose and is indeed necessary. For the fathers of the Philosophers, as well as those most skilled in Divine Wisdom <term>Theosophy: in this context, the study of God through mystical insight rather than the modern movement</term> who adhere to the sacred scriptures, have said that this Void is **Nothing**. 

Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure linked to the origins of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy</note> calls this a "horrible Shadow, destitute of all form"; the Cabalists call it the "Potential Principle looking toward nothing." Plato, in his *Timaeus*, says it is a thing perceptible without the senses, and hardly credible through false reasoning, making it out to be a mere dream. And Augustine says: *When I conceive of something unformed, I understand it as "nothing" before I understood it at all, just as darkness is seen by seeing nothing, and silence is heard by hearing nothing;* hence he seems to compare it to Darkness and silence. Job says: *God stretches out the North over the empty and the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing. Job 26:7.* And elsewhere: *He reveals foundations out of the darkness, and brings the lethal shadow out into the light. Job 12:22.* 

By these words, he seems to argue that the Empty, the Void, Nothingness, Darkness, and the Shadow are the same thing. They are "Empty" and "Void" because all fullness comes from GOD; but truly, GOD—the parent of light—had not yet shone upon the world. Therefore, insofar as the first matter of the world <term>materia mundi prima: the raw, chaotic substance of the universe before creation</term> was destitute of all grace and deprived of goodness, it was called the Empty and the Void—indeed, even darkness and a lethal shadow—insofar as it entirely lacked the rays of life. 

Thus the earth was said to be empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss, before the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters. But after the appearance of the said Spirit, it is said: *And GOD called the dry land Earth, and GOD saw that it was good, and it produced tender plants and seeds of every kind, and trees bringing forth fruit, etc. Genesis 1.* Therefore, the earth—formerly empty and void—has now been made full of divine grace. From this, it is rendered not empty but fertile; not void, but completed on all sides by the divine fire of incorruptible rays. 

*The hand of the Almighty created the world from unformed matter. Wisdom 11:17* <note>The text cites Wisdom 11:12, but refers to the famous passage in 11:17</note>. Here, "the hand" indicates the Word or the Spirit emanating from His mouth. Hence the Apostle Peter says: *The heavens existed of old and the earth out of water and through water, by means of the word. 2 Peter 3.* That is, by holy emanation. Through this light (says John) the world was made. Indeed, where the rays of this informing divinity are absent, there is the "greatest vacuum"—that is, the absence of completed form. 

And this is why a vacuum appears so "horrible" in the kingdom of nature; for every thing, by a natural appetite, desires above all else to be "informed" <note>To be "informed" here means to be given a specific shape, essence, and purpose by God's light</note>. Therefore, it is the habit not only of particular nature, but also of that Universal Nature (the parent of all particulars), to utterly abhor and avoid deformity. 

From this it is clear that all fullness in nature comes from the divine abundance. By its own power, this abundance fills everything in the world so that, out of nothingness and the void, something actually formal and relatively existing may be made. They received this gift of existence from Christ, or Wisdom; whence it is written that *Christ fills all things. Ephesians 4.* And elsewhere: *The holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world. Wisdom 1.* From this it follows that unless GOD had filled everything in the world, there would be a vacuum and nothingness in the world; but because He created all things by His very presence, it is necessary that nothing empty exists in the world.

### CHAPTER XIII.

#### That it was the will of GOD that the fixed stars should be created in their sphere, and that they were made in a moment.

We have stated in the preceding sections that God was moved to mercy—not by any external necessity, but by His own voluntary and innate impulse—to create the heavens, the earth, and even the stars within the heavens, along with the rest of the things in <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "terra" (earth) indicates the sentence continues on the following page: "...in the earth."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 174 regarding the creation of the world. The previous page ended mid-sentence with "things in [the earth]." # Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

the earth, which He created with things numbered, and this is also by the testimony of the Royal Prophet <note>The "Royal Prophet" refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, from whom we have:

> *Give thanks to the Lord of lords, who made the heavens in wisdom, for His mercy endures forever; who established the earth above the waters, for His mercy endures forever. Who made the great lights, for His mercy endures forever; the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night, for His mercy endures forever. Psalm 136.* <note>The text cites Psalm 135, following the Vulgate numbering.</note>

This is assigned in its own property to the first numbering or <term>sephirotic</term> <note>Referring to the Sephirot, the ten emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> emanation, namely *Ehieh* <note>original: "Ehieh," the Hebrew name of God meaning "I AM."</note>, which name presides over *Keter* <note>original: "Cheter"</note> or the Crown, and is ascribed to the Father and to Mercy. From this, we have the reason why God, being free in Himself, willed to create the world with its creatures: namely, because of His sheer clemency and mercy toward "deformed" things. That is to say, out of empty things and those veiled by darkness or lethal shadows, He would procreate good things adorned with divine beauty. He infused into every creature a living soul or spark from His own luminous source, by which it might live and exist in its own being. From this, the creatures first desire to return immense thanks to Him, and then they proceed to perform faithfully the duty assigned to each by God and the commands of the Creator. Regarding this giving of thanks, we read in the Royal Psalmist:

> *Praise God from the heavens, praise Him all His angels, and all His powers. Praise Him, Sun and Moon, praise Him all stars and light, praise Him heaven of heavens, and all waters that are above the heaven; let them praise the name of the Lord, for He spoke and they were made, He commanded and they were created. Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit or wind of storms, which fulfill His word, etc. Psalm 148.*

Here he runs through all creatures, both terrestrial and aquatic. But to declare the office of the stars as well, we say with the Prophet in the place cited before, that He made the Sun to have dominion over the day, and the moon and other stars—both fixed and wandering—to have power in the night, and this on account of His kindness. As for the substance or consistency of the stars, both fixed and wandering, it seems to be very clean and pure, the better to receive their luminous forms from the Creator. This also seems to be confirmed by these words: *The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God, much less men, Job 25:5.* From this speech, it seems they are very pure, though not absolutely pure when seen in the presence of the Deity. Yet if they were not very pure and polished in their substances, they would be least capable of receiving such splendid forms; for as <term>Plato</term> rightly says, form is given by the Creator according to the merit of the matter. Truly, since their substance varies in purity, it is said by the Apostle: *That star differs from star in clarity [glory], 1 Corinthians 15.*

It remains now to discuss in a few words the property and influence of the fixed stars. Among these we read that, as God extended the heavens, He alone made <term>Orion</term>, the Pleiades or <term>Hyades</term>, and the stars of the southern chambers, *Job 9:9.* <note>The text cites Job 32:4, but the quote is from Job 9:9.</note> And elsewhere, mention is made of the circuit of *Arcturus* or the belt of *Orion* in *Job 38.* The Prophet also speaks thus: *It is God who makes Arcturus and Orion: He turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night; Jehovah is His name, Amos 5.* All these stars of the firmament our great God—great in Power, whose wisdom is beyond numbering—counts; He counts however many stars there are, and called them by their own names, as David testifies, *Psalm 147.* To these He undoubtedly assigned names based on their various properties, thereby declaring that many hidden properties exist within them beyond that common and vulgar one—namely, that they have dominion over the night. For it is not likely that He would have assigned them various brightnesses and figures if they had no other faculties over creatures. This is especially true since the Prophet adds, *However many they are, our great Lord calls them by name, being great in strength or power, whose wisdom is without number.* From this it is argued that He who is great in power and of innumerable wisdom also assigned various powers to the innumerable stars of the firmament. This can also be understood through these words: *Do you know the laws of Heaven? Do you set its dominion upon the earth? Job 38:31.* By these, the Creator seems to indicate that the heaven, through its army [of stars], is accustomed to operate strongly and in various ways upon the earth. For this reason, the heaven is most aptly compared by some to a husband, and the earth to a wife; and consequently, every particular star of the firmament of heaven has a particular power of influencing particular things—animal and vegetable as well as mineral.

For example, it has been handed down and proven by experience itself, that the <term>stella polaris</term> (Pole Star), called <term>Alracuba</term> <note>An old name derived from the Arabic *al-rukbah*, referring to the Pole Star (Polaris).</note> by the Egyptians, having the nature of Saturn and Venus, attracts to itself the <term>magnete</term> (loadstone), as appears in a mariner’s needle; and the same magnet attracts iron to itself, provided that the <term>adamas</term> (diamond) is not present, for the diamond by its presence hinders the influences of the said star. And <term>Cichus Esculanus</term> <note>Cecco d'Ascoli (1257–1327), an Italian encyclopedist and astronomer.</note>, writing on the sphere in the place where he speaks of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, affirms that each of the twelve signs receives its particular and special name from the nature and property of some animal of the earth, because the nature of one seems to symbolize the nature of the other. And <term>Moses Arabicus</term> <note>Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), the Jewish philosopher who wrote in Arabic.</note> says that every animated thing claims for itself a peculiar star in heaven, from which it draws and receives influence every moment to protect and sustain its essence, and he says this was done by divine command and will. Thus the stars in the body of the Ram [Aries] in heaven have a relation to such animals on earth, and the Scorpion of the former to the scorpion of the latter, and so with the rest. For this reason, therefore, <term>Diodorus Siculus</term>, speaking generally, quite sensibly confesses that the lower is ruled by the higher, and that the lower world is continuous with the higher. In our discourse *On the physical subject of the macrocosm*, where I spoke at sufficient length regarding the origin of the fixed stars, I proposed a certain doubt: namely, whether the fixed stars were created on the fourth day of creation along with the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>, or at least on the second day. There we expressed our reasons by which we proved it likely they were established on the second day of creation. Indeed, if we consider the orders of the <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself.</note> or the "numberings" of the Kabbalists and the reason for their influxes, we will perceive that just as the influx of *Keter* <note>original: "Cheter," meaning "Crown," the highest Sephirah.</note>—which is the Crown or first numbering—occurs through the Seraphic order of angels into the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" sphere that drives the rotation of all other celestial spheres.</note>, so *Chokhmah* <note>original: "Hochma," meaning "Wisdom."</note> flows through the order of Cherubim into the starry heaven. If that heaven were empty and without stars, it would receive those influences from *Chokhmah* in vain. But let us proceed briefly to the production of the planets or wandering stars and their creation in their orbs.

It is most certain, and to be conceded without controversy, that all stars are created by God himself, as we have confirmed by many testimonies of holy scripture. *The Sun (says Moses), the Moon, the stars, and other things God created for the service of all nations under heaven. Deut. 4:19.* How each of these stars has an intelligence presiding over it—which receive influxes from the "luminous gates" called Sephirotic—and what the duties of said angels are, both in the ethereal heaven and the elementary region, and who is their Prince, we shall discuss copiously in the second member of this part.

In this place, however, we shall chiefly hold discourse concerning the noblest creature of the celestial bodies: the king of stars, the corporeal Emperor of the heavens, the heart of the firmament, and the clearest eye of the world—namely, the visible Sun. To arrive at a better understanding of it, we shall first speak a few words concerning the invisible and uncreated Sun, as it is the life and light of this created sun.

**Creating**

    - **Primary**, which: Sweeps the spirit of the world along with its motion; animates and illuminates that spirit with its Light, and provides life to composite creatures; fosters and preserves all things with its Heat.
    - **Secondary and by effect**, which: Generates and corrupts; multiplies by its own seed; illuminates the bodies of the stars, and infuses them with the seed of life.

**Created:** in which these things are especially to be considered:
- **Dignity**, which arises: From its origin and lineage; From light and grace; From the command it holds over the material world; From its primary and principal or royal office: for it is the house or palace of the archetypal king <note>original: "regis archetypici." - **Passion and Suffering** in the deprivation of its light and, as it were, its life <note>This likely refers to eclipses or the setting of the sun.</note>.

# CHAPTER XIV.

## Second Part.

### Concerning the Uncreated Sun.

Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, to whom various philosophical and "Hermetic" writings were attributed.</note> seems to recognize that the whole and entire world constituted from the elements proceeds and is led by Him who is abundantly full of the fertility of all things, of both one and the other sex, containing in Himself every power of generating without any other assistance. For this reason He is called PAN <note>original: "PAN poetis dicitur," meaning "The All" or "The Universe."</note> by the poets, as if to say the "Total" and the "Universe." The Arcadians, thinking Him to be the sun, worshipped Him as the true GOD. Their error, indeed, seemed to lie in this: they falsely accepted and worshipped the creature in place of the creator, and the visible and created sun in place of that invisible and uncreated one—that is, the royal palace in place of the King of Kings, who built it and inhabited its center. Concerning this uncreated and invisible sun, not only the wiser of the Philosophers but even the Holy Scriptures have made rich and copious mention. For among those most skilled in Philosophy, Plato (indicating that admirable harmony which exists between that sun of the world and the sun of the highest order) calls the mundane <note>Belonging to the physical world.</note> sun the "shining son of the Supreme Good"—not the first son, but the second one, through whose mediation we arrive at the knowledge of the first. For in that glorious work of the creating...

And it is seen more in this solar palace of his because it is the most pure of all visible bodies in this world, and more polished than them, and more worthy to receive a wonderful form of this kind. From this it is manifest that because this solar vessel is capable of such a supereminent and excellent form, it becomes worthier than all other bodies in the world; for, as *Plato* testifies, form is given in perfection according to the merit of the matter.

It is certain, therefore, that this divine Sun is God himself, illuminating all things from the beginning, both secretly and manifestly, of whom King *David* speaks thus: *The Lord God is a Sun giving grace and glory, Psalm 84:12.* From him, therefore, the material Sun received its power of life, so ample that it not only illuminates and warms all things in this visible world with heat, but also rains down the act of generation and <term>vivification: the act of giving or restoring life</term> upon lower things, by the divine will, and that liberally. This we also have explored and confirmed from the exact words of the Prophet: *In the light of Jehovah we shall see light, Psalm 36:10.* This discourse is not to be understood regarding hidden and barely visible light, but also regarding that visible light, as if the creature had said: *In the light of Him who placed his tabernacle in the sun, we shall see light.* But concerning the manner in which this invisible light is rendered visible through the property of this visible vessel, we shall speak more broadly below. To confirm the origin of its vivifying property, the *Psalmist* speaks thus: *The fountain of life is with thee, Psalm 36:9.* This is to be understood not only of the life of the soul, but also of that of the body, according to that passage of the sacred page: *God of the soul and the body, the strong God of spirits, the God of all flesh.*

We conclude, therefore, that this sun in the *Archetypal* world is called God illuminating all darkness, or the Word of the Lord from which all things come, in which is life, and that *true light of the world, John 1.* Or Wisdom, which is the brightness of the eternal and almighty light, and compared to the Sun, is far more excellent in light; which, descending by emanation into the angelic world, is called the first-created wisdom, and by the *Kabbalists* the great Angel *Metatron* <note>A powerful archangel in Jewish mysticism, often described as the mediator between the divine and the material worlds.</note>, by whose rays the seraphic region of angels is illuminated and animated by fiery love. In the celestial world, it descends from *Tiphereth* into the heart of heaven and appears visibly in the solar organ. Hence it is clear that in the Ideal world or the heaven of heavens, this sun reflects its ardor into itself, in which state it is absolutely formal, without any respect to created matter. In the angelic world, it appears to the angelic and purely spiritual bodies with its invisible rays, which clothe the clear spirit of the intellectual heaven; and light of this kind is by no means subject to bodily eyes. But in the ethereal world, it appears visibly and joyfully, like a messenger to creatures, driving away nocturnal darkness, principally in that clear place (in which rays are infused and received immediately through the ministry of the Archangel *Michael* <note>In Western esoteric traditions, the Archangel Michael is frequently associated with the sun and the element of fire.</note>, and also in other places, as much in the planetary regions as in the regions of the elements by reflection). Finally, this Divine Sun plunges itself even deeper into the multitude of matter, for he foretold that he would dwell in darkness, either in the thick cloud which he sometimes makes his tent (*2 Chronicles 6:1* and *Job 22:15*) or in the fleshy house of man, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit, or the earth itself which is said to bring forth the Savior. And the uncreated Sun dwells in such dark places centrally in that sun which the mystical Philosophers have called the *Central Sun* <term>Central Sun: A spiritual or alchemical sun believed to reside at the center of the earth or within the heart of man, acting as the internal mirror of the outer sun.</term>, which has a continuous relationship with the celestial sun, just as the celestial sun does with those super-celestial things, since they are least of all distinguished in essence. Hence, therefore, was the error of those who, in *Arcadia* and *Scythia* or *Tartary*, falsely adored the visible and created sun as God; indeed, among the *Egyptians*, the Sun was held in such reverence of worship that not only was a noble temple dedicated to it, but also one of the five notable cities of *Egypt*. Whence it is written that the *Babylonian* king shattered the houses and statues of the sun in *Egypt, Jer. 43.* And elsewhere, one of the five cities of *Egypt* is called the *City of the Sun, Isa. 19.* Their error, he says, is egregious because they celebrated with blind and darkness-covered worship a vain cult: the garment for the thing clothed, the palace for the lord, the body subject to changes for the immortal soul, the illuminated thing for the illuminating essence, and finally the creature for the creator. But if anyone were to behold that invisible sun, which dwells in the sun's tent, with the hidden eyes of the heart and mind, and were to contemplate the creator in the solar creature, he certainly cannot be deceived in his adoration; for to venerate an angel in place of *JEHOVAH* is a sin—wherefore it happened that the Angel did not permit *John* to adore him, *Rev. 19:10*—but to adore the name of Jehovah in the Angel...

The wise Philosophers say that in whatever thing a matter has its origin, in that same thing it is accustomed to end; whence if we wish to seek and prove the beginning of the mundane sun, we shall best perceive it from its end. Now, in the accounts of the saints, we have these words: *Your sun shall no more go down; your moon shall not wane, because the Lord shall be your light in Jerusalem; Isaiah 60.* And with this place agrees that of John: *And the city needs neither sun nor moon to shine in it; for the clarity of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb: and the nations shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it, Revelation 21:23.* By these things it is indicated that in the final days of the world, this heavenly sun will cast off its thick and dark garments and will appear just as it truly is. For there is no truth except in the true light of the world, which reveals all fictions and reduces them to nothing by the Lydian test. For by an examination of this kind, the moon in the final days will have the clarity of the sun by laying aside its created garments; and the truly central and divine Sun, by stripping off its thick and created clothing, will be in its naked and clear nature, providing light to the blessed servants of God in their purification and, as it were, resurrection—not otherwise (but in a far more excellent degree) than the common sun or the sun visible in the sky. But the Holy Bible also seems to confirm those things which were said above: for it is said that God fills all things: *That from God and through God are all things, Romans 11; that God is the father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all, Ephesians 4:6.* And that *God works all in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* Whence, since He Himself is the only truth, it is necessary that nothing be true unless it is of His essence. Wherefore we say finally that just as God was the beginning of solar beauty—that is, if His glory is the cause of the excellence of the solar creature—once the fiction is laid aside, it will be far more beautiful, just as it was in the beginning, that is, in its first emanation, when it was called <term>Hochma</term> <note>Hebrew: Chokmah, or "Wisdom," the second Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing the first spark of creation.</note> or divine wisdom, which is the brightness of the clarity of the Almighty. So it was in the beginning, and its beginning shall be justified by the end, inasmuch as He is the Alpha and Omega, *Revelation 1,* the beginning and the end. Hence the Apostle says, *God shall be all in all when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father, 1 Corinthians 15.* Whence also He said elsewhere, *When I am exalted, I will draw all things to myself,* that is, all that which is of purity and truth; for nothing is to be considered as nothing in its mere nature, nor as void and empty.

But let us proceed rapidly to the nature of our created sun, that is, the solar creature.

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...the heavens were made firm, and all their powers or hosts by the breath of his mouth, Psalm 33. <note>original: "spiritu ab ore eius omnes virtutes seu exercitus eorum"</note> And that distinguished priest Ezra denotes this with these express words: *the stars were established by the word of the Lord*, 2 Esdras 16. <note>The text cites "Esdr. 4. 16," referring to the apocryphal Fourth Book of Ezra.</note> However, to treat the particular manner of this creature’s origin and to immerse oneself in its mysteries will seem somewhat difficult for a human, unless we look into the Holy Scriptures with lynx-like eyes. Regarding its matter, therefore, it is certain that it possesses the consistency of the clearest, most polished, and highly spiritual earth, which emerged from the darkness (after being reflected into the center of the world by the bright rays of divine wisdom, as was declared in our history of the physics of the Macrocosm). By the help of divine rays, it was exalted in the center of the heavens like something cast in a mold, and illuminated on all sides by the rays of divine grace and beauty. 

In this same way, the body of Adam was formed from choice clay, animated and quickened by the breath of life and the bright spirit of the Almighty, and formed in the image of the Almighty. So too the earth was said to give birth to the Savior; and our Savior, rising from the tomb and emerging from the gap of death or the lethal dark shadow like a morning star, ascended into heaven clothed on all sides with a celestial spirit. Why then should the created sun refuse the "earth" as the parent of its consistency? For the sun is the condensed spirit of a celestial nature, in whose center the uncreated light of the world placed its tabernacle, as the royal Psalmist teaches us. 

Furthermore, we see that just as our Savior rose from the darkness of death and the abyss of the tomb on the third day, so too after the third day in creation—and not before—was the sun created. Until the fixation of the earth in the center of the world (or its suspension over nothingness) was achieved, no mention was made of the creation of the greater light. From this, it is likely that the sun ascended from the earth, stripped of dark filth, as if from a tomb; for in the sun is the tabernacle of the invisible and divine sun, which stands in relation to that highly polished body as a most brilliant soul. 

But however we read it, that ethereal matter is so involved in a spherical manner, and in its consistency so pure, that it is called by the wise man a "vessel," the admirable work of the Most High (Ecclesiasticus 43). And in what is announced elsewhere: *The sun, the work of the Lord, is full of his glory* (Ecclesiasticus 42); and elsewhere, *that he placed a tabernacle in it*. It is clear that it is a vessel naturally very clean and polished, for otherwise it would not be capable of containing a form so pure and simple—since form is usually granted according to the merit of the matter. 

And yet, it is impossible for matter so exquisitely pure to be found throughout the entire created spirit that it could merit a form as pure and simple as that divine essence, which is without any stain or impurity. Whence it is written first of the angels, and then afterward of the stars, that in respect to the lynx-like purity of the divine essence, they are not pure. Regarding these stars, it is written: *The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God*, Job 25:5. Of those angels, indeed, we read these words: *Behold, God found wickedness in his angels, etc.*, Job 4:18. <note>The source text cites Job 14.17, but the quote corresponds to Job 4:18.</note> For it is impossible for a created thing to be made equal in its Being to the essence of the Creator. 

But truly, among all visible bodies, it is certain that the solar substance is the purest. This is declared because the visible glory of God is indicated more to mortals in the sun than in any other creature of the world. And from this, it is said by Augustine that as much light as something has in itself, by so much more does it seem to claim God for itself. Hence also the wise man says of the sun: *The sun, illuminating all things, looked upon them, and its work is full of the glory of the Lord*, Ecclesiasticus 42. From this, it is evident that the presence of that divine glory denotes the purity of the subject into which it enters. For in holy scripture we read everywhere that the Holy Spirit does not descend except into a pure spirit or a clean heart—that is, into a purified subject. For such must be the respect between the bridegroom and the bride, between Cupid and Psyche, <note>A classical allegory where Cupid represents Divine Love and Psyche represents the Human Soul.</note> between Christ and the Church, between the mind and the spirit, or there will be no firm bond and union between them.

From this, therefore, we ought to gather that insofar as the mundane sun is a creature and a kind of shadow of the majesty of the archetypal sun, it is in no way to be worshiped as God by mortals who are consistent and not seized by diabolical madness. To do so would be to adore the house instead of the master. This is exactly what those twenty-five men did who (as Ezekiel witnesses) stood between the porch and the altar with their faces toward the east and worshiped the rising of the sun, having their backs against the temple of the Lord. Of them, God speaks thus to the Prophet: *Is it a light thing that they should commit these abominations which they commit here, filling the land with iniquity, etc.* Ezekiel 8:16. 

The sacred page also reproves this in express speech: *You shall not look at the sun, the moon, or the stars, or any of the host of heaven, to bow down and worship them*, Deuteronomy 4. It is as if He had said: "Jehovah is the only and unique Creator God; you must offer worship to Him alone, and not to the images created by Him—that is, to the creating Lord, and not to the created servant or minister." The sun, says the wise man, has the Lord as its maker, at whose words it hastened its journey. Elsewhere this is expressly explained in this manner: "God created the sun, moon, stars, and others for the service of all nations under heaven"; therefore He forbade them to be adored and worshiped. It is as if He said, "I am the Creator, therefore the things I created are not to be worshiped, but I alone, the Creator." 

How ridiculous it would be to a wise man to revere a servant with honor and not think of the Master, or to bestow the least praise on minor things while rejecting and neglecting the greater! What, I pray, is a body without a soul, or something unformed without its form imparting life and glory? Surely it is nothing—void, and clearly a deformed and horrendous shadow—as if one were to choose a shadow for the true God, but reject the true subject as nothing. This indeed is the way of the worldly, overwhelmed by darkness and ignorance, choosing things that appear to be but are least significant, instead of those things which truly are but are least seen, just like the blind. Open, therefore, you blind mortals, those eyes which Adam closed because of his sins, and close your carnal eyes, which in a deceptive manner think they see those things which are not, but are truly unable to penetrate to the things that are.

### CHAPTER XV.

## *On the manifold Power and usefulness of the Sun.*

The primary power of the Sun consists in its light, motion, and heat, just as its secondary power is accustomed to flow from these same effects; we shall therefore speak at somewhat greater length about both, as they are mixed with one another: and first, concerning Light.

As it is certain, and confirmed by what has come before, that GOD is the fountain of light, this primary light made its first act or motion through its own emanation. By this, the "first moved" <term>primum mobile: In the old geocentric model, the outermost sphere that moves all others.</term> of the world—that is, the highest circle of the thin "world-spirit"—was carried around, and by its motion all the enclosed spheres are also rotated along their perimeters. Furthermore, the effect of this mobility or "moving act" is heat, just as, conversely, the dull and unfeeling act of rest is the parent of cold. And although it is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Bible that God is always remaining in Himself and least subject to change, yet in respect to His Wisdom emanating from His bright fountain, He is "more mobile than all mobile things," Wisdom 7 <note>original: "Sap. 7," referring to the Wisdom of Solomon 7:24.</note>. By this, it is manifest that He includes all things in His nature, both the moving and the resting, and that He ordained and brought forth both darkness and light.

How and by what reasoning this solar matter receives visible light from the invisible sun, we shall say in a few words. It was declared before that the substance of the sun is pure and clear in its nature, so that it might be a vessel and a work worthy of receiving the rays of so divine a form. But indeed, according to the opinion of Algazel <note>Algazel: The Latinized name for Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian philosopher and theologian.</note> regarding the nature of a mirror, if the spirit in the sphere receiving the rays is too rare <term>rare: thin or low-density, the opposite of dense.</term> in its consistency, it does not become bright when light is cast into it; that is, it is not illuminated because it does not submit to color, and consequently, it is neither colored nor visible. Hatten <note>Hatten: This likely refers to Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose "De aspectibus" was the standard medieval textbook on optics.</note> also confirms this in his *Book on Optics*, saying that a thing is not visible if it has no color, for (he says) a visible thing exists only according to the light in the thing seen, but visible light only occupies what is colored. Moreover, the reason why a subtle and thin spirit is not seen, even in the presence of light, is that it is necessary for the thing seen to be "resistant" to the sight. From this, some might conclude that the sun's substance cannot be most pure, clear, and transparent in its being, but must have a certain opacity and consequently a dark condition, without which it could not be seen or appear as a bright, colored thing: for thus we see the image of a thing appear in clear water, crystal, or the purest air for the reasons brought forward before. To this doubt we respond briefly, in the words of Algazel in the place cited before, by saying that no part of the stellar sphere placed before the visual power is receptive or retentive of the sun's light, except for its denser part, which we call the "star" itself. Thus, if the sun's substance, clear and pure as it is, had been thin in its physical dimension, no color would appear on its surface, and no spherical shape would be clearly visible. But because it is massive in quantity and of a globe-like containment, the light renders it more colored the more deeply it penetrates, and its rays are gathered together into the center of the body of the globe. We see this form in waters which, though most pure and clear in their substance (and consequently receiving no impression of an object’s light in a small quantity), nevertheless receive the images of those standing by because of their density and depth (as is also read in the story of Narcissus <note>A reference to the Greek myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool of water.</note>), as experience testifies. We say, therefore, that the deep center of the solar body is the darkest part of the whole body, from which it follows that, because of its depth, that place resists the gaze of the "bright spirit" looking into it more strongly. Then, the rays dispersed invisibly on all sides through the edges of the spherical body, and striking together at the center—like a multitude meeting at a center point or unity—create by that union not only a strong reflection, which is the source of solar heat, but also visible light that is most pleasant to the sight. Thus they say the visible stellar body is brought forth by the gathering of invisible parts of the ether, and also visible clouds from the invisible air, and visible lightning and comets from the more active consistency of the same, and even indeed the flame of terrestrial fire. Hence it was said by the Apostle that we must believe through faith that visible things were first made from invisible things <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:3: "so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."</note>. Thus also God, clothing the fiery air, is called a "consuming fire," and Wisdom is said to be "brighter than the light of the sun." We see this confirmed by the practice of the common "burning mirror" <term>burning mirror: A concave mirror used to concentrate sunlight to start fires.</term>, which, by drawing all the solar rays on its circular surface into the unity of its center, reveals them—from an insensible and barely visible nature—into the likeness of a visibly burning fire; and by directing that ray far off with a violent reflection, it thus destroys houses and towns from a distance by that fire. This, therefore, is the reason why visible light of this kind is produced and drawn together in the solar disk from the rays of invisible Wisdom; by means of this work, the spiritual light, spread invisibly through the vast spirit of the world, reveals itself visibly in a transparent colored medium to direct and govern visible bodies in their remote places. And certainly, many benefits of this visible light are recounted both from the sacred fountain and by philosophers. For we read written in the Holy Scriptures that its splendid face and its arrival in the world after the darkness of night provides joy, comfort, and motion to creatures; it expels the "light-shunning" spirits and restrains their violence, just as conversely its absence inclines one toward sadness, horror, and from motion to rest and lethargy. Hence we read that, as we have it in the Wise Man, "what is brighter than the sun?" Ecclesiasticus 17 <note>original: "Eccl. 17," referring to Ecclesiasticus (Sirah) 17:31.</note>. So its presence is very pleasing and useful not only to brute animals but even to men themselves: "The sun has risen," says the Prophet, "and the lion cubs are gathered together," etc. Psalm 104:22. And some...
