...will do, <note>original: "Exorto sole quid facit bestia? quid homo?"</note> *When the sun has risen, what does the beast do? What does man?* And in another place we have, *You commanded the sun's splendor on the fourth day to serve the future man,* <note>original: "4. Esdr. 8."</note> 4 Esdras 8. And elsewhere, *God created the Sun for the service of all nations,* <note>original: "Deut. 4."</note> Deuteronomy 4. Regarding its absence, Genesis speaks thus: *As the sun was setting, a horror invaded Abram,* <note>original: "Gen. 15."</note> Genesis 15. From this it is argued that the absence of the sun is the time most suited for horror and fear. Furthermore, the light of the sun is an ornament of exceptional value, not only to the earth but also to the heavens; it is understood concerning its splendor where it is said that *He adorned the heavens with His spirit.* From this spirit, which first gave life to the sun, all celestial bodies—both the wandering planets and the fixed stars—principally acquire their beautiful brilliance. This is despite the opinion of Cicero and certain others that all stars, with only one exception (namely the moon), claim their own light and splendor for themselves. However, other Philosophers seem to perceive more correctly—namely, that the other stars, and especially the planetary ones, do not have a light appropriate to themselves, but rather they maintain that these are ignited and illuminated by the Sun along with the Moon. Thus we also observe that although the earth has a soul appropriate to its body (in the manner of the lunar body), it is nevertheless illuminated in the daytime by the sun’s splendor and is moved by it in a hidden manner. And hence Heraclitus quite deliberately called the Sun the *fountain of celestial light*, and others maintain that it is called *Sol* as if *solus* <note>The author uses a traditional Latin etymology: "sol" (sun) derived from "solus" (alone/only).</note> because it alone out of all the stars is so great. If you were to remove the sun from the world (says Heraclitus), what is our twilight if the soul is missing? No pulsing vein is felt there, no judgment resides in the senses, no vital habit or any breath is in it. And hence it is that by some the Sun is called the **heart of heaven**, because just as in the heart there exists a fountain of blood that moistens and waters the other members of the human body and infuses vital motion, so in the sun there seems to be the vegetation and preservation of all things, both lower and higher, because it breathes life and heat through its light. As such, it is defined as a simple act, turning all things toward itself with life-giving heat, permeating all beings, and leading their qualities and virtues through all things while dispersing darkness and gloom. Wherefore, in the middle, Apollo seems to sit upon the gleaming throne of heaven, with golden hair and shining in a glorious manner, imparting his lucid influences to the other creatures of the world, both celestial and terrestrial. But the Platonists have expressed this in a few words, and as if in a single phrase, asserting that the **soul of the world** is included in the sun, and, as the sacred text has it, that light—which gives life to all things—*set its tabernacle in the sun*. If this light were taken from the world, it would be necessary that the world and its creatures immediately become soulless and recede into that nothingness from which they were first made; for by that bright Word all things were made (<note>original: "vti D. Iohannes ait"</note> *as Saint John says*) *and without it, nothing was made.*

Hence the Academics <note>Followers of the Platonic school of philosophy.</note>, following the example of that supreme sun, acknowledge that the mundane sun is unique in itself—that is, in essence and light—but they nevertheless make it manifold in its rays. This follows the example of the first essence, which is unique and most simple in itself, most divine and immobile, yet is manifold insofar as it is disseminated among its creatures. Just as when the sun contracts its rays into itself, all things are dark, so too when the divine sun turns away His face, all things are disturbed and return to their own nothingness, as is read in the *History of the World’s Harmony*. But we also draw this in express speech from the sacred fountain: *wisdom is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, simple, manifold, having all power, etc.* <note>original: "Sap. 7," referring to the Wisdom of Solomon 7:22-23.</note> Wisdom 7. From this they teach us that although in its essence it is unique, it is nevertheless manifold in respect to the rays which it disperses everywhere and into every subject of this world, without which nothing exists. This is also confirmed in that it is said to contain all power in itself, as in its essence consists the life of every thing: *in it is life, etc.* <note>original: "Ioan. 1"</note> John 1. Upon this foundation Orpheus fixed his opinion: *that all things were full of Gods*; but they referred all these Gods, like the rays of one essence, to that one great God, Jehovah or Jove. For the confirmation of the aforementioned discourse, we have this written by the royal Psalmist: *When God hides His face from His creatures, they are troubled; when He takes back their spirit—that is, that bright form of life—they expire and return to their dust; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated by His goodness,* <note>original: "Ps. 104. 29-30."</note> Psalm 104. From this it is clear that just as the rays of divine light or the invisible sun are acts of life (which He also rains down liberally upon creatures from His solar temple), so it is necessary that if those rays are taken away, the creature is suddenly reduced to nothing. Finally, there is still another use for this kind of mundane solar light: namely, that it distinguishes times into their divisions and subdivisions. Whence it is written: *that the sun being made, the days, light, and years were separated by the knowledge of the Lord, whose precept they keep, and they are divided by the wisdom of God,* <note>original: "Eccl. 23," likely referencing a commentary or variant of Ecclesiasticus/Sirach.</note> Ecclesiasticus. So also it is said of wisdom: *that she gives knowledge of the beginning, the end, and the midpoint of times; the changes of the solstices, the varieties of seasons, and the circuits of the year, etc.* <note>original: "Sap. 7"</note> Wisdom 7. From the act and liveliness of the solar light—since its soul, namely Wisdom (according to Solomon), is *more mobile than all mobile things* (Wisdom 7)—motion is generated. By the power of this motion, the Sun rises and sets, so that both day and night might be brought into the world for the benefit of man. Now, this motion is procreated by the act of light, for the bright Word of God is the first actor both in the motion of the sun and of the rest of creatures; for light acts, and by its action produces motion in nature, which thereafter is the parent of heat—generating, fostering, and nourishing all things, as will be discussed more broadly below. Hence the wise man says: *Great is the Lord who made the Sun, at whose word it hastened its path,* <note>original: "Eccl. 43"</note> Ecclesiasticus 43. This indicates that not only was the creature of the sun created by the word and speech of Almighty God, but it also seems to have received life (which is light) and motion (which is the effect of acting light) from Him, as the sequence of words suggests. Indeed, just as the hidden spirit of wisdom is the soul and beauty of the sun itself, sent down from the bright gate of the Kabbalists <term>Tiphereth: The sphere of 'Beauty' on the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, often associated with the Sun and the heart.</term>, so by the motion of this vessel (which is an admirable work of the Most High), the entire universal world-spirit is ruled, quickened, moved, and governed, not otherwise than the whole mass of the human spirit and body is governed by the fiery power of the heart...

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical exploration of the sun's influence on the physical world, specifically how solar motion and heat generate atmospheric phenomena. # On the Efficient Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena.

<term>Atmospheric Phenomena</term> <note>original: "Meteororum." In this period, "meteors" referred to all phenomena in the atmosphere, including wind, rain, and clouds, rather than just space rocks.</note> is stirred up to fulfill the appetite of the will, which is why Solomon says that by the turning of the sun, it hurries as it circles, and returns according to its circuits, *Ecclesiastes 1.* And from this it arises that the winds are called the children of the Titans, Astraea, and Aurora, insofar as they are born from solar motion and heat, as Aristotle himself says; yet we define winds as agitated air. However, that this solar motion—both the daily, swift motion and the natural motion—comes from a single spirit operating in many ways, we are taught in this: *because from him and through him are all things*, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> testifies. He, for the quickening of the world, acts voluntarily in the <term>First Mover</term> <note>original: "primo mobili," the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries the others</note>, by whose motion the solar sphere is swept along with all the others from the east to the west according to that word of David: *The sun, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, will rejoice as a giant to run the way; his going out is from the end of heaven and his circuit even to the end of it, nor is there anyone who can hide himself from its heat, Psalm 19.* And in this sense, the sun is said elsewhere to know its own setting. But truly, this celestial body has another motion assigned to itself, insofar as it is a peculiar creature within the great living being <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul</note>: thus we see man by his will—as an effect of the prime mover and as if in the first mover of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being viewed as a miniature universe</note>—sweep the entire mass of the creature here and there, while nevertheless the heart in his center has its own peculiar and appropriate motion, namely in <term>systole and diastole</term> <note>the contraction and expansion of the heart</note>, distinct from the motion of the will, yet still depending on the will of the creating mind. In the same way, the Sun, insofar as it is a body, is seen to move slowly through its own resistance against the motion of the First Mover, namely from the west toward the east; by this motion we measure and outline the space of a year. In this motion, the sun is said by Solomon to turn from the north to the south and again from the south toward the North: *It circles,* he says, *through the south, and turns to the North, etc. Ecclesiastes 1.* It is as if he had said: it goes toward the winter solstice or the Tropic of Capricorn, and returns to the summer solstice or the Tropic of Cancer, by which motion the annual circuit of the year is completed.

Finally, just as motion is the most proximate and immediate effect of emanating light, so also heat, as an effect, proceeds immediately from motion, just as it is demonstrated in the friction of iron or a hard thing against another hard thing. We must therefore briefly discuss solar heat as the effect immediately following motion. *Ecclesiasticus* <note>The Book of Sirach</note> seems to attribute a triple property to the sun, namely: *to burn, to blow out fiery rays by reflection, and to blind the heavens with the brilliance of its rays, Ecclesiasticus 43.* Regarding the heat coming from its motion, it is most certain that it comes either immediately from the solar nature—since it is fundamentally its nature to blow out fiery rays from its body, no differently than we see warm breaths coming out of the mouth of an animal—or it arises due to the various reflections of its rays against the earth or clouds, according to the variety of the angles of resistance, which produce both intensity and weakness. For direct rays striking perpendicularly produce stronger effects in heat because of the stronger resistance; hence we read in express words, *that the Sun at midday burns the earth, and in the sight of its heat, who can stand? Ecclesiasticus 43.* By which we understand that for those to whom the sun is at the meridian or mid-heaven, especially when it passes near the Tropic of Cancer, it brings forth a more vehement heat because its rays strike more perpendicularly. Furthermore, wherever the sun's rays strike in the summer season, whether from the rising to the midday or from that point toward the setting, it burns greatly, because of the perpendicularity of the rays with the climate. Thus it is said, *that the sun rising over the flower, with heat, withers the grass and its flower falls, James 1.* And elsewhere, *Tomorrow when the sun grows hot, there shall be help for you, etc. 1 Samuel 11.* From this it is clear that the sun's heat is present to creatures sometimes as a benefit and sometimes as a punishment, for indeed it is a work full of the glory of the Lord, who acts either benevolently or severely according to His good pleasure, but especially so that it may serve man, for whose benefit and use the rest were created, whence it is written: *You commanded the sun's splendor on the fourth day to serve the future man: 4 Esdras 6.* Hence it is that the sun was produced into the power of the day, as the Psalmist says: *Psalm 136:8.* where by "day," life can be understood, both in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The universe</note> and the Microcosm, just as conversely death and deprivation stand for night and darkness; for the prince of darkness is the destroyer of life, while the commander of light is the author and creator of life. For this reason, the sun is called "fecund" by the Philosophers, and full of the power of generating many things. Although we have many life-giving virtues from the other stars and planets, this nevertheless happens through the power of the sun, which warms them with its seed and life-giving virtue. For it is the opinion of the most excellent Philosophers that the Sun is like a **celestial rooster**, insofar as it makes the army of the heavens pregnant; for the celestial bodies are like hens, in that they receive the seed and the generable and heating virtue from the Sun no differently than a hen receives hers from a rooster. In a similar way, I say, this rooster of the ether communicates and disperses the lucid virtue of life and generation everywhere, like the benevolent nurseries of divinity (which divinity was said by Hermes Trismegistus to be abundantly full with the fecundity of both sexes) into the stellar bodies, as if into wombs of various conditions, and consequently raining various natures upon the earth according to the properties of the stars. For it must be certain and determined that just as God, the author of light and of all acts, motions, and heats springing from it, is one and simple, yet is accustomed to operate in various forms within Himself according to the different nature of the receiver—just as the sperm of a man cast into the womb of a cow, a dog, or a horse is observed to produce various effects—so also says the *New Light* <note>original: "Nouum Lumen." A reference to the alchemical text *Novum Lumen Chymicum* by Michael Sendivogius.</note>, that nature is simple and always the same, but all alteration is in respect to the places in which it operates uniformly in its being, but in various forms in respect to the variety of reception. Likewise, we notice that fire acts in various ways in respect to the variety of resistance in the things receiving it.

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

Among these celestial matrices <note>In this context, "matrices" refers to "wombs" or formative environments that nurture life.</note>, however, the moon is that common one which receives "seeds" just as immediately from the sun as it does mediately—that is, indirectly—from the higher stars. She distributes these everywhere to the air, water, and earth, for she is the common matrix for all classes of stars. Therefore, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and the soul.</note> and many others conclude that in Phoebus <note>A poetic name for the sun, often associated with Apollo.</note>, who shines with a golden mane and holds the world’s scepter and helm like a king, all the virtues of the celestial beings reside. Proclus also testifies that at the sight of the sun, all the powers of all celestial beings are gathered into one and, as it were, collected; we believe these are finally scattered into this lower world through fiery conduits. 

Does not yearly experience also prove this? As the sun turns toward us, the earth grows green and flourishes; when it stands perpendicularly above us, it greatly warms and matures the crops; but as it hastens toward the winter quarter and departs, the plants and herbs lose their flowers and are seen to languish more and more every day, as if by a disease. It seems that the sun does all this by means of its beneficial heat, which either cherishes and gives life through its moderation, or destroys and scorches through its harshness; or finally, in its absence, the vegetable and animal things it once quickened are observed to fade and grow numb in the torpor of the cold. In this same sense, Plato says:

> That the Sun is a celestial fire, ripening <note>original: "decoquens," literally "cooking down" or "digesting."</note> all things by its heat which pertain to the food of the "great world-animal." By "food," he means the creatures of the world, with which he wished to fill the world for its own preservation; these are brought to perfection and maturity by the solar "concoction."

Sacred scripture seems to agree with his words where it is said that the Sun guards the furnace in the works of heat—that is, in the ripening of those things that are in the world. Indeed, its rays, with their tempered heat, are so effective and penetrating that they descend even to the bowels of the earth. There, the sun first "cooks" and perfects the metals, which the elementary fire later purifies and cleanses through its own trial. Because of this life-giving disposition and beneficial power, the ancients imagined him to be the inventor of medicine; and insofar as he is the parent of life (for he generates all things by his heat), he is called by the Platonists the ***anima mundi*** <note>Soul of the World.</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that just as Jehovah, in his own nature, is inclined toward both severity and mercy in his luminous gateway <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>The sixth Sefirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing Beauty, Compassion, and the Sun.</note>—since that attribute stands in the middle between <term>Ehieh</term> <note>A Divine Name associated with the highest crown and pure mercy.</note>, the Father or head of mercy, and <term>Adonai</term> <note>A Divine Name often associated with the physical world and judgment/severity.</note>—he is nevertheless more inclined toward life than destruction. Nonetheless, since nothing under the sun is immortal, it is necessary that just as a creature is generated and preserved by the life-giving rays of life given from the "tabernacle in the sun" for the preservation of mortals, so too is it corrupted and perishes, or rather is dissolved, by their absence or by a fiery and angry aspect. Hermes Trismegistus elegantly confirms this:

> The sun and the moon were allotted the increases and decreases of all bodies;

He says this not because these creatures usually perform such things by their own power, but insofar as they are the organs through which God performs such deeds.

But now we shall proceed to describe his honor and dignity, which the Wise Man clearly expresses in these words:

> *The sun, lighting all things, is the work of the Lord, full of his glory*: Ecclesiastes 43.

Hence, elsewhere he calls the sun an "admirable vessel" and the "work of the Most High," as the place in which (according to the Psalmist) that royal light of life 

> *placed his tabernacle*, Psalm 19:4.

That is, it resides in that place as the soul resides in the body; from which, according to the common laws of created nature, it liberally and sumptuously distributes the benefits of life to the creatures of the world in its circuit. For indeed, 

> *in the Word was life, and that life was the light of the world*,

as Saint John teaches us. Similarly, this Word strengthened the heavens, and his Spirit brought forth all the virtues of life into the light. Although this Spirit is not confined within the solar vessel, that "admirable vessel" nevertheless abounds with its presence and glory. Thus, the sun is called the giver and distributor of life, growth, and increase, not only to celestial bodies but also to earthly ones. Therefore, because of its surpassing glory and dignity, and because of its dominion over other creatures, it is called by the Platonists "King and Emperor," holding the scepter and government of the world—both because it is seen to sit upon a throne of visible glory with a shining golden mane, and because we perceive, taught by experience itself, that all the virtues of the celestial beings reside in it. Some, wishing to make the nobility of this subject known to us in another way—especially Orpheus and others of the Platonists—imitating him, declared that it is the "faithful eye of the world," since nothing in the world is more sharp-sighted; for in it, as in a most brilliant mirror, all things are seen, brought out of darkness into light, and present themselves to the sight of the creature. 

Others, wishing to express the praises and dignity of the sun differently, have called it the "heart of heaven," and this is by no means foolish. For Heraclitus says:

> If you take the sun out of the world, what is our poor little body if the soul is missing? No pulsing vein would be felt there, no breath of life, and finally no motive, life-giving, or natural force throughout the entire human body. Just so, in the sun—as if in the heart of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the Universe.</note>—the movement, growth, life, and preservation of all the members of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to Man as a reflection of the Universe.</note> (both higher and lower) are seen to exist. For it is accustomed to breathe out life and heat in the manner of the Divine Unity—or, let us say, from its center or middle point, or the uncreated light dwelling centrally within it, shaping it and adorning it with rays of life through the medium of its created light, or rather its illuminated spirit. Indeed, by reason of the Divinity that inhabits it, there is nothing visible in the world that represents the image of the one God in three persons in a single essence more than this excellent vessel, full of divine glory; for in its entire essence (as if its body), it holds the icon of the Father; in the emitted rays, the icon of the Son; and in the effect of both—namely, the life-giving heat—the icon of the Holy Spirit.

# On the Efficient Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena.

<margin>Dionysius on</margin>the life-giving Holy Spirit, from whom all gifts of life originate; thus it happened that Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note>, following Plato’s concept of the Sun, calls it the "visible statue or image of God," and Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> calls it the "image of divine intelligence." Furthermore, even those of the Academy <note>The followers of Plato.</note> acknowledge it to be unique in itself—that is, in its essence and light—and yet multiple in its rays, according to the pattern of uncreated emanation. This emanation is one in itself, but is said to be manifold because its rays are scattered everywhere through the world among creatures. By a similar reasoning, Wisdom—which is brighter than the sun—is simple and unique in its nature; yet, in respect to its manifold communication, it is called "multiple" by the wise man. He says: "Wisdom is a holy spirit of intelligence, unique or simple, manifold, more precious than the Sun and light, and when compared to the light, it is found to be above every arrangement of the stars" <note>original: "Sap. 7," referring to the Book of Wisdom 7:22-29.</note>. For this reason, Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher.</note> seems to observe that the Sun is called Apollo from *a* <note>original: "α," the Greek letter alpha used as a prefix for negation.</note> meaning "without" and *poly* <note>original: "πολὺ."</note> meaning "multiplicity," since he is the only one who appears to have the power of the stars and the heavens in his own authority. But Speusippus the Platonist says the Sun is called Apollo because its power consists of many fires; for in it alone are the shining powers of all the stars deeply hidden, so that the aspects of the stars can do nothing or bring anything to completion until they have been made "pregnant" by the shining seed of Apollo. Hence, he is called the "cock of the heavens," indicating that in effect Apollo is both one and multiple, and thus both those philosophers can be reconciled into one view. The Latins call the Sun *Sol*, as if he were "the only one shining" <note>original: "Solum lucentem."</note>, as some would have it. And the Assyrians call him *Adad*, which in their language also signifies "the only one." The Hebrews call him *Shemesh* <note>original: "Semes."</note>, which can be interpreted as "his own," because the light and the power of light are proper to him. But while he is called Apollo as "the only one," he is also called Phoebus in the heavens from another perspective—namely, from his appearance and splendor. On earth, they call him Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here representing the sun's heat when applied to the terrestrial realm.</note>. Finally, he is the visible tabernacle of the invisible God, or of the holy spirit of intelligence, made in the image of his creator or Lord, most full of the glory of the creating Lord, but by no means to be worshipped in place of the Lord dwelling within him.

->Therefore, we turn toward the rising sun in our prayers, not as if to a statue or an image, but to the uncreated Lord—in whose image the sun itself was made—who dwells in it and from it liberally flows the necessary benefits of created nature. Him alone we ought to worship and revere, to whom be the highest glory and highest praise, and adoration from the whole human mind, forever and ever.<-

From this it is clear that this admirable work of the Most High is a creature that humbly offers its obedience to its creator or lord—not only in this, its vessel, which abundantly shows forth glory to worldly things, but as one existing everywhere through his presence. By this, the error of those philosophers is clearly revealed who strongly defend the idea that this eternal light, dwelling exuberantly in the sun, acts in nature by necessity or compulsion. However, we read that the sun’s obedience in observing the commands of its lord is perfected in three ways: namely, either by its duty and direct motion according to the laws of nature; or by retrograde motion, contrary to the order of nature; or by rest; or by celebrating its creator in praises and offering him immense thanks for that glory with which it is endowed above other worldly creatures. Its obedience in its direct motion is explained in these words: *The Sun that he made is the great Lord, at whose words it hastened its journey* <note>original: "Eccl. 43," referring to Ecclesiasticus/Sirach 43:2-5.</note>. Furthermore, it obediently performs its duty in illuminating and heating according to the will of its creator. For as the sun was created for the power of the day, as the Prophet says in *Psalm 136:8*, or for the ministry of light to all nations under heaven as is found elsewhere <note>original: "Exod. 4," though the sun's service to nations is more commonly cited from Deuteronomy 4:19.</note>, so it is said that the Sun *goes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber*—that is, from his rising—and *he rejoices like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit even to the end of it, and there is nothing hidden from his heat* <note>original: "Psal. 19. 5," referring to Psalm 19:5-6.</note>. By these words, its obedience is explained, both in the duty of illuminating and in its daily and direct motion moving at the will of him who rotates the *primum mobile* <note>The outermost sphere of the universe in ancient astronomy, which drives the motion of all other spheres.</note>, and also in its property of heating. But its obedience in its duty of heating, according to the will of its lord, is also explained by what is written: *The sun shall not burn you by day* <note>original: "Psal. 121. 6."</note>. And elsewhere, with the opposite effect: *The sun at noon parches the earth; who can endure in the sight of its burning?* <note>original: Sirach 43:3.</note>. From this it is manifest that this creature burns with its heat when it pleases its lord, and sometimes acts beneficially and gives life without scorching or drying up. In this way, we have seen how this solar creature obeys the pleasures of its creator in its duty, according to the ordinary laws of created nature. Furthermore, it is seen to act by divine command outside and plainly against the ordinary laws of nature. Thus, sometimes by the will of God, it moves backward against its ordained progress in its daily motion; and sometimes we read that it stood fixed for the space of a whole day, as in *Joshua 10*. And elsewhere: *When God forbids it, the sun does not rise, and he seals up the stars* <note>original: "Job. 9. 7."</note>. Regarding its former obedience, it is said in the sacred page: *The sun stood still in the midst of Heaven, and did not hasten to set for the space of one day* <note>original: "Jos. 10."</note>. In the latter case, we read that *the sun returned ten lines by the degrees it had gone down on the sundial in the days of King Hezekiah* <note>original: "Isa. 38," referring to Isaiah 38:8.</note>. Finally, it is not to be doubted that this glorious creature is endowed with an intellectual spirit, no differently in its great mass than a man is in his own; for just as He breathed the breath of life into man's face, so in that sun He placed His tabernacle. Therefore it is evident that both of them are temples of the Holy Spirit, and consequently it is within the will and power of the sun—and those things which are animated by the sun through the incorruptible spirit—to pour out praises to its creator, just as it is in the power of man. Hence the Psalmist says: *Praise the Lord, Sun and Moon; praise him, all you stars and light* <note>original: "Psal. 148. 3."</note>.

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

Thus those three in the fiery furnace <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, from the Book of Daniel.</note>, glorifying God with one voice, said: *Sun and Moon, bless the Lord; praise and exalt him above all forever.* So too is it said elsewhere that the Sun "knew its setting" (*Psalm 104:19*). From these few examples, it is right to gather how great the obedience of this solar creature is toward its Creator. Thus man—a vessel most excellent in his creation but most perverse by nature—should yearn to perform his obedience and duty according to the will of his Creator. He should strive with the greatest effort so that, in the manner of the sun, he might shine in such glory as the solar creature radiates by its righteousness. For according to the Evangelist, the righteous shall shine like the Sun in the kingdom of their Father. Indeed, we believe that the image of Adam living in Paradise before the Fall was everywhere radiant and splendid, gleaming with the glory of the divine light dwelling within him, as a vessel formed by the very finger of God, the Light-Father. Do we not read that the stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God and entrusted to Moses, gleamed with a sapphire brilliance to the eyes of those looking upon them? So too do we read that the face of Moses (even though he was stained by the mark of mortality) so excelled in light that the Israelites were unable to look upon his face without a veil or covering. How much more, then, would Adam have shone, who was not yet contaminated by the slip and stain of mortality before his disobedience?

Finally, we come to the "passion" <note>In this context, 'passion' refers to suffering or an undergoings of change—specifically the miraculous darkening of the sun.</note> of the sun, by which we gather it has been affected several times in this world’s age, not only from the Sacred Scriptures but also from the authority of trustworthy authors. *The sun shall be darkened in its rising,* says the Prophet (*Isaiah 13*). And elsewhere: *Your sun shall no more go down, for the Lord shall be your light, O Jerusalem* (*Isaiah 60*). And in Joel we find: *The sun shall be turned into darkness before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes* (*Joel 2*). And elsewhere: *The sun and moon are darkened* (*Joel 3*), so that in its place the Sun of Righteousness may rise for those who fear the Lord, as we have in the prophet Malachi (*Malachi 4*). Also in Ecclesiastes we have: *The sun, the light of the stars and the moon, shall grow dark for man* (*Ecclesiastes 12*). And in St. Matthew: *The sun will be darkened immediately after the tribulation of those days* (*Matthew 24*). Finally, during the passion of the "primary sun" <note>Referring to Jesus Christ as the spiritual Sun.</note>—or rather, during the death and passion of His very tabernacle <note>The physical body of Christ.</note>—the "secondary" and celestial sun lost its light and was obscured. It was as if, when the life of its fleshy tabernacle failed, the celestial sun also suffered a <term>syncope<note>A sudden failure of strength or light; a fainting of the star.</note></term>, or a deprivation of its radiant form for a great span of time, through an inseparable consensus. Regarding this deprivation of solar life or form, Eusebius writes: *In the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad, a solar eclipse occurred, greater and more excellent than all that happened before; at the sixth hour, the day was turned into such a dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and there was an earthquake in Bithynia.* Thus he writes; similarly, Lucian of Antioch, the Martyr, while in his torments, cried out this to the judges of the infidels and the executioners: *Search your annals and you will find that in the time of Pilate, while Christ suffered, the day was interrupted by darkness as the sun was obscured.* Furthermore, it is most certain, and confirmed by logic, that this solar passion was wonderful and miraculous, far above ordinary solar eclipses (in which the Sun does not actually fail, but the body of the moon is merely positioned between its sight and our eyes). The first reason is that this passion occurred against the order of natural solar eclipses, which never happen when the moon is full; yet this was at the moon's opposition to the Sun. Instead, this failure and "syncope" of the Sun happened immediately after the opposition of the luminaries. Second, the part of the sun toward the east was veiled and shadowed first, and that same part was later re-illuminated first; from which it is clear that it happened contrary to the common laws of nature. The third reason (and that which would seem monstrous and incredible to all) is that in the hour of the eclipse, the moon moved against its own natural course—namely from East to West—whereas its natural motion is from West to East; and then, immediately after the passion ended, it was observed to travel in its natural motion. From these things, it must be concluded that this passion and failure was real and according to the nature of the Solar body itself, and not merely in respect to us (which, as has been said, is not a true passion in the sun).

And for this reason, this passion or failure was universal, which cannot happen to them from the moon's interposition between the earth and the sun. We conclude therefore from these things that, in the first place, when the life of the tabernacle of the uncreated Sun on earth failed, that sun in heaven was also affected as if by a syncope; it seemed to be lifeless and deprived of its radiant form. It was as if that radiant spirit, establishing its temple and tabernacle in both subjects, hated such an inhuman and cruel act and turned its radiant face away from both worlds for some space of time. We see also from this that the solar body is a creature subject to the will of GOD, either for life or for the deprivation of its light. Consequently, we see that GOD does not act in this world necessarily or as if coerced by the ordinary course of nature, despite that foolish assertion of the <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens moved by fixed, necessary physical laws.</note></term>.

Finally, that the sun will be transfigured from its current state on the last day and rendered seven times more splendid in its light—that is, shedding its corruptible garments to put on its incorruptible and immortal nature and be transmuted—seems confirmed primarily by the words of the Prophet: *The light of the Moon itself (he says) shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold* (*Isaiah 62/30*). And he teaches this more clearly when he says elsewhere: *Your sun shall no more go down, and your moon shall not be diminished, because the Lord shall be your light, O Jerusalem* (*Isaiah 60*). John in the Apocalypse seems to agree with this speech, saying: *The City has no need of Sun or moon to shine in it, for the brightness of GOD will illuminate it, and its lamp will be the Lamb.* Here and there it is declared that the spirit of Wisdom will be far more excellent than any brightness of sun or star. By laying aside the solar creature which it wore when it "placed its tabernacle in the sun," Wisdom will reveal itself in its own inaccessible splendor and light, the sight of which no mortal in this state of mortality can behold; but

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...when the righteous, like the sun (as St. Matthew has it), shall shine in that kingdom of their father <note>Matthew 13:43</note>, then they will see him, having stripped off their earthly garments, as he truly is. Thus *Alpha* shall be turned into *Omega* <note>original: "Alpha conuertetur in Omega"</note>; the beginning shall meet with its end. Just as things began in unity, so they shall have their end in unity. From God are all things, and into God all things shall return, for in him we live, move, and have our being (*Acts 17:28*). From him and in him is the life of all things (*John 1*). He will then be all in all, once Christ has obtained the kingdom of the father. He is the father from whom all things come, and the primary principle of such an end. He alone is the one who works all in all; He is the father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all; for he gives life to all. Indeed, he himself, lacking nothing, gives life and inspiration and everything to all. Finally, from him and through him and in him are all things, to whom be praise and honor forever (*1 Corinthians 15, 1 Corinthians 8, 2 Corinthians 5, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6, Acts 17, Romans 11*). And in this, many of the philosophers who were hidden in the deeper divine mysteries have agreed. Among them, the Zohar <note>original: "Zoar," referring to the foundational text of Jewish Kabbalah</note> says that all things are nothing but one in respect to God, though in respect to us they are many. Plato and Parmenides say that whatever exists, insofar as it is in God and proceeds from him, is nothing but one. Hermes, in his Emerald Tablet <note>original: "Tabula Smaragdina," a foundational text of Hermeticism/Alchemy</note>, says: just as all things were by the mediation of the one, so all things were born from this one by readoption. And Proclus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who sought to synthesize Greek philosophy into a single system</note>, in his *Theological Problems*, says: as all things proceed from one alone, so also they hasten continually to return to that one. And these things find all the greater peace and concord the more closely they approach that one and participate with it.

Plato also speaks thus in his letters: All things proceed from the most high, and they strive with the greatest effort to return to him again, as being that in which their final rest and the protection of their essence consists; and so it is with the rest.

By these things we have it confirmed that all things are truly nothing but one, yet they are "many" in the imagination of common men. It is the nature of such men to look back at those things which appear in an external manner—things which seem to exist but in the truth of the matter are nothing (and they ignore the central things which are least seen, yet are the truth itself, and the one, and the same). This is no different than how infinite rays are continuous with the same solar body or essence, and are by no means divided from the identity of the sun.

Therefore, it is certain that although worldly people attribute the acts of enlivening and life, of heating, ripening, multiplying, illuminating, and nourishing to the solar creature—and sometimes the Holy Scriptures, speaking in common language, attribute these effects to it and other creatures—nevertheless, speaking truly, God works all these things which are done within his creatures. The creatures merely serve in the place of instruments <note>original: "organorum loco"</note> to produce such effects. For example, we do not say that the flute made this or that harmony, or that the sword wounded this or that person, but rather the blower or musician, or the soldier, or some other man doing the wounding. Nor do we say the wagon transported such weights into the city, but rather the horses. Nor is it to be said that the human body truly does this or that, but rather the internal agent—the "prime mover"—who leads it according to his will and pleasure. Nor does a mirror burn things from a distance, but rather the rays emitted from the sun. Nor does the sun even emit its own rays, but rather he who informs and enlivens the sun, and who carries it from the east to the west and back again from west to east, and again makes it stand still to fulfill his commands.

Therefore, the acts of angels, stars, and all other creatures are truly to be attributed to God, since it is from him that *they live, move, and have their being*, as the Apostles and the Poets, agreeing on this, affirm (*Acts 17*). And if you say that God moves nothing toward evil, I respond: if you can assign some other primary act co-eternal with God—thereby creating not one God, but two co-eternal Gods—then perhaps some credit might be given to your objection. But we shall speak of these things more clearly below.

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II, Lib. IV. Membr. I.

...[of] himself, "God created the sun, the moon, the stars, and others for the service of all nations under heaven" (Deut. 4). He does not say that He created the Sun by His word, and then afterwards the other stars from the Sun; rather, by His own word, according to His own specific ordination and will, He created the Sun separately along with the others. Thus, He made each of them distinct from one another in shape, property, and position; which is why it is said that He counted the number of the stars and called as many as there are by their names—our Great Lord, with many powers and virtues. By this, the Prophet seems to suggest that He assigned various names to them based on their various properties and virtues. We are persuaded of this because in the linking of his words he says, *our Great Lord and of many virtues*. In the same way, Adam is said to have given names to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven—names that were undoubtedly not frivolous or empty, but suited to the property of each. By these things we are reminded that all the stars in heaven were created distinctly from the sun, and yet on the same day—indeed, even in the same moment—no differently than the earth and any species of plants or animals, though distinct from each other. These things received from the Supreme Creator a soul and a corporeal existence distinct from the rest, for in His word alone is the life and existence of every thing. And just as we see that the earth is illuminated at intervals and by turns by the solar face, which produces day in whichever hemisphere it faces, so too we are taught by daily experience that the moon receives its waxing and waning from the splendor of the Sun. Yet, it is certain that both the earth and the moon exist in their own proper natures even when the solar light is absent.

But here, finally, a double question may arise: do all the stars in Heaven receive visible light from the Sun or not? And then, is any star altered or strengthened in its action or influence by the aspect or luminous virtue of the Sun? Regarding both at once, we say (as we have related before) that Cicero and others assign a proper light and splendor to all stars, with only one exception <note>original: "vna tantummodo excepta" — referring to the moon</note>. However, the greater crowd of philosophers maintains that the stars have very little light or beauty of their own from their creation, but rather they claim they are ignited and illuminated by the Sun. For this reason, Heraclitus called the Sun the fountain of celestial light.

But as far as our opinion is concerned, we say either this last opinion of the Philosophers appears false and inconsistent, or that history recorded by Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian</note> regarding the universal eclipse of the Sun is far from the truth and a mere fable. In that history, he tells that the day was turned into murky night, so much so that the stars were seen in the sky. If, therefore, this eclipse was that universal one during the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ in that very hour—as he himself seems to infer—during which there was no interposition of the moon <note>The author argues that because Christ's crucifixion occurred during Passover (a full moon), a natural solar eclipse caused by the moon was impossible; therefore, it was a supernatural darkening of the Sun.</note>, it follows that this was a true failure of the solar light. Consequently, the Sun, having no light in itself, could not give light to others as they likewise failed; and yet, in that same failure, the bright stars showed themselves to the eyes of men.

In any case, it is likely that although some of the stars had sparks of light for their own ornament at the instant of their creation, they nevertheless receive a notable and excellent splendor from the solar rays, which are held back by no failure of their own. This is no different than what one may see in the globe of the earth and the moon. But because the highest activity of any thing—whether greater or lesser—is seen in the increase and decrease of its light, it is certain that the power and virtue of any of the wandering stars <note>term: "erraticarum" — the planets, which "wander" across the sky compared to the fixed stars.</note>, and indeed even of the fixed stars, becomes more fit and inclined to pour out such and such influences (whether simple or fixed) upon the lower things, whether by the conjunction of rays, by opposition, or by a trine, square, or sextile aspect <note>These are "aspects" in astrology—specific angles between celestial bodies that determine their combined influence.</note>. For example, when the Sun joins with Saturn, it produces sad, melancholic, and heavier effects, both in the upper elements and in the earth itself. Therefore, at this time, the daemons <note>note: In this context, "daemons" refers to mediating spirits or intelligences, not necessarily evil beings.</note> or Saturnine angels have stronger effects in the elements, because the great angel Metattron <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Kabbalistic tradition, often associated with the presence of God or the Sun.</note> (or Michael, the Prince of the whole celestial host, who is the governor of the sun) seems to assign dominion to the prince of the globe of Saturn, namely *Caphiel*, over both the ethereal and elementary world; and so it is with the others.

Furthermore, the various effects of the Sun running through each house are seen and noticed every year. For instance, passing through Aries, it usually procures dry and violent winds (such as those that tend to blow in the month of March), and so on for the others.

The essential cause of this effect is the will of GOD, dwelling in the solar organ. By His gaze and intuition alone, or by a ray emitted to a star or the center of some organ, and with that divine spark reigning in it—assigning life and being to the whole composite—it is immediately received in a joyful and obedient manner, as if by a messenger and a brother of the same uncreated parent, from whom that spark of light was also derived. Hence "like rejoices in like" and nature delights in nature. Whereupon He suddenly seizes the nature of the whole stellar body, and the daemons ordained for the service of that star, to fulfill and perfect the will of the Commander in the ordinary course of the world—whether it be in procuring winds, or in bringing forth and drawing out rains, hail, snow, frost, or rime from the treasury-chest of GOD; or finally, in producing lightning, thunderbolts, thunder, comets, and other ignited meteors, both manifest and hidden. ### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...for himself, **God created the sun, the moon, the stars**, and other things for the service of all nations under heaven, according to Deuteronomy 4. He does not say that He created the Sun by His word and then afterwards the other stars from the sun; rather, by His own word, according to His own specific order and will, He created the sun separately along with the rest. For this reason, He made each of them distinct from one another in shape, property, and position. Thus it is said that our great Lord has counted the number of the stars and called as many as there are by their names, and with great strength and power. By this, the Prophet seems to imply that He assigned various names to them based on their various properties and virtues; we are persuaded of this because, in the phrasing of the words, he says, *our Lord is great and of many virtues*. So also **Adam** is said to have imposed names upon the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven—doubtless not frivolous or empty names, but ones suited to the property of each. By these things we are reminded that all stars in heaven were created distinctly from the sun, and yet on the same day—indeed, in the very same moment—not unlike the earth and every species of plant and animal. Though distinct from one another, they received from the Supreme Creator their own soul and a corporeal existence separate from the others; for in His word alone is the life and existence of every thing. And just as we see that the earth is illuminated at intervals and by turns by the solar face, from which day is generated in whichever hemisphere, so too are we taught by daily experience that the **moon** receives its waxing and waning from the splendor of the Sun. Yet, it is established that both the earth and the moon exist in their own proper natures even when solar light is absent.

But here, finally, a twofold question can arise: do all stars in the Heaven receive visible light from the Sun or not? And then, is any star altered or strengthened in its action or influence by the Sun’s aspect or its lucid power? To both questions at once we say (as has been reported by us before) that **Cicero** and others assign to all stars, with only one exception, their own light and splendor. However, the greater crowd of philosophers maintains that stars have very little of their own light or beauty from their creation; instead, they repeatedly say the stars are ignited and illuminated by the Sun. For this reason, **Heraclitus** called the Sun the "fountain of celestial light."

But as far as our own opinion is concerned, we say either that this last opinion of the Philosophers is false and inconsistent, or that the story told by **Eusebius** regarding the **universal Eclipse of the Sun** is a mere fable far removed from the truth. In that story, he relates that the day was turned into a dark night, so much so that the stars were seen in the heaven. If, therefore, this Eclipse were that universal one at the passion of our Lord **Jesus Christ** in that very hour—as he himself seems to infer—during which there was no interposition of the moon, it follows that this was a true failure of solar light. Consequently, the Sun, which had no light in itself at that time, could not give light to others as they likewise failed; yet, even in that same failure, the bright stars showed themselves to the eyes of men.

In any case, it is likely that although some of the stars had sparks of light for their own ornament at the instant of their creation, they nevertheless receive a notable and remarkable splendor from the solar rays, which are repressed by no failure of their own. This is no different than what one may see in the globe of the earth and the moon. Furthermore, because the supreme activity of any thing—be it greater or lesser—is discerned in the increase or decrease of its light, it is certain that the power and virtue of any of the wandering stars <note>The planets</note>, and indeed the fixed stars, is more fit and inclined to pour out such-and-such influences (whether simple or fixed) upon the lower realms through the conjunction of rays, or by opposition, or by a **trine, quartile, or sextile aspect**. <term>Aspects: The angular distances between celestial bodies that astrologers believe determine their influence. Trine is 120°, quartile (square) is 90°, and sextile is 60°.</term> For example, the Sun joining with **Saturn** produces sad, melancholic, and heavier effects, both in the higher elements and on the earth itself. Therefore, at this time, the "Saturnine" daemons or angels will have stronger effects in the elements, because the great angel **Metattron** (or **Michael**, Prince of the entire celestial host), who is the presiding officer of the sun, seems to assign dominion to the prince of the globe of Saturn, namely **Caphieli**, over both the ethereal and elementary world; and so it is with the others.

Furthermore, the various effects of the Sun as it runs through each **House** <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> are clearly noticed every year. For example, when passing through **Aries**, it tends to procure dry and violent winds (the kind that usually blow in the month of March), and so on for the others.

The essential cause of this effect is the **will of GOD** dwelling in the solar organ. By His gaze and intuition alone—or by a ray emitted to the center of a star or "organic" body—and with that divine spark reigning within it and assigning life and being to the whole composite, the command is immediately and joyfully accepted with obedience, as if by a messenger and a brother of the same uncreated parent from whom that spark of light was also derived. Hence, **like rejoices in like** <note>original: "simile simili gaudet"</note> and nature delights in nature. From this, the Sun suddenly seizes the entire nature of the stellar body, and the spirits <note>original: "dæmones"</note> ordained for the service of that star, to fulfill and perfect the will of the Emperor <note>God</note> in the ordinary course of the world. This might be in procuring winds, or in bringing forth rains, hail, snow, frost, or rime from the treasury of God’s storehouse; or finally, in producing lightning, thunderbolts, thunder, comets, and other ignited meteors, both manifest and hidden. We have expressed a model of this assertion here for the better comprehension of the readers' capacity, regarding the production of winds; in which demonstration the ray of the will—

Thus it is said that **GOD** has placed his tabernacle <note>original: *tabernaculum*; a reference to Psalm 19:4, suggesting the Sun is the "dwelling place" or tent of the divine presence</note> in the sun, and for this reason it is said elsewhere that any given thing claims as much of **GOD** for itself as it is capable of receiving light. Thus the wise man says: *the sun giving light looked upon all things, and his work is full of the glory of the Lord.* <note>Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 42:16</note> And David calls that soul, or created light, the Sun that gives life and glory <note>original: *Psal. 148. 12*; in modern Bibles this context is found in Psalm 84:11</note>, to which even the solar creature, along with the Prophet, can directly say: *if you light my lamp, O **JEHOVAH** my **GOD**, you will make my darkness shine.* <note>Psalm 18:28; original cites Psalm 18:29 following the Vulgate numbering</note>

In the aforementioned demonstration, therefore, we have an image of the three persons of one essence; namely, **יהוה** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God, translated here as Jehovah</note>, the source of the divine essence, as the Father outside of all things; the Word or the emanation from the source, as the Son within and outside all things, insofar as he is not divided from the Father, by whom the heavens were established; and the holy Spirit of discipline <note>A reference to the "Holy Spirit of discipline" from the Wisdom of Solomon 1:5</note>, flowing into all virtues or forms from every side, who, though arranging a tabernacle in the sun, is nevertheless not enclosed within the sun. He is in all things and outside all things, insofar as he proceeds from the source and the emanation simultaneously, yet his essence is not divided from them, as it is indivisible in all things.

And in this way you have it demonstrated how **GOD** gives life and inspiration <note>original: *inspirationem*; literally a "breathing into"</note> and all things to everyone, and by what means *in him we live, move, and have our being.* <note>Acts 17:28</note> Similarly, how *there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, etc.* <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note> Not that we are born from the sun, but that man, the Lord of all creatures, is adorned in his own spirit with such a divine breath <note>original: *afflatu*</note> as the sun, which is the most full vessel of the glory of the Most High. Indeed, all remaining creatures, although they have not received this divine gift in the same measure as the sun and man, have received it as well; wherefore both are called sons of God.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *That GOD created also a Microcosmic sun, by whose rays—illuminated by GOD—He is sometimes accustomed to perform miracles and acts beyond the laws of nature, even greater than those of the Macrocosmic Sun, which is established for the ordinary measurement of the year and the seasons. Finally, that it is the property of the invisible Sun present everywhere (by which these other suns are illuminated) to perform even greater works.*

<term>Microcosmic: referring to the 'little world' of the human being, which was believed to be a miniature reflection of the 'Macrocosm' or the great universe.</term>

From the properties of the sun that we have brought forward above, it has been clearly explained that **GOD** made the sun to rule over the day, *Psalm 136:8* <note>original: "in potestate diei"</note>; that is, so that it might look upon all things with its illumination. Likewise, it was made so that the days, the light, and the years might be separated, which was nonetheless done by the Lord through the science operating in the sun, *Ecclesiasticus 43* <note>The source text cites chapter 53, but this is a likely error for chapter 43, which discusses the sun's role in the heavens.</note>, as He who placed His tabernacle in it, *Psalm 19*. Furthermore, we have said that worldly things revive, multiply, and are warmed by means of the sun’s central power, and that the earth, the heavens, and the air are affected with various properties according to the sun's various aspects. Indeed, we have already expressed above, and will explain a little more broadly below, how they are sometimes disturbed and agitated by every kind of **meteor** <term>meteor: in this period, the term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</term>. All these things are so regular and ordinary in the course of nature that we would say they are produced not miraculously, but according to the paths of nature, so that not only Astrologers (by the varying positions of the stars) but even common folk and peasants are accustomed to predict and foresee these occurrences through diverse observation.

But truly, since He has established the temple of His Holy Spirit within the external man—in whose body, though it be vile, **Jesus** is said to dwell—by His own particular and proper breath, just as He placed His tabernacle in the worldly sun, so without doubt **JEHOVAH** acts as wonderfully in man through His wisdom dwelling in man's internal spirit as He does through that wisdom inhabiting the solar spirit of the world. For the works of **GOD** are wonderful everywhere, which He performs in wisdom. Yet, nonetheless, we shall find, if we look into the matter a little more accurately, that the delights of wisdom are with the sons of men, *Proverbs 8*. From this, He is accustomed to bring forth far greater things in man and through man’s organ than in the worldly sun. Indeed, this power of His is so excellent above that of the world that the worldly sun is sometimes observed to offer remarkable obedience to it. Thus said Joshua—or rather the word of **GOD**, or this Holy Spirit of discipline dwelling in Joshua:

-> Sun, stand still against Gibeon, and do not move; and the Sun stood still in the midst of heaven, *Joshua 10* <-

and it did not hasten to set for the space of one day. Furthermore, by the prayer of Hezekiah, his spirit was so pleasing before **GOD** that the Sun was forced to step back in its natural course and return against the laws of nature, *Isaiah 38* <note>The text cites chapter 39, but the miracle of the sun's shadow moving backward is recorded in chapter 38.</note>. Moreover, if it is within the power of the sun to produce clouds and winds in the ordinary way, it is within the power of the illuminated spirit to produce even greater things. For when the heavens were as brass and no rain was granted by God to the children of Israel, by the power of that spirit reigning in Elijah a small cloud like a man’s hand ascended from the sea, and immediately the heavens were darkened with clouds and wind, from which came a great rain, *1 Kings 18:41*. So also, lightning <note>original: "fulgur"</note> descending from heaven by the power of Elijah destroyed the captain with his fifty men, *2 Kings 1:12*. Thus, by the operation of that spirit in Moses, thunder and hail were brought forth from heaven; for when Moses extended his staff toward heaven, **Jehovah** brought forth hail and sounds <note>original: "sonos," meaning thunderclaps</note>, and fire ran along the ground, *Exodus 9*. And by the power of that spirit in those three chosen and illuminated men cast into the fiery furnace, all the violence of the fire was taken away so that it did not burn them at all. And by this most powerful spirit in **Christ**, the stormy tempest of the sea was mitigated in a moment, demons were cast out of human bodies, diseases miserably afflicting the wretched were cured, the dead were called back to life, fish and loaves were multiplied, water was changed into wine, and finally (and what is the miracle above all) the rage of death and the devil was suppressed, and the mortal body was made incorruptible and immortal; and finally, the worldly and celestial sun itself was forced to suffer at the passion of that body and be deprived of its light.

Hence it was that the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of his *Ethics* confessed that man is of such excellence and sublimity that he is in a way the end of all things. And **Hermes Trismegistus** says that man is a great miracle, a living being to be adored and honored, for he passes into the nature of **GOD**, and is as if he were **GOD** himself. And **Zoroaster** says: *you must ascend to the light itself, and to the rays of the father, from whence a soul was sent to you clothed in much mind.* And in another place **Hermes Trismegistus** says: *it will behoove you to ascend above the heavens, and to be far away from the choirs of demons.* And **Pythagoras** says: *if you, leaving the body, pass into the free ether, you shall be an immortal **GOD**.* But the Holy Scriptures, describing this more clearly, say: *He who adheres to **GOD** shall become one spirit with Him*, and elsewhere, *At last we shall be transformed into the same image.* Finally, as pertains to the other acts and wonderful operations of the illuminated human mind, from which it is manifest that the internal man is more excellent in dignity and efficacy than the worldly sun...

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...and is to be preferred, on account of that sacrosanct gift, namely the **God-like breath** <note>original: "spiraculum Deiforme"</note>, which was imparted to him by the Creator.

Hence, we also read in scripture that all creatures were ordained by the Creator for the use of human beings; and we are told by the holy elder <note>Likely a reference to a Church Father, such as St. Basil or St. Ambrose, in their commentaries on the six days of Creation (the Hexameron).</note> that the sun was made on the fourth day so that it might serve the human being yet to come. We could discuss infinite matters regarding these things here, but since the Holy Scriptures are everywhere filled with them, we shall return to the power of the said illuminated spirit in its aerial home. This spirit is present everywhere throughout the world and fills all things, according to that saying of the Prophet: *To you the Seraphim and Cherubim do not cease to cry out; heaven and earth are full of the majesty of your glory.* <note>A reference to the "Sanctus," a hymn based on Isaiah 6:3 and Ezekiel 3:12.</note> Therefore, it also works everywhere according to its own good pleasure, commanding its angels as if they were ministers who carry out its word and will, whether to produce fiery, windy, cloudy, or hail-filled **meteors** <term>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</term> to fulfill its purposes. It does this sometimes from its tabernacle in the Sun, sometimes from the human tabernacle, and most often from that vast worldly spirit which it fills on every side by saying "Let it be," and it is done. That is, by casting out a ray of its will to this or 그hat quarter of the world, immediately the angel having dominion over that quarter is moved, and sends out his windy legions to fulfill the commands and will of his most high Lord; hence the royal Prophet says:

> Angels of GOD, most mighty in strength, doing his word, listening to the voice of his word, ministers doing his pleasure. *Psalm 103:20*. And elsewhere: Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a burning fire. *Psalm 104:4*. <note>original: "Qui facit angelos suos ventos, & ministros suos ignem urentem."</note>

Hence also Baruch says, *The wind that blows through all regions obeys God in its blast.* <note>Baruch 6:60.</note> But regarding these things, we shall speak more broadly below.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### How the wisdom of God is the primary author and actor of the winds, both in the Microcosm and the Macrocosm.

In the preceding chapter, we said that angels are sometimes winds, and occasionally burning flames. But truly, how that great angel—who is the emanation or brightness of the omnipotent power—is the great Lord over these angels and governs them to perform the Father's will in the form of winds, we shall declare more fully in the following section. For we read, *that God or Divine Wisdom bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet; and he ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew or glided upon the wings of the wind.* <note>2 Samuel 22:10–11 and Psalm 18:9–10.</note> From this discourse, it is clear that just as the **Seraphim** are ministers burning with fiery love and serving before God, so indeed the **Cherubim** are aerial ministers, by whose act or movement in the air the winds are produced. Thus it is said that He ascended upon the Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the wind—that is, the aerial spirits existing under the power of the Cherubim and having power in the air—from which the winds are said by the Prophet to *perform the commands of God.* <note>Baruch 6:60.</note>

We have described this matter more fully before: how the will of God, included in the word "Let it be" <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, travels and is sent out with the emission of the Word to any creature. When the spark of that Word or Spirit joins with the spark dwelling in that creature (for both its formation and preservation), it seizes that creature entirely to fulfill the Creator's will without any resistance. This cannot be otherwise, because God is the sole Actor in every creature. Hence it happens that a creature, whether spiritual like the angelic ones or corporeal, is always ready at hand to fulfill the will of God—that is, to carry out His word and consequently His pleasure, according to that verse cited above: *Angels of God, most mighty in strength, doing his word, listening to the voice of his word—that is, by the word, doing his pleasure.*

And therefore, these intelligences are called "winds" insofar as the air is disturbed by their breath and movement at the divine will, and that quarter of the world is said to move from which these angelic spirits carry the spirit of Wisdom. They are moved at Wisdom's nod, wherever or whenever she wishes; whence it is said, *In her will the North wind blew.* <note>Ecclesiasticus 43:17.</note> But also elsewhere in clearer speech it says, *He who fits the weight to the air or wind, and weighs the waters in measure, makes a statute for the rain, and a path for the lightning of the thunders.* By this discourse, it is denoted that God, by His wisdom, fits the air in its light nature, and by agitating it through His ministers, He produces winds; and by compressing it to a denser degree, He procreates clouds, from which rains then arise. Likewise, by another adaptation and formation of the air, He produces the lightning and the thunder. For His flame-vomiting ministers are the formal causes of the inflamed air, just as they themselves are called winds in their invisible nature—which are heard but by no means seen.

From this, it is certain that the internal act of the winds or the angels disturbing the air is immediately from God; that is, a ray of the divine will joined with His own ray, which is of the same essence. For this reason, it is necessary that they be moved and incited with all effort to fulfill the divine will.
