### Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member I.

that thing is created by the agitation and action of the Word or of Divine Wisdom, as if by a leaf acting in the midst of the world, and this happens immediately, with no sublunary causes <note>Causes occurring beneath the moon, i.e., in the earthly realm of change and decay.</note> intervening, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and the Christian Philosophers of our own century have falsely believed.

We conclude, therefore, that nothing is clearer or more certain than that the winds are both ordained by God and procreated in His wisdom; and finally, they are sent forth into the open air of the world to execute the will of the Creator. This is indicated in the Sacred Font <note>The Bible.</note> in express words in this manner: the Psalmist says, *God brings forth the wind out of his treasuries* (Psalm 135:7). And elsewhere: *He drove the East wind in the heavens and by his power he brought in the South wind* (Psalm 78:26). Moreover, Job says that *God made a weight for the winds* (Job 28:25). And Moses says: *God sent a wind so that the waters might be calmed* (Genesis 8). And elsewhere: *Jehovah brought an East wind upon the land all that day* etc. (Exodus 10) *and he sent a mighty West wind* etc. And elsewhere: *a wind went forth from Jehovah and scattered quails brought from the sea toward the camp* (Numbers 11:31). Thus it is in other passages, from which it is clear enough that all winds come immediately from God, and they can by no means move or blow unless they are animated and incited by Him. 

Here it must be especially noted that God emits His ray, which produces these worldly blasts, from His various organs—namely, sometimes from a thick cloud, as in a hurricane <term>Ecnephia: a storm-wind breaking out of a cloud</term>, a fire-spout, or a whirlwind, and also blasts derived from His lightning; for after lightning or thunder has ceased for the day, winds very often tend to occur. Furthermore, it is also said that God flies upon the wings of the winds in the time of thunder, as will be discussed more widely below. Sometimes He accomplishes the effects of His will through the human temple in the form of wind, or in the repression of winds: Then, says Matthew, *Jesus, rising, commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm* (Matthew 8). Similarly, He emits His ray from the spiritual temple of Elijah to lead clouds and winds into the sky. 

From this, the infinite power of the "illuminated man" <note>A person spiritually enlightened by God, capable of understanding or influencing nature through divine grace.</note> is declared, which is accustomed to operate against the foreknowledge of soothsayers, diviners, and astrologers. Concerning this spirit of the illuminated man, Daniel speaks thus: *The King asks a mystery, which the wise men, the magicians, the diviners, and the seers are unable to show you; but there is a God in heaven revealing mysteries* (Daniel 2:27-28), that is, in the heaven of both the Microcosm <note>Man, the "little world."</note> and the Macrocosm <note>The Universe, the "great world."</note>. Whence, through this spirit, Daniel explained the dream and performed many other miracles which the wise men of this world could not understand by their own prudence. 

Finally, He is accustomed to emit His power from His excellent Macrocosmic organ, constantly governing worldly nature and preserving it according to the laws ordained by Him in the beginning. Therefore, the worldly spirit is rotated by His internal spirit, which is also to be gathered from these words of the wise man: *The sun, surveying all things in its circuit, the spirit goes on and returns into its circles* (Ecclesiastes 1:6). 

Furthermore, we gather from these words of the Prophet that this spirit, which emits winds from the four quarters of the world, is one and not multiple, although it is said to blow from diverse places: *Come, spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again* (Ezekiel 37:9). By these words, he indicates that there is but one "blower" or breathing spirit, though the winds are various; but back to the point. We see, taught by experience, that diverse ordinary winds are agitated every year by the worldly sun according to its various positions. It is observed every year that in the hottest time of summer, when the Sun enters the first part of Leo, the Dog Star <note>Sirius.</note> rises; this is preceded for the most part by eight days of those Northern winds which they call the Precursors <note>original: "Prodromos."</note>, as they run before the Etesian winds <term>Etesiae: annual Mediterranean winds that blow for 40 days in summer</term>. For two days after the rising of the Dog Star, those winds called the Etesian winds begin, which are Northern winds lasting for forty days. So too the setting of the constellation of the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergiliarum."</note>, which occurs 44 days after the autumn equinox, begins the Winter, which the wintry North wind is accustomed to accompany. Note also that Southern winds follow the Etesian winds and last until the rising of the star Arcturus (which rises eleven days before the autumn equinox). Furthermore, the West Wind <note>original: "Favonius."</note> is said to blow frequently from the western corner in the spring time, namely at its beginning; and the East Wind <note>original: "subsolanus."</note> from the east around the rising of the Pleiades, which rise at 26 degrees of Taurus; and so it is with the others. 

By these things we see how the worldly winds are excited in an almost customary manner from different quarters of the world, by grace of the sun's rays receiving its own rays in different ways upon different objects in heaven—both from their own properties and from the various methods of reflection, and also from the diverse mixing of celestial natures. All these objects, animated and made "pregnant" as it were by the solar rays, rain down forces into the sublunary air that differ from each other in nature and condition. This happens by the annual decree of the Creator placed in the sun, whose internal spirit, acting as the ruler and governor of the entire world, acts in a diverse manner upon the spirit of the world, so that the various natures in it—weighed in equal scales by the justice of the Creator—might be respected and preserved. Thus, various species of things in heaven as well as on earth and sea, and also in the air, are generated, multiplied, sustained, and altered by corruption according to the order of Nature. All these actions in the world depend on the Word of the Lord, who *placed his tabernacle in the sun* (Psalm 19:4). I mean that high and eternal spirit, *creating the heavens, stretching them out, establishing the earth and those things which sprout from it, giving breath to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those walking upon it* (Isaiah 42:5). Of whom it is said: *God does according to his will both in the powers of heaven and in the inhabitants of the earth, and there is none who may resist his hand or say, "Why have you done this?"* (Daniel 4:35). 

However, that all these things which seem to be cast out from the Sun are the works of God, and not of any creature, we gather from these words of the holy Priest: *God is most strong, who is the truth, and he turns the heaven in a circuit* (3 Esdras 4:34). Similarly, the wise man: *The beauty of heaven is the glory of the stars, God illuminating the world in the heights... he has encircled the heaven in the circuit of his glory, the hands of the Most High have opened it* etc. (Ecclesiasticus 43:9-12). Consequently, every influence from the heavens, every structure on the lands or in the sea, or any imperfect mixture in the air, is without doubt (with no subordinate cause interposed) from God, who is the author of all, *from whom, in whom, and through whom are all things*, as the Apostle holds.

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors <note>In the early modern period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>

How ridiculous then are the schools of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, who fashion so many fantastical efficient causes for the winds—namely, a hot exhalation seeking the heights, the heat of the sun elevating it and summoning it from the earth, and the intense cold of the middle region of the air. I leave this for you to consider, you who are raised up on the more precise wings of doctrine and the knowledge of truth.

Not without reason was man called **the microcosm** <note>Greek: *ὁ μικρόκοσμος*; meaning "the small world."</note> by the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle.</note>, insofar as he possesses the greatest likeness and analogy to the great world <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe.</note>. For he enjoys the same elements as that world, which are accustomed to act and be acted upon among themselves through similar actions and passions, as much in the one world as in the other. Indeed, it seems that the lesser world received the parts of its substance and being from that greater world, if we consider the matter a little more accurately; for in time and order, the latter preceded the former. Whence Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of wisdom texts (Hermetica) that bridge philosophy and religion.</note> did not hesitate to call man the son of the world, just as the world is the son of God.

And indeed, if we carefully weigh the words of the Prophet, we shall find them relevant to the Philosopher's proposition, where he speaks thus regarding the resurrection of the bones: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again* (Ezekiel 37:9). By these words, he seems to imply that life comes from that spirit which God bestowed upon the world for its existence and vivification. But however that may be, it is a certain and well-worn truth that just as God created one world by His breath of life, so also He created the other. That is, just as the Spirit of the Lord, which was carried over the waters in the great world, provided them with fiery vigor and created and animated its moist spirit, so indeed for the creation of man, He breathed the breath of life into the created spirit of man, whence *man was made into a living soul* (Genesis 2:7). I, says God, *creating the heavens and establishing the earth and those things which sprout from it, give breath to my own people, to him who is upon it* (Isaiah 42:5). From these things we gather that the life not only of the world but also of man took its beginning from the wind or divine inspiration.

Furthermore, just as we see the common spirit of the world divided into four elements, so too not only the human spirit (which we also call air) but also the body participates in these elements. Indeed, we see that the air of both worlds enjoys its own proper sun: for the heart performs its office in the human spirit no differently than the Macrocosmic sun does in its own. But truly, we see with open eyes that just as man’s primary power was from the inspiration of Him who placed His tabernacle in the sun, and he received the parts of his constitution from the air and elements of the world, it is necessary that there be a continuous relationship both between the incorruptible spirit in the sun and that in the heart—seeing as both are but a single thing in essence—and also between the air of the world and that of man. Both are from one and the same source, and both enter into this same common office with one another: namely, that the bright spirit of the Creator flies upon the wings of both winds or spirits, and is carried as if by a vehicle or chariot.

And just as in the world that aerial spirit is divided into three regions, of which one is placed before the other in dignity and purity, so indeed is this spirit in man. It is divided into the **animal and intellectual spirit** in the brain (or the highest heaven), related to the Empyrean or Angelic spirit of the world; and the **vital spirit** in the heart, compared to that ethereal world; and the **natural spirit** in the liver, having respect for the sublunary region of the world <note>The author is mapping the three "spirits" of traditional Galenic medicine—animal, vital, and natural—onto the three layers of the universe.</note>. From this it arises that there is such a great proximity—indeed, even a continuity—between these two spirits and bright souls, which are in effect of one essence governing them, so that in later time, namely for the Microcosm, it cannot exist without the assistance and presence of the former. For this cause Heraclitus said quite sensibly: *If you take the Sun out of the world, what is our little body?* If the soul be absent, no pulsing vein is drawn there, no vital breath is in it, no respiration at all.

And it is from this that the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> maintained that man cannot be generated by man unless the sun is assisting, etc. Whence comes his axiom: *The Sun and man generate man.* For this reason, therefore, man (for we are now dealing with his sympathy with the worldly spirit) is said to live as long as he breathes. Therefore, antiquity rightly ascribed the spirits—which the more excellent physicians estimate as the "innate heat"—moving the body, exciting the senses, and nourishing thoughts and minds, to the sun (which moves all things like an instrument, and is the organic cause of all living things through that incomparable spirit which inhabits its center). These spirits, according to the testimony of Homer, are said to be present in us daily in such a way as the worldly Sun, Prince of the planets, breathes out, moves, radiates, and prepares, concocts, and refines through the medium of the sublunary air. 

Which air alone, on the testimony of Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> and also by experience itself, whatever its state may be, we are compelled—whether we wish it or not—continually and necessarily to inhale. By the aid of the lungs, we draw it through the mouth and the rough artery <note>The trachea.</note>, and from there again into the left chamber of the heart, which is most full of the spirits that enliven the body and restore and nourish the animal power. In addition to this, we receive it into the brain through the nostrils, and into the entire body—which is entirely "breathable" <note>Original: *conspirabile*; a term used in early medicine to describe how the body is porous and can "breathe" through all its parts.</note>—through the connections of the arteries and the pores. It is from this, therefore, that according to the state of the air in the sky and the sun in the air, we find our own spirit also disposed, wandering everywhere in the blood, the viscera, and through the flesh. ### Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. IV. Membr. I.

...more than in another, we feel our spirits to be either duller, slower, and more prone to melancholy, or sharper, lighter, and more inclined to joy. This, indeed, can be seen and noticed not only in humans, but even in the brute animals themselves. For it is natural for beasts and birds to be cheered, to chirp, and as it were to laugh in clear air and a limpid sky, but during a dark, gloomy, and cloudy sky where rain is present, to be saddened and as it were to groan, which is confirmed for us by the following speech of the poet <note>Virgil, in his *Georgics* (I. 418-423), describing how animals sense changes in the weather.</note>:

> *The paths have changed, and Jupiter, moist with the south winds,*
> *Thickens what was just now thin, and thins what was thick;*
> *The forms of their minds are turned, and their bodies*
> *Now conceive other motions than those they felt while the wind drove the clouds.*
> *Hence comes that chorus of birds in the fields,*
> *And the joyful cattle, and the ravens exulting from their throats.*

From this it is clear that the spirits of men are refreshed by the clarity of the world’s light, and on the other hand, the sublunary world itself <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the region below the moon (Earth), which was thought to be subject to change and decay.</note> seems to be refreshed and to rejoice at the clear sight of the sun. This is because by the presence of divine glory—which is in the sun as if most full of divinity—any spirit, whether in the world or in the creatures within it, is irradiated, exults, is excited, and seems to leap with cheerfulness. For there is a perpetual appetite in matter to be shaped by the beauty and lucid presence of the Creator; thus, the more it is deprived of Him through sad obscurity, the more it is disturbed. It seems to approach the boundaries of privation and, consequently, to move further away from the lucid act of the Creator. Yet, as Augustine and others testify, the more light something has within itself, the more it seems to claim of God for itself.

Therefore, it is for this reason that in sad, thick, and dark air, the lower world seems to mourn, be disturbed, and saddened. Through consensus and a close kinship (so to speak), the spirit of man also seems to sicken and be disturbed, so that even in bodies that have not moved beyond the limits of health, one seems to be affected by an unexpected sadness, heaviness, and grief. It is as if one were to say that because God hides the splendor of His face, both the spirit of the world and of its creatures are affected by the sickness of grief and sadness. Indeed, we read this very thing in the express words of the prophet: *All creatures look to God; when God gives to them, they gather; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated; when He hides His face, they are troubled; when He takes back their spirit, they expire.* <note>Original Latin: *Omnes creaturæ inquit à Deo habent expectationem... Pfal. 104.* This refers to Psalm 104:27-30.</note> This speech arises as much from the visible light which has its origin in God—and the visible light is the image of the invisible—as from that invisible light from which we primarily have our life and Being.

<margin>§</margin> But I will gird myself more closely to the matter and say that if there is such a relationship between the spirits of both worlds <note>The Macrocosm (universe) and Microcosm (man).</note>, if the life of both is an inspiration or breath and a life-giving wind proceeding from the mouth of the Almighty, and if the disturbances of one follow those of the other, then it must consequently follow that the various agitations of the winds or air of the one produce similar effects in the other. 

Regarding the microcosmic winds, and the four quarters of them corresponding to those of the greater world, we have spoken clearly in our treatise *On Mystic Anatomy*. There, we compared (not without wit) the <term>Spleen</term> <note>Original: *Lienem*. In humoral theory, the spleen was the seat of black bile and melancholy, associated here with the North.</note> with the northern region, the <term>liver</term> <note>Original: *hepar*. Associated with the hot/moist South.</note> with the southern, and the region of the <term>chest</term>, where the seat of the <term>heart</term> resides, with the corner of the East where the Sun rises, and finally the fourth part of all the viscera with the West. Therefore, we do not intend to say more about them in this place. 

But as far as the present purpose is concerned, it is certain that just as the benign property of God produces gentle and beneficial winds both in the world and in man for the life and recreation of both the elements and the elemental beings, so for example, <term>Ehieh</term> <note>A Hebrew name for God, "I Am," associated with the highest Sephirah.</note> graciously rains down benevolent influences and breaths through the lucid gate of <term>Cheter</term> <note>Keter, the "Crown" (the first Sephirah).</note> or the Crown. These incline toward fiery love in the world, by which means the world was created. Likewise, <term>Elim</term> <note>A divine name associated here with mercy.</note> rains warmth and moisture into nature through its lucid gate <term>Chesed</term> <note>Chesed, "Mercy" (the fourth Sephirah).</note> into the creatures of the world, via the sphere and star of Jupiter. It pours out benevolent breaths of life, which is why Jupiter is called the "benevolent planet" in the procreation of living things and the preservation of their life. 

So also solar influences from the gate <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>Tiphareth, "Beauty" (the sixth Sephirah).</note> distribute and breathe out the heat of life to creatures everywhere, and by these the world is wonderfully recreated. Hence we see the spring winds produced by the breathing of benevolent winds—sometimes blowing through the earth with a suitable dryness and gently drying it, as in the month of March, and sometimes moistening the field with pleasant and fertile rains, as in the month of April. By their breath, both the earth of the Macrocosm and the entire mass of the Microcosm are purified and receive the necessities of life. 

The western and eastern winds also greatly favor human life; they are observed to breathe utility into both plants and other living creatures. These benevolent breaths are exhaled by God, full of mercy and clemency, in His beneficial property. Hence in the springtime the blood is renewed. Breaths of this kind occur in every season of the year, according to the good pleasure and mercy of God toward men, by which they live healthily and for the most part escape from diseases. 

But truly, in His other property contrary to this, He is noted to act contrarily; for in His wrath He is observed to act severely with the sublunary spirit, and also with the waters and the earth and their creatures, on account of the sins of men. Whence it happens that in His name <term>Elohim</term> <note>The Hebrew name for God associated with judgment and severity.</note>, exhaling the effects of His property through the lucid gate of <term>Binah</term> <note>Binah, "Understanding" (the third Sephirah), which Fludd links here to Saturn and severity.</note> into the sphere of Saturn...

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.
<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, snow, and lightning.</note>

From Saturn, these influences are then rained down into the elemental region. This usually results in a severe treatment of the world and its creatures; that is, by God turning His face away from His creations and binding the heavens with thick and opaque clouds, fostering winter chills and their effects, and by stirring up and agitating the actions of human life. It is for this reason that northern winds procreate cold, which is most opposed to the life of mortals and induces stupor and insensibility. Furthermore, sometimes **Jehovah** <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible.</note> in His wrath pours out fiery breaths and burning spirits from the fiery gate of *Geburath* <note>original: "Geburath"; the Sephirah Gevurah, representing Might or Severity.</note> by the power of His name *Elohim Gibbor* <note>original: "Elohim Gibbor"; meaning God the Mighty.</note>, through the sphere of Mars, under the guidance and leadership of *Samael*, the fiery angel who is malicious toward the life of creatures. From this follow lightnings, flashes, and hot, ignited winds; because of these fiery emissions of **Jehovah**, He is called a consuming fire, both in the Great World <term>Macrocosm</term> and the Little World <term>Microcosm</term>. Furthermore, the ultimate extremity of severity in God is seen in the property of His surname *Adonai* <note>original: "Adonai"; meaning The Lord.</note>, which sends back the influx of His will from the shining gate of *Malcuth* <note>original: "Malcuth"; the Sephirah Malkuth, or Kingdom.</note> through the body and sphere of the Moon, whence come floods, inundations, and vehement rains in the Great World; and in the Microcosm, such diseases as dropsy, catarrhs, and other watery ailments. Hence arises the occasion for diseases, both cold and hot, joined with dryness or moisture, as will be discussed in their proper places.

Therefore, in the attribute of His clemency, the first of which is called *Ehieh* <note>original: "Ehieh"; from Exodus 3:14, "I Am that I Am."</note>, moved by mercy, He is changed into the condition of a father; and in this sense it is said: *God said this, creating the heavens, stretching them out, establishing the earth and the things that spring from it, giving breath to the people, and spirit to those who walk upon it.* <note>Isaiah 42:5.</note> In this speech, the Prophet shows that God, in His first attribute, created and generated as it were the world, and then afterward the rest of the creatures, both vegetable and animal, and especially man by His breath or spirit; and in the manner of a father, He looks upon His children with clemency and as it were paternal love, and preserves them by the continuation of that same breath or spark of life. Furthermore, in respect to this attribute, it is said that God created all things that they might exist, and He made the nations of the world healthy, and there is no medicine of destruction in them, nor is the kingdom of the underworld upon the earth; and that He did not make death, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living.

In the second attribute of His benevolence toward created things, by reason of which He is called *El* <note>original: "El"; a Hebrew name for God implying power or kindness.</note>, He treats His creatures benevolently; and moved by mercy, He is accustomed to remove them from those curses with which He sometimes afflicts them for their sins. This is evident in the recovery of Miriam <note>The text uses "Maria," referring to Miriam, the sister of Moses.</note> from her leprosy, for whose healing Moses bent God with prayers through the name *El*, saying: *El, na, rapha, na, la*, that is, *O God of grace, heal, I pray, her.* In this sense, David also said: *Heal me, O Jehovah, for my bones are troubled.* <note>Psalm 6:3.</note> In this place, he also seems to imply that the medicine of **Jehovah** is His grace, mercy, and kindness; whence he says elsewhere: *I cried out to You and You healed me, and You kept me alive so that I should not go down into the pit.* <note>Psalm 30:2-3.</note> And elsewhere: *Your mercy is from the heavens; O how precious is Your kindness and mercy, when the sons of men take refuge under the shadow of Your wings.* <note>Psalm 36:7.</note> And the Apostle says that mercy and grace far surpass the nature of sin. <note>Romans 5:20.</note> And in another sense: *Your visitation preserves my spirit.* <note>Job 10:12.</note> Hence Jupiter is called the favorer of human nature. Finally, in Your third attribute, namely that by which the influx of graces and beauty rains into the sphere of the Sun through the shining gate of *Tiphereth* <note>original: "Tiphereth"; the Sephirah Tiferet, meaning Beauty or Harmony.</note>, that is, grace and beauty, it is read that *the Sun is giving glory and grace.* <note>Psalm 84:11.</note> And elsewhere: *The fountain of life is with You.* <note>Psalm 36:9.</note> Hence the Sun is called by philosophers the author of life and the father of multiplication among the worldly organs. Furthermore, from the surname of God *Sadai* <note>original: "Sadai"; Shaddai, the Almighty.</note>, from the shining gate of *Iesed* <note>original: "Iesed"; the Sephirah Chesed, meaning Mercy or Loving-kindness.</note>, that is, redemption, we have the benevolent influxes of redemption and salvation, concerning which attribute the King understands when he says: *You shall save men and beasts, etc.* <note>Psalm 36:6.</note>

In the first of the attributes tending toward severity, from which He is called *Elohim*, which passes through *Binah* <note>original: "Binah"; the Sephirah of Understanding, often associated with restriction or form.</note>, He pours punishments and slaughters upon the earth. For in this, God is accustomed to exercise His power by punishing the wicked, and the ministers in this attribute are those angels who are called *Bene Elohim*, that is, the sons of *Elohim*. *Elohim*, therefore, signifies terror and the earth, and its place in the world is the north, from which all evil comes. Such influxes pass through the sphere of Saturn, which is why this planet is called the "Greater Malefic" by astrologers. In this kind of attribute, God persecuted the Egyptians with palpable darkness and similar plagues, and also when **Jehovah** sent down great hailstones from heaven, with which He slew the enemies of the Israelites. <note>Joshua 10:11.</note> By the same reasoning, He produces earthy and stupid effects in man, and even melancholic and timid ones, through those angels. Thus it is said that Miriam appeared white with leprosy—an evil which He afterward healed in His mercy by changing the surname *Elohim* into *El*. And elsewhere: *Jehovah struck the people of Ashdod with hemorrhoids.* <note>1 Samuel 5:9.</note> And in this attribute, it is said that **Jehovah**, meeting Moses on his journey, wished to kill him. <note>Exodus 4:24.</note> And elsewhere: *I will cause terror to rule over you, with consumption.* <note>Leviticus 26:16.</note> Similarly, in this attribute He poured His evil spirit into Saul, taking away the good spirit which He had granted him in *El* or grace; and in infinite other instances. Similarly, in such a disposition of His, joined with that of *Elohim Gibbor*, He is described in such a form of terror in the persecution of the unjust: *Smoke went up in His anger, and fire from His face burned; coals were kindled by Him. He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under His feet. And He ascended upon the Cherubim, He flew upon the wings of the winds. He made darkness His secret place, His pavilion round about Him: dark waters in the clouds of the air. At the brightness before Him, the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightnings.* <note>Psalm 18:8-14.</note>

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...more than in another, we feel our spirits either duller, slower, and more prone to melancholy, or sharper, lighter, and more inclined toward joy. Indeed, this can be seen and noticed not only in human beings, but even in the beasts themselves. For it is natural for beasts and birds to be cheered, to chirp, and as it were to laugh in clear air and a bright sky; but in a dark, gloomy, and cloudy sky when rain is present, they become sad and seem to groan. This is confirmed for us by the following verses of the poet:

> But when the storm and the shifting moisture of the sky 
> Have changed their paths, and Jupiter, wet with southern winds, 
> Thickens what just now was thin, and thins what was thick, 
> The images of their minds are turned, and their bodies 
> Now conceive different movements than those they had while the wind drove the clouds: 
> Hence comes that chorus of birds in the fields, 
> And the joyful cattle, and the ravens croaking with triumph.
<note>This is a quotation from Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 1, lines 417–423. Virgil explains that animals react to changes in atmospheric pressure and humidity, which Fludd interprets as a shift in their "inner spirits."</note>

From this it is clear that the spirits of men are refreshed by the brightness of the world’s light, and likewise the sublunary <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> world itself seems to be refreshed and to rejoice at the clear sight of the sun. For by the presence of divine glory—which is most full of divinity in the sun—every spirit, both in the world and in the creatures within it, is irradiated, exults, is stirred up, and seems to leap with joy. For there is a perpetual appetite in matter to be formed by the beauty and bright presence of the Creator; thus, the more it is deprived of Him through sad darkness, the more it is disturbed. It seems to approach the boundaries of "privation" <note>A philosophical term meaning the absence of a natural quality, often associated with decay or non-existence.</note> and, consequently, to distance itself from the bright act of the Creator. Yet, as Augustine and others testify, the more light a thing has in itself, the more it seems to claim of God for itself. 

Therefore, it is for this reason that in sad, thick, and dark air, the lower world seems to mourn, to be disturbed, and to be saddened. Through a shared feeling and a close "kinship" (if I may call it that), the spirit of man also seems to grow sick and disturbed, so that even in bodies that have barely strayed beyond the limits of health, they seem to be affected by an unexpected sadness, heaviness, and grief. It is as if one were to say that when God hides the splendor of His face, the spirit of both the world and its creatures are affected by the sickness of that very grief and sadness. We read this very thing in the express words of the Prophet: *All creatures,* he says, *look to God; when God gives to them, they gather it up; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated; when He hides His face, they are troubled; when He takes away their breath, they die.* <note>original: "Psal. 104"; reference to Psalm 104:27-30. Fludd links the "breath" or "spirit" of the Psalm to both physical air and divine light.</note> This discourse has its origin both in visible light and in God; visible light is the invisible image of Him from whom we fundamentally have our life and Being.

But I will gird myself more closely to the matter at hand and say: if such a relationship exists between the spirit of each world—if the life of both is an inspiration, or a breath and life-giving wind proceeding from the mouth of the Almighty—and if the disturbances of one follow those of the other, then it must consequently follow that various agitations of the winds or air in the one produce similar effects in the other. 

Regarding the winds of the <term>Microcosm</term> (the Little World, or Man) and their four quarters corresponding to those of the <term>Macrocosm</term> (the Great World, or Universe), we have spoken clearly in our treatise *On Mystical Anatomy*. There, we compared the Spleen to the northern region, the Liver to the southern, the region of the chest (where the heart sits) to the corner of the East where the Sun rises, and finally the fourth part of all the bowels to the West. Therefore, we do not intend to say more about them in this place; but as pertains to the present purpose, it is certain that just as the benign property of God produces mild and beneficial winds in both the world and in man for the life and recreation of the elements and their compounds, so for example **Ehieh** <note>original: "Ehieh"; the Hebrew name of God meaning "I Am."</note> graciously rains down benevolent influences and breaths through the bright gate of **Cheter** <note>original: "Cheter"; the Sephirah Kether, meaning "The Crown."</note> (or the Crown). These incline toward a fiery love in the world, by which the world was created. 

Likewise, **Elim** <note>original: "Elim"; a name of God signifying might.</note> rains warmth and moisture into nature through its bright gate **Chesed** <note>original: "Chesed"; the Sephirah of Mercy.</note> into the creatures of the world, through the sphere and star of Jupiter, and pours out benevolent breaths of life. Hence Jupiter is called a benevolent planet in the procreation of living things and the preservation of their life. In the same way, the solar influx from the gate of **Tiphereth** <note>original: "Tiphereth"; the Sephirah of Beauty, associated with the Sun.</note> distributes and breathes out the heat of life to creatures everywhere, and by these the world is wonderfully refreshed. Hence we see the spring winds produced by the breathing of these benevolent spirits: sometimes blowing through the earth with a suitable dryness to dry it gently (as in the month of March), and sometimes moistening the field with pleasant and fertile showers (as in the month of April). By their breath, both the earth of the Macrocosm and the entire mass of the Microcosm are purified and receive the necessities of life. Even the western and eastern winds greatly favor human life; they are observed to breathe utility into both plants and other living beings. These benevolent breaths are exhaled by God, who is full of mercy and clemency in His beneficial property. Hence, in the springtime, the blood is usually renewed; such breaths can occur in any season of the year according to the good pleasure and mercy of God toward men, by which they live healthily and for the most part escape disease.

198 Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

<margin>Psalm 17</margin> With these words, the Prophet <note>Likely referring to David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> perfectly denotes and describes the mixed power of Martial fire <note>Associated with the planet Mars.</note> combined with the horrendous and fearsome shadows of Saturn. This represents the quality of <term>Elohim Gibbor</term> <note>Hebrew: "God the Mighty," the divine name associated with the Sephirah of Gevurah (Severity).</note>, the gate of <term>Geburah</term> <note>Gevurah: The attribute of Strength or Judgment.</note> joined with that of <term>Binah</term> <note>Binah: Understanding, often associated with Saturn in Hermetic Qabalah.</note>. In this severe quality of the second order—by which He is called *Elohim Gibbor*—God emits His outpourings through the bright gate of *Geburah*. He puts on a fiery nature and is called a "consuming fire." His ministers, who carry out this specific quality, are the fiery angels, <margin>Psalm 104</margin> of whom the Psalmist speaks, saying that He "makes His angels winds and His ministers a flaming fire." <note>original: "facit angelos eius ventos & ministros suos ignem ardentem"</note> Hence Job also says: "Will you send forth lightnings, and they will go, and say to you, 'Here we are'?" <margin>Job 38</margin> In this sense, the Prophet speaks elsewhere: <margin>Psalm 18:8</margin> "He rained down coals upon the wicked, fire and sulfur, and the spirit of storms is the portion of their cup." And elsewhere: "Smoke rose from the nostrils of Jehovah, and fire from His mouth... and shooting forth lightnings, He scattered them." Furthermore, in another place, he describes how God, in His burning heat, is accustomed to afflict the impious through the mediation of His fiery ministers. "Will you be angry forever?" (says David). "Pour out your heat upon other nations that do not know you, for the consumer has consumed Jacob," <margin>Psalm 7, 9, 5</margin> where by "the consumer" he understands a minister or an afflicting angel of God. And elsewhere: "You multiplied lightnings and troubled them." <margin>Psalm 17</margin> Similarly, He sent a rainy flame of sulfur and whirlwinds upon Sodom and Gomorrah for their sins. <margin>Genesis 19</margin> And elsewhere: "Fire coming out from the presence of Jehovah took the life from the sons of Aaron, and they died before Jehovah." <margin>Leviticus 10:12</margin> And elsewhere: "A fire going out from Jehovah consumed those 250 men who had offered incense." <margin>Numbers 16:35</margin> And elsewhere: "The burning wrath of Jehovah shall remain in this place, and shall not be extinguished." <margin>2 Kings 22</margin> Moreover, it is said that vengeful angels of a fiery disposition are the ministers in this action, as fire is admitted from Jehovah into Babylon, which shall finally and for a long time be inhabited by demons. <margin>Baruch 4:35</margin>

But it must also be observed that this fiery quality of God operates sometimes visibly and sometimes invisibly upon disobedient men. Finally, this malignant fire frequently operates within the <term>macrocosmic spirit</term> <note>The "world-soul" or atmosphere of the universe.</note> to cause either the disturbance or the total destruction of that "smallest world" <note>The human body, or Microcosm.</note>. We gather this from many passages of Holy Scripture. <margin>Wisdom 19:13</margin> "By the power of lightnings," says the wise man, "punishments come upon the wicked." And elsewhere, the Holy Page speaks thus of the human spirit corrupted by the vengeful fire of God: "The anger of Jehovah was kindled against Israel, and the plague was restrained from proceeding further; there were those who died from that plague, 24,000." <margin>Numbers 25</margin> Furthermore, elsewhere, the arrows of God are plagues, "the poison of which the spirit of man drinks up." <margin>Job 6:4</margin> And elsewhere: "Let the plague cleave to you until it has consumed you." And elsewhere: <margin>Deuteronomy 28:12</margin> "Jehovah will strike you with consumption, and with a hot, burning, and parching fever, and with drought and blight, and they shall pursue you until you perish," and so on in other cases. From these, it is clear enough that just as lightnings are subtle and fiery winds sent by God to exercise His will here on earth, so also febrile and pestilential winds in the "human air" <note>The vital spirits or breath within the body.</note> are very similar to them in nature, operation, and effect. Just as winds breathed into the earth cause earthquakes, and as those produced in the air by the severe quality of God produce black clouds and make the sky, air, and sea tumultuous, so too do similar effects—procreated by external winds—arise in the air, the humors, and the human "earth" <note>The solid parts of the body.</note>.

The reason is readily available: because, <term>namely</term>, the Microcosmic air is the son of the Macrocosmic air, and is linked to it by such a natural bond that the one (of the Microcosm) cannot live, exist, or remain without the other. Hence Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and all those most skilled in medicine, posit that a change in the human air occurs following the alteration of the world’s air by the winds, both in sickness and in health; they have explained this abundantly in their books on *Epidemic Diseases*, on *Ephors*, and on *Flatus* <note>Intestinal gas or "winds" in the body.</note>. Hence we also read in Isidore that the North Wind <note>Septentrionalis/Boreas</note> makes the air pure and clear, hardens bodies, and closes the pores, whereby it purifies the humors, makes the spirit of man clear, aids digestion, rectifies pestilential air, and assists the power of generation. Thus Aristotle maintains that if the wind is northerly during conception, the infant will be male; if southerly, female. And Constantine <note>Constantine the African, a medieval medical translator.</note> says in Book 5, Chapter 1, that the North Wind represses bad humors, though it also sometimes induces dryness of the chest, a cough, and roughness of the lungs; it makes the limbs numb and makes <term>Phthisis</term> <note>Tuberculosis or "wasting disease."</note> severe, and this is because of its cold and dry disposition.

Similarly, the South Winds <note>Australes</note> make the air thick and cloudy, open the pores, multiply rains and sometimes thunder, and corrupt the air, etc. And Bede recognizes that the South Wind acts in the human air and body just as it does with the sky and earth of the world; hence he says that it opens the pores of the body, hinders the power of sensation by thickening [the spirits], and induces a heaviness of the body. In this, he seems to agree with Hippocrates, who also arrived at this opinion: that this wind dulls the hearing, makes it difficult, affects the head, and does not bind or strengthen the humors, but rather dissolves them, calling them out from the interior toward the exterior, and bringing pestilential diseases, along with many other things of which we speak more fully in our *Preternatural History of the Microcosm*.

We conclude, therefore, that since three spirits are reckoned in this world—namely the Divine (which is primary), the Mundane, and that of the creatures—and because these spirits are derived successively from one another (namely, the secondary is driven either peacefully or tumultuously by the motion of the first, in the manner of a body moved by a soul either gently or violently, and again the third by both), it is necessary to believe that all these spirits, when put into action, are considered and held to be blasts and winds. But this is the greatest difference between these spirits: the first is uncreated, splendid, and primordial, animating the others—the light of the world and the breath of life; the two lower ones are air, blast, spirit, and of a foreign, moist nature.

For He is the God and Lord of both soul and body, the mighty God of spirits, and the God of all flesh, as we read in the Bible of all truth, *Numbers 16:22.* To Him, therefore, be praise and honor forever; to Him we must also turn our thoughts with all our soul and heart, and entreat Him with faithful prayers, that by His benevolent breath, full of mercy, He might deliver us from our infirmities and preserve us unharmed until the end from His destroying spirits or ministers. ### CHAPTER XIX.

## That clouds, snow, hail, frost, and other such dark meteors are procreated by the winds of God in the air; and how God is the sole and unique author and actor in their creation.

That God is the actor and origin not only of the winds but also of all other <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note>, and that He works through various "organs" of the world for their procreation, the wise man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach).</note> demonstrates to us most clearly and in truly golden words:

->*The firmament of the height is his beauty, the appearance of heaven in a vision of glory. The Sun, when it appears, announcing at its rising: a wondrous vessel, the work of the Most High. At noon it parches the earth, and who can endure its burning heat? As one guarding a furnace in the work of heat, so the Lord is great who made it, and by His words it hastens its journey. And the moon in all things in its season shows the timing and the sign of the age. From the moon is the sign of a feast day, a light that decreases at the end of the month; according to its name it increases wonderfully in its completion, a vessel of the camps in the heights, shining gloriously in the firmament of heaven. The beauty of heaven, the glory of the stars, the Lord illuminating the world in the heights; at His holy words they shall stand in judgment, and they shall not fail in their watches, etc. Ecclesiasticus 43:1–12.*<-

By these words, the wise man first clearly denotes that the stars are the only "organs" of heaven by means of which God illuminates all things and operates upon the lower things for the procreation of every kind of meteor. Hence he calls the sun a "wondrous vessel," because in that which is called the "work of the Most High," it is recognized as a creature and not the creator. How God acts through the sun is explained there: namely, by heat and fervor, by which the "human furnace" is preserved in its work of heat—that is, all things are generated, preserved, and finally, having been brought to the period of a new generation in the circle of nature, they perish; that is, they are deprived of their preceding form. Furthermore, with the lunar organ, He distinguishes the seasons of the year into days and months. 

Finally, he concludes that it is not the sun, but the Lord in the sun or any other star, who is the beauty of heaven, according to that saying: *By His spirit He has adorned the heavens, the glory of the stars, Job 26.* <note>original: "Spiritu suo cœlos ornauit"</note> Whence it is said: *The Sun giving grace and glory, Psalm 84:12,* and the "illuminator of the world"; thus He is handed down as the light of the world, by which the world was made, *John 1.* Therefore, by means of such visible organs or instruments of the world, God produces His meteors in the sublunary world. Indeed, the said wise man seems to confirm this immediately in the following verses:

->*Look upon the rainbow, and bless Him who made it; it is very beautiful in its brightness. It encompasses the heaven in the circle of its glory; the hands of the Most High have fitted it. By His command He has hastened the snow, and hastens to send forth the lightnings of His judgment. Therefore the treasures are opened, and the clouds fly out like birds. In His greatness He has placed the clouds, and the hailstones are broken. At His sight the mountains were moved, and by His will the South wind breathed. The voice of His thunder has struck the earth, the storm of the North wind and the gathering of the spirit; and like a bird lighting to sit, He scatters the snow, and pours out frost like salt upon the earth. The cold North wind blew, and the crystal froze in the water, etc. Ecclesiasticus 43:12.*<-

By these words, it is clearly indicated that God is the author of all kinds of meteors: namely, the rainbow, snow, hail, mist, cloud, wind, thunder, lightning, storm, the gathering of spirits, frost, ice, etc. We say that the generation of clouds is ordained by God according to the order of the mundane nature, and then God mostly operates from His "solar tabernacle," and also by means of other celestial instruments—

...in the heavenly bodies, by the observation of whose courses astrologers are accustomed to judge changes in the air: or He <note>Referring to God as the primary actor.</note> uses a human instrument to produce them. The "Philosopher" mentioned here likely refers to Aristotle, who discussed weather in his *Meteorologica*.</note>, according to the Philosopher, since they are observed to be stirred by the sun in its ordinary annual course. We read, therefore, that the winds alter the air into any given disposition. For the **North Wind** <note>original: "Aquilonaris"</note> produces cold and converts the air into snow, frost, rime, and hail, and is accustomed to drive away the rain. The **South Wind** <note>original: "Auster"</note> produces clouds by thickening the air, bringing storms, rains, and lightning and thunder, and it even renders the air contagious to animals. The **East Wind** <note>original: "Eurus"</note> scorches the fruits, stirs up storms at sea, and both heats and disturbs the air; hence the Psalmist says: **With the East wind you break the ships of the Ocean** (*Psalm 48:8*). Finally, the winds are the occasions for all <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, rather than just space rocks.</note>, for every substantial transformation of the air, and even the agent of alteration; they were the minister of the division of the Red Sea, and again of its rejoining and bonding; the author of the bringing of locusts into the land of the Egyptians and their subsequent expulsion, and the transportation of quails into the camp of the Israelites; the disturber of the Ocean; and finally, the procreator and generator of all things in this world, whether imperfectly or perfectly mixed. Indeed, the winds are the performers of the will and voice of the Lord, who, dwelling centrally within them, moves them wherever and however He pleases; hence they are called the breaths of God, **which He is accustomed to send into the world to fulfill His pleasure** (*Job 37:3*).

We say, therefore, that the Name or Word of God primarily moves the winds, which in their external form are nothing other than air in motion, but their internal part is the clarity of the Almighty, by which they are animated, governed, and arranged according to the will of the Creator to carry out God’s commands. Therefore, when God wishes to create rain clouds in the world, a greater ray of His will joins with its likeness in the wind—specifically the **South Angel** <note>The angel associated with the South Wind.</note>, or <term>Uriel</term> <note>Uriel is the archangel typically associated with the South and with the element of fire or light.</note>, who presides over the Southern region—in a greater proportion. Thus, the wind is accustomed to blow from that dominant corner; but in a smaller proportion, He sends a ray of His will to its likeness in the North wind—that is, to its soul. Therefore, that wind also blows, but not in such a proportion as its opposite, the South Wind. In this way, the intermediate air is converted, through the opposition and compression of its parts, first into a misty substance and then afterward into the consistency of a dense cloud. By the dissolution brought about by the Word or Wisdom of God, these clouds turn into rain, either to make the earth more fertile or to submerge it. That clouds proceed from the blast of the winds is taught to us by experience, since clouds are rarely absent when the South Wind blows. Furthermore, we see clouds of every condition not only moved and stirred into the opposite quarter by the predominant wind, but they are also miraculously sustained in this by the divine Word acting within them, unless they are resolved into rain by divine operation and so fall. Indeed, David seems to confirm this in these words, declaring the act of the Word's power in the melting of snow: **He sends out his word and melts them; as soon as his wind blows, the waters flow** (*Psalm 147:18*). That clouds are sustained by the winds is clear from another passage: **Jehovah bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet; and he mounted upon a Cherub, and flew upon the wings of the winds** (*Psalm 18:10*), because <term>Cherubim</term> <note>High-ranking angels; here, they are described as "airy" beings who animate the atmosphere.</note>, being airy angels, are animated and led, and Jehovah is said to sit upon them. Wherefore it must be said that just as Wisdom is the soul or central life of the said angels, so indeed they are the soul and life of the air in which they move; hence they are called angels of great strength, carrying out the word of God and His pleasure (*Psalm 104*). For this reason, we say that God alone is the creator of clouds and their sustainer in the heavens, according to that passage in Job: **God fits the weight to the air or wind, and weighs the waters by measure; he makes a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder, etc.** (*Job 28:25-26*). It is as if he had said: God is the **Alpha and Omega**, the beginning and the end, the first and last actor in the production of meteors, being present everywhere. And He moves the first part of Himself in the angel, who, obeying His will, moves first in the air in the form of wind with his legions; and then He fits the air into the nature of wind, or the thickness of a dense cloud, from which the rains receive their laws, or He reduces it into the property of lightning. And yet, it is not the angel but God, or Wisdom within the angel, who is most rightly said to do all these things, since He is the true and only actor in these matters.

# Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...the wise man says that the upper clouds distill dew by wisdom, Proverbs 3:20 <note>original: "Prou. 20"; the author likely refers to Proverbs 3:20, though the OCR reflects a different numbering.</note>. From these things it is clear enough, against the false assertion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed weather was caused by natural vapors and heat/cold cycles rather than direct divine action.</note>, that neither vapors emerging from the earth or waters, nor the cold of the middle region of the air thickening and supporting that imaginary vapor, is the material or efficient cause of a cloud. Instead, it is the air itself, applied and thickened by the opposing or transverse breath of God: that is, by the ray of wisdom of the angels, who are snatched and driven to carry out the will of their Creator.

The situation is similar in the generation of snow, hail, and frost, except that in such a creation the North Wind <note>original: "Ventus septentrionalis"</note> holds dominion. Its role is to constrict the air into a cloud—air that had been reduced by the South Wind <note>original: "flatu Australi"</note>, though blowing at a milder degree—and to harden it. For just as it is the nature of the South Wind to soften, melt, and dissolve, so it is the nature of the North Wind <note>original: "Aquilonis"</note> to harden and constrict. That God alone is the producer and effecter of such meteors <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and lightning.</note>, through the mediation of His angelic ministers, is proven by these testimonies brought forth from the sacred fountain: **Who (says God) fathered the frost of heaven? Job 38:29.** <note>original: "Iob. 28, 19"</note> As if by such a question He were arguing that no one did except Himself alone. And elsewhere, **God sends snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes; He casts down ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? Psalm 147:16.** By which He seems to imply that God, through His winds—and especially the North Wind <note>original: "Boream"</note>—creates snow from the air gathered by the milder breaths of the South. Wherefore He says: **The mighty God by His breath produces snow and ice, Job 37:10.** <note>original: "Iob. 27. 9"</note> And elsewhere: **The North Wind produces cold.** Furthermore, ice and frost are created from the thickening of dewy air while God blows from the north; hence we read: **Ice comes forth from the womb of the dew, Job 38:28.** And elsewhere, **While God blows, the ice hardens like a stone of water, etc. Job 37:10.** <note>original: "Iob. 27. 9"</note> In this discourse, the matter of ice, as well as its form and author, along with His instrument, are explained: namely, the dewy matter, the watery stone-like form, and God as the agent working through His windy instrument. From these things, therefore, the error of the pagan philosophers concerning the matter and efficient cause of these types of meteors is evident.

### CHAPTER XX.

### Concerning the single efficient cause of flashes, lightning, thunderbolts, and thunder; likewise concerning the author of sulfurous smoke and flames.

Just as the Creator of all things makes His angels winds, so also He makes His ministers a burning fire or flame, as the royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> testifies in Psalm 104:4 <note>original: "Ps. 103. 104"</note>. Moreover, we call lightning and flashes air animated by their presence and clothed in their fiery form; indeed, we gather this also from the logical flow of this discourse: **God fits the weight to the air, and weighs out the waters by measure; and He makes a way for the lightning of the thunders**, where He seems to fit the air in its weight so that through it, as through a medium, His fiery spirits may make their way to fulfill the will of the Creator. Job seems to imply this in another place: **The clouds scatter His light, which illuminates all things round about, wherever the will of the Creator drives them for everything He commands them upon the face of the world, whether for a scourge or for mercy, Job 37:11-13.** <note>original: "Iob. 28. 25"</note> And elsewhere: **Behold, God extends His light over the clouds, and covers the roots of the sea, Job 36:30.** <note>original: "Iob. 37"</note> And elsewhere: **Will you send forth lightnings, and will they return to say to you, "Here we are"? Job 38:35.** <note>original: "Iob. 36"</note> Are we not also made more certain of the efficient cause of lightning from these words: **Fire coming out from the presence of Jehovah consumed the sons of Aaron, Leviticus 10:2.** And elsewhere, **Fire having gone out from Jehovah consumed the 250 men who had offered incense, Numbers 16:35.** Finally, in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> we have it that **lightnings, voices, and thunders proceeded from the throne of God:** by which it is clearly denoted that flashes and lightnings proceed immediately from God. 

This discourse should be understood in this way: the Divine Essence, in its wisdom or emanation, agitates its likeness in the fiery spirits (by means of which a fiery angel exists and remains such as he appears in the air at the time of lightning; for the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing, but more abundantly in the angels). He urges and moves a part of Himself, as it were, to perform those things which are ordained by the moving Father. These fiery spirits in their motion disturb the air, massing and constricting it into dense clouds; and on the other hand, the spirits of nature opposed to them, blowing from an opposite region of the world, wage a vehement war and violently break out from their moist embrace and the dense prison surrounding them. This is not something those fiery or watery spirits or demons do on their own, but rather what God is accustomed to effect by a double ray emitted from His essence acting within them. And this is the reason why many thunders are heard at the same time, rising from different corners of the world; whence Daniel says: **the four winds of heaven fought upon the great sea, Daniel 7:2**—that is, in the open air. By "winds" the Prophet understands the angelic intelligences who preside over the four corners of the world. But concerning these we shall discourse more clearly in the second book of this member, God willing. Yet we have other testimonies of Holy Scripture everywhere dispersed that prove this our single efficient cause of all things, especially that God alone (with no other subordinate efficient cause mediating) is the author and actor in thunder, lightning, and all other luminous meteors whatsoever. For in one place it is said: **Smoke went up in His anger, and fire from His face glowed, coals were kindled by Him, etc. At the brightness in His presence the clouds passed away, hail and coals of fire; and the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice, etc. Psalm 18:8-13.** <note>original: "Psal. 17. 9"</note>

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II, Lib. IV. Membr. I.

By this discourse, it clearly appears that God performs all these things. Although we may say in our common speech that the lightning and thunder "happen," or in a more mystical sense, that angels set the air on fire by their fiery presence, the truth is that God is present in the fiery angels, and God is in the dense clouds or the watery spirits, bringing all these things to their conclusion to fulfill His commands. Thus, the Holy Scripture rightly says that *in God all things live, move, and have their being* <note>original: "Act. 17. 9."; the author likely refers to Acts 17:28</note>. And elsewhere, *God works all in all* <note>1 Corinthians 12:6</note>. And again, *God the Father from whom are all things* <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note>. 

Therefore, how foolish, dull, and over-subtly argued is that opinion and assertion of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who sought naturalistic rather than divine explanations for physical phenomena.</note>—both the pagans and those of the Christian order—who presume to assert that lightning is merely a "hot and dry exhalation" leaping from the earth. They claim that by the sun’s power, these vapors are raised into the middle region of the air, and being enclosed there by a cloud and driven by the force of the local cold, they catch fire. I leave it to you, looking into this matter with clear eyes and weighing it in the scales of justice, to judge: Is this matter of lightning and thunder something of so little consequence (as these Aristotelians think), or is it of a far deeper profundity and inscrutability? In the Holy Scriptures, these are called the fires of God leaping from His mouth and throne, and the voices and sounds of God. 

For this reason, some philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of the thunderbolt, judged it not to be a work of nature, but the immediate effect of the Most High God. Indeed, this work seemed so marvelous to the pagans that they doubted its origin greatly and argued among themselves. For **Empedocles** thought that lightning and the flash of light were fire generated by the rays of the sun descending downward and being intercepted by clouds. **Anaxagoras** maintained that this fire was a portion of the ether, which he believed was sent down from on high and driven into the place where the clouds consist. Although Aristotle himself and Seneca attempted to refute these opinions, they nevertheless seem far more probable and relevant to the matter than those of Aristotle and his followers. 

This is also declared clearly enough by arguments drawn from experience itself. For, good God! How destitute of reason are those who are accustomed to attribute the wonderful effects of thunder to the power of an "earthly exhalation," or to the weak faculty of an earthly fire? For we see that by the action of a thunderbolt, wine is drawn out of a barrel with a sudden rush without the vessel being touched at all; a sword is broken in its scabbard, gold and silver in a purse, and the bones within the fleshy home of a man; sudden winds are created in the air, forests are burned, stones are crushed, huge towers are suddenly torn down, and infinite other wonders are performed. It is extremely difficult to give a ready reason for these things. Indeed, there seems to be a sense and reason within the lightning, by which they show obedience to the Creator; they are said to "bless" Him in the Holy Scriptures, thereby indicating to us Christians that there is within them a certain Angelic virtue very close to the divinity. Governed by this, they go forth violently when sent, and say with reverence to the Creator, *“Behold, here we are”* <note>Job 38:35</note>. 

Truly, its spirit is so subtle and its life so agile, as we find written by one skilled in these mysteries: "Angels are much brighter and more splendid than spiritual bodies, which a man can hardly admit or comprehend; for by reason of their subtlety, they can pass through and penetrate all things without any hindrance and without any corruption, like lightning." The human soul can do the same, since God likewise created it from the same source from which the angels were created <note>original: "Lib. de secretis creationis" (The Book of the Secrets of Creation)</note>. By this, he seems to hint that the substance of an angel, of lightning, and of the human soul is of the same matter, which he is inclined to call the **sixth essence** <note>term: sixth essence; a substance even more refined than the "quintessence" or fifth element, often associated with the divine or the soul.</note> in many places. And indeed, just as the substance of an Angel is hardly seen except in its "airy clothing"—which it illuminates in the manner of the spirit of the sun, which is illuminated by its internal soul—so also the internal part of lightning is an angelic power and essence, veiled in airy garments. 

It is from this that so many wonders arise from lightning, far surpassing the deaf nature and disposition of a mere "exhalation." For experience has revealed here in England, in the county of **Devon**, that thunder coming from the North sent a "fiery stone" <note>A "thunderstone" or "ceraunius," which people then believed was a physical projectile launched by lightning.</note> into the kitchen of a certain nobleman. Rolling from that place into the hall of the house and passing between the feet of a man there, it rendered him temporarily insane and raging. Passing from there into a chamber, by its mere sight, all the window glass on that side was perforated in infinite places, as if they had been pierced by needles; and so, penetrating through a thick wall and leaping out of the house, it buried itself in a hard rock in a wonderful manner. 

Furthermore, in **Ireland**, two women seeking wood and traveling through a field were delayed on the road by a certain horrendous thunder. One of them was struck with fear and trembling, calling out to God and hurrying toward a tree. The other seemed not at all disturbed, but behaved in an impious manner, holding the voices of the thunder in derision and contempt. Striking her buttocks with her hand, she turned her rear toward the place from which the sounds were issued. It happened that the first woman, moved by the fear of God and His voice, escaped safe; but the buttocks and hindquarters of the other were immediately torn and mangled by the thunder, and thus that blasphemous woman died miserably. 

But to come closer to the foolish assertions of these Aristotelians: one day, some merchants and others were in the company of a certain **Peripatetic** (a young man of good character who lived in the city of **Shrewsbury** <note>original: "Salopiensem"</note>, where he worked in literary matters and was held in high esteem by everyone there for his knowledge of philosophy). While they were traveling together through the wide Shrewsbury plain, they noticed dense clouds approaching them with sounds and thunder, and the greater part of them began to fear vehemently.

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

But that young man, wishing to show himself well-versed in the knowledge of **Peripatetic** <term>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who favored naturalistic explanations over supernatural ones.</term> philosophy, counseled them and persisted in boldly persuading them not to fear. He affirmed that this phenomenon was common in nature and happened by chance as an external occurrence. He claimed there was no danger in it, asserting that the flame was produced solely from a hot and dry exhalation from the womb of the earth, sublimated into the middle region of the air by the power of the sun’s rays. He attributed it to that **antiperistasis** <term>A philosophical concept where a quality, like heat, is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, like cold.</term> which he said existed between the coldness of the place and the heat of the received exhalation. However, it turned out differently for him than for all the others, and differently than he himself thought: for he was instantly killed by the lightning, while the rest, struck only by stupor and fear, fell to the ground. In this way, the blasphemy of this man, deceived by Aristotelian arguments, was judged by the just judgment of God.

In the year 1623, near the town they call **Croydon**, situated only eight miles from the city of London, around the month of July, certain people were preparing hay in the field of a certain nobleman. As they were drying it in the sun, they noticed voices and thunder approaching with horrendous lightning. Consequently, they divided themselves into two groups or pairs, standing not much more than two arm-lengths apart from each other, gathering together to remain safer from the rage of the storm. Under one tree sat three young women with a certain boy; under another stood two or three men. 

As the storm approached (wonderful to relate!), the thunder could do nothing against those under the first tree while one of the aforementioned young women remained under it, as if she alone had been marked on her forehead by God so that the evil spirit might not bring any harm to her. For this reason, prompted by some instinct—I know not what—while the thunder and heavy rain were falling, she proposed to leave that tree and hurry to the other. Addressing the others, she said, "I shall hasten to the other tree; do you wish to come away with me?" But the others refused. When she had gone only five or six paces, immediately the other two and the boy remaining under that tree, who had been unwilling to leave with her, were struck by lightning and killed. No other sign appeared on them except a tiny scraping of the bark. The young woman who left escaped safely to the men drying hay under the other tree. 

But what seemed an even greater miracle: a fire in the form of a globe, descending from the top of that tree all the way to its root, rolled over the ground like a wheel. It passed near the other tree under which the girl stood with the men. By its presence and passage, those standing there were not only stunned and astonished by stupor and fear, but the tree itself, moved by a certain remarkable reverence, seemed to incline itself toward that wheel and humble itself in a kind of bow. Indeed, it seemed to that robust man who was leaning against the trunk that his back was broken by the immense leaning of the tree. From this it is clear that there is a greater mystery in lightning and thunder than the **Peripatetics** could ever comprehend. Therefore, true Christians ought to devote themselves to the sense of the Holy Scriptures rather than to the vain and barely probable imagination of the pagan Aristotelians, since the certainty of the divine sparks and the vanity and absurdity of the latter have been clearly declared in the preceding pages.

Furthermore, another wonderful example of this astounding meteor <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> in nature presented itself last year, 1624, in the month of July, near the town of **Windsor**, where one may see a royal and well-fortified palace or castle, not eighteen miles distant from the city of London. For while two women with three girls were gathering ears of wheat scattered everywhere through the field after the harvest, an astounding thunderclap suddenly came upon them. The eldest of the girls, seeing the lightning flying everywhere through the air and appearing before her eyes in an oblong form with sharp tails, was greatly moved and disturbed in spirit beyond all the others. She cried out to her mother, "Fie on this lightning and thunder! I cannot endure it; I wish I were home!" 

When she was admonished by her mother and another honest woman (who before her marriage was a servant or maid in my own house) to leave off her frivolous and contentious talk and call upon God, she nonetheless neglected prayers to God and continued to make her exclamations against the loathsome appearances of the meteor. Consequently, the others attempted to protect themselves from the violence of the storm under the branches of two tall trees. But that girl, with a joking and cheerful face, leaning her back against the trunk of a very tall oak, said that she was placed as if in a royal throne above the others and was secure from the storm. The other woman, formerly my servant, had her arm resting in the lap of the said girl, and her younger sister was not far from them, while the mother of the girl was under another tree five or six paces away. 

It happened suddenly that a certain ball of fire, falling from a cloud onto that huge tree, stripped its bark in three places from the top to the root without any interruption of the parts, with a most violent and sudden force. It scattered fragments of it everywhere for almost a mile. Meanwhile, the substance of the trunk and the internal body was not immune from that triple wound, but hollow wounds were inflicted to the depth of a finger, long and continuous, from the highest branches down to the root, as if by plowshares. This was undoubtedly the work of the finger of God or some administering angel. Thus it happened that the girl, who thought herself most safe and protected from all violence, was suddenly killed in the blink of an eye by a force that cannot be explained in words. The woman who was once my servant was deprived of the use and feeling of the arm that had been resting in the girl's lap; she ran through the field or road in a frantic manner, crying out with a loud voice and looking up at the clouds: "Holy God, open Your clouds and Your gates, that I may enter, nor...

Finally, all other **meteors** <term>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including lightning, rainbows, and comets.</term>, whether composed of sulfur or a more subtle illuminated substance—such as comets, the **will-o’-the-wisp** <note>original: "ignis fatuus"</note>, and others of that kind—claim this same efficient cause for themselves: namely, God himself, who is accustomed to produce them by means of his flashing angels. Yet it is not the angels who do this, but God himself *in* the angels and *through* the angels. Just as the angels vary in their composition, they produce meteors of varying condition, property, and even constitution. Thus we observe some to be comets, fiery columns, burning spears, or **chasms** <note>original: "chasima"; a term used for openings or "gaps" in the sky during auroras or storms</note>; and others to be flashes, lightning bolts, or sulfurous rains; and finally others to be the will-o’-the-wisp or flames emerging from the earth. Nevertheless, there is only one single act: one God remaining in His essence, who acts variously—not by reason of Himself, but by reason of the object which receives His rays in different ways. This occurs in respect to the various angelic bodies which are distributed into different portions of the world’s air by a primary internal act; these portions differ in density, rarity, and quality, as trustworthy writers testify.
