That God is the cause—both primary and immediate (for there is no regard for place or time before God, who is the Alpha and Omega)—we gather from Holy Scripture, where we find it written: *God moves the earth out of its place, so that its columns tremble; he transfers mountains, etc.* <note>Job 9:5-6</note>. And elsewhere: *The earth trembles at the look of God.* <note>Psalm 104:32</note>. Hence, the royal Psalmist said in another place that *the deepest footprints of the earth are in the hand of God.* Similarly, it is denoted there that He brings about this perturbation of the earth in the character of His severity and wrath; for an earthquake is always an act in the **Macrocosm** <term>The "great world" or universe, viewed as a reflection of the human "microcosm."</term> that is "beyond nature." Thus it was said of the wrath of God against the Israelites: *The earth shook and moved, the foundations of the heavens were disturbed, because He was angry.* <note>2 Samuel 22:8</note>. Moreover, we gather from many places in Scripture that **Jehovah**—sometimes surrounded by a thick cloud, and most often clothed in an angelic body—produces these stupendous meteors. *Behold,* (says Saint Matthew) *there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and his appearance was like lightning, etc.* <note>Matthew 28:2</note>. By these words, it is implied that the Angel of God was the efficient cause of the earthquake; after expressing the effect in the words "Behold, a great earthquake was made," he explains the reason or efficient cause in the following words: "For an angel of the Lord descended." The manner by which he did this was his "lightning-like aspect," which is the essential flash and splendor of God shining forth from the angelic composition. For angelic bodies are said to be mirrors receiving the splendor of divinity, as will be explained more fully below. Hence David said: *The earth trembles at the look of God.*

From these things, therefore, it appears clearer than the midday light how impious and profane is that opinion of the **Heathens** <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; referring here to pre-Christian Greek philosophers like Aristotle.</note> who say that an earthquake is nothing other than a violent eruption of a multitude of winds trapped in the bowels of the earth. They wrongly take the wind or the air—which is merely the organ or vehicle of the divine "look" that works these wonders—for the cause itself. In doing so, they fall into a notable form of idolatry, injuriously and vainly attributing the acts of the Creator to the creature. But truly, if they were willing to look at the mystery of this matter with eyes a little more accurate, they would perceive a matter of deeper significance, and they

For common experience teaches us what hidden events follow an earthquake, and what wonders accompany its effects—namely plagues, famines, and the observation that sometimes the earth itself is seen to groan with fiery sighs and roar with a lowing sound like a lion. To assign all these wonders to wind accidentally trapped within the earth will appear (as it will seem to any rational person) utterly absurd. We, however, shall produce from among a thousand examples just one from our own Europe that is worthy of admiration. On the day of the Conversion of St. Paul <note>January 25th, 1348</note> (says the *History of Venice*), around the first hour after midday, while Doge Andrea Dandolo, the 54th governor at that time, was in power, a massive earthquake arose. It shook the city with such motion and violence that various structures, both public and private, collapsed under its force. Thus the towers of the churches—namely St. Sylvester, St. Vitalis, and St. James of Lorio—together with the roof of St. Angel and the left portion of St. Basil, fell to the ground and were laid low. This earthquake lasted more or less for the space of fifteen days, and by its shock many pregnant women suffered miscarriages. Furthermore, a most contagious disease followed this event, which began with a swelling in the groin <note>Symptoms of the Bubonic Plague</note>, which was immediately followed by extreme heat with pain and heaviness of the head, so that their memory was taken from them. It was observed that those suffering from this infection generally exchanged life for death within three days. Indeed, out of a hundred persons, scarcely ten were counted who escaped the scourge of death, so that throughout the entire city nothing was in use except tears, groans, funerals, doctors, and the visiting of the sick. Finally, at the end, a plague began to rage and attack with such atrocity and severity that everywhere men, infants, and women of every age who suffered the infection suddenly fell dead even in the streets. Thus, relative dared not offer help to relative, nor friend to friend; likewise, children were forced to refuse and avoid their parents, and parents their children. The physicians themselves took flight in terror, and funeral pomp was by then unknown; instead, without ceremonies, the nobles were dragged to the pit in the manner of the common poor. This contagion held its growth from the beginning of the spring season until the first of May, and only then (with few survivors remaining) did it begin to decrease.

What then? O, the vain invention of the Greek philosophers! Even though they are almost eyewitnesses to the wonderful effects of earthquakes (for *Diodorus Siculus* and *Herodotus* have narrated wonders regarding earthquakes happening in Greece), they still desire to assign their stupendous effects to such a frivolous cause as mere air or wind shut up in the cavities of the earth.

But in this place, we shall set about reciting the various theories of the philosophers concerning earthquakes, so that you may more easily discern how inconstant and unstable they are in their opinions. This usually arises because they were ignorant of the true foundation of atmospheric phenomena <term>meteororum: used here in the archaic sense to mean any atmospheric or geological phenomenon like rain, wind, or earthquakes</term> and the secret action of the Divine Word.

**Posidonius** said the cause of this was wind trapped in the cavities of the earth, in which he seems to agree with the **Peripatetics** <term>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</term> who say that it is caused by vapors obstructed in the bowels of the earth. These vapors, finding no way out and being expanded and thinned by the sun's rays during the day, shake the sides of the earth seeking an exit, and thus, breaking out, they cause an earthquake. The Assyrians, and the Babylonians above all others, wish it to be produced by the power of a certain planet or by the aspect of its rays meeting with those of the sun in the center of the earth. **Anaxagoras** thinks it is created by a storm of time from air retained in the earth. And so you see that many have said many things, yet have indicated nothing certain about its origin or efficient cause. In truth, God is the immediate cause of this thing, looking upon the earth from an angelic body with the appearance of His wrath; He performs and acts all these things in the strength of His arm, as was declared in the preceding pages. Therefore, let the praise and glory of such a great miracle be attributed to Him alone forever.

The sacred text also teaches us that God is the sole efficient cause of springs and rivers, where it is read: *He sends forth the springs through the valleys, so that they walk between the mountains, to provide drink for all the beasts of the field* <note>original: "Qui emittit fontes per valles, vt inter montes ambulent, vt potum præbeant omnibus animantibus agri"</note>, Psalm 104. And elsewhere, *When the Lord strengthened the fountains of the deep, wisdom was with him, etc.* <note>original: "Cum roboraret Iehoua fontes abyssi, sapientia erat cum eo, &c."</note>, Proverbs 8:28. By these, it is clear that God or divine power is the cause producing springs and rivers, and not the vapors of the earth, as the Peripatetics falsely supposed.

Finally, God is the unique maker of the sea storm, inasmuch as He acts from a whirlwind to such an effect, no differently than He is said to have spoken to him <note>likely referring to Job</note> out of the whirlwind. This also seems to be confirmed by these words of the Royal Psalmist: *Those going down to the sea in ships (he says), they see the works of the Lord and His wonders in the deep; and He speaks, and makes the breath of the whirlwind blow, and lifts up its waves; they mount up to the heaven, they go down even to the depths, etc.* <note>original: "Descendentes ad mare nauibus, ipsi vident opera Iehouæ, & mirabilia eius in profundo, dicitque, & flare facit spiritum turbinis..."</note>, Psalm 107:23. Furthermore, we read elsewhere, *You shall break the ships of the ocean with the East Wind* <note>original: "Oceani naues perfringes Euro"</note>, etc., Psalm 48.

## Corollary to the Microcosm.
<note>The "Microcosm" (Little World) is a traditional philosophical term for a human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the "Macrocosm" or the entire universe.</note>

We have received from the doctrine of both the Theosophers <note>Mystical philosophers who seek direct knowledge of the divine</note> and the more learned Philosophers that four things were created in the world according to the likeness of the Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint</note> and the first Idea. Two of these were created in a natural way by the best and greatest Creator—namely, the world and man—while the others were fabricated by the craftsmanship of the human creature, man: specifically the Ark or Tabernacle of the Covenant built by Moses, and that notable Temple built by Solomon. Just as those natural things were created according to the image of the Archetype, so indeed were the artificial things fabricated according to the example of the natural ones. For thus in the world we have three regions, of which one excels the other in dignity: namely the supreme, which is the most excellent essence of all, called *Empyrean* <note>The highest heaven, literally "of fire"</note> from its fiery nature. Indeed, just as fire is more eminent in dignity than all other elements, and purer and simpler in essence, so for that reason the Empyrean heaven is the head and Prince over the other two lower ones. Therefore, it is assigned as the seat for the purest and simplest creatures of all—namely the Angels and the intelligences flashing with divine splendor.

Then follows the middle region, participating in both extremes, which is called *Ether*, because it seems to be composed of the supreme fire and the lowest air. Therefore, it is not as pure as that supreme region, nor so impure, thick, and unclean as that lowest one, but consists in a middle state. Finally, the lowest is thicker in quantity than the higher ones, more imperfect in quality, and subject to all changes—namely the agitation of winds, the procreation of clouds, the crying out of thunders, and the inflammation of lightnings, fiery whirlwinds, and other luminous meteors <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain and lightning</note>, the wetting of rains, the flooding of waters, the insane and furious violence of winds breaking out from the earth, the power of whirlwinds, and infinite other things happening contrary to the peaceful laws of nature. Furthermore, in man—who was fabricated in the image of the world (whence he is also called the "Son of the World" by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy</note>)—we have an intellectual heaven assigned to the divine mind and its angelic sparks, whence also his head is the seat of the "Holy of Holies." In the middle region or celestial spirit is the seat of life and the living soul; while his thick air, along with the external seat of this human temple (namely the body), is subject to so many and such great changes and the effects of "meteors" tending toward both generation and corruption, that it ought most aptly to be compared to the lowest region of the world.

But Moses in the construction of his Tabernacle, and Solomon in that of his Temple, confirmed this same thing by reason: For their first part is uncovered and left open to the common air, subject to winds, rains, hail, snow, and other atmospheric impressions observed to form below the lunar circle—and finally, it is subject to all alterations and changes. Therefore, common men of every kind, as well as animals, approach this part, where by reason of continual sacrifices there is a constant alternation of life and death. From this it follows that this part is applied fittingly to the disposition of the elementary world, inasmuch as it is composed of water as a fluid and unstable substance; whence the world is truly called [a place] of darkness and obscurity. For this reason, the Tempter is sometimes called the Prince of Darkness, sometimes the Prince of the World, and sometimes the Prince having power over the air. The second part of the Tabernacle or Temple is covered, and shines within with gold, and is illuminated by a lampstand with seven branches, which without doubt denote as many planets. Hence, this region of the Tabernacle undoubtedly represents the celestial world in the Macrocosm, participating in light and darkness—namely, fire and thin water. From this, the heavens were called by the Hebrews *Esh-shamayim* <note>original: "Eschamaim" from "Esch" (fire) and "maim" (water). This is a traditional etymology suggesting the heavens are a balance of fiery and watery natures.</note>. From these things it is clear that the substance of the heaven is indeed a body, but incorruptible, imbued with a certain intellect by which it is governed and to which it is joined, so that this matter is neither free nor wandering. The rational soul in man, or the Microcosm, has such a relationship to his body. The third part of the Tabernacle or Temple was the Holy of Holies, bearing the likeness or image of the intellectual world, which is the fiery seat and domicile of the angels and abstract or separate intelligences (who are the ministers of the living God). This is also signified therein because two golden Cherubim, with wings extended lengthwise, cover and overshadow the mercy seat. Furthermore, we have all these regions in the human temple, differing in every way in purity and impurity. From this it follows that, just as in the greater world we have all influences from GOD through the most pure and fiery world into that which lies immediately below it—namely, by means of the *Sephiroth* <note>The ten emanations of God in Kabbalah through which the universe was created</note> through the angelic or empyrean region into the ethereal one, and likewise the ethereal into the sublunary, elementary...

->### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.<-

...aforementioned, in which so many and such great transformations occur in the world; so indeed in the human world, the mental power through the intellect exerts its influences upon the ethereal region, in which the life-force resides. Finally, by these influences, the "aerial spirit"—dispersed everywhere through the body and the blood vessels—is ruled and governed for the fulfillment of human life and its preservation. Truly, we possess the essences of these [human] regions from the regions of the Macrocosm <note>The Great World or Universe</note>. Beyond that double breath—namely, that common one which the Creator assigned to the world for its completion, and that specific one which He Himself breathed into the face of Adam as the "breath of life" <note>Latin: *spiraculum vitae*; a reference to Genesis 2:7</note>—it is necessary that the particles of every Macrocosmic region attributed to man in his creation should concur toward the perfection of the regions of the Microcosm <note>The Little World or Man</note>. Furthermore, by the same reasoning, it is clear that the lowest region of the Microcosm (the air within us), when burdened and disturbed by the presence of various "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon like wind, rain, or lightning, not just space rocks</note>, continually communicates with the human air. Indeed, this common air, inhaled and breathed in through the nostrils, the windpipe, and the pores of the Microcosm, joins with the air enclosed within the man. Through this communication, the human air participates in and possesses the natures and impressions generated first in the Great Air [the atmosphere], and afterwards dissipated through it, as if enclosed in "seed-beds." 

Just as in the Macrocosm, God rains down the influences that create all meteors—both favorable and malevolent—through His "luminous gates" into the angelic world, and from there into the celestial world, which finally disseminates them everywhere through the elemental world; so indeed God is the general actor in all these things. His act is the effect of His Word dispersed everywhere, whether as Wisdom, or as a luminous emanation and emission. Therefore, it is also manifest that all diseases produced in man proceed from God in no different way than those meteors in the Great World. But truly, just as the outpourings of the divine will first descend through various orders of angels according to a varied logic, and these angels then pour them into the stellar bodies of the ether—from which they finally flow into lower things for the procreation of meteors and impressions of every kind—so indeed the winds, as if they were spirits and angelic impressions (both occult and manifest), are the ministers of God. They act first in the open air, so that afterwards, in various ways and paths, they may act upon the human air to execute the will or pleasure of GOD, whether for good or for evil. Hence, it is for this reason that, as was said regarding the Great World:

> *At the brightness before him clouds passed, hail and coals of fire; and the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice, and coal of fire; he sent his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them, etc. Psalm 17:12-14.* <note>Original: *psal. 17. a 9.* In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:12-14.</note>

Where by "arrows" the rays of lightning can be understood; whence it is said elsewhere:

> *The direct emissions of lightnings shall go forth, and they shall be exterminated from the clouds as from a well-curved bow, and shall fly to a certain place. Wisdom 5:22.* <note>Original: *Sap. 5. 22.* A reference to the Book of Wisdom, often called the Wisdom of Solomon.</note>

In the Microcosm also, God acts in such a way by means of the Microcosmic spirit—namely, by kindling a fire in his aerial spirit no differently than in the Macrocosmic air.

Wherefore Job breaks out into these words:

> *The arrows of the Almighty are heavy within me, their poison drinks up my spirit, and the terrors of God, set in array, fight against me. Job 6:4.*

And elsewhere: *Jehovah shall make the pestilence cleave to thee until thou be consumed; Jehovah shall strike thee with a wasting disease and heat.* This, however, happens in the wrath of Jehovah, of which it is spoken thus: *The wrath of Jehovah becomes like a consuming fire.* And elsewhere: *God shall consume the wicked with fire.* And regarding this elsewhere: *Pour out thy heat upon other nations.* Furthermore, even the leprosy falling upon Miriam can be compared to snow. But regarding these things, we speak most abundantly in our *Preternatural History of the Microcosm*. Now, however, we shall descend with a light leap to the description of the angelic ministers of GOD, whose duty it is to carry out the commands and pleasures of GOD.

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member II.

...since the opportunity arises, we shall discuss their names, composition, differences, and properties, both in general and more specifically.

Regarding their names, therefore, they are not to be imposed upon them out of necessity or from their true essence—as if they should be openly named and called upon exactly as they are in their true natures—but rather, these names are merely **mnemonic tools** <note>original: *lignacula memoratiua*; literally "memory-pegs" or "little wooden tokens of memory"</note> handed down to the wise through revelation. By means of these names, angels are understood by men and held in memory. For not all divine power is hidden within the spoken sound itself. In this way, there is also the ineffable name, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah</note>; and yet, when Moses asked, "What is your name?", God answered him, **I.H.V.H.** <note>original: *i. h. u. h.*; the Latinized letters of the Hebrew name</note>, saying: "This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation." The <term>Tetragrammaton</term> is, therefore, the name of eternity, but for mankind, it is only a memorial, since no name can be composed of any human voice that could equal the nature of the Divinity. For this reason, <term>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Better known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> says that the names of God used by men are to be uttered based on a specific property and not at all from His essence. For example: <term>Ehieh</term> <note>original: *Ehieh*; "I Am," from Exodus 3:14</note> from eternity; <term>Adonai</term> <note>original: *Adonai*; "Lord"</note> from Lordship; <term>El</term> <note>original: *El*; "God" or "Mighty One"</note> from fortitude, and so on.

By the same reasoning, it is difficult and impossible to name the Angels or "Intelligences" according to their true essences, as they are most full of the divine essence. But in truth, as wise men have known the angels through their works, so they have assigned names to them, both general and specific. For example: by a general name, the first order of the highest Hierarchy is called <term>Seraphim</term> <note>original: *Seraphin*; "The Burning Ones," associated with divine love and fire</note> from love and fiery ardor; <term>Cherubim</term> <note>original: *Cherubin*</note> from wisdom and knowledge; <term>Thrones</term> <note>original: *Throni*</note> from Justice, and so forth. So also the **Archangels** and angels are named after their office as messengers. Furthermore, specific names are assigned to particular angels for the same reason—namely, from their condition, office, or virtue. Just as <term>Raphael</term> <note>Meaning "God heals"</note> is named from medicine and healing, <term>Gabriel</term> <note>Meaning "Strength of God"</note> from manliness, <term>Uriel</term> <note>Meaning "Fire of God"</note> from his fiery nature, and so on. Nevertheless, it remains extremely difficult to utter their proper and essential names because we are ignorant of their essence; consequently, the frailty of mortals prevents and forbids finding them, except insofar as it has been granted to us through divine revelation.

Hence, it was for this reason that the most contemplative wise men formed the names of angels for themselves from numbers and figures according to their intentions, just as children are taught to compose words from letters—whether Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, or Egyptian. This is not because the voices themselves require such letters, but because our weakness is so great that such characters are required for the sake of memory, and such names are formed from letters and characters. Therefore, names of this kind are like <term>markers</term> <note>original: *notamina*; signs used for remembrance</note> (as <term>Johann Reuchlin</term> <note>1455–1522; a German humanist and scholar who pioneered the study of Hebrew and Kabbalah among Christians</note> has it) which first strike our senses either by their shape or sound. Then, the imagination is excited by the sense, so that the imagination moves the memory, the memory moves the reason, reason moves the intellect, the intellect moves the mind, and finally, the mind moves the angel. From this, it is clear that the angel is stirred by us in this way to fulfill our pious will, and not that we are stirred by the angels. For GOD and the angels are not moved by syllables and words or common prayers, but we are moved by them; they lead us so that we may have a "moored" confidence in them. For example (to use the words of <term>Reuchlin</term>), when bringing a ship to port, sailors are accustomed to throw a rope or cast a cable to pull the land—which is nonetheless immovable—by which effort they pull themselves toward the land. In clearly the same respect, through signs of this kind presented to the senses, we seem to pull the invisible Divinity toward us, when in reality we, who are movable, pull ourselves toward the immovable Divinity.

It is for this reason, therefore, that we use signs, characters, voices, hymns, and other ceremonial rites in our invocations of GOD and the Angels for our help—not, I say, that we may move them to us, but conversely, that we may elevate ourselves to them by this means. But to the point.

### CHAPTER II.
->*On the Essence and Composition of the Angel: What is its external part, and what is its internal?*<-

**A** great dispute and discrepancy has arisen among the more skilled philosophers and theosophers <note>Theosophers were those who sought direct knowledge of the divine through mystical insight</note> concerning the *Angelical consistency*. Some (among whom I name Damascene, Thomas Aquinas, and Dionysius) affirm that the Angel is absolutely incorporeal. Yet Basil, Origen, Gregory, and Hermes Trismegistus, along with the entire school of the Academics <note>The followers of Plato</note>, maintain that the angel is a corporeal substance. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, says in express words that demons are "aerial and fiery animals," and consequently he seems to assign aerial bodies to them. Indeed, elsewhere he does not hesitate to assert that from the beginning of their creation, angels had aerial bodies formed from the purer part of the upper air, suited for acting but not for suffering; however, the evil angels were changed by their fall, their bodies taking on the quality of thicker air, so that they might be able to suffer and be tormented by fire. Basil teaches us what kind of bodies were assigned to angels by God at creation: namely, he says they are thin, aerial, and pure spirits. Artephius, in his *Key of Wisdom*, says that the "external" of the Devil is air, but his "internal" is fire; for this reason, he teaches that it is very easy for the Devil, by means of his external part, to join with the aerial spirit within a human being, and in this way produce feverish diseases.

As for our own opinion, it is most certain and proven by clear reason that Basil, Gregory, Origen, and all the Academics did not deviate from the truth when they said that demons or angels are, in their external part, embodied out of air. Thus, according to the thickness or thinness of the air and its various changes, different orders of demons are found in the world, differing from one another in nature and condition. For just as it is observed in the order of nature that thin air is nothing but pure fire, and moderate air is nothing but wind, and thick air passes into the nature of water (the density of which is eventually earth itself), so too, for this very reason, some demons are fiery, others aerial, others aqueous, and some terrestrial. Consequently, in respect to their external part, all are merely aerial—that is, subtly corporeal, insofar as they are made of air.

For who, having been even slightly involved in philosophy, can be ignorant of the fact that rain-water was previously a dense cloud, and that the dense cloud was previously derived from a type of misty vapor? And that misty vapor, which is usually visible to the eyes, was once an invisible vapor, which is the first step in the progression from moderate, invisible air to that which is thick and visible. This alteration happens through degrees of thickness. By the same logic, it is necessary that we consider the varied constitution of angels; from this arises the mystery of angelic mutation from one species to another, from a visible form to an invisible one, and vice versa. Thus it is certain that angels, insofar as they are aerial, are to that extent corporeal. For unless air in its invisible nature were corporeal, it would be impossible for it to be condensed into a visible body; for that which makes something such is always more so in its beginning, and certainly nothing can give what it does not possess. But air, by addition, creates clouds, water, and earth through the process of condensation; therefore, it undoubtedly possesses a corporeal nature within itself, otherwise it would be impossible for it to be altered into the form of a body. This, then, was the reason why some demons are fiery: namely, those who are clothed in the thinnest and rarest

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.
<note>The "efficient cause" refers to the secondary agent or force that brings something into being; here, the author explores how angels or spirits act as the drivers behind weather phenomena.</note>

Dd 2
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

...truly: other winds, which are clearly clothed in middle air, are denser in their bodies than those fiery ones, and so it is with the rest. From this, we conclude that however angels are understood within their spheres, they ought to be accepted as having bodies—though they appear to differ among themselves in rarity and purity according to whether they participate more in this or that element.

For this reason, beyond doubt, Orpheus seems to recognize that there is one type of body which consists only of fire—that is, one whose external as well as internal nature is fiery—and he calls demons <note>The author uses "demons" in the classical sense of *daimones*, or mediating spirits, rather than purely evil entities</note> of this kind "supracelestial." Another type is tempered by a mixture of fire and air, and these demons are called "aerial" and "ethereal." If water is added to these, a third genus of demons arises, who are called "aqueous"; these are sometimes subjected to [lower realms], and if a subtle earthy element is joined to them, they are called "terrestrial" demons. By this, he seems to suggest to us that the bodies of angels appear to differ among themselves according to the varying temperament—the thinness or thickness—of the spirit of the world.

But let us now proceed to a clearer demonstration of this matter. We have in the universe of things only two principles proposed to us: namely, the universal Creator, or the uncreated light that forms all things; and the creature, which constitutes all things in heaven and on earth by means of that said uncreated light. Regarding the creature, St. Peter taught us that it is water, just as he called that light the Divine Word. Here, therefore, we have the external and internal of all creatures. The internal (I say) has its beginning from the incorruptible Spirit of God, which is said to be in all things (according to the *Book of Wisdom* 12 <note>Wisdom of Solomon 12:1: "For thy incorruptible Spirit is in all things."</note>), so that life and being may be imparted to it—that is, to every creature. Among these, we establish that angels and "intelligences" are of the first order and intention; that is, they are closest to God in their essence and excellence, and contiguous to God in the purity and thinness of their external consistency. 

Thus, just as God is the simplest essence, entirely free of matter and sufficient unto Himself without any help from matter (and is therefore rightly called "Identity" and "Unity"), so too the angel is a creature and not the creator, insofar as—besides the ray of that uncreated divinity which is its internal part—the angel possesses a created external spirit to complete the mass of its body, however subtle it may be. For this reason, the angel is said to stand apart from the dignity of "Identity." Because it is fashioned out of two things, it is not ineptly called <term>Alterity</term> <note>original: *Alteritas*; a philosophical term for "Otherness" or being distinct from the Primal One</note> by those most skilled in philosophy and theosophy. This "Alterity" presupposes the number two (the binary). From this, it is evident that just as God in His nature is absolute simplicity, so the angelic nature is the highest degree of composition. This is no different than how the number two is the first "confusion of units," or the first immersion of unity into multitude—the primary step in composition. It is like the number ten, which is a "joint" or "link" <note>original: *articulus*</note>; it is the root to a hundred (which is a square) and to a thousand (which is a cube). For the "link" is the first step in the composition of numbers after the "digits," which are simple numbers, as will be seen more clearly in the following demonstration.

Or look at it this way: This angelic "Alterity" is the number two, fashioned from the Divine Unity (which is its formal and internal light) and a created unity (which is the subtle aerial part, or the thinnest proportion of the primordial water). This latter is the angel's external and corporeal part. Therefore, it is certain that the number two is the root of all composite things in the world. Since its square is four, it signifies those four elements which, when multiplied in their root, produce the elements in the form of a cube; these are the final species in composition, just as the number one thousand is the final end of numbers. 

Furthermore, just as Unity (or the light of God, or the pure Word) is the primary form in composition (the angelic form), so the angelic nature is the form for the "celestial" composition, which consists in the number three (the ternary). This composition, in turn, acts as the form for the sublunary elements and those things constituted by them. This is the reason why, according to the wise, every hidden work, every effect of a meteor, and every property of an animal, vegetable, or mineral has its own angelic virtue flowing into it from heaven and the stars themselves. Indeed, for this reason, Orpheus and the Pythagoreans said that "all things are full of Gods," all of whom they referred back to a single Jove, the God of Gods. But the Platonists said "all things are full of Forms," which they likewise referred back to a single Soul of the World. The former made their demonstration from the cause (the *a priori*), namely the angels, whom they related to the one God; the latter demonstrated from the effect (the *a posteriori*), namely from the Soul of the World, which they placed in the ethereal heaven. This Soul is that angelic force infused by God by which heaven is animated, and which liberally rains down new forms into the various spheres of the elements and their species.

From these things, we see how angels are composed of an internal and pure part—which is the divine light, with whose glory they are more or less filled—and of a very thin mundane spirit as their external part. This spirit also differs in thinness, purity, and subtlety. Thus, those who are purer and thinner are more capable of grace, while those of denser bodies are less so; for the further matter is from grossness, the nearer and closer it is to God. Hence, we read in the more secret writings of the Cabala and "theography" <note>Divine writing or description of God</note> that the angelic nature, because of its purity, is very close to the First Light, which is God. The closer it is, the more it draws from the luminous fountain, and the more it receives <term>Theophany</term> <note>original: *Theophania*; the manifestation or appearance of God</note>—that is, the light and splendor of God. Thus, the first light descends from the Father of Lights first into the angels of the first order, by whom it is then infused into those of the second order, and so on.

But so that these things may be understood more clearly, I would have you know the opinion of "the Archangel" <note>Likely Archangelus de Burgonovo, a 16th-century Franciscan who wrote on Cabala</note> in his *Cabalistic Dogmas*: "Whatever," he says, "departs from God—the first and purest Act—must necessarily enter into matter." Wherefore, those natural philosophers describing the breadth of beings placed at the summit "Pure Act" without matter...

In which you see that the upper part of the **material pyramid** occupies barely a third, so that there seem to be three parts of the **formal pyramid** <note>The pyramid representing divine light or "Form."</note> for every one part of the material pyramid. 

Furthermore, from the third division in the highest region toward the seat of God, you see the material pyramid gradually and step-by-step diminish as it ascends. Therefore, it is most certain that the closer an angelic creature is to the divine nature, the more the matter in its composition is rendered purer, thinner, and rarer, and is consequently smaller in proportion. As you see in that demonstration, the more that pyramid tends toward the point <term>cone/apex: Fludd uses the word "conus" to refer to the sharp point of his triangular diagrams</term>, the more it is enclosed by a greater portion of the formal pyramid—the emanation sent out from God. 

Thus, the closer an angelic order approaches God in its nature—that is, the subtler and rarer it is in matter—the fuller and richer it is in divine form. From this pyramidal proportion, it is right to gather the dignities, exaltations, and differences of the angels: for the more the internal nature of the angel (which shone forth from God as pure form) is submerged in a multitude of matter, the more it is lowered in rank and honor. 

Hence it follows that, according to the observations of *Dionysius* <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, the historical authority on the nine choirs of angels.</note>, the Order of the **Seraphim** excels the **Cherubim** in dignity and excellence. This is because the highest Seraphic portion in the material composition is at the very point of the material pyramid, which is contiguous with God himself. For this reason, the angels of that order are those who are said to stand immediately in the presence of God, and consequently, they are the ones who immediately receive the fiery or luminous influxes from God. These they afterward send down to the **Cherubim**, just as the **Cherubim** send them to the **Thrones**, and so on successively through the remaining orders. Thus, the further down the orders are moved in their position, the more remote they are from the dignity of the divine presence. 

Those deeper in <term>theography: the study of describing or mapping divine things through diagrams and writing</term> seem to argue this with even clearer words, which are of this sort: "The simpler the substance of the angel, the further it stands from the dominion of matter; and the more the angelic order is absent from the multitude of matter, the more expressly the likeness of God shines back in it, as if in a very clear and polished mirror." Consequently, the Divine splendor is clearer in such an angel, and the "influence of happiness" <note>original: "influentia fœlicitatis"</note> is more abundant, more vivid, and worthier. 

Hence *Dionysius* says: "Those who are of a higher order receive the light of God more abundantly than those who are lower, and these share the light they have received with others who are lower; for this law of participation is observed among the angels." Thus he speaks. 

But this is explained even more clearly through a certain demonstration in our physics, in the *History of the Microcosm* <note>Robert Fludd’s major work, "Utriusque Cosmi Historia," which explores the human being as a "Little World" reflecting the universe.</note>, where we mentioned the harmony of the internal man, which we have expressed again in this place for a better understanding of this matter.

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

In this figure, then, that proportion is clearly explained by which any angelic order abounds in both matter and form, and also by what proportion the divine emanation immerses itself into the multitude—that is, into the depth—of the **formal pyramid**. <note>The "formal pyramid" represents the descending light of God, while the "material pyramid" represents ascending matter.</note> Furthermore, in the contemplation of this image, you will see with open eyes how all things have proceeded from God, and how they shall return to God, according to that saying of the Apostle: *And consequently how one is all, and all, in the end, are nothing but one.* <note>Fludd is likely referencing Colossians 3:11 or 1 Corinthians 15:28 regarding God being "all in all."</note> Moreover, in the proper study of the **formal pyramid**, you will perceive what the Kabbalists understood by their great angel *Metattron* <term>Metatron: In Jewish mystical tradition, the highest of the angels who serves as the celestial scribe or the mediator between God and the universe.</term> or the emanation from *Ehieh* <note>original: "Ehieh," the Hebrew name for God meaning "I AM."</note>, which is that wisdom so often cited in the scriptures; and what the Platonists meant by the **Soul of the World**; what the poets meant by *Pan* and *Panthea*; and how an angel is an "alterity"—namely, created from a pyramid that is material in respect to its outer self, and an uncreated or formal pyramid in respect to its inner self. <note>Fludd views angels as "mirrors" that reflect divine light into the material world.</note> For this reason, angels are called mirrors, looking up at the divine lights. Finally, you will see what created nature is—namely, the **material pyramid**, which is made from the primordial water—and what uncreated nature is—namely, the **informing pyramid**, which is nothing other than the emanation or flowing-forth of divinity into the spirit or worldly water. This water was once overwhelmed by darkness and formless, but is now informed by the divine presence; that is, it is a mixture of the lights of divine emanation with the substance to be recreated, since without this, it could not persist for even a moment of time. From this, therefore, it was said that *all things are made by the Word*, and *without Him nothing was made that was made*; hence we say that God fills everything and everywhere; hence the Apostle said, *In God we move, and in him, through him, and from him all things are.* But indeed, the Angels are called creatures of the "first composition," because their matter, the thinnest of all, first received the effects of the creating emanation, which is therefore called by the wise man the first of all creatures.

But lest you misunderstand me when I make mention of pyramids—since the word "pyramid" seems to sound mathematical, and furthermore I have described them in a mathematical fashion, namely with a base and a cone—I wish you to understand that I mean a **physical pyramid**, and not a mathematical one. Although I was forced to describe the former by the latter (as it is more commonly known), by a physical pyramid I mean the **world spirit** <note>original: "spiritum mundanum"</note>, which, ascending from the earth to the periphery of the world, always renders itself gradually thinner and more subtle in its ascent, until in its apex it reaches the extreme perfection of rarity, beyond which matter cannot ascend. But that which is beyond the grasp of matter must necessarily belong to the divine essence. Does not experience itself seem to declare this same thing? For all coincide in this—the physicists as much as those most skilled in theology—that water is subtler than earth, air than water, fire than air, ether than fire, and the **Empyrean spirit** <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most refined heaven of pure light.</note> is subtler than ether; and this spirit also has its own degrees up to the cone of the physical pyramid. Here, therefore, we have expressed the material pyramid both physically and mathematically, so that what has been said by us may be more easily grasped by you.

#### Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member II.

In a similar way, we delineate the **formal pyramid** <note>The "formal pyramid" represents the descending light of God’s active power, which gives shape and "form" to the universe.</note> both physically and mathematically in this manner.

Therefore, by the contraction of the parts of each physical pyramid—both the formal and the material—they shall stand by themselves and in their separate positions, as can be seen in number 2 of the aforementioned demonstration.

But indeed, the proportion of the mixture of the one **formal pyramid** (namely, when combined with the **material pyramid**) is indicated according to God's decree by the place of intersection through which the **sphere of equality** passes. <note>original: "sphæra æqualitatis." This is the point in Fludd's cosmology where light and matter are perfectly balanced, often associated with the Sun or the human soul.</note> This is because, in that specific place, matter and form are equal, as is declared by the conforming adaptation of each in the second figure of the aforementioned demonstration.

You see clearly, then, the reason why the Kabbalists <note>Fludd frequently references Christian Kabbalah, a Renaissance movement that integrated Jewish mystical traditions with Christian philosophy.</note> called an angel **Alterity** <term>Alterity: From the Latin "alteritas," meaning "otherness" or "difference." Fludd uses this to explain that angels are not pure unity like God, but are composed of two different principles: light and spiritual matter.</term>. This is because an angel is constituted from two things; they call God, however, **Identity** <term>Identity: From "identitas," meaning "sameness" or "unity."</term> and **Unity**, insofar as He is purely formal and self-sufficient, without any regard to matter. Hence, in respect to this property of self-sufficiency, He is called **Shaddai** <note>original: "Sadai," a Hebrew name for God (El Shaddai), traditionally translated as "Almighty" or "The All-Sufficient."</note>, which means "He who is sufficient in Himself."

But **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic theologian.</note>, **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Church Father who wrote extensively on the nature of angels.</note>, and others of that sect will reply: "We acknowledge that there is matter in the Angels, but we deny that this matter is corporeal; for we assert that it is purely spiritual." To them we respond: a star should not be removed from the designation of "body" simply because it is the denser part of the spirit of its own sphere—which spirit is ethereal, and consequently, extremely thin and rare. Furthermore, a body, however rare and invisible it may be, is no more to be removed from the laws of bodies than one that is coarse and visible. Yet we see that a star is a visible, dense body; must it then be denied that the **ethereal spirit** is likewise a body, even if it is invisible? Since of its invisible parts...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the nature of angels, specifically addressing the metaphysical composition of their "bodies." Fludd is arguing against the idea that angels are purely incorporeal, suggesting instead that they possess a "spiritual body" made of highly refined matter (rare matter), which mirrors the divine light of God.</meta>

# Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...by adding together, is a visible body produced? Therefore, whatever can be understood within the laws of rarity and density <term>rarity and density: in 17th-century physics, these terms describe the "thickness" of matter—rarity refers to thin, gas-like states, while density refers to solid or liquid states</term> can be called (and not without justice) a body. In the same way, since a cloud is a dense form of air, why should its "rare" state not also be called a body, since the thing that produces it is itself of that nature? What? Is it because it is a natural body that it cannot therefore be a spiritual body? *The Apostle says:* <note>Paul the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 15:44</note> *The body that is sown in corruption rises in incorruption; the natural body will be changed into a spiritual body.* 

It is therefore no more impossible for a sublunary spirit, or an ethereal one, or even an empyrean or angelic one to be a "rare body"—and consequently for angelic creatures to make themselves corporeal by their presence—than it was for that corporeal body of our Savior. After His passion, His body was made incorruptible and, through its purity and subtlety, was raised and sublimated all the way to the throne of God, where He is said to sit at the right hand of the Father; and yet, He did not lose the name of "body." For this reason, we should not be faulted for assigning an external corporeal nature to angels of any order, because all matter—whether it is subject to corruption or of a celestial and incorruptible nature—is contained within the limits of corporeal substance. For who can rightly deny that water turned into vapor is a body, just as much as it is in the form of water? Or that the tip of a material pyramid is any less a "body" than its base? The whole difference lies in rarity and density. But truly, because something is a dense body, it does not exclude the possibility of something being a rare body. Therefore, I hope it has been explained clearer than light that angels, regarding their external aspect, are corporeal and not incorporeal, as some have previously thought.

But as for their internal nature, we say that it is **uncreated light**. Thus, the external part of angels is like a highly polished, clear, and spotless mirror, receiving into itself the ineffable likeness of God. For within it shines, as in a clean and pure mirror, the divine splendor emanating immediately from the Divine Majesty. Hence (as was declared in the preceding pages), angels are called *Agalmata* <note>original Greek: αγάλματα, meaning statues or images; Fludd interprets this as "clearest mirrors"</note>, which is to say, clearest mirrors receiving the light of God. For this reason, an angel is said to be the image of God, the revelation of hidden light, a most polished and pure mirror without blemish. *Dionysius, On the Divine Names, Chapter 6.* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance angelology.</note>

For they receive through influence the light of the Deity, which in itself is incomprehensible and invisible, and they show it, emit it, and reveal it to others of a lower order. The angel is called a "mirror" because it can receive light, and it is called a "most polished mirror" because of the complete purity of its substance. Another author says that angels are "intellectual lights" receiving light from the First Light. That emanation descending into the bodies of angels, as well as into other creatures through their mediation, is what the Cabalists call *Hochma* <note>Hebrew for "Wisdom"</note>, namely Wisdom. For this reason, the Wise Man <note>referring to Solomon</note> calls it the "first creature," as it proceeds immediately from the Father like a son from a radiant source. Solomon describes this Wisdom as a holy spirit of intelligence, more mobile than all things that move, reaching everywhere because of its purity. He says it is in its essence a "vapor of the power of God," and a certain pure emanation or flow of the glory of the Almighty God, and the brightness or splendor of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of His goodness. *Wisdom 7.* <note>A reference to the deuterocanonical Book of the Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7.</note>

Hence, according to the doctrine of the Cabalists, this spirit is that great angel *Mettatron* <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Jewish mysticism, often seen as the mediator between God and the world.</note>, whose role is to animate the entire universe, and whom the Platonists were fond of calling the "Soul of the World." But they understood this clarity only insofar as it is allowed within a created spirit. We say, therefore, that this clarity, first striking the angelic spirit, primarily shaped it by its presence. For this reason, it is also said that the Name of God is in the angel—that is, the Divine light or the Word that gives life to all things, and which primarily moves within the angelic composition. From this, angels are the ministers through whom, as instruments, the Word of God is perfected in this world. Therefore, the Psalmist says: *Angels of God, most mighty in strength, doing His word, hearkening to the voice of His speech, His ministers who do His pleasure, Psalm 103.* And elsewhere: *Behold, I send my angel before you; listen to his voice, because my name is in him, Exodus 23.*

We conclude, therefore, that an angel is composed of a **created spirit**, which is its external part and serves as its body, and **uncreated light**, shining immediately from God, which is its internal part by which it is animated. By means of this composition, an angel is sometimes called "angel" or "alterity" <term>alterity: the state of being "other" or distinct from God's absolute unity</term> in the Holy Scriptures, in respect to the composition of its whole from two parts (namely, the internal and external). Yet in another place, it is called **JEHOVAH** in respect to its internal part alone, which is the emanation of God. Thus, sometimes it is said that an "angel" was in the burning bush, and sometimes that "Jehovah" spoke to Moses from the bush. For this very reason, the name of God is assigned to the angels of God, such as *Gabriel, Michael, Raphael,* and so on. <note>The suffix "-el" in these names is the Hebrew word for God.</note>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member II.

### CHAPTER III.

### *Concerning the General distinction of Angels, and then afterwards concerning the particular division of the good Angels.*

Since it is a well-known and commonplace fact, established not only by the experience of Christians but even by that of the Pagans, that there are spirits both evil (which they call <term>cacodemons: from the Greek *kakos* (bad) and *daimon* (spirit), referring to malevolent entities</term>) and good: we have deemed it worthwhile, first of all, to distinguish the intelligences according to this general division of theirs, based on the opposition of their properties and conditions. Therefore, we distinguish the angels at their primary root as follows:

We distinguish Angels into:
*   Good or Luminous <note>original: "Lucidos"; see Section A.</note>
*   Evil & dark. Concerning which, see the following chapter.

This great opposition within the Angelic condition resides in the diverse properties of the Creator, which vary according to the ten names attributed to Him by the Hebrews according to the sense of the Holy Bible. According to the arrangements of these names, various influences flow into this world through the <term>sephiroth: the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals Himself</term> (also called "numberings" or "luminous gates"). Some of these influences tend toward clemency and benignity, which are carried downward by the mediation of the good angels; likewise, those that incline toward severity are assigned to the punishing angels, who strike with the blow of divine wrath—as will be discussed more abundantly below. According to these two most opposite properties, men of the world have discovered various forms of knowledge: namely, **Good** knowledge, which occupies itself with God (the source of all goodness) and His administrative good angels; and **Evil** knowledge, which concerns the works of the Devil (who is the dealer of all malice or dark effects). To outline this for you methodically, we have compiled it into this distinction:

Knowledge in this world is either:

**I. Of the Good, and it is:**
*   **Theosophy** <term>Theosophy: "Divine Wisdom," knowledge focused on God and the spiritual realm</term>, which occupies itself in two matters, namely:
    *   The knowledge of the word of God, and the instruction of life according to His word.
    *   The understanding of the governance of GOD through the Angels (whom the holy page calls <note>original: "vigiles" — referring to the "Watchers," a class of angels mentioned in the Book of Daniel</note> **Watchers**), as well as the discernment of the mystery of the angels themselves.
*   **Androsophy** <term>Androsophy: "Human Wisdom," knowledge pertaining to the natural world and human society</term> given to man, namely:
    *   The science of natural things.
    *   Prudence in human affairs.

**II. Of the Evil, and it is:**
*   **Cacosophy** <term>Cacosophy: "Evil Wisdom," the corrupt inversion of true wisdom</term>, the members of which are:
    *   Contempt for the word of God, and living according to the will of the cacodemon.
    *   Ignorance of the governance of God through His Angels.
    *   To despise the protection of the good Angels, and to embrace the society of malignant demons.
    *   Idolatry and Atheism.
*   **Cacodaemony** <term>Cacodaemony: The practice or study of demonic arts</term>, of which there are also two members, namely:
    *   The science of poisoners <note>original: "veneficorum" — this term often encompassed sorcery, herb-craft used for harm, and literal poisoning</note> in nature, and the use of such things.
    *   "Prudence" in all arts inclined toward the ruin of the human race, and the practice of those arts as an insult to God and to the loss and destruction of man.

But to return to the proposal: we distinguish the good Angels in various forms, according to the various dimensions of the world—that is, according to the orders of the heavens from which the world is fashioned.

<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning. The "efficient cause" refers to the active agent—in this case, angels—that makes these events happen.</note>

Good angels are distinguished either:
*   With respect to the division of the world, and thus they are called:
    *   **Super-celestial** <note>original: "Supercælestes"</note> see B.
    *   **Celestial** <note>original: "Cælestes"</note> see C.
    *   **Elemental** <note>original: "Elementares"</note> see D.
*   As they appear to symbolize with the holy letters <note>Referring to the Hebrew alphabet</note> as shown below.

We call those "super-celestial" who belong to those nine orders which are said to be contained within the <term>Empyrean heaven: the highest part of heaven, thought in ancient cosmology to be the abode of God and composed of pure light or fire</term>. These appear to be organized and explained in various ways by the <term>Theosophists: scholars seeking direct knowledge of the divine</term>; we proceed, therefore, as follows:

<margin>B. The super-celestial Angels are divided by:</margin>

Theologians have placed the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones** in the higher distinction or Hierarchy as super-celestial spirits, gazing upon the rank and condition closest to divine providence. Of these orders, the highest regards the goodness and fiery love of God; the second, His essence and wisdom; and the third, His prudence and justice. **Isaiah chapter 6** makes mention of the **Seraphim**, and Holy Scripture does so in many other places where these spirits are described as being closest to God in order. To the **Cherubim** is assigned the guardianship of Paradise, and elsewhere: *God ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew upon the wings of the wind.* (**Psalm 17** <note>Modern Psalm 18:10</note>). Many sacred biblical passages also speak of the **Thrones**, namely **Ezekiel chapter 1**, the **Apostle in Colossians 1**, and **Revelation** in many places.

In the second Hierarchy are placed the **Virtues**, **Powers**, and **Dominions**, as world-spirits whose duty is more closely adapted to the governance of the world. The highest of these commands and gives orders to the lower ones; the second administers in the heavens and ordains the laws of fate; the third strives with great effort to ensure that those things which presume to disturb the divine law in any way are hindered. The Apostle speaks of principalities, powers, and Dominions in the place cited above, namely, **1 Colossians 16** <note>Colossians 1:16</note>.

In the lower Hierarchy, they describe the **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**, whose duty it is to descend to care for lower things. For the first order of this distinction cares for public affairs—namely, Princes, Magistrates, and Provinces or kingdoms, each according to their own. Among these, 72 are numbered by the <term>Cabalists: practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</term>, to whom 72 portions of the earth are committed by Divine providence, which are for that reason called kingdoms.

The second order is concerned with sacred matters and assists upright men on earth, and is said to offer prayers and sacrifices to GOD. Furthermore, seven from among them are dedicated to the governance and direction of the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> in the heaven, as will be discussed more broadly below. ### Section I. Part IV. Part II. Book IV. Member II.

On earth, these angels are of great importance for providing care, as they are accustomed to being present with individuals and, indeed, to caring for every creature—be it animal, vegetable, or mineral. St. Paul discusses these principalities in various places, and Archangels and Angels are mentioned everywhere throughout the sacred pages.

From these sources, it is clearly evident that each of these hierarchies has a special relationship to a person of the Most Holy Trinity: the highest relates to the divine essence; the middle relates to the emanation, or the Son, as it regards the monarchy and <term>Economy of the heavens: the divine administration or management of the universe</term>; and the lowest has respect for sublunary things <note>Items "below the moon," meaning the earthly realm subject to change and decay</note>, as it is present with the forms and virtues of the inferior world and is seen to administer to them.

To this effect, the royal Psalmist <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms</note> seems to speak in very few words, saying: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their virtues by the spirit of his mouth* <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt caeli, & spiritu ab ore eius omnes virtutes eorum"; Psalm 33:6</note>; where the Lord or the Father created the heavens through the Word or the Son, and every virtue and influence through the Spirit proceeding from both, and so forth.

Following the division of the ancient Hebrews, we see the same orders of angels—both in number and effect, though varying in their names—according to the series of the luminous gates or <term>Sephirot: the ten attributes/emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</term>, or the "numberings" of the Kabbalists <note>Scholars of Jewish mysticism</note>, through which various influxes of divine properties descend to the lower things. For as we have declared elsewhere, the influxes of **Kether** <note>The "Crown," the highest Sephirah</note>—over which the name of God **Ehieh** <note>original: "Ehieh," meaning "I Am"</note> presides—descend through the order of the **Seraphim** according to the doctrine of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian who defined the nine choirs of angels</note>. Likewise, according to the sense of the ancient Hebrew Doctors, it is taught that through the order of the angels **Haioth Kadosch** <note>The "Holy Living Creatures"</note>, God grants the gift of being via the name **Ehieh**; through the **Ophanim** <note>The "Wheels"</note>, God <note>original: "Ælohim"</note> distinguishes Chaos; through the **Aralim** <note>The "Valiant Ones"</note>, **Jehovah** provides the forms of universal matter; and so it goes with the others, as will be clearer in the following sections.

Other Hebrew Doctors have given almost the same names to these angelic orders, though changing the sequence: namely, **Cachmalim**, **Cherubin**, **Tarsisim**, **Arelim**, **Seraphim**, **Malachim**, **Ophanim**, **Issim**, **Elohim**, to which they also desire to add the **Ben Elohim**, who look over spirits both good and evil (of which more below). All these names were explained by the Doctors from the holy fountain of the sacred page itself. For Ezekiel speaks of the **Chasmalim** <note>The "Brilliant Ones" or "Amber ones"</note>. Genesis, Exodus, and the Psalms mention the **Cherubin**. Ezekiel also names the **Tarsisim**, though common interpretation offers "angels" or "messengers" in its place. Ezekiel also has the name **Ophanim**, just as **Issim** is expressed by Solomon. They took **Elohim** from the first book of Kings, where the <term>Pythoness: the Medium or Witch of Endor</term> said to Saul: "I saw Elohim ascending from the earth"—that is, "gods" according to the common edition. Moses and Job mention the **Bene Elohim** <note>Sons of God</note>, some being good, while Job mentions the evil ones in another place.

It is not irrelevant to note that although only nine orders of angels are noted by the wise or more secret theologians, there is an innumerable multitude of individual individuals of each of those species, which they have called "armies." They divided each of these orders, primarily according to the partition of the celestial Zodiac, into twelve parts, the first member of which division they called **Mizaloth** <note>The "Constellations" or Zodiac</note>. Then, they partitioned each of these twelve members into thirty portions, which they called "cohorts," and they called this subdivision **El**, which consequently contains under itself thirty cohorts for each of those twelve, making a total of three hundred and sixty cohorts of Angels.

Afterward, they assign another subdivision which multiplies that 360 by 30, producing the number 10,800; they call this subdivided member a **Legion**. They multiply this number again by 30 and produce what they call a **Rihaton**, consisting of 324,000. Furthermore, they multiply this number by 30 and the result is the number they call **Chitton**, which is composed of 972,000. Finally, they multiply that product again by 30, and the resulting number will be 29,160,000. From all these, the total sum is one million, six hundred and fifty-five thousand, one hundred and seventy-two <note>The author's math here follows a specific Kabbalistic calculation rather than a standard multiplication of the final product</note>, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, who made all these angels "ministering spirits," about whom more will be clear in the following pages.

The Platonists, however, maintain that there are as many legions of inferior spirits as there are stars in the heaven, and they say there are as many spirits in each legion as there are stars in the heaven. Some Kabbalists strenuously defend the idea that angels do not only correspond with humans in many natural things but also in number, asserting that there must be as many humans to be saved as there were rebellious angels who fell from heaven in the conflict and battle between Michael and Lucifer; and again, that there will be as many damned as there were angels on Michael’s side who gained the victory over the fallen angels.

But whatever the opinion of the Kabbalists and Platonists may be regarding the number of angels, we gather from the sacred scriptures that there are many myriads <note>Groups of ten thousand</note> of angelic spirits. In many places, David says: *The chariots of God are two myriads, many thousands of angels; the Lord is among them, the Lord of Sinai, dwelling in the Sanctuary* <note>Psalm 68:17</note>. Furthermore, Christ speaks of many legions of both his Father and of Satan. Both Augustine and Gregory maintain that the number of good angels transcends all human grasp; to which, on the contrary, respond the innumerable unclean spirits, there being as many existing in the lower world as there are world-spirits in the upper world. Certain theologians have also confessed to having received this from oracles. Celestial demons are called **mundane** <note>original: "mundani"; meaning "of the world" or "cosmic"</note> by the more secret theologians. Furthermore, those who dwell in the firmament and its stars are called **Olympic**; it is their duty to decree fates and administer fated events to those below, according to the will and permission of God. Thus it happens that neither an evil demon nor an evil fate can harm one who "sits in the aid of the Most High" <note>A reference to Psalm 91:1, "He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High"</note>.

Moreover, it is decreed for each of these spirits to bring about what the star to which it is attached portends. However, they can bring nothing from potentiality into action without divine permission, for God alone is the one who grants them the power and the execution, since to Him, as the Creator of all things, it is granted that super-celestial, celestial, sublunary <note>Earthly</note>, and even infernal things obey and submit.

As for the demons presiding over the **fixed stars**, those who hold their realms in the Zodiac preside either over the triplicities—namely fiery, airy, watery, or earthy.

Others are set over individual whole signs, namely: ***Malchidael*** over *Aries*; ***Asmodel*** over *Taurus*; ***Ambriel*** over *Gemini*; ***Muriel*** over *Cancer*; ***Verchiel*** over *Leo*; ***Hamaliel*** over *Virgo*; ***Zuriel*** over *Libra*; ***Zarachiel*** over *Scorpio*; ***Advachiel*** over *Sagittarius*; ***Hanael*** over *Capricorn*; ***Cambiel*** over *Aquarius*; and ***Barchiel*** over *Pisces*. Indeed, the names of the angels of any sign are usually derived from the harmony they have with the name of the thing they are set over. Thus from *Aries* comes ***Ariel***; [similarly] ***Telechiel***, ***Suriel***, ***Tommiel***, ***Sartamiel***, ***Betuliel***, ***Masniel***, ***Acrabiel***, ***Chefitiel***, ***Gediel***, ***Deliel***, and ***Dagymiel***. It is as if we were to say in Latin letters: *Ariel*, *Tauriel*, *Geminiel*, *Cancriel*, *Leoniel*, *Virginiel*, *Libriel*, *Scorpiel*, *Sagittariel*, *Capriel*, *Aquariel*, and *Pisciel*.

Regardless, it is certain that each of these signs has its own peculiar prefect or angel. The <term>Cabalists: scholars of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</term> believe John understood this in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note> where, in the description of the **Heavenly Jerusalem**, he mentions the twelve gates of the city. By the twelve gates, he understands the twelve celestial signs, which Plato calls the "gates of heaven." The Apocalypse says that in each of these gates there is an angel, for it explicitly assigns twelve angels to the twelve gates of the heavenly city. And just as there are three Eastern, three Western, three Southern, and finally three Northern signs of the Zodiac according to the doctrine of the Astrologers, so the revelator <note>John of Patmos</note> recognizes and assigns three gates to the eastern region, as many to the west, and likewise three to the south and as many to the north.

### Section I, Portion IV, Part II, Book IV, Member II.

Furthermore, the **Kabbalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism who sought to understand the hidden relationship between the eternal and the mortal</note> assign a lower angel to all the **decans** <note>10-degree segments of the zodiac</note> of the signs—which the Astrologers call "faces"—and even to the **quinaries**, which are the half-parts of a face. According to their opinion, every angelic **triplicity** <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: fire, air, water, or earth</note> also enjoys its own angelic prefect.

That every planetary sphere also has a spirit or presiding **Intelligence**, by whose mediation the world is governed in succession, is testified by Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot famous for his works on cryptography and angelology</note> in a specific treatise dedicated to Emperor Maximilian. Through these spirits, all things that exist in heaven and air, and those that live and grow on earth, are fatefully disposed according to the will of the Creator. Their Prince or superior prefect assigned to the governance of **Saturn** is called *Zabkiel* by the Magi, as some wish; others call him *Oriphiel*. Succeeding him is *Zadkiel*, or *Zachariel*, who presides over **Jupiter**, as does *Zamael* or *Samael* (or as others prefer, *Camael*) over **Mars**. *Michael* presides over the **Sun**, although some assign *Raphael* as its prefect; *Haniel* or *Anael* over **Venus**; *Raphael* over **Mercury**, though some attribute *Michael* to it; and *Gabriel* over the **Moon**. And it seems that John in the Apocalypse, chapter 1, understands these spirits ruling the planets when he says: *And from the seven spirits who are in the sight of the throne of God, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Et à septem spiritibus qui in conspectu throni DEI sunt &c."</note> Raphael also understood this when he said to Tobit: *I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before Jehovah.* And Gabriel said to Mary: *I am Gabriel, who stands before God (Luke 1).* And elsewhere it says to Daniel: *Behold, Michael, one of the princes, came to my aid (Daniel 10:13).* Zachariel was also the good angel of the Prophet Zechariah, of whom he writes: *The angel who spoke in me went forth, and said to another angel, "Run," etc. (Zechariah 2).* These princes or prefects have many cohorts of lower spirits under them within each of their jurisdictions. At the will of their leader (and according to God's commands), these spirits are constantly showered upon the lower realms by way of **influence** <note>term: <term>influence</term> — in astrology, a literal "flowing in" of celestial power or spiritual energy into the material world</note>; this happens more abundantly according to the dominance of the star in heaven which they are said to inhabit. And these lower angels or demons take their general names from their star. Just as we say "Frenchman," "Englishman," "Spaniard," or "Italian" to mean a man born in France, England, Spain, or Italy; so by the same reasoning we speak of **Jovial**, **Saturnine**, or **Martial** spirits, who are the inhabitants of those celestial spheres.

However, the angels under the empire, nature, and disposition of the Great Archangel **Gabriel** tend to vary according to the various positions of the lunar sphere under the signs of the Zodiac, which the Astrologers have called **Mansions**. These mansions are 28 in total, and therefore the angels governing them are called by various names, which we list in order as follows: *Geniel, Enediel, Amixiel, Azariel, Gabriel, Dirachiel, Scheliel, Amnediel, Barbiel, Ardesel, Neciel, Abdizuel, Iazeriel, Ergediel, Ataliel, Azeruel, Adriel, Egibiel, Amutiel, Kyriel, Bethnael, Celiel, Requiel, Abrinael, Aziel, Tagriel, Alheniel, Amnixiel.* All of these have great power both in the various changes of water and air, and in the alterations of terrestrial things.

Finally, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, there are other angels to whom the four watches of the night are committed, of whom Christ speaks thus: *And if he comes in the second or third watch of the night, etc.* Others are placed over the four seasonal guardians of the year, according to those four solar stations that occur in Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn <note>The spring equinox, summer solstice, autumn equinox, and winter solstice</note>.

The name **Michael** is assigned to the great solar angel because of awe and admiration, as if we were to say, "Who is so strong?" <note>A common etymological interpretation of Michael: "Who is like God?"</note> Regarding the origin of this angel, his illustrious lineage, his immense power in the world, and his dominion over both good and evil angels in this world, we shall speak more extensively in the following sections.

**Raphael** is named from the "Medicine of God," just as **Gabriel** is named from "manliness" <note>or "strength of God"</note>; **Uriel** means the "fire" or "light of God."
