Winds (whose souls we have said in the preceding sections are angels, either openly and manifest or occultly bright) we categorize either as invisible and subject only to hearing, or visible and bright—such as lightnings, fire-whirls <note>original: "presteres"</note>, flashes, and similar visible **meteors** <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning, not just falling stars.</note> which are driven in the air by violent motion, no differently than those winds which are visible. From these kinds of winds, then, as the first movers in the elementary world, all other meteors are produced and procreated, whether bright or dark: namely Comets, chasms <note>gaps in the clouds or sky</note>, "beams" of light, lightnings, flashes, fire-whirls, "leaping goats" <note>original: "capræ saltantes"; a term for flickering atmospheric lights</note>, *ignis fatuus* <note>Will-o'-the-wisp</note>, and sulfurous flames which the earth vomits up. These come from bright winds and are manifest to fire—which in their nature are nothing besides the most subtle air, animated and agitated by a fiery soul. But truly, clouds, mists, vapors, snow, hail, stones, hoarfrost, and ice come from **occult** and less manifest winds as efficient causes, and from occult and dark air contracted into such dark shapes. Regarding these occult and least visible winds, we shall say a few words in this place, and that in the common manner.

## CAP. III.

It is also called *Vulturnus* <note>The South-East wind</note> by some because of its rapid nature; for it is accustomed to blow violently and fly high, being observed to behave like a vulture <note>original: "vulture"; a play on the name Vulturnus</note>. By its nature, this wind is stormy, hot in itself, and dry, but it does not abound in dryness as much as the **Caecias** does, because on one side it faces the damp South wind. For this reason, it is often observed to gather clouds, just as, in respect to its dryness and heat, it is sometimes observed to dissipate gathered clouds throughout the air and fill the atmosphere with smoky mists and thick vapors. Because of this, it often deceives the sight, making visible objects appear larger than they truly are.

For a fuller explanation of the qualities of these winds, I refer and send you to the following volume which, God willing, will treat the nature of health and disease.

# CHAPTER IV.

->Description of the West wind with its wings or collateral winds,<-
->and of the meteors which they are accustomed to produce in the air.<-

That general wind blowing from the corner of the west, whose midpoint is cut by the **equinoctial line**, is called *Favonius* in Latin and *Zephyrus* in Greek—that is, "bringing life and vigor." This is the prince of those winds that blow from the west. In its nature, this wind is cold and humid in a most temperate degree. It has the *Aphricus* <note>The South-West wind</note> as its "right wing" or collateral wind, and the *Corus* <note>The North-West wind</note> as its left.

The collateral wind **Aphricus** is therefore that which blows from that point of the western horizon intersected by the **Tropic of Capricorn**, namely, from the winter solstice. Its disposition is to incline somewhat toward southern heat, but western cold chiefly abounds in it. This wind is accustomed to blow impetuously in turns, whence it is stormy and sometimes accompanied by clouds.

The other "wing" of the **Favonius** turning toward the North is that wind which blows from that point in the west which the **Tropic of Cancer** cuts, namely, from the summer solstice. This is called *Corus* in Latin and *Argestes* in Greek—that is, "impetuous and stormy." In its condition, it is somewhat inclined away from the humidity of the **Favonius** toward the dryness of the North. Thus it is naturally prone to producing hail, snow, and cold, and is humid by turns; while it blows, the clouds in the sky are observed to be dark, although for part of the day it may be serene, dry, and finally humid. Furthermore, sometimes due to more intense humidity, it brings haily or snowy rains, and occasionally—more frequently in summer—it brings the most vehement thunder, lightning, and horrendous storms.

Concerning the production of these qualities in both the "macrocosm" and "microcosm" <note>original: "vtroque mundo"; the world and the human body</note>, whether regarding disease or health, we shall speak copiously in the following volume, God assisting.

# CHAPTER V.

->On the North wind with its two companions and<-
->their effects in the air.<-

The North wind, called *Boreas* in Greek, is the principal wind of the North, and it usually blows directly from the **Pole Star**. In its condition, it is extremely cold and dry. It is the task of this wind to cleanse and purify the air of the thick humors produced by the South wind. According to the testimony of Holy Scripture, it is accustomed to drive away rains, though it sometimes produces hail and snow—specifically at that time when the South wind blows strongly against it. This occurs when a louder noise is heard; for then it condenses the air into clouds, and sometimes, especially in summer, it is observed to produce thunder.

Its "left wing" is called **Aquilo** <note>The North-East wind</note>, which blows from that point of the eastern region where the polar or **Arctic circle** cuts the horizon. This wind in its condition is very cold and dry, but truly somewhat...

The right wing of the North Wind <note>original: "Boreæ"</note> is that wind called **Circius** <note>original: "Circium"; likely the North-Northwest wind</note>, and this blows from that point of the west where the Arctic Circle is observed to intersect the western horizon. ### CHAPTER VI.

->*On the three Southern Winds, along with their conditions in the production of meteors.*<-

**F**inally, the **Cardinal** <term>Cardinal: refers to the four principal directions—North, South, East, and West</term> and principally reigning wind in the south, which is said to blow from the Antarctic pole, is called **Auster** <note>the South wind</note>, named, as some would have it, from "drawing up" <note>original: "hauriendo"</note> waters. This wind is hot and humid in its nature; thus it is accustomed not only to gather thick and constant clouds but also to pour out heavy rains. It tends to produce lightning, to make the air thick and dense, to nourish mists, and also quite often to flash and give forth great peals of thunder. Furthermore, just as the North Wind is a hard wind that hardens humors, so the South Wind is soft and softening.

Its right wing blows from the place of intersection made by the Antarctic circle on the Eastern Horizon and is called **Euro-Auster** <note>the South-Southeast wind</note>. In its quality, it is hot and humid, but indeed because of its aspect toward the Eastern corner, it is somewhat hotter and not entirely as humid as the South Wind. It is a cloud-bearer and sometimes a producer of thunder.

Its left wing is the **Austro-Africus** <note>the South-Southwest wind</note>, which blows from that point of the western Horizon where the Antarctic circle intersects it. This wind produces stormy winds, which are sometimes accompanied by clouds and thunder.

From this, therefore, you see what those learned by common insight and experience perceive: that nearly all **meteors** <term>meteors: in the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, snow, or wind, not just falling stars</term> proceed from the winds. But truly, the pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> seemed to us to be ignorant of the internal essence of these winds; they carelessly claimed their internal agent was merely exhalations springing from the earth and animated by the heat of the sun. However, we are taught by Saint John that it is not known where the winds arise or where they go, and that the spirit <note>the Latin word "spiritus" means both "spirit" and "breath/wind"</note> is accustomed to blow where it wills. And the Prophet says that Jehovah made his Angels winds, and his ministers a burning flame. By this speech, he clearly seems to explain that there are two kinds of winds, after the manner of Angels: those that are heard and not at all seen, which are hidden; and those that are seen and are bright, but are not heard at all except through their effect, as are lightning and flashes in thunder. And so, almost weary and fatigued by the exhaustion of such great labor, we gladly place an end to this volume (not without perpetual grace and blessing to God our Creator for such great favor and illumination).

# ON A CERTAIN UNIVERSAL EXPERIMENT 
# WHICH DEMONSTRATES THE ORIGIN OF 
# METEORS AS IF WITH A POINTING FINGER.

->*A brief prelude, in which the logic of this spiritual machine is clearly explained through another machine, which has been quite often described and demonstrated by us before.*<-

In the first tractate of the First Book of our *History of the Macrocosm* <note>original: "Macrocosmicæ nostræ historiæ"; Fludd’s massive work on the structure of the universe</note>, we took care to illustrate a certain figure concerning a particular spiritual experiment. Although we provided many other experiments and demonstrations almost everywhere in that discourse to support our reasoning, we nevertheless decided that our primary intention should be drawn from that very illustration which we depicted at the end of Chapter 6 of the first Book of that history. ### Universal Experiment

L. M. is the neck of the matrass <term>matrass: a glass flask with a round body and a long neck, commonly used in early chemistry and physics</term> whose orifice L. is submerged in the water.
N. is the hole in the lid, through which the part of the neck submerged in water enters.
M. is the portion of the matrass divided into twelve equal parts.
O. is the body of the matrass, standing upright.

We think it worthwhile to proceed quickly to the properties and use of this instrument. First, it must be observed that when the body of the matrass (O) is heated, the air trapped within it is thinned <note>original: "subtiliatur" — in early modern science, heat was thought to make substances "subtle" or less dense</note> by the external heating warmth; once thinned, it requires a larger space to contain its existence. Thus, a greater portion of air—which had been gathered and contracted in the hollow of that body by the cold—now thinned and dilated more or less by the heat, requires a more ample place for its existence. For this reason, a portion of it is forced to exit into the open air while the vessel or body of the matrass is heating. 

Consequently, once the opening of the matrass neck is placed into the water (while the vessel is still warm), as that body gradually cools, the water is drawn up and rises into the neck of the matrass by degrees: specifically from degree 1 to 2, and then from 2 to 3. The reason for this is as follows: the action of cold is in every way the opposite of heat. Therefore, if it is the nature of heat to thin and to require a larger or more spacious place for the thing it has thinned or attenuated, it follows that, conversely, it is the nature of cold to thicken [inspissate] and gather the substance that was dispersed and rarefied by heat, reducing it into a narrower place. 

Thus, as the strength of the heat gradually vanishes and the power of the cold subsequently grows stronger, a greater portion of air is expelled from the hollow of the vessel by thinning. Because the water acts as a barrier, new air sufficient to match the growing strength of the spirit <note>original: "spiritus" — here referring to the "vital" or active quality of the air</note> cannot be drawn into the belly of the vessel. Therefore, it is necessary that a portion of water supplies the defect of the air and is raised into the neck of the matrass in place of the air. This happens because the thinned air, which once filled the entire cavity of the body, is now contracted into a narrower place by the binding and freezing faculty of the cold; it would leave a vacuum in the vessel (which is in no way permitted by nature) <note>This refers to the "horror vacui," the ancient belief that nature abhors a vacuum and will move matter to prevent one from forming</note> unless the water supplied the filling of that space, as has been explained more extensively elsewhere.

Once the body of water has been drawn up and elevated in this way, due to the successive creeping in and abundance of cold, any future increase in cold or heat will necessarily be discerned with open eyes. For if either the air surrounding that vessel, or something more solid applied to or touching the vessel, grows warm, then the more intense that surrounding air or applied object is in heat, the more the water will decline downward toward the box. For example, if the water stood at degree 6 or 7 in the neck due to a state of cold, then with an increase in heat—whether in the surrounding air or by applying a hand or another object to the body—the water will descend through as many degrees as the proportion of heat has increased in the enclosed air.

The reason for this is readily apparent: as has been said, the greater the proportion of heat, the greater the thinning or rarefaction of the enclosed air. And the rarer and thinner a thing becomes, the more it seeks a wider and more free place for its existence. For a single handful of water dilated into air requires ten times as much space to be contained as it claimed for itself in its liquid consistency; the same ratio or proportion exists between air and fire, for air ignited by heat migrates gradually into the thinness of fire. 

Therefore, the air enclosed in the body of the vessel—which was formerly contracted by cold and reduced into a narrower place—is now dilated by the approach of heat and thrusts the water that had risen in the neck downward, so that it may acquire a larger or narrower place for itself according to the greater or lesser degree of its rarefaction. Are we not taught by experience that water reduced into vapor by the violence of fire requires a vast place for its freedom? Whoever prepares himself for a more exact inquiry into this matter, we wish them to be referred to the experiments brought forth by us in Chapter 2, Experiments 12, 13, and 16, and in Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, Chapter 1, Rules 6 and 7, where we have clearly expressed the infinite faculty of nature dilating itself. 

Furthermore, this is explained even more evidently to the unlearned by means of gunpowder <note>original: "pulvere Bombardali"</note>; a small portion of its earth-like substance is usually converted into a great smoke like a huge cloud, snatching and shattering everything with it if its spacious freedom is hindered. Likewise, in the extraction of *aqua fortis* <note>original: "aquæ fortis" — nitric acid</note> composed from saltpeter and vitriol, we observe the receiving vessel containing the greatest spirits leaping forth from the orifice of the retort. We conclude, therefore, that heat, by dilating, causes the air enclosed in the body to repel the water raised in the neck, so that the dilated air may acquire a larger place for itself, according to the greater or lesser dominance of the heat's effect on the enclosed air.

But indeed, as the effect of heat decreases and grows faint, and the cold gradually revives and predominates, it is necessary that every power and operation of the preceding heat be removed, and that, on the contrary, the properties and acts of cold—which are opposite to those of heat—be produced. Thus, just as the water elevated in the neck was pushed downward by the act of heat, so now a contrary effect is produced by the contrary affection of cold.

The reason for this matter is as follows: since it is the property of heat to thin and rarefy, in which act a wider space is required to contain the thinned substance,

## CHAPTER III.

->On the various uses of this experimental instrument.<-

Although the chief aim in demonstrating such an instrument is to derive a most suitable observation of atmospheric phenomena from its double action of contrary motion, it is my intention here to speak briefly regarding its common use, which is relevant to our subsequent contemplation.

By its general constrictive action—that is, the rising of water through the contraction of air—we perceive the logic of **Density** or the thickness of any thing; this action of nature proceeds from cold (as you have seen reported above). Conversely, through the action of dilation, by which the water is propelled downward due to the dissipation and resolution of the enclosed air, we perceive the cause of **Rareness** or subtlety in nature, which property is derived from heat. From this it is certain, and we are made more sure beyond all doubt, that nothing in the entire kingdom of nature can be rarefied or thinned except by the mediation of light or fire (whether visible or invisible), the effect of which is heat. Conversely, nothing can be condensed, constricted, or thickened where darkness does not hold dominion, since its effect is cold, as was clearly explained in the location cited above.

Its more specific use is manifold: first and most evidently, it is accustomed to indicate the natural state and temperament of the external air regarding heat and cold. For the higher the water tends through the degrees of the neck, the greater is the dominion of cold in the air. Thus, in any quarter of the year, as well as on any day of the week, we can judge the degrees of cold by the rise of the water; indeed, within the same day, we will perceive the conflict of solar heat and cold, and many other things worthy of observation. Furthermore, by the same logic through the contrary motion, we will derive the dominion of heat in any quarter, day, or hour of the year. Such observations are of no small importance in the unfolding of nature and its mysteries.

Moreover, those same effects are usually provided by added heat or cold. Thus it happens that if we apply only the hand over the bottom of the glass matrass <term>matrass: a glass flask with a round body and a long neck, commonly used in early chemistry</term>, the enclosed air—thinned by the heat of the applied limb—forces the water downward in the blink of an eye. Once the hand is removed from the vessel, the water immediately longs to return to its original place assigned to it by natural cold.

Finally, by proper observation of such an instrument and vigilant attention to the movement of the water, we can measure the heat of chemical furnaces. For if we have two such instruments ready, one exposed to the mildness of naturally affected air, and the other applied to a vent breathing from a furnace, they will yield a ratio for adapting the artificial heat of the one to the natural heat of the other. At last, the one applied to the artificial heat will be rectified in its degree by this natural one. From this, it will be very easy to derive a unit of proportion in artificial heat in this way: namely, by adapting the degree of natural heat in the air to that artificial one. For example, if the heat in the naturally placed instrument has pushed the water back only to degree 7, but the heat of the instrument applied to the furnace has depressed it to degree 4, then I may observe that the artificial fire exceeds the natural one by only three degrees. Therefore, if the natural heat in the air should decrease later and the water rises to degree 8 or 9, I will expect the water in the instrument applied to the furnace to rise by the same proportion to degree 5 or 6. Thus it always maintains its triple proportion in distance, which is to be ascribed to the artificial heat, and so on for the others.

Now I shall proceed to the second part of this book, where, God willing, we shall discuss the specific contemplation of the generation of atmospheric phenomena, having taken into account the action or property of this pneumatic <term>pneumatic: original "spiritalis," referring here to the air or "spirit" contained within the device</term> instrument.

# Universal Experiment

## SECOND PART OF THIS
### *Experimental Book.*

### CHAPTER I.

### *On the primary reason for condensation and freezing.*

Just as you have heard from us in previous sections that heat and its effects flow from God in His manifest state <note>original: "Deo patente" — God as He is revealed to the world through light and action.</note>, so too we have shown that coldness and its effects lead their primary origin from God in His hidden state <note>original: "Deo latente" — God in His retracted, unrevealed state of pure potentiality.</note>. Yet coldness (though born from the womb of darkness and matter <note>original: "hylæ" — Hyle is a Greek-derived term for the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</note>) was not prior in actual time or place until heat also claimed its essence in the world. For coldness is recognized in the world only insofar as it is in every way opposed to heat in nature and property. Nevertheless, God-hidden is thought by us mortals to be older in time than God-manifest, because before the creation of the world He was unknown and, as it were, idle in respect to human capacity. For this reason, He is called <term>A E N</term> <note>original: "Ayin" — a Hebrew term meaning "Nothing" or "Non-being," used in the Kabbalah to describe the Infinite (Ein Sof) before it reveals itself.</note> by the Kabbalists and Hebrew Rabbis; that is, "nothing" and "non-being," since He is known only to Himself and exists within Himself. Indeed, those skilled in the occult philosophy have described Wisdom as such before the construction of the world: namely, as a dark principle, having action only in potentiality. For this reason, they frequently called it the <term>Dark Aleph</term> <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the "Dark Aleph" represents the divine source before the first light of creation emerged.</note>; that is, that which has not yet shone forth from the darkness, but has reflected its rays into itself. Hence Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and scientific writings are attributed; a foundational figure for Renaissance alchemy.</note> said: *The Monad generates the Monad and reflected its heat into itself.* If, therefore, all heat and fervor comes from revelation and from this outflow—that is, from the revealed divine act, namely the emission and emanation of divine brightness from the center of darkness to its circumference, when the hidden God is turned into the manifest God, or the Dark Aleph into the Bright Aleph—it follows that all chill and cold are produced by the contrary reasoning. This occurs, namely, by the contraction of the divine rays into themselves, in which act the airy medium, deprived of heat (as heat arises from the act of emission and not the retraction of divine light), gives place to cold. This quality holds its name and dominion from the deprivation of heat, just as dryness arises from the absence of moisture. And the more God contracts or hides His act within Himself or His center, the more cold abounds, and dense, earthly shadows hold dominion. Therefore, in such a case, the air is turned into thick and dark clouds, into rain, into snow, hail, and even into frost. For Wisdom (which is the life of the world-spirit, and consequently of the entire world), by retracting itself from the circumference toward the center, also contracts the spirit. To this spirit, Wisdom is life, just as the soul is to the body. Furthermore, the appetite of created matter for its central, creating form is so immense that it follows that form by a certain natural instinct and remains obedient to it, both for expansion and contraction, according to the will of the creating spirit—almost as if it vehemently feared that by forsaking the benevolent rays of its creator, it would be rendered deformed and clearly nothing, just as it was in the beginning. Hence it is that in this world we have so many contraries consisting of a binary nature (for which reason the number two is called the number of confusion and imperfection by the followers of Pythagoras <note>Ancient Greek philosopher who believed numbers were the fundamental building blocks of reality; two was seen as "discord" because it breaks away from the unity of "one."</note>), namely: darkness and light, night and day, the Devil and God, death and life, rest and motion, nothing and something, sin and justice. A prince of light presides over some of these, and a prince of darkness over others. Nevertheless, in reality, through a central consideration, all these are but one. Whence it is certain that the One is all things; or as we have it in the Sacred Scriptures, Christ or Wisdom is all things—the beginning and the end, the Alpha and Omega, the center and the circumference. Nonetheless, in respect to the variety of actions, without which there would be no mutability in the world, and no generation or corruption in the nature of things, this One seems to be divided and distributed into various things as far as we mortals are concerned. For by an absolute, general contraction of the divine rays that create all things in themselves, it is necessary that the world be reduced to nothing. By a particular contraction, it is necessary that the individual person to whom that deprivation or retraction pertains should also suffer death, or tend closer to death, the more effectively God calls back or contracts the rays of His benevolence into Himself. This is also to be gathered clearly enough from these words of the Royal Prophet: *When God hides His face, the creatures are troubled; when He takes away their spirit, they die and return to their dust; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated:* Psalm 104:29.

Where, by the "hiding of His face," is understood the turning away or contraction of His life-giving rays, more or less into Himself; by "taking away" is meant the absolute contraction, from which comes the complete deprivation of life, the removal of vital motion, the fixing of the body, and its reduction to dust. But indeed, by the "sending forth of His spirit," the dead rise again, the sick are restored to their former health and are refreshed by good, and they are seen to remain in a state of unity and specific existence.

And hence the Royal Prophet says: *Life is present in the benevolence of Jehovah.* Psalm 30:6. And elsewhere: *The fountain of life is with thee.* Psalm 36:9.

# On the Generation of Atmospheric Phenomena <note>original: "De Meteororum Generatione" — In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and wind.</note>

And elsewhere, the extension of life is the kindness of GOD, Psalm 90:14. And Job said, *His visitation has preserved my spirit, Job 10:12.* And Moses: *Jehovah your God himself is your life and the length of your days;* but of these things, we shall speak more clearly at another time.

From these things, therefore, it appears more clearly than the midday sun (unless I am mistaken) that cold arises through the contraction or reflection of the divine rays into themselves—that is, the absence of heat. From this cold, freezing, stillness, and the removal of motion are produced, and consequently death or the deprivation of life. It is for this reason that the Earth, being the lowest or most extreme order in the nature of things, is the most still, immobile, and fixed, as if it were saturated by a thickening and contracting coldness. Therefore, the primary origin of freezing and constriction comes from GOD lurking centrally <note>God "hiding" within the center of His own being.</note> and contracting and reflecting the rays of His goodness into Himself (as Hermes Trismegistus holds), or as the prophet David suggests, *by hiding his face*, or by receiving his spirit back into himself in Psalm 104. Conversely, the primary beginning of resolution <note>original: "resolutio" — here meaning the melting or breaking down of solid matter.</note> and expansion comes from God being manifest <note>original: "Deo patente" — God revealed in action.</note>, emitting the rays or the spirit of His goodness everywhere, here and there according to His pleasure. This follows the words of the royal prophet: *creatures are renewed when God sends forth his spirit*; or as Hermes Trismegistus says, *When Poimandres <note>The "Divine Pymander" or "Shepherd of Men," the personified Mind of God in Hermetic texts.</note> wished to reveal himself, all things were turned into a most pleasant light, etc.* But we shall deal more extensively with this revealed principle, or the primary light brought into the light, in what follows.

->### CHAP. II.<-

->### *On the primary occasion and origin of thinning*<-
->### *and expansion.*<-

**W**e have indicated that the primordial cause of condensation and thickening was the effect of the hidden God—namely, cold. Now, however, we think it necessary to demonstrate that the cause of thinning <note>original: "subtiliationis" — the process of making matter "subtle" or less dense, such as water turning to steam.</note> and expansion flowed originally from the efficacy of the action of the manifest God. Thus, according to the meager capacity of humans, the "Dark Aleph" <term>Aleph tenebrosum</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here representing God's first, unmanifest state of potentiality.</note> or the hidden God is thought by the Kabbalists to be at rest—that is, idle and not at all active, and consequently existing in potential. He has no regard for anything, which is why He is called <term>NIHIL</term> <note>original: "Ayin" — Hebrew for "Nothingness," the infinite source before creation.</note> by the Kabbalists. In the same way, on the opposite side, they understood the "Light Aleph" to be the manifest God—that is, God acting, revealing Himself, and illuminating and creating all things by His emanation and His luminous Word. Similarly, just as it is the nature of cold to condense, thicken, rest, and act very little (unless it is by reacting—that is, by repelling the assaults of the heat's action), so we see by the contrary way that it is the nature of heat to thin, never to rest, but to always be engaged in action. Therefore, coldness is its opposite. From this, it is right to consider that heat is the offspring and firstborn of the manifest God's acts, just as coldness is the immediately proceeding child of the hidden God.

Cold holds its place and sequence in that progression which occurs from the hidden God to the manifest God—that is, between God having regard for nothing, and God intent upon the formation of the world or its creatures. Thus it happens that the source of cold is potentiality alone. Although it is a quality, it is nonetheless potential in itself and is not brought into action except in relation to heat; hence its name is defined in relation to heat, nor does it usually act except insofar as it is pushed back, reverberating the actions arising from heat. Therefore, cold rests with darkness by a natural instinct, while with light, the heat reigns and acts. And hence it is that, while heat is observed to contribute most to the generation of things, coldness is always the companion of deprivation. Yet it is certain that both these contrary qualities emanate from a single God in essence, though differing in property, which is why the Wise Man says: *Ecclesiasticus 7:14. Good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches are from God.* For that same nature which is the author of generation is also the author and occasion of corruption. Thus, when God hides His face—that is, inclining toward His own occult nature—cold reigns and heat fades; but when He sends forth His spirit—that is, manifesting or revealing Himself—the effect of heat is increased. 

Therefore, by God considered in His simple essence, without any regard for creation, we understand the hidden God. But by "the Word," the Holy Scriptures signified the second person, the first emanation into the world, the uncreated light in the world, through which all things were made and without which nothing was made, as it is found in John. Therefore, the Word acts in its own power, and the effect of its action produces heat. Heat, in imitation of its divine parent, always longs to move and never rests from action, but labors by expanding and thinning, and strives to destroy those things which coldness has constructed. From this come death and life, generation and corruption; from this, the thick and the subtle, the heaven and the earth, the light and the dark, motion and rest. But the royal prophet taught us clearly concerning the different disposition of these qualities, along with the primordial principle of each, in these words: *He casts down his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? Sending forth his word, he melts them; as soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow. Psalm 147:17.* From this discourse, one may gather that God, in His cold property, thickens the thin air into ice and snow and frost (as was clearly explained in the preceding verse). But through His Word—that is, through the revelation of Himself—those things thus thickened and condensed by the cold are again dissolved by thinning, and are led back from terrestrial thickness into water, and from water into air.

### Universal Experiment

### A Corollary from the Demonstration.

All these things, which have just been recounted concerning cold and heat, are best demonstrated by their effect through the medium of our experimental machine <note>This "experimental machine" is a thermoscope, a precursor to the thermometer, which Fludd used to demonstrate the expansion and contraction of air.</note>. For regarding the nature of coldness in particular, we observe that when it predominates in the open air or in the body of the flask, the water is raised higher and higher. We have the reason for this at hand: namely, because the enclosed air, which was previously dilated by external heat, is now—with the arrival and assault of cold—contracted more and more according to the intensity and dominion of that cold. This contraction happens by necessity and natural instinct; but truly, because a vacuum is not permitted in the nature of things <note>original: "vacuum in rerum natura non admittitur" — This refers to the Aristotelian concept of *horror vacui*, or "nature abhors a vacuum."</note>, it is necessary that the water touching this enclosed air must fill that space which the air had previously occupied due to its dilation. Thus, the water is visibly elevated upward because of the presence of intense cold, and the more that cold dominates, the more the water will be lifted up by degrees. Conversely, when heat predominates in the external air or on the surface of the vessel, the internal air (the air trapped in the vessel) will dilate for the reasons we alleged above. In its dilation, it requires a larger space to be contained. Hence, the water—which had been drawn up by the previously dominating cold—now descends to give place to the dilating air. It is seen to lower itself by as many degrees as the heat is observed to prevail over the cold. Accept this as a general consideration of this machine in relation to natural reality. Now, however, we shall move on to more specific matters.

# PART III.

## On the detailed investigation of Atmospheric Phenomena <note>original: "Meteororum" — In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and clouds, not just falling space rocks.</note> based on the observation of the properties of this machine.

### CHAPTER I.

#### On the Origin of the Winds.

Elsewhere we have declared at length, and this according to the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, that God is the act of acts, the Creator of creatures, the light of lights, and the fountain of life and motion. This fountain of all things, this primary spirit of spirits, this unity of unities, or center of the universal circle, sent forth His Word. This is to say, He manifested His light, which was once contracted and hidden within Himself (that is, hidden centrally). Through this emanation of His divine light or Word—which is the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), considered by Fludd to be the active power behind creation.</note>, or the divine Word itself, or the light in the world which the world did not comprehend—He miraculously brought all things existing only in potentiality into light and Being. This is according to the words of the Royal Psalmist: *By the word of the LORD the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth, Psalm 33.* Or as Saint Peter has it: *By the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water, 2 Peter 3.* Therefore, this light—creating all things and moving all things from the center—having completed the third day of creation, placed its tabernacle in the sun <note>original: "posuit tabernaculum suum in sole" — A reference to Psalm 19:4, suggesting the sun is the physical dwelling place of God's creative spirit.</note>; that is, in the central habitation of the sun, as the most beautiful of all creatures and the most worthy of cleanliness and purity. From the fountain of the sun, therefore, is the spring of life, the emanation of both celestial and elemental light, and the soul and act of the universal spirit. Consequently, all other stars obey it, just as they would an emperor holding a throne and scepter. Even the Wise Man <note>Solomon, traditionally the author of Ecclesiastes.</note> seems to acknowledge its power over the worldly spirit, expressed in these very clear words: *After the sun sets, it pants again toward its place where it rises; it hastens to the south and circles the North; and the air (or as Jerome translates it, the spirit) hastens on its circling course; or as Pagninus has it here: The wind goes circling thereafter, and the wind returns to its circuits. Ecclesiastes, Chapter 1.* And indeed, since the soul and act of the world comes from the invisible or internal sun establishing its tabernacle in the visible sun, there is no doubt that all force and motion of the worldly spirit takes its origin from that source. Consequently, every motion or agitation of the universal air comes from the sun's center, as if from the innermost active principle of all things. Yet wind is said by the ethnic philosophers <note>Non-Christian or Pagan philosophers, specifically the Greeks and Romans.</note> (whose doctrine the Christians of our age follow as if they were the chief priests of divine matters) to be nothing other than "moved or agitated air." Therefore, it follows that all motions of the high air, from whatever land they arise, are stirred up by an internal central principle of this kind, though by different means. But we have this confirmed not only by the Holy Scriptures, but even by the prince of the Peripatetics himself—namely Aristotle—even if he contradicts himself in this. By him, the winds are called (not unwisely in this case) the sons of Titan, Astraea, and Aurora <note>Figures from Greek mythology representing the sun, the stars/justice, and the dawn.</note>, inasmuch as they are procreated by solar heat, since it is the sun's role to make the air thin and rare, and this especially at Dawn. Yet they are also said to obey the commands of Juno <note>The Roman goddess often associated in alchemical and natural philosophy with the element of Air.</note>, insofar as they do not blow except in the aerial medium.

# On the Generation of Meteors.

...which is named Juno <note>In the symbolic language of the time, the goddess Juno was frequently used as an allegory for the element of Air.</note>. From this it is demonstrated clearly enough that Aristotle and Solomon agree on this point: namely, that the air or the wind is governed by the rays and motion of the sun. But truly, it is certain and confirmed by the experience of skilled astronomers that the variety of the winds' motion happens due to the various aspects <note>original: "aspectibus" — In astrology, "aspects" are the specific angular relationships (like squares or trines) between celestial bodies.</note> or reflections of the sun and the other erratic stars <note>term: erratic stars <gloss>the planets, as opposed to the "fixed" stars of the constellations</gloss></term>. Since indeed all stars receive their life and luminous being from the sun, it follows that all the actions of the planets—flowing from their various mutual aspects—originally proceed from the Sun’s soul or its central unity. This is not surprising, since we see different effects arising from the same fire. For example, fire warms gently, it parches and burns without mercy, it moistens by accident (which happens by thinning the substance), and yet, by the dry removal of moisture from calcined earth, it both vivifies and destroys; by reflection it torments bodies more severely, and when contracted into an angle it penetrates vividly, yet when spread out it vanishes. 

In the same way, the sun acts in different ways according to the different media through which it passes. For example, in the air it warms pleasantly; in water its heat is more tempered; sometimes it fosters the earth and causes the grass, herbs, and trees to grow; and sometimes it burns and cracks the earth and its fruits with its excessive heat. Nevertheless, the sun is always the same in its essential temperature, nor is any variety seen in it except because of the diversity of the media and bodies it acts upon. For in the open air it fosters gently, but by means of a burning mirror <note>original: "speculo ardente" — a parabolic or concave mirror used to concentrate sunlight to start fires.</note> it burns cruelly; yet it is always the same in itself and of the same power. It is only observed to act differently according to the nature of the passive receiver. For example, in the heavens it communicates its rays to the planetary bodies, which in turn—by secondary or tertiary reflection, that is, from one planet to another according to the distance of their locations, the difference of their bodies, and the variety of their aspects—produce various effects in the elements. 

Hence it is that when God wishes to create this or that effect on earth according to the order of nature, He looks toward this or that planet, by whose aspect the other planets also look upon each other. From this, various winds arise, whose "souls" are nothing other (as was copiously declared before) than spirits or demons, sent down from the various celestial worlds or planetary orbs by occult influences. Thus we said in the preceding pages that the Angel presiding over the sun is <term>Metattron</term> <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Kabbalistic tradition, often viewed as the celestial scribe or the "lesser Yahweh" who mediates between the divine and the material.</note>, whom we explained to be nothing other, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, than that primary emanation or that lucid Wisdom created before all things, by which all things were afterwards created. All good angels are accustomed to obey and comply with him, just as the other stars are secondary to the sun in power, light, and dignity; and consequently, so are all those angelic presidents or Intelligences to whom the command of those bright orbs is attributed. This is because, by his wise wisdom from his central palace existing in the heart of the visible sun, they fulfill the commands and will of the invisible sun, as their divine and universal Lord.

### *Correlation to the property of that machine of ours.*

GOD, the source and supernatural origin of Light and consequently of heat (which is the effect of light), placed his tabernacle in the sun. From this natural fountain, He gives fiery power to the heaven and the elements; then to the elementary parts, both celestial (such as the erratic and fixed stars) and sublunary <note>term: sublunary <gloss>literally "under the moon"; the realm of the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) where things are subject to change and decay</gloss></term>, among which the lightning-fire and the terrestrial fire claim the first place for themselves. If, therefore, the aerial spirit is altered by immediate fiery heat, or by violent agitation or motion (as is evident in the collision of two bodies or the revolution of a wheel), it arises primarily from the Sun in respect to its natural principle. The Sun received its central power—both moving and agitating as well as heating—from God by means of His angel Metatron. 

We see, therefore, that by means of Heat, whose father is the sun, the universal spirit (and consequently the particular spirit) is governed, and by dilation is moved and led around, just as the human breath is drawn in and exhaled by means of the human soul. Therefore, the particular spirit enclosed in the glass or <term>matrass</term> <note>A matrass is a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck used in laboratory experiments.</note> is dilated by the presence of heat, and in its dilation, it requires a larger space; thus its thickness, which the cold had gathered, is now dissipated and driven into the part opposite to the seat of the heat.

So also in the generation of Winter winds, it is certain that the sun itself holds the first place. The reason is at hand: namely, because when the sun predominates in the regions beyond the equinoctial <note>The southern hemisphere.</note> and warms those places in a wonderful way due to the perpendicularity of its rays, it is necessary that the air—which was condensed by cold during our summer time while the sun was inhabiting Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo—should now (during our winter time) be dissolved again by the near presence of the sun. It becomes thinned, and because of its thinness, it requires a larger space to be contained. Wherefore the thicker part of the air tends toward the opposite part or pole of the world, mostly from the South toward the North, and this with more or less violence according to the greater or lesser action of the sun in the air of that open region. Hence it happens that Southern winds are so frequent in our winter time: namely, because of the thinning of the air in the Antarctic part of the equator, which is caused by the presence of the sun, whereby it happens that the air of that quarter or region is so rarefied...

...it crosses the limits of the equinoctial line <note>The Equator</note> and seeks the northern parts in a violent manner, and from this those Southern winds are generated. Their blasts are usually accompanied by rain because that air, receding from the Antarctic region toward the Arctic, possesses a **solar soul** within itself. It is carried by means of this soul, which is why those winds are hot. However, this rarefied air, mixing itself with the dense northern air, immediately thickens it; and by its own soul, it dissolves that thickened air into droplets of water; but more on these things below. Do we not see all of this expressed through the contemplation of our machine? <note>Fludd refers to his weather glass or thermoscope, described in previous chapters, which models the expansion and contraction of air.</note> There, the enclosed air is condensed by cold, but made thinner by heat, and in its rarefaction, it compresses the waters and requires a more spacious place.

As for the Northern wind, the reasoning is the same as its opposite. For when the air in the southern parts during the night—warmed by the clear and powerful presence of the sun, and heated due to the power of reflection or the multiplied influences of a certain planet—seeks the Northern part (first the Torrid zone, then the Temperate, and finally that Frigid zone where our **antipodes** <note>term: antipodes <gloss>the people or places on the opposite side of the earth</gloss></term> dwell), it does so in the form of a southern wind. In its expansion, it always pushes the dense air before it toward the Arctic pole, no differently than we see in our machine, where the air enclosed in the cavity of the glass vessel <note>original: "matracei"</note> pushes the dense waters before it during its expansion. 

Then that air, following in the form of the South Wind and so animated by solar rays—partly by the extreme cold of the pole, partly by the compression of the place, and partly by heat—is violently driven by its own inclination from the Northern part toward the equator. And if it is strongly fortified by rays and spirits together with those of an approaching planet (especially if it be **Mars**), that blast occurs with lightning and thunder, such as we very often see happen in summer. But if the enclosed animating spirits are weak, then they come with snow and extreme cold, such as we see in winter. 

But here we make it known especially that if that wind happens among the Antipodes as a Southern wind in the summer time (especially when the sun is in Cancer or near that tropic), then we are taught by experience that the air—driven from the South by rarefaction and passing through Arcturus—does not produce snow or hail from the North because of the sun's proximity to that region, but for the most part produces rains that are cold due to the nature of the place. This happens because the solar rays, having now become more powerful in the Northern parts due to the direction of their reflection, and mixing themselves with the expanded air (inasmuch as they animate it and push it toward the North), act strongly against the cold nature of the pole and loosen it. 

Do we not perceive this very same thing with open eyes through the properties of the preceding machine? Even that which was cited above from the wise man <note>King Solomon</note> seems to confirm this more than sufficiently. He says: *The sun rises, and after it has set, it pants again toward its place where it may rise; it hastens to the south so that it may circle to the North; circling in its conversion, the air (or as others prefer, the wind) hastens on, and returns according to its circuits.* <note>original: "Ecclesiastes 1:5-6"</note> By these words he seems to hint that the winds are animated by the solar spirit, whose internal spirit is the uncreated light itself, which placed its tabernacle in the sun. This spirit, as it is a spirit, breathes centrally within itself and circumferentially in the air (the created spirit or external wind); that is, outside of itself to fulfill the will of its father. 

Hence the Prophet said: *The wind performs the command of GOD.* <note>original: "Baruch 5:6"</note> And the Evangelist: *The spirit blows where it wills.* <note>original: "John 3:8"</note> And the royal Psalmist: *He who brings forth the wind from his treasuries—that is, from the hidden bosom of the air or heaven.* <note>original: "Psalm 135"</note> So also it is said: *That Jehovah brought an east wind upon the land all that day and night: And Jehovah turned a very strong west wind, etc.* <note>original: "Exodus 10:13"</note> And elsewhere: *He drives the East wind into the heavens, and by his power he brings in the South wind, when he had rained flesh upon them.* <note>original: "Psalm 78:26"</note> And elsewhere: *God fits a weight to the wind (or the air) and weighs the waters by measure.* <note>original: "Job 28:25"</note> From which it is manifest that God (or the Word, or Wisdom), looking upon Himself from His palace, or leaping forth according to His pleasure, gives a soul to the winds; indeed, He is even present in the winds, which is confirmed by Psalm 18:8: *Jehovah, sitting upon the Cherubim, flies upon the wings of the wind;* and elsewhere: *He who makes the winds his angels and flaming fires his ministers;* and elsewhere: *By the breath of God, ice is congealed, etc.*

However, it must be understood here that the southern wind, violent among the Antipodes, is the cause of the Northern wind among us, and vice versa, for the reasons we cited above.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the origin of Clouds and consequently of rains.

The procreation of clouds and rains is brought about by clearly the same reasoning. For the air is dissipated in the equatorial parts by rarefaction proceeding from the solar rays, near or beyond which line the solar rays strike perpendicularly. The dissipated parts are forced toward the Temperate Zone, which is now chilled and consequently condensed because of the sun's long absence. Thus it happens that this rarefied air—driven by the rarefaction of the South wind and animated by the thinning solar spirit—mixes itself with the air of the Temperate and Frigid Zones. By the compression of its parts, it changes that air into a dense vapor, which then migrates into the substance of a mist, a small cloud, or a great cloud. This, in turn, is ready to be liquefied into water droplets and converted into the nature of rain because of the central heat of the rarefied air inspired into it by the sun. We see in our experimental instrument <note>Fludd’s weather glass or thermoscope</note> that the air itself, enclosed in a flask <term>matrass <gloss>a round-bottomed glass flask used in chemistry</gloss></term>, dilates itself by contact with heat. In its dilation, it requires a more ample and spacious place, wherefore it tends downward against the quarter of the heat dilating it, with a motion so strong—indeed, contrary to the nature of its body’s lightness—that it even drives and urges the dense mass of water before it. By these things we are taught that air dilated by solar heat moves for the most part either to the right or to the left in the world, and recedes on light wings from the seat of heat (namely, the solar place). This happens many degrees faster than in the glass, both because of the immense motion of the sun in the open air and because dilated air is not so much attacked or repelled by thickened air as it is by thick and dense water. It follows, therefore, that if air applied or joined to air usually procreates denser air, it is necessary that such a thickening of the air creates a medium composition between water and earth of a moderate substance. For it is necessary that there be a medium between two extremes: namely, water and air. But truly, those more skilled in natural philosophy have frankly acknowledged the condensation of air into water, and again the rarefaction of water into air. Therefore, the medium between such a starting point and end point is vapor, and a denser or looser vapor usually procreates such a cloud as it is itself, which cloud is finally resolved into drops of water. Therefore, thinned air, mixed with thick air, passes into a cloudy vapor, which is finally seen to drip into rain. But even this—even if some were ignorant of the opposite—we can prove by ocular experience, passing from the lesser to the greater in this way: If a part of the subtlety of the air is usually transmuted into the substance of water, much more so is that air when joined to thicker air. But a part of the thinned air usually migrates into the substance of water; the major premise is evident, but the minor is explained by the following experiment:

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s discussion on the movement of air and the formation of weather patterns. -># Universal Experiment<-

...let the whole vessel, except for its top, be covered, and let a gentle fire be lit beneath it—whether from coals or a lamp, it does not matter. You will perceive with your own eyes that once the lower part of the vessel is heated, the air contained within the glass will be thinned <note>original: "attenuabitur," referring to rarefaction</note> by the heat of that place. But since a larger or more vast space cannot be obtained for the body of the thinned air due to the solid composition of the glass, it is necessary that in the cooler part of the vessel—namely, the top—the air reveals itself in a denser and more visible form than it was before. From this, it will first change into a white smoke, and then gradually into drops; this process has indeed been proven by me quite often. By a clearly similar logic, in the dissolution of water into air, which occurs through its strong boiling, we observe that a wind is first stirred up, and that wind accompanies the vapor, which then later vanishes into the air. So also (since the logic of contraries or opposites is the same) the air heated by the sun's warmth is easily condensed into a cloud in the cold alongside dense air. This is even more true due to the abundance of material to be condensed, since the aforementioned experiment shows that this same thing is usually achieved by the simple condensation of air. 

Whence it is clear how absurd is that opinion of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, whose physical theories Fludd frequently challenged</note> who affirm that the cause of clouds is the freezing of vapors from the earth and water in the middle region of the air due to the quality of that place. Similarly, we are taught by experience that clouds and rains are so rare in the summer time because of the strong dominion that the solar rays have in our air; for the more the air is subtle and rarefied, the further it is from thickening into a cloud. But if by chance the thinned air is gathered together by opposing blasts and migrates into the existence of a cloud, then it is for the most part mixed with such great fiery spirits that thunder and lightning flashes arise from it.

### CHAPTER III.

#### *On the origin of springs and consequently of rivers.*

From the preceding points, relying both on philosophical speculations and on experimental practice, we consider it demonstrated more than enough that the air filling everything in this world is expanded in its regions by the power of heat (the common source of which we have said is the sun itself). By this expansion, the air requires a larger place to receive its expanded substance—upwards and downwards, as well as to the right, the left, before, and behind. 

But conversely, we have explained that this universally dispersed air is condensed, gathered, and contracted into one place by the presence of cold, more or less according to the greater or lesser predominance of that quality. We have also noted that just as expanded air requires a larger place for itself, so too when its members are contracted, it is content with a narrower place. Since this is indeed the case, it follows that in the summer time, the reason for the diminishing and drying up of springs and rivers is *not* due to the evaporation of their water into the air, according to the opinion of the Peripatetics. For if this were so, it would follow that solar heat was not the cause of the thinning of the air, but rather of its thickening. If the aquatic substance of the springs and rivers were evaporated into the air, then it would be necessary for the air to be thicker in the summer time; consequently, the sun, by its proximity and the direction of its rays, would not rarefy the air but rather make it thick. Yet we are taught that the property of heat is to rarefy and not to thicken—a fact we also draw from the property of our aforementioned experiment, since the air contained in the matrass <note>A matrass is a round-bottomed glass flask used in alchemy and early chemistry</note> is expanded by the presence of heat, just as it is thickened again by the assault of cold.

But to make a further inquiry into this matter, let us see, I pray: if the substance of rivers and springs is converted into air during the summer, what finally becomes of that superfluous air, since the extreme heat of the sun always tends toward the thinning of the air? Certainly it is not converted into clouds, because in the summer time—and especially when the sun is heating in an extreme way—clouds are not so frequent, nor is rain in such abundance. Indeed, as it is held in the Sacred Page <note>A common term for the Bible</note>, "the heavens are as brass and dry," and any clouds that are present are sterile. 

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:23</margin>

From this it follows that, contrary to the doctrine of the ancient philosophers, there is another cause for this flowing away of rivers, springs, and ponds, and another path for them, though invisible and quite hidden. That is to say: the air of the hemisphere, being greatly thinned and requiring a wider and vaster place for its existence, thrusts the waters of the springs downward into their whirlpools and causes the moisture to descend into the innermost parts of the earth. Is this not the same thing shown by the ocular demonstration of our machine? In it, we see that by the presence of heat, the air contained in the matrass requires a larger place for itself through expansion. There, the heat in its expansion does not convert the nature of the water in the lower vessel (which had been raised through the neck) into dense air—since such a sublimation would be entirely against the laws of the nature of heat—but visibly thrusts that water downward to its deep hiding places and penetralia, from which it had first been raised upward by the effort of the cold. 

But perhaps someone will raise a question about the place where that water, so depressed among us in the summer time, is moved, since the sources from which it comes are hidden from us. For without doubt, it is necessary that the waters of the springs are always in motion. To this we respond with the Holy Bible: "they return to the sea from which they first came," <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7</note> yet the sea does not seem to grow, because the sea distributes that portion of water which the hotter quarter of the world rejected to the winter quarter of the world. For beyond any controversy, by as many degrees as the Northern <note>original: "Boreali"</note> hemisphere of the world excels in heat and dryness, by that many degrees the Southern <note>original: "Australe"</note> hemisphere prevails in cold and moisture.

This is indicated exactly both by philosophical reasons and by this practical experiment of ours. For unless the contact between the elements of water and air were so tight that one could not be separated from the other, that monster in the nature of things—namely, the Vacuum <note>Early modern scientists generally believed a "perfect vacuum" was impossible in nature</note>—would be admitted. From this it follows necessarily that where air recedes through vessels closed on all sides, water follows there also, because of the natural embrace of one with the other. This has been exactly demonstrated by us through the conclusion of *Rule 7, Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, of the Technical History of the Macrocosm*, where elemental motion is discussed. The Rule is as follows: *The substance of the element of water is contiguous with the air by a tenacious bond, so that there is no distance between them.* From this it happens that water is raised upward with the air. And at the end of that rule, an experimental demonstration follows, which we have expressed in this place.

On the other hand, it is the property of heat to thin and expand the air, as is shown in the preceding demonstration. > *Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. Genesis 1:9.* <note>original: "Congregentur aquæ quæ sunt infra cælum in locum vnum vt confpiciatur arida & fuit ita, Gen. 1. 9."</note>

Now, God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering together of the waters He called Seas. But in passing, some might object to what we write here: that if this were true, then the winds would blow more abundantly and copiously at that time when the cold in our Zone is more intense; yet, in the time of frost and hoarfrost, the air is found to be coldest; therefore, at these times, the air will be more centrally contracted, and consequently, the rivers will be more abundant and the springs more flowing and full.

To these we respond that the cause of the outflow and more copious flow of springs is not only from the cold of the region in which they flow, which contracts the local air and consequently draws upward the waters hidden in the earth (due to the proximity and connection of water with air), but also the heat of the opposite region thinning the air is quite suitable. For example, in our winter weather, when the sun occupies the spaces beyond the equinoctial region—namely toward the Antarctic pole, passing through Scorpio, Sagittarius, and especially Capricorn—the air of that place or region of the earth is thinned due to the direction of the solar rays and seeks a more spacious place everywhere (that is, circularly) for its expanded existence. From this, it happens that the springs of that place are pushed down toward the bowels or center of the earth. For this reason, that hot action very easily provides the "hot matter" <note>Fludd often treats "heat" or "thinned air" as a physical substance that can be displaced.</note> for the multiplication of the Northern springs. This matter, once offered, then later—by its absence, or the weakness of solar heat in Northern parts (that is, due to the slant and weakness of the rays hitting them, where the dominion of cold contracts the air)—is carried upward and fills the springs copiously. 

But it is certain that water cannot be raised by the northern cold any more than in that proportion by which the southern heat pressed it into the earth. If it happened otherwise, then a vacuum would be left in the nature of things, which is most absurd and abominable to nature itself. And hence it is that, although rivers flow into the sea (according to the words of the wise man <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full."</note>), yet the sea does not overflow, nor is it fuller at one time than another. For there is a circular motion in nature, but it admits no increase or decrease. 

And although we see that floods occur and rivers overflow their banks in their northern parts, we are taught that this usually happens more copiously from rains, which occur because of the extreme thinning of the air in southern places. In this process, a large portion of that thinned air, by means of the southern wind, is led into northern parts, where it is reduced into clouds by the local cold and finally, by its own heat which it receives from solar rays by way of thickening <note>original: "via inspiffationis"</note>, is immediately dissolved into rains. ->Corollary.<-

What need is there for more words? Do we not see in the observation of our present machine <note>Fludd’s "weather glass" or thermoscope</note> that by the approach of heat to the matrass <term>matrass: a glass flask with a long neck used in alchemy and early chemistry</term>, the air is dilated, and that in this dilation it requires a more ample place for its existence? This is proven by the fact that we observe with our own eyes that the water—which had been raised many degrees into the neck of the matrass by the presence of cold—is gradually beaten back downward by the dilation of the air. Indeed, this experience was quite costly and laborious, even truly quite dangerous, for certain common chemists; for in the making of nitric acid <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid</term> from saltpeter and vitriol, the spirits leaping out from the small mass contained in the retort, on account of the dilation of the nitrous air, were not contained by the vast glass vessel or receiver, but (I speak from experience) they miserably shattered that vessel into infinite particles, accompanied by a horrendous sound like that of a handgun <note>original: "sclopeti"</note>, so that they might acquire a broader field in the open air for their existence.

Hence, therefore, is the reason for the diminishing of springs in the summer time: namely, because by the presence of solar heat, the air in our Zone is thinned <note>original: "attenuatur"</note>, as one may see through a diligent intuition of the properties of our machine; wherefore the dilated air does not attract the waters upward to itself, but on the contrary thrusts the terrestrial waters downward. Thus we see in paralytics, that because the nerves are relaxed by thinning, they are not stretched and do not pull the limbs toward motion to perform their functions, but vice versa we note them falling downward toward the earth—that is, being pressed downward toward the earth. Do we not observe this very same thing in the action of this instrument of ours, whose water, raised by cold, is gradually driven downward by the presence of heat and the rarefaction of the air? 

In like manner, we see in the winter time that the air is contracted by cold, and in its contraction the springs overflow with water and the rivers swell with waves. We have said this happens because of the constriction of the air, which for its own movement also moves the water itself—which is, as it were, its servant and handmaid. It moves it, I say, either by fleeing from the center toward the circumference (and this in its hot and dilated condition), or by contracting from the circumference to the center (and this in its cold, or contractive and gathering, nature). Behold the sign in our machine, where by the contact of cold, the air contained in the matrass is so condensed that it raises the water by many degrees high into the neck of the matrass, through which the cold is intensified in its nature; from which it is clear that this is the reason why waters are raised high from the central recesses of the earth: namely, by the presence of winter’s cold.

# CHAPTER IV.
->On the origin of Luminous Meteors, and how they are procreated in rarefied air.<-

Since, therefore, ocular experience teaches us that the more the air is heated, the rarer and subtler it becomes; it follows conversely that the rarer and purer the air is, the closer it approaches the nature of the luminous and fiery spirits of the element of fire. Just as, on the other hand, it is clear that the more the air grows cold, the more dense it is rendered. Wherefore the first degree of condensing air is into the consistency of vapor; the second into the consistency of mist; the third of a cloud; the fourth of rain; the fifth of snow; and the last of hail and ice. 

Such also is the relationship of degrees in the thinning of air from its middling state up to its extreme limit at the sphere of fire: namely, wind, will-o'-the-wisp <term>ignis fatuus: "foolish fire," a phosphorescent light seen over marshland</term>, a falling star, lightning, a flash, a column of fire, and other kinds of comets. All these fiery meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning</note> have air rarefied by fiery heat for their existence. 

But here we think it must be diligently observed by us that the "hidden" part—that is, the greatest spiritual part of the air—is light. It vivifies the air itself no differently than a soul vivifies an animal, and agitates it everywhere according to its will. Therefore, the hidden or internal part of the air, which dwells in its center, is pure fire; just as its manifest or external part is a certain moist substance, covering and enclosing that hidden light no differently than a body encloses a soul, or a dense cloud encloses lightning. For the fiery or central substance of the air is pure fire, which God, in the first creation when He said "Let there be light," breathed into the universal spirit of the world. By stripping off its moist garment—or by making the hidden manifest and the manifest hidden—the moist invisible air is changed into invisible fire. 

But truly, just as we see the external and manifest air itself (though invisible) first take on the appearance of visible vapor and then a dense cloud through contraction; so also we shall perceive the hidden or fiery invisible air change first into the substance of a flash and lightning, and then, in a tighter contraction, into a visibly fiery meteor, namely a comet, a falling star, a will-o'-the-wisp, and other things of this kind. Therefore, the "point from which" <note>original: "Terminus ergo à quo"</note> the air tends from its middling nature by thinning is a fiery existence; but the "point toward which" it is accustomed to migrate from its middling nature is the nature of a dense cloud. From this it is clear that in ordinary air there is an aptitude either toward a dark nature by virtue of thickening, or toward a luminous existence by way of rarefaction. And in this way, both dark and luminous meteors are produced in the world, from which then both the internal and the external—that is, both the soul and the body—of any thing, whether simple or composite, is derived.

Taking up this path myself, and desiring to direct the needle or edge of my mind toward the **Polar Star of radiant truth**, I do so first for the honor of our God (whom it is fitting to revere sincerely above all things as the sole and unique Creator of the world and ourselves, offering Him the inward sacrifices and libations of our heart), and then for the benefit of Christian men. My hope is that they, sticking and adhering to the mud of the Heathens, and long captured by the pitchy and dark snares of human demons, may gradually redeem themselves as much as they are able. In this volume, therefore, you have a **Sacred Philosophy** published by us, which swallows up that profane philosophy of the Heathens like a single morsel; it is like a second Michael or Angel of truth, thrusting the sad and following Dragon of Heathen errors from the heaven of truth into the rude abyss of ignorance and deformity. This is not *my* work (I say), but you have here the divine operations, acts, and wonderful works of the **Word** dwelling in the womb or vitals of the **moist nature** <term>natura humida: Fludd’s term for the primal watery substance of the universe, which he believed was animated by the Divine Spirit</term>—that is, reigning everywhere in the world—designated and depicted to the life. I speak of the true "moist nature" or **Psyche**, that most beautiful creature, animated and adorned on every side in a wondrous and inexplicable way by divine light or emanation; that is, impregnated by a most powerful desire, the offspring of Jupiter, or rather radiant Wisdom and fiery love, most full of the Son of Jehovah. By His presence, all things that were once empty and void are now finally found full, fertile, and most exuberant with divine gifts. This is not *my* work, I say, but that which was described and outlined by the finger of the Almighty in the universal book of nature, expressed by me—the poorest philosopher and minister of the Creator—with an artificial pen and such paper. Indeed, I have not dared to produce anything in this philosophy that I have appropriated to myself or invented, but whatever it is, I have it entirely supported, confirmed, and established upon the firmest columns: either by the testimony of **Holy Scripture** (which has always been especially dear to me and closest to my heart), or by the consensus of the **Theology of the Fathers**, and especially the **Hebrew Doctors** <note>Jewish Rabbis and scholars</note> most skilled in the **Cabala** <term>Cabala: a tradition of Jewish mysticism that Fludd integrated into his Christian Neoplatonism</term>, or by the ocular demonstration of a certain proven machine <note>Referring to Fludd's weather-glass/thermoscope</note>. Finally, we assert that the use or benefit of this our philosophy is twofold: in the first place, it teaches Christian men, most desirous of true philosophy, to read the works of **Aristotle** cautiously (if they do not yet cease to persist stubbornly in his doctrine), and to give no more faith to his sayings than either the true harmony of the philosophy of reason suggests, or the Christian faith (whose anchor is the Holy Bible) and consequently the authority of said Bible indicates in express words, or ocular experience confirms. But if anyone, neglecting or repudiating these triple testimonies, proceeds in an insane manner—and I know not by what madness—to immerse himself further and more deeply into Aristotelian Philosophy without further doubt, we can boldly and confidently pronounce him not only a rebel against God and his own nature, but also to be raving without reason in a beastly manner. Therefore, I would wish no one to judge this our Sacred Philosophy before it is read seriously by him, and every member of it is weighed with a right, equal, and sincere judgment, as if in the scales of justice. Once this is done, and a comparison is made between this our Philosophy and that of Aristotle, it will be permitted to go to the left, or at least to seek the goal of one's philosophy toward the right...

<summary>Fludd presents his "Sacred Philosophy" as a divinely inspired alternative to Aristotelian (Peripatetic) physics, which he views as a diabolical "veil" hiding the truth. He justifies his work using a combination of Scripture, the Church Fathers, the Hebrew Cabala, and empirical evidence from his "weather-glass" experiments.</summary>
