<meta>This page continues Fludd's polemic against Aristotelian (Peripatetic) philosophy. He argues that his "Mosaic" philosophy is superior because it identifies God as the immediate cause of natural phenomena, whereas Aristotle mistakenly attributes these effects to natural elements like "exhalations" and "humors."</meta>

# Universal Experiment

He may choose whichever he prefers, for his will in this matter will be pleasing to me. But if anyone prepares himself to choose, embrace, and gladly follow this philosophy of ours—or rather, not ours, but that of **Moses** and the **Holy Scripture** themselves—we declare that he will avoid a double inconvenience and, consequently, obtain a double benefit. Specifically, he will escape the useless waste of a **seven-year period** <note>original: "Septennii"; the traditional length of a university course in the liberal arts and philosophy</note> spent on the vain philosophy of the Peripatetics, and at the same time, he will not receive the deep-rooted impression of their false doctrine in his mind. Those engaged in medicine as well as theology in this age—being seduced by false principles or foundations—are infected by these harms and are quite often forced to wander astray in their studies.

Hence it is that the physicians of this school or sect have made the "efficient causes" <note>the primary agency that produces an effect</note> of diseases to be **heat, cold, moisture, dryness, yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile**. Regarding the divine act and angelic power—by which God, in His attribute of severity, is accustomed to operate malignantly upon human humors—they have not even spared a thought. Therefore, being poorly instructed by the doctrine of **Aristotle**, they have accepted the effects and natural organs in which God and His angelic ministers act as if they were the efficient causes themselves.

Similarly, some Christian theologians who are followers of the Peripatetic school do not blush to create a distinction between **Theology** and **Sacred Physics**. By separating the rays of divinity from created nature, they assert that God is not at all present in nature. And so, they have imagined many "actors" in nature besides the one and only God, the sole actor in the world without whom nothing exists. Thus, with their Aristotle, they want fire, the sun, the stars, and their influences to be the actors and authors of all lower things, even though the **Sacred Scriptures** acknowledge that the one and only God does all things, in and out of all these things. 

These theologians, along with their master, report that winds proceed from exhalations rising from the earth by the power of the sun and stars; and yet, the **Holy Page** <note>original: "pagina sacra"; a common term for the Bible</note> makes God the author of the wind. It is the same in infinite other matters. Our Christians have learned all these errors with such labor and weariness, and over such a long duration of time from Aristotle’s *Physics*, that even if they find the contrary in the sacred writings, they are nonetheless unable to root out and cast them from the treasury-chest of their mind and memory where they are so firmly impressed. They do not know the way to correct themselves and they scorn being taught.

And yet, among both Christian philosophers and those skilled in **Theosophy** <note>divine wisdom</note>, there are some who candidly acknowledge the crookedness and weakness of Aristotelian doctrine, but they do not know how to correct it properly. For **Freigius** <note>Joan Thomas Freigius (1543–1583), a German philosopher</note>, a man very well-versed in Aristotelian philosophy, after he had mentioned the efficient causes of windy meteors, immediately departed from Aristotle’s opinion and broke out into these words: 

*“Although the entire dispute about winds, as with other meteors, is full of the admirable works of God—for which no firm and sufficient causes in nature can be brought forward—nevertheless it is useful to see how far human reason can progress. Indeed, the Sacred Scriptures say that God produces the winds from His treasures, whence we hear their blasts, but we know not whence they come or whither they go.”* 

(This from Freigius, book 25, on the cause of winds). And the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>original: "The Philosophical Pearl," a famous encyclopedia by Gregor Reisch first published in 1503</note>, in the chapter on lightning and thunder, writes thus: 

*“Certain philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of lightning, judged it to be not a work of nature, but an immediate effect of the Most High God.”* 

And so says that author. And **Johannes Velcurio** <note>1490–1559, a commentator on Aristotle and physics</note>, a man very profound in Peripatetic philosophy, in Book 3, Chapter 6 of his *Commentary on Physics*, says this: 

*“The Sacred Scriptures do not clearly agree with the Physicists concerning the origin of springs and rivers, which Ecclesiastes (Chapter 1) testifies flow from the sea through various channels and passages and flow back to their sources, saying: ‘All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from whence the rivers come, they return to flow again.’ However, Aristotle and the Peripatetic physicists say that the matter of these is partly vapor resolved into water and liquefied by cold and heat together within the earth, etc.”* 

So says he; and it is thus in many other things which would be too long and tedious to recount here. By these things, they seem—provoked by a good conscience—to argue that all meteors proceed **immediately from God**, and that the Aristotelian doctrine is in every way most opposed to that fountain of all truth. But I advise that everyone use his own judgment in this matter.

The **second utility** which a diligent regard for this kind of philosophy will seem to bring to the reader is that it is impossible but that, by the study of this philosophy, he should creep gradually and step by step into the true mysteries of theology. Thus, he will find himself very well and radically versed not only in Philosophy but also in the foundations of **Theography** <note>likely "writing of God" or "divine description"</note>. For the reader will find a Philosophy so natural to a Christian, united by spiritual instinct, and connected to the light of the intellect, and inclined toward the true knowledge of God.

This is unlike that of **Aristotle**, which is suited to a Heathen and his faith, bound to his vain fantasy and least of all to the mind, and consequently prone to producing **Idolatry** in the world. For the philosophy proposed by us teaches and warns to attribute uniquely to the Creator of all what is His own; but this Aristotelian one, by arrogantly stealing divine right, attempts to ascribe it to its own "nature." Thus, it longs to arrogate to creatures those things which belong to the Creator alone, falsely detracting from God His right and His act. 

His philosophy (I say) writes that all meteors proceed not from the immediate power of God, but in a way that is "accidental" to its nature. For instance: 
* **Winds** from a hot and dry exhalation, raised by the force of heat and pushed downward by the act of cold. 
* **Clouds** from vapors exhaled from water and earth by the same act, and condensed by the cold of the middle region of the air. 
* **Thunder** from a conflict made between the water of a cloud and fire arising from an exhalation enclosed in the cloud through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when surrounded by cold</note>.
* **Whirlwinds** and tempests, both in the sea and air, from dry but not-at-all-inflamed exhalations (the same matter he imagines for earthquakes). 
* **Presters** <note>original: "presteres"; fiery, destructive whirlwinds or lightning bolts</note>, which are horrendous, from fiery exhalations easily inflamed. 

He even affirms the matter of **Comets** to be such. He makes the "actors" of all these things to be either the rays of the stars or the accidental encounters of contrary qualities in the elements. In all of these, he makes no mention at all of the true Author of all these wonders. Thus, he seems not only to distract his Christian followers from divine worship, but by his false doctrine, he causes them to forget Him in the hardships and dangers of storms—He who truly is the ordainer of such weather because of the sins of men, and the one producing the immediate causes through angels.

He contends that phenomena like wind, thunder, and disease are caused directly by divine or angelic action rather than the "exhalations" or "humors" described by secular philosophers.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Fludd's discussion on meteorological phenomena, transitioning from the "Macrocosm" (the outer world) to his upcoming work on the "Microcosm" (the human body). It reinforces his central thesis: that natural events are direct acts of God and his angels rather than purely physical processes.</meta>

### On the Generation of Meteors.

Hence it happens that because of the ignorance of this world, many—not knowing the true author of these evils <note>Referring to destructive storms, lightning, or plagues</note>—ignorantly cease to call upon Him for His mercy and help and to urge Him with due prayers. Thus, they are destroyed and in various ways exterminated by **Jehovah's** destroyer, or by His wrathful **Angels** who disturb the air, seas, and earth in a stupendous manner. But it is the task of the philosophy brought forth by us to attribute all these things justly to God, as is right; we acknowledge—led by the authority of the sacred page <note>The Holy Scriptures</note>—that He acts by means of Angels, that is, in angels and through angels as the instruments and vehicles of His will. We say without hesitation, supported by His testimony, that the air is moved, led, and governed by the word of God, insofar as it floats in the word of God which encompasses all things; and it is led by the Angels of God appointed for this purpose (whose duty it is, as **David** testifies, to perform the word of God) whenever, wherever, and however God wills.

And although this very thing may seem absurd and trivial to some disciples of **Aristotle**, nonetheless, Christians—weighing all these things on the scales of truth and penetrating the mysteries of divinity with sharper eyes—will perceive that this matter is profound and of the greatest importance. This is because it concerns divine honor: it ensures that Christians truly and fundamentally know and understand that storms and other related operations do not arise from their own motion and "Aristotelian nature," or by random chance, or in such an inept manner as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> have attributed to them. Rather, they proceed from divine providence and the citadels of divine treasures hidden in the air, and are sent down from above into this lower world. Thus, if dangerous storms ever arise, people may call upon God, so that He (as the sole producer of storms) might be willing to mercifully avert that danger and in its place bestow kind rain, and at the same time defend, protect, and preserve the fruits of the earth along with men and livestock from all evil; and so that they might furthermore consider whatever else can redound to the honor of God.

The same is also to be thought concerning **Microcosmic** <note>The "Little World," or the human body as a reflection of the universe</note> meteors and their effects. Regarding these indeed—as they relate to health and disease in the Microcosm—we shall deal more fully in the following volume (if the supreme deity is favorable). We have proposed to rightly distinguish that volume with the title <term>The Final Causes of Meteors</term> <note>original: "causæ meteororum finalis"</note> or <term>Sacred Medicine</term> <note>original: "Medicina Sacra"</note>. In its first part, the **Citadel** or fortress of health is described; in the second, the siege, assault, and invasion of the fortress of health by a "diseased enemy" is expressed; in the third, the expulsion of that diseased enemy who has violently entered the fortress of health, and the restoration of that same violated or weakened bulwark, is treated. 

In the meantime, let us be allowed to breathe for a moment, while the Creator of the world is fortunately present for you and us; I shall never cease to trumpet forth His praises both with heart and pen. Under Your wings, therefore, O **JEHOVAH STRONG GOD**, I implore You to keep me safe from the viperous tongues of critics <note>original: "Momorum"; referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism</note> and envious men, so that I may serve Your divine Majesty with a sincere mind and an upright spirit as long as I remain among the living,

->for Yours is the virtue, the praise, and the power<-
->forever.<-
